For example, it might involve the design of governance models to incorporate the input from different stakeholders in the recurrent refinement and modification of the rules and policies that guide everyday algorithmic decision-making on what content and behavior on the platform is accurate and/or appropriate. The desired outcome of such cooperation with stakeholders and facilitation of conflict resolution may be greater organization-stakeholder fit and ultimately platform legitimation [28] with regard to how algorithms are used to moderate content creation and consumption.
Thus, we view it as an algorithmic design and adaptation process through which the platform performs its lead role as arbiter of conflicts among different stakeholder groups, creating forums and shaping a stakeholder interaction space that allows for the incorporation of stakeholder interests into the ongoing design and adjustment of governing algorithms. For example, YouTube stakeholders include, among others, creators, consumers, and advertisers who may choose to interact with the platform's algorithmic governance models in different ways, through the decisions they make, the behavior they show, the direct feedback they give, and more generally the data they provide as input into training and adjusting the machine learning algorithms throughout iterative cycles [2,28,39]. While stakeholder governance theory tends indicate that forums are sub-organizations within the focal organization, such as the board of directors, [3:500], which would potentially work toward the common interests of all stakeholders or resolve conflicts between them, in platform settings such as YouTube the platform itself, where stakeholders interact with each other directly, represents the forum where conflicts should be resolved.
In what follows, we present the findings of our in-depth study of YouTube and its stakeholders and the subsequent theory development with the intention to extend the literature on on platform governance and algorithmic governance on platforms more specifically.
We conducted case study research with the goal of theory development. New theoretical concepts and relations presented in our final model were grounded in data [8]; they capture the phenomenon of platform users participating actively as stakeholders in the governance performed by algorithms (as per our research question). The principle of emergence [25] guided our investigation, while we also kept in mind that our grounded theory research requires an open mind but not an empty head [11]. For this reason, stakeholder governance theory [9,17,26,38,42] also guided our empirical analysis and investigation of the case, shaping our research design with a strong emphasis on abduction [43].
The rationale for selecting the global video streaming platform YouTube as the case was its suitability for shedding light on algorithmic stakeholder governance, as the case scores high on two key variables of interest. The first variable was algorithmic governance, which involves the use of computational techniques for implementing platform rules and policies, while relying on as little human intervention as possible to ensure scalability. YouTube's business model is highly dependent on such automated content moderation practices, as it allows the platform to govern the vast amount of video content uploaded by users. The second variable of interest was stakeholder governance that involves the idea of bringing the interests of multiple stakeholders into governance by managing and sustaining stakeholder relations. Given that video content is generated and shared by users, and that they engage with this content (e.g., by viewing, liking, or reporting it), algorithmic stakeholder governance is very salient and particularly important on this well-known video sharing platform. Finding an "extreme case" [21] with high scores on both these variables was important to answer our research question at the unique intersection between algorithmic governance and stakeholder governance in platform settings. Even though there was an inextricable link between data collection and analysis in our study [8], for simplicity, we discuss data collection first, followed by data analysis in the following subsection.
We collected data from a variety of sources within YouTube's platform ecosystem, including interviews, forum postings and official YouTube press releases (see Table 1 and Figure 1). We conducted 66 semi-structured (recorded and transcribed) interviews with three relevant groups, that is, YouTube creators (n = 24) and YouTube consumers (n = 26), as well as YouTube advertisers, executives, and platform complementors (n = 16).
Our sample of creators ranges from small and occasional creators to regularly engaged creators, and up to a handful of YouTube 'superstars' with hundreds of thousands and even millions of followers in some instances. In addition, we interviewed different types of consumers, ranging from occasional viewers to regular viewers, and up to frequent users, covering all adult age groups. Video content produced by the creators and viewed by the consumers covered a range of topics such as technology/science, gaming, beauty and lifestyle, family, and music/dance. Furthermore, we were able to recruit several YouTube advertisers, executives, and platform complementors to participate in our study. Job titles included: director of digital marketing (expertise in YouTube advertising), head of digital marketing (expertise in YouTube advertising), chief marketing officer (expertise in YouTube advertising), manager in media planning (expertise in YouTube advertising), YouTube manager in advertising, YouTube manager branded content/influencer management, YouTube software engineer, YouTube analytical lead, YouTube agency account executive, corporate YouTube creator coaches, social marketers, and selected social media entrepreneurs. Table 1 describes the characteristics of study participants.
In addition to the interview data previously described, following the example of previous information systems (IS) research [39,48], we identified relevant forum postings and official press releases using a combination of keywords including but not limited to "YouTube," "data," and "algorithm." We harvested user comments posted on videos associated with these key terms, providing us with 2,917 posts (419 pages of text). Furthermore, we collected relevant material from official press releases (the official blog for the latest news) published by the YouTube executive team (n = 35, resulting in 81 pages of text).
In the selection of interviewees and data to be collected, we used the technique of theoretical sampling, which is typical for grounded theory analysis. "Theoretical sampling does not aim to identify representative populations, but rather to enrich the emerging concept," being driven by the desire "to understand the nature and dimensions of emerging conceptualizations further" [8:3]. After algorithmic stakeholder governance emerged as our core category of analysis, we started to explore concepts and relationships between the aggregated dimensions that help explain this phenomenon. While the initial set of interviews was focused on how YouTube's creators and consumers interact with YouTube and its algorithms, in later interviews, we realized that we needed to further substantiate and extend these findings by investigating in greater detail the practices by which algorithmic stakeholder governance occurs, as well as the platform-side practices by which governance gets delegated to the machine (affecting our sampling decisions for interviewing YouTube executives and platform complementors). Finally, we realized that it is pivotal to strengthen the perspective of YouTube advertisers resulting in additional interviews with marketing experts with an expertise in YouTube ads in later stages of the writing process. As a result of these theoretical sampling procedures, our theoretical model gradually evolved to focus on various interrelated concepts that explain algorithmic stakeholder governance.
Given the inextricable link between data collection and analysis in our study, the topic of primary data collection slightly shifted over time [11]. Initially, when interviewing creators, we were particularly interested in the process of content creation and how creators interact with the platform and its algorithms. Among others, we focused on creators' perceptions of the rules and algorithmically mediated policies that they must comply with, and how YouTube algorithmically controls and governs user content and behavior. From the consumers' perspective, we asked questions related to individuals' video preferences, browsing, and viewer behavior. We also focused on consumers' perception of YouTube's algorithmic governance, including their experience of YouTube features, such as the recommender system that proposes content that may be of interest to them, and how they perceive YouTube's efforts to censor content. Furthermore, we interviewed YouTube advertisers, executives, and corporate platform complementors. Topics we covered included advertisers' experience on launching ads on the platform, and YouTube executives and complementors insights about the YouTube ecosystem and role of advertisers. A few core themes that emerged from the data in early phases and that guided data collection and analysis in subsequent stages include the penalization of creators via "strikes," perceptions about algorithms versus human content moderation, how YouTube influences their users through nudging and advertising, and how users share feedback with YouTube-all relevant topics that helped us to investigate algorithmic stakeholder governance in depth.
In our data analysis, we used various techniques of grounded theory [8,11] (see Figure 1). First, we engaged in iterative coding which helped us develop indicators. We began this project with a broad research interest in users' experience and interaction with the YouTube platform and its algorithms. Through an iterative process in which we constantly revised the coding scheme for our multi-source data and compared emerging findings with relevant literature, we ultimately narrowed our research scope to focus on algorithmic stakeholder governance (see Table 2 for final data structure). Then, we abstracted indicators to dimensions, and ultimately to concepts. For example, the dimensions misrepresentation, marginalization, and manipulations were aggregated to the concept of unintended consequences (see Table 3). Finally, we accounted for the dynamic interrelationships between concepts, which allowed us to capture the feedback loops and relationships between different concepts. Our theory was developed through many iterations [8] in which we cycled back and forth between indicators, dimensions, concepts, and literature about the phenomenon of using algorithms as tools of stakeholder governance.
Second, adhering to common standards in grounded theory research, we engaged in constant comparisons when analyzing our data [8]. Doing so allowed us to capture different standpoints and attain more depth when making sense of our findings. For example, we compared indicators that emerged from the interviews with different types of creators, ranging from those who only occasionally upload content, to those who view their work on the YouTube platform as a full-time career choice. We also compared indicators developed from interviews with creators, consumers, and advertisers. Understanding the differences and similarities between all instances of data and codes allowed us to triangulate insights obtained from multiple perspectives, and ultimately ensure theoretical saturation of all concepts and the relationships between them, once we realized that adding further instances or slices of data did not substantially alter our theorization of algorithmic stakeholder governance.
Finally, we also addressed preconceptions. While it is impossible to completely avoid that the authors' convictions influence the judgements they make in the research process [8], we attempted to avoid basing our data collection and analysis on a priori theory in the domain of study. While the first author was leading the data collection and analysis, all three coauthors deeply engaged with the primary data, allowing the team to collectively manage bias.
Founded in 2005, YouTube is a leading global video streaming platform, currently ranked as the second most popular website worldwide. 4 The YouTube platform facilitates uploading, viewing, commenting, advertising, and sharing of video content, ranging from documentaries and educational videos to video blogging. YouTube content is consumed by as many as two billion logged-in users every month. 5 In a press statement published in 2017, Susan Wojcicki, 6 former CEO of YouTube, described the platform and its major value proposition as follows:
As the CEO of YouTube, I've seen how our open platform has been a force for creativity, learning and access to information. I've seen how activists have used it to advocate for social change, mobilize protests, and document war crimes. I've seen how it serves as both an entertainment destination and a video library for the world. I've seen how it has expanded economic opportunity, allowing small businesses to market and sell their goods across borders. And I've seen how it has helped enlighten my children, giving them a bigger, broader understanding of our world and the billions who inhabit it. (Susan Wojcicki, CEO YouTube) (YouTube press release #5)
As a foundation for addressing our research question "how are platform stakeholders algorithmically governed?," we start by reviewing YouTube's key stakeholders including their different interests and concerns regarding algorithmic governance (see Table 4). The table highlights that stakeholders in our case have multiple different economic and noneconomic interests, creating possibilities for conflicts. Key interests of creators include
The restricting or removing of content that is considered inappropriate and does not adhere to the platform's guidelines, achieved via the enforcement of rules and policies using a combination of human reviewers and machine learning.
The creators' desire for creative freedom which can be at odds with consumers' demands to be protected from harmful or misleading information, as well as their wish to access diverse content.
The user perception that algorithmic policing distorts their understanding due to flawed and erroneous content moderation.
The crafting of machine learning models to suggest tailored and personalized content to individual platform users based on their known or presumed preferences, values, and beliefs.
The consumers' desire for relevant, entertaining, diverse, and highquality content versus advertisers' goals to reach target audiences
The user perception that algorithmic stakeholder governance, in its effort to recommend content on the platform, inadequately restricts some content while promoting other content, with potential negative effects on individual cognition and behavior.
The automated financial incentivization of creating and sharing new content that generates substantial user interest and engagement.
The creators' desire for monetization opportunities and expressing themselves freely to engage their followers versus advertisers' concerns about brand reputation and brand-safe content.
The user perception that algorithmic stakeholder governance in form of algorithmic monetization tends to treat less mainstream, minority, or fringe points of view, in a disadvantageous manner.
The implicit approval of a platform's algorithmic stakeholder governance system and practices, demonstrated through acts of ignoring and bending behavior.
The acknowledgment and acceptance of the platform's data collection practices that provide input to algorithmic governance without deeper consideration.
The willingness to modify one's actions to align with the platform's guidelines as algorithmically implemented and enforced in the form of codified rules and policies.
The stakeholders' efforts to flag undesirable content to a platform's algorithmic governance system by offering judgment and context, potentially prompting a human review.
The negative evaluation of other stakeholders and their (inappropriate) content on an ethical basis, followed by reporting it to the platform.
The recognizing of specific cases that necessitate more comprehensive and qualitative evaluations by humans, prompting stakeholders to request reviews by human moderators  monetization and audience reach, while advertisers' primary interests include content safety and reaching the target audience, and consumers' interests include getting access to diverse, entertaining, and safe content.
YouTube knowingly uses sophisticated algorithms to govern its interactions with these stakeholders on the platform, thereby, substantially reducing the need for costly human content moderation. Extensively using algorithms is critical to the survival and growth of YouTube because it ensures the governance of user interactions and content on the platform is executed in a highly cost-efficient way, which aligns well with a platform business model focused on scaling the userbase and increasing revenue. Resembling the "lead role" perspective in stakeholder governance (see background section), the following analysis explains how YouTube uses algorithms in an attempt to largely automate the resolution of conflicts among its major stakeholder groups.
In examining how YouTube manages the platform's multifaceted relationships with stakeholder groups, including creators, consumers, and advertisers, our findings directed us to the notion of algorithmic stakeholder governance. We define this emergent new form of stakeholder governance as a process through which algorithms are designed and used to shape interactions and create forums "where conflicts among stakeholders can be addressed" [3:500], ultimately with the goal of bringing stakeholders' interests into the governance of the platform [3,9,29,32,42]. Algorithmic stakeholder governance comprises three elements: algorithmic policing, algorithmic recommending, and algorithmic monetization.
Algorithmic stakeholder governance needs to resolve stakeholder conflicts to be effective. Stakeholder conflicts refer to disagreements or disputes that arise between stakeholders on the platform who have different interests. The three conflicts that emerged from our data are the freedom of speech, the information diversity, and the content safety conflict (see Table 3). However, algorithmic stakeholder governance is a difficult undertaking and may also result in unintended consequences, which refer to various issues, challenges, and potential negative consequences stemming from algorithmic stakeholder governance, including misrepresentation, manipulation, and marginalization (see Table 3).
The findings we present in the following unpack how the different elements of algorithmic stakeholder governance, stakeholder conflicts, and unintended consequences relate to each other, 7 before presenting our findings about stakeholder participation.
YouTube harnesses extensive user data to train and deploy machine learning models that autonomously filter shared content on the platform. This approach enables the platform to "make YouTube a safer community" 8 by automatically identifying and filtering out hate speech, violence, extremism, or any other inappropriate content, as well as videos that may spread harmful misinformation. In pursuit of this goal, algorithmic policing is a key component of YouTube's algorithmic stakeholder governance system. This involves the restricting or removing of content that is considered inappropriate and does not adhere to the platform's guidelines, achieved via the enforcement of rules and policies using a combination of human reviewers and machine learning.
YouTube has always had a set of Community Guidelines that outline what type of content isn't allowed on YouTube. (. . .) We enforce these Community Guidelines using a combination of human reviewers and machine learning, and apply them to everyone equally-regardless of the subject or the creator's background, political viewpoint, position, or affiliation. Our policies aim to make YouTube a safer community while still giving creators the freedom to share a broad range of experiences and perspectives. 9   The governing algorithms can take various actions when content is found to be in violation of community guidelines. These automated decisions may undergo some selected human moderation (i.e., by employees), either before or after the initial identification. With its "4Rs" principle (removing, reducing, raising up, and rewarding content), YouTube has developed a system that allows the platform to take nuanced action based on the severity of the detected violation. For example, rather than removing content, YouTube has the option to implement age-gating, a measure that would require videos to remain on the platform while ensuring that only users aged 18 and above, who are logged in, can access them:
That's why we address misinformation on our platform based on our '4 Rs' principles: we remove content that violates our policies, reduce recommendations of borderline content, raise up authoritative sources for news and information, and reward trusted creators 10   It is difficult to design algorithmic policing in a way that fully incorporates the different perspectives of all different stakeholders, who have their own interests, preferences, and (political) points of view. Yet, our findings indicate that many stakeholders favor that YouTube has implemented some sort of content moderation (if done "correctly"), in particular to protect the most vulnerable, which are children: I think it's good that they removed people who utilize the platform for hate crime, wrongful use of political agendas, you know, anything that can be used to harm another individual or party, I feel like it's very justified. Because, you know, the wrong person can draw a pretty big crowd. And, you know, if you want to turn people negative, you can easily influence them view via YouTube, and, you know, that platform. So, I feel like it's, it's a very good thing that, you know, they hop on the bad people like that. I agree with it. (YouTube creator #23)
The platform demonstrates its lead role in using algorithmic policing as an attempt to address the freedom of speech conflict in a way that is cost-effective and scalable. This conflict refers to the creators' desire for creative freedom which can be at odds with consumers' demands to be protected from harmful or misleading information, as well as their wish to access diverse content.
Our findings reveal that on the one hand, creators and consumers stressed the value created by curtailing less desirable content. Many consumers applaud YouTube's efforts in protecting the community from content that glorifies hate crime, pushes wrongful political agendas and spreads fake news, sharply condemning such content.
I think it's good that they removed people who utilize the platform for hate crime, wrongful use of political agendas, you know, anything that can be used to harm another individual or party, I feel like it's very justified. Because, you know, the wrong person can draw a pretty big crowd.
And, you know, if you want to turn people negative, you can easily influence them view via YouTube, and, you know, that platform. So, I feel like it's, it's a very good thing that, you know, they hop on the bad people like that. I agree with it. (YouTube creator #16) Yet, they also pointed out the risk of deliberate censorship being employed by the platform, indicating that these practices would not conform with creator's "right" to be able to voice their opinion via free speech. Some expressed the desire to allow more content on the platform, calling for the platform to minimize their content moderation practices and letting users decide themselves how to make sense out of a message. Creators across the (political) spectrum were generally critical of YouTube's rather opaque algorithmic policing practices, and some blame the platform for attempts at silencing and "getting rid of alternative political philosophies" (YouTube creator). Some felt that it jeopardized the very function of YouTube which is the sharing of ideas within a likeminded community. One content creator reported:
The scary thing is that they can literally just get rid of your channel if they don't like what you're talking about. None of these guys [content creators banned in the past] were-they weren't trying to incite violence. I mean, there are people that are unpopular on YouTube that actually tried to incite violence . . . But the point being, they just didn't . . . If they don't like what you're talking about, they can get rid of your entire channel. But again, that's obvious censorship, right? (YouTube creator #4)
Several content creators and consumers mentioned how difficult it is to find the balance between allowing content and curtailing content. One consumer explained that "there are things that obviously need to be censored, and no doubt need to be removed,' while at the same time, 'we live in a society right now where we're constantly struggling with having a right or ability for free speech:" I guess I would probably have to say it kind of feel like it's a double-edged sword. I feel like there's a really fine line, it's a blurred line. There are things that obviously need to be censored, and no doubt need to be removed, but at the same time, we live in a society right now where we're constantly struggling with having a right or ability for free speech. I feel like we're allowed to have free speech in our opinions, but there comes a point where a line needs to be drawn. (YouTube viewer #10) In order to manage this balancing act, YouTube seeks to create a forum for creating and viewing content by providing a creative and entrepreneurial, yet also safe and protected environment.
While algorithmic policing is implemented to resolve the freedom of speech conflict, it does not come without unintended consequences. One unintended consequence that emerged from our data analysis is misrepresentation, which revolves around the user perception that algorithmic policing distorts their understanding due to flawed and erroneous content moderation.
At its core, this refers to YouTube facing challenges in satisfying the desires and preferences of different stakeholders representing diverse opinions and perspectives and incorporating their interests and voice fully into the governance system. Several content creators and consumers expressed concerns about YouTube's inconsistent content classification, pointing out that the algorithmic decisions related to policing are prone to inaccuracies. Many reported that they were left with the feeling that the "algorithms and machine learning . . . it doesn't always work," and that YouTube's algorithmic practices, such as moderating content via algorithmic policing, would be "blatantly inaccurate and dangerous."
I think hiring more human beings to go through content to flag it, because, you know, these algorithms and use of machine learning to do that, it doesn't always work. To flag content that might be, you know, blatantly inaccurate or dangerous to public safety. (YouTube viewer #14)
For example, one viewer pointed to past instances where YouTube incorrectly labeled content as fake news, emphasizing the need for certainty that it violates the guidelines before removal:
They would have to be 100 percent sure that it's fake news before they take it down because if it's not . . . it could be something that they consider fake news but it's not really fake news. (YouTube creator #10) Some content creators explained that the sudden deletion of videos, or even entire channels, without prior warning would be detrimental for some content creator's careers, given that it put them at risk to lose their fan base that may have taken them years to build. One creator expressed this concern in the following way:
The scary thing is that they can literally just get rid of your channel if they don't like what you're talking about. None of these guys [content creators banned in the past] were-they weren't trying to incite violence. I mean, there are people that are unpopular on YouTube that actually tried to incite violence . . . But the point being, if they don't like what you're talking about, they can get rid of your entire channel. But again, that's obviously censorship, right? (YouTube creator #4)
The success of YouTube is frequently attributed to its ability to "accurately predicting the videos you want to watch." 11 Given the vast number of videos available on YouTube (500 hours of videos were uploaded on YouTube every minute in 2022 12 ), recommendations are a crucial tool to improve the user experience. To this end, algorithmic recommending is another important component of algorithmic stakeholder governance. This involves crafting machine learning models to suggest tailored and personalized content to individual platform users based on their known or presumed preferences, values, and beliefs.
When recommendations are at their best, they help users find a new song to fall in love with, discover their next favorite creator, or learn that great paella recipe. That's why we update our recommendations system all the time-we want to make sure we're suggesting videos that people actually want to watch. 13  Through its recommendations, YouTube ensures that consumers are exposed to content tailored to their interests. Simultaneously, algorithmic recommending enables content creators to attract more consumers to their channels, potentially leading to monetization through advertising revenue for both the creators and YouTube. For example, when consumers express interest in a particular topic by watching a video, the platform's algorithms recommend similar content based on their past viewing history. As a result, algorithm-driven recommender systems play a crucial role in assisting consumers in discovering and watching new videos uploaded by content creators. As one consumer explains:
When I go on to the YouTube homepage, it has an idea of what I watched the last time I was there. So, the recommendations for the next video, for me to view are usually something that I'm probably interested in watching. (. . .) for example, if I'm watching something about a product, they're either that exact product reviewed by someone else, or they're very similar makeup products that I might be interested in. So, I think they do a good job with the algorithm. (YouTube viewer #16) Algorithmic recommending is enabled by advanced machine learning technology, including deep generation models and deep ranking models, for the implementation of content recommendations. Through ongoing design, iteration and maintenance, these models are continuously updated and refined. 14 The individual models learn and improve by themselves based on a diverse set of data points they receive, including the consumers' viewing history, search queries, and interests, along with data that assesses the quality of specific videos. As described by one YouTube executive, this data may encompass a user's historical preferences, like a preference for shorter or longer videos. Additionally, it incorporates information about user engagement, such as likes and comments, on videos from other users:
It's all about the user itself. Has the user been often on YouTube? Has the user been interested in that particular content or no, like how often this user goes on like YouTube. If that user is interested in watching like a long video versus like a short video. That second sort of big bucket and it's a really important bucket is everything around like the social aspects of like how often that video is actually being watched, is there any likes, how many comments, like, you know, some of the feedback. (YouTube executive #4)
In summary, YouTube is known for "one of the largest scale and most sophisticated industrial recommendation systems in existence" 15 and the recommendation system has evolved into a pivotal tool for enhancing watch-time and user engagement on the platform.
Algorithmic recommending enables the platform to perform its lead role in stakeholder governance by facilitating more accurate and appropriate matches between creators or advertisers and consumers, creating a forum for consumers to consume the content and ads that align better with their individual preferences. To this end, algorithmic recommending helps to resolve the information diversity conflict, which is the consumers' desire for relevant, entertaining, diverse, and high-quality content versus advertisers' goals to reach target audiences.
While many YouTube consumers appreciate video content tailored to their interests, several have expressed frustration with YouTube's hyper-personalization. Instead of enhancing their experience, this often leads to overexposure to topics they are only marginally interested in. For example, one consumer shared that after searching for "how to make a pivot table in Excel," he was bombarded with ads related to higher education and Google Sheets, despite only having a temporary interest in the topic. I don't think they do the greatest job of showing me content. It's always like, tailored to me. And I think sometimes I . . . look up random things on YouTube, and I feel like once I look up one thing that's outside of what they usually show me, like, it just floods my feed . . . for example, I'm a, I'm a graduate student. So I googled how to make like a pivot table in Excel. And yes, there's an interest of mine. But I didn't want like, all these ads about going back to school and Walden University and . . . . how to use Google Sheets. (YouTube consumer #15)
The consumers' interest of not being overexposed to targeted content and advertising is at odds with the interests of advertisers to place their personalized ads in front of the right target audience-which is individuals who have a potential interest in the product or services being advertised. This may be niche audiences, such as high net-worth individuals interested in purchasing a home. Advertisers reported that YouTube helps them to "basically reach an audience that we could refine very nicely based upon this niche:"
We have actually had good success on YouTube here in my current company, because we sell a beautiful luxury product . . . So YouTube has allowed us to basically reach an audience that we could refine very nicely based upon this niche audience that we're going after. We're going after very high net worth individuals with a very visual, esthetically beautiful ad. (YouTube advertiser #15) To this end, advertisers seek to run YouTube ads that generate impressions, referring to ads "getting eyeballs in front of them," or clicks that, ideally, lead to conversions, such as product purchases:
You need to be very careful with the audience that you're trying to attract, and ensuring that you're reaching those folks who are most likely to want to interact with your assets [advertised products], and then move on for whatever we're going to consider conversion, whether that's actually clicking through or just simply, getting eyeballs in front of them . . . .and then making sure that you have appropriate measurement of those interactions that you're having with your customer. (YouTube advertiser #13)
One unintended consequence of algorithmic recommending that became salient in our data analysis is manipulation. This concern stems from the user perception that algorithmic stakeholder governance, in its effort to recommend content on the platform, inadequately restricts some content while promoting other content, with potential negative effects on individual cognition and behavior.
Manipulation on YouTube can manifest in various ways. One significant concern in this context involves what are commonly referred to as "rabbit holes." In these instances, users who follow content recommendations and ads may inadvertently find themselves exposed to more "extreme" content that reinforces stakeholders' existing views and beliefs while not exposing them sufficiently to a variety of content. Several interviewees voiced concerns about the risks associated with these rabbit holes and their potential to influence consumers' cognition and behavior.
I have heard some friends experience, saying that they (. . .) have watched a video or two on YouTube. And now they're in this rabbit hole, like right wing conspiracy theories (. . .). Even in my own experience, like YouTube doesn't really show me like leftist, or even much liberal stuff, even though I've tried to make the algorithm show me more of that. (YouTube creator #16) Furthermore, advertising in form of influencer recommendations also received critical scrutiny. YouTube influencers with specialized expertise in specific topics and significant follower bases on the platform were seen as having substantial influence on their followers, in some cases also nudging stakeholders to behave in ways that was not necessarily aligned with their own interests and thus not beneficial to them. In this context, stakeholders voiced concerns about the ambiguous distinction between authentic product reviews by influencers and undisclosed advertisements. They suggest that the motivation of some content creators might be focused on monetizing content and pleasing advertisers, rather than prioritizing the best interest of consumers: Cause there's a lot of influencers that, um, you know, just are not quite clear about, you know, advertising products (. . .) Just like not making it completely transparent that they are being sponsored or got something for free and they actually doing whatever advertisement, whatever testing of the project, talking about It. (YouTube consumer #3)
In general, some study participants raised concerns about the naivety of other consumers, noting that many of them appear to be unaware of the potential for manipulation on the platform:
It's straight-up manipulation across the board now. The worst part is that people aren't aware and most don't understand what's being done to them. In my opinion, banning all kinds of psychological manipulation to make someone buy things they don't want or need is the way to go. (YouTube user post)
Given the polarization and heated political debates surrounding the 2024 U.S. presidential elections, such manipulation was perceived to be particularly concerning.
Finally, YouTube utilizes algorithmic monetization 16 techniques as an integral component of its algorithmic stakeholder governance system. This involves the automated financial incentivization of creating and sharing new content that generates substantial user interest and engagement. While only the most successful content creators can anticipate acceptance into the YouTube Partner Program (YPP) and commence earning revenue on the platform, YouTube has evolved into a significant source of income for a considerable number of creators (with estimates suggesting that it benefits millions of them):
Being accepted into the YouTube Partner Program (YPP) is a major milestone in any Creator's journey. As part of YPP, Creators can start monetizing their content, receive email and chat support, and get access to the Copyright Match Tool to help protect their content. 17  YouTube has achieved greater scalability of video monetization by automating the process. Its algorithms assess a video's eligibility for monetization based on engagement metrics, including total viewing time and the number of subscribers, and consider additional factors such as the video's copyright status and the channel's adherence to YouTube's Community Guidelines:
YouTube uses machine learning, because it's more efficient to filter out the content that needs to be demonetized (. . .). And I understand why they're using it because there are so many videos on YouTube. And it's very difficult to hire individual people to try to filter like this, just the vast amount of videos that people post on YouTube every day. But also, I think that the algorithm, more often than not, will just blatantly censor or demonetize. (YouTube creator #14) Overall, algorithmic monetization serves as a powerful incentive for content creators to generate content that aligns with the interest of consumers, drawing in an audience and, consequently, boosting watch time and user engagement on the platform. As one YouTube executive reported:
YouTube is a monetization platform (. . .) YouTube can encourage users to stay on the platform and watch more content, that's ultimately what the algorithm is trying to do. (. . .) The vision is to have people stay engaged with the platforms (. . .) they are going to see more videos and stay in the platform as opposed to just watch one and just leave, which is a bit of a challenge with YouTube. (YouTube executive #4)
Algorithmic monetization enables the platform to facilitate better alignment and incentivization of content creation with advertisers' interests, ensuring that content viewed as appropriated by advertisers gets monetized while inappropriate content gets demonetized. To this end, algorithmic monetization is an attempt to balance conflicting interests and resolve the content safety conflict which captures the creators' desire for monetization opportunities and expressing themselves freely to engage their followers versus advertisers' concerns about brand reputation and brand-safe content.
One creator explained that examples of controversial topics may include "depression" or "CBD oil," given that this is "just a topic that advertisers aren't happy to be in front of." Even if this content may not be banned from YouTube, creators are being discouraged to post such controversial topics, given that they will not be able to monetize these videos: I made a video this year about CBD oil, and that's just a topic that advertisers aren't happy to be in front of (. . .) It was demonetized because they say, 'Oh. It's a controversial topic' (..) It [the video] doesn't get promoted. Or, if I have made videos about mental health, talking about suicide, talking about depression, you can't monetize it, but, therefore, the algorithm does not care to promote it whatsoever. (YouTube creator #2)
The well-known YouTube adcalypse 18 is a major event showcasing this conflict. In 2017, YouTube took major measures to shield advertisers and their ads from being associated with controversial content, thereby demonetizing content by thousands of content creators. Some content creators felt that this incident showed that YouTube would prioritize advertisers over content creators' interests.
Oh, adpocalypse was like a time. in YouTube. I think it was like couple, I would say maybe three or four years ago, when a lot of the youtubers that I watched, they were talking about how their ad revenue from the videos that they posted were being decreased by a very large amount from the AdSense . . . it was caused by YouTube. And as a result, a lot of people were losing money. And like it was just losing a lot of money from their videos. And it was mostly impacting the individual content creators. And it seems like YouTube was shifting their focus from helping support the individual content creators, and giving more reference to the corporate companies. (YouTube creator #23) While creators expressed concerns about restrictions in monetizing their videos and valuefree expression, advertisers are concerned about content safety. One advertiser explained that YouTube has stepped up efforts to ensure content safety over the past few years, and shared the detrimental effects of what can happen in it is not taken seriously by the platform. She shared that in a former job, in which she was responsible for advertising toys for children, these products were placed on a pedophile channel, causing a "a little mini crisis." Such events can have major reputational effects: I think they definitely, at some point, they had issues with brand safety 100 percent and like even I experienced them as an advertiser, our ads appeared on a pedophile channel. It was horrible. So yeah, and then a reporter actually took a picture of that and wrote an article about it. So there's like a little mini crisis . . . their brand safety was not at the appropriate level. (YouTube advertiser #14) Several study participants reported that YouTube has recently stepped up its efforts to ensure content safety. It allows advertisers to make very targeted choices about which content their ads appear next to, and advertisers can even exclude certain channels. For example, advertisers can direct the YouTube system to not show ads next to political and religious topics or news channels, to avoid placing their product next to emotionally triggering content such as wars.
I also think what's nice about advertising on YouTube and on the Google platform in general is that it allows for a lot of brand safety. You know that your campaign is not going to be running on anything that is offensive or that is going to be threatening the brand in any way . . . . they have been like, further dividing up and contextualizing their audiences and creating more and more affinity segments that are more and more granular by the year. So you're able to create, like, a very tight targeting system, and they're also pretty extensive with the content and the topics that you're able to exclude on the Google ad platform. . . . They also have, like, keyword block lists. (YouTube advertiser #16)
While algorithmic monetization is an attempt to balance conflicting interests and address the content safety conflict in both an effective and cost-efficient, scalable way, it does not come without unintended consequences. Some creators and consumers on the platform blame YouTube for attempts to silence "unpopular" or less mainstream content and "getting rid of alternative political philosophies"-thereby prioritizing the interests of advertisers. We label this as marginalization, referring to the user perception that algorithmic stakeholder governance in form of algorithmic monetization tends to treat less mainstream, minority, or fringe points of view, in a disadvantageous manner. This particularly refers to content that YouTube classifies as borderline problematic. While some advertisers do prefer to not be associated with this content for content safety or because it does not align with their value proposition, this content does not meet the requirements of being deleted from the platform yet.
Our findings reveal that monetization does not seem to be very uncommon. Several creators explained that some of their content has been demonetized in the past, particularly, resulting in creators not being able to "use the one [video] anymore:" I remember getting some sort of a notice in YouTube that some of my content had been flagged, and I think it was demonetized. Essentially, I can't use that one [video] anymore. I can't get any sort of monetization out of it. (YouTube creator #14) Marginalization was deemed problematic when it negatively impacted YouTube content associated with political and social movements supporting historically disadvantaged communities. For example, one interviewee sharply condemned that content addressing the #BlackLivesMatter movement posted by a well-known and respected black influencer was inadequately promoted on YouTube. #BlackLivesMatter promotes anti-racism and "builds power to bring justice, healing, and freedom to Black people across the globe." 19 Given the importance of the movement for the black community, this action, reflective of YouTube's content moderation practices, was strongly condemned by one of the creators: I view content from [name anonymized]. And he's like, a really notable figure like in the black community. And he talks about social injustice, he talks about building black businesses. And sometimes when he gets like too deep into his topics, they will flag his videos. So I think that they do pull down some of the Black Lives Matter videos. (YouTube creator #13) Some stakeholders of the platform reported that YouTube treats minorities unfairly, not necessarily by deleting their content but also by inadequately recommending content or allowing creators to monetize videos of interest to the Black community, resulting in this content being less prominent on the platform. For instance, one interviewee mentioned that she could only discover content specifically focusing on "African American or textured hair" if she included these specifics in the search system:
If you use just software to promote or push content, you're most likely going to only push content that might not look like red hair, you know, things of that nature (. . .) If I type in hairstyles, YouTube is not necessarily always going to populate, you know, African American or textured hair until you start adding those specificities. (YouTube consumer #15) In sum, algorithmic stakeholder governance heavily depends on the utilization of tracked data about each user and their interactions with the platform, as well as machine learning algorithms for recommending, policing, and monetizing content. With this objective in mind, YouTube publicly commits to having implemented adequate measures to ensure that its algorithmic stakeholder governance helps to mitigate conflicts between the different stakeholder groups, by facilitating a forum for creating, consuming, and advertising content that is moderated in appropriate and accurate ways.
YouTube's different algorithmic stakeholder governance practices, and their unintended consequences, result in a variety of stakeholder participation behaviors, allowing creators, consumers, and advertisers not only to build bilateral relationships with the platform and share feedback with its algorithmic system, but also to engage in direct, multilateral interactions among each other. These range from unreflective endorsing to critical reporting.
Some creators, consumers, and advertisers displayed passive response behaviors through unreflective endorsing of content, inadvertently reinforcing the status quo of the algorithmic stakeholder governance system. Unreflective endorsing was often driven by stakeholders' indifferent attitude towards the appropriateness and accuracy of the platform's algorithmic stakeholder governance practices. We characterize this unreflective endorsing as the implicit approval of a platform's algorithmic stakeholder governance system and practices, demonstrated through acts of ignoring and bending behavior.
Many content consumers understand that the YouTube platform collects data on their preferences and actions, such as sharing, liking, or following content, and that this data is used to personalize video recommendations based on behavioral patterns, among other goals. Likewise, creators and advertisers are aware that the platform automatically vets their content and ads before they go live on YouTube, for example to check for proprietary content, such as background music. To this end, we observed a willingness among consumers to engage with advertising and curated content in exchange for free access to video content, as well as an acceptance of the YouTube practices by creators and advertisers as it allows the platform to effectively place their content in front of their target group. Within this context, one aspect of unreflective endorsing is "ignoring." This refers to the acknowledgment and acceptance of the platform's data collection practices that provide input to algorithmic governance without deeper consideration.
For example, some stakeholders agree to the platform's data-related terms and conditions without thorough review. Although participants in our study acknowledge their lack of clarity about how YouTube utilizes their data, and the accuracy and appropriateness of the platform's algorithmic stakeholder governance, some mentioned that they simply tick the terms and conditions box without full comprehension. One consumer explained: They use our data-but the security-you don't know where the data goes and what they do with it and how they use it. So, it's scary when you understand this. But they don't make it obvious, that's the problem. . . . Regulations are very important too, you know. I'm not sure that everybody reads all their privileges. Everyone just ticks the terms and conditions box. (YouTube consumer #1)
As this evidence suggests, the continued use of the platform by stakeholders reflects silent acceptance and consumption of this directed content, inadvertently reinforcing the algorithmic stakeholder governance.
The second aspect of unreflective endorsing involves bending behavior, defined as the willingness to modify one's actions to align with the platform's guidelines as algorithmically implemented and enforced in the form of codified rules and policies. Our research indicates that some content creators, consumers, and advertisers actively choose to alter their behavior, thereby contributing to the reinforcement of existing algorithmic stakeholder governance practices.
For example, behavioral adjustments were notably prominent in the context of creator responses to algorithmic monetization. As mentioned earlier, this algorithmic stakeholder governance practice stands as a significant source of income for the most successful content creators, motivating them through financial incentives to produce advertiser-friendly content that resonates within the YouTube community. Many creators harbor a fear of demonetization, as it significantly impacts their earnings derived from the platform. Strategies to avoid this include steering clear of contentious topics, resulting in content that adheres to YouTube's community guidelines but falls outside the realm of advertiserfriendly material. For instance, a creator expressed her readiness to avoid swearing in her videos to enhance the likelihood of her content qualifying for algorithmic monetization:
Once I do monetize, I know that, you know, the swearing, those kinds of things that have to stop, and I'm totally comfortable with that. I won't have any issues with that. But for right now, I'm just kind of being myself. (YouTube creator #19) Likewise, advertisers reported their willingness to redesign their ad content, which is vetted by YouTube's algorithms and occasionally (temporarily) rejected by the system due to concerns about compatibility with the platform's guidelines. They indicated that they had no problem making these adjustments to ensure compliance. Overall, compelling evidence suggests that the different stakeholders of YouTube are willing to adhere to the platform's guidelines, rules, and policies, and some of them are even willing to modify their behavior to ensure their continued ability to upload content and avoid being subjected to algorithmic policing, as this quote exemplifies:
It's just that when you try to post like controversial topics, I think YouTube kind of blocked you. Because I know like when a lot of people were posting videos about Coronavirus, and as soon as I mentioned Coronavirus, their video would get pulled down or taken down. So I tried to stay away from my controversial keywords so that my video doesn't get like pulled down. (YouTube creator #13) In summary, endorsements in form of ignoring and bending can be rather passive behaviors that reinforce algorithmic stakeholder governance. However, our data also points to more active response behaviors which we explain in the following section.
Our findings suggest that the unintended consequences in form of misrepresentation, manipulation, and marginalization may prompt stakeholders to take action, striving to have their voices heard and their interests more fully represented and incorporated into algorithmic stakeholder governance. 20 In this regard, creators, consumers, and advertisers have the option to actively engage with YouTube or the other stakeholders, and advocate their specific interest, by redirecting algorithmic stakeholder governance, through a process we refer to as critical reporting. We define critical reporting as the stakeholders' efforts to flag undesirable content to a platform's algorithmic governance system by offering judgment and context, potentially prompting a human review.
The initial aspect of critical reporting involves judging, encompassing the negative evaluation of other stakeholders and their (inappropriate) content on an ethical basis, followed by reporting it to the platform. For example, YouTube consumers might encounter creator or advertiser content that violates community guidelines (e.g., age-restricted content), indicating a lapse in accurate algorithmic policing, recommending, or monetization practices. In response, they can report other users and their content by clicking on a "flag"shaped icon located below the video. The YouTube website 21 explains this process:
We rely on YouTube community members to report content that they find inappropriate. Reporting content is anonymous, so other users can't tell who made the report. 22   Through enabling content reporting, YouTube asserts an active involvement of its stakeholders in algorithmic governance. According to YouTube, stakeholders are not solely impacted by the platform's decisions but also hold the potential to influence and shape its algorithmic stakeholder governance system. This empowerment allows stakeholders to signal about content deemed inappropriate and advocate for their own interests. Some YouTube consumers feel a significant sense of responsibility in this regard, perceiving themselves as partners or even aligned entities with the platform. They adopt a proactive stance, expressing solidarity with the platform in their efforts to remove inappropriate content ('we are taking all of this down'):
But there was a point in time when somebody was recording children's YouTube videos and telling them to do horrible things to themselves and their families. And that was good to have you to, like, step in and say: "Hey, we're taking all of this down. This is inappropriate." (YouTube consumer #15) Creators, consumers, and advertisers have mixed sentiments about the act of judging content. While some acknowledge that flagging content theoretically empowers them by providing a means to voice their concerns and advocate for their interests, others express some disappointment or frustration with YouTube's algorithmic stakeholder governance. Given that diverse stakeholders, particularly creators and consumers, engage in collective forum of interactions facilitated by YouTube not all of them are successful in having their voices fully heard. They remain realistic about the probably limited impact of their flagging efforts: I guess it gives a lot of power to the viewers to flag content for YouTube (. . .) I think like, as soon as someone flags it, they kind of pause, whatever the link is. And then they takes a couple of days for the video to come back up. But they should have a better process for that. (YouTube creator #13)
The second aspect of critical reporting involves contextualization. Oftentimes, YouTube's machine learning algorithms make automated filtering decisions that creators, consumers, or advertisers consider to be inappropriate or unfair, because they result in misrepresentation, manipulation, or marginalization. In such instances, particularly they may request a review of their own or others content by human moderators, aiming to potentially reassess or reverse automated policing or monetization decisions. This process, referred to as contextualization, involves recognizing specific cases that necessitate more comprehensive and qualitative evaluations by humans, prompting stakeholders to request reviews by human moderators. These requests may arise due to YouTube providing limited information about why video content might be filtered or deemed guideline violations. One content creator elaborates: Sometimes it's hard as a YouTube creator, to really determine if your video is going to get flagged or not, by talking about certain topics, and you may have a topic that doesn't seem controversial to you, but then to YouTube, it does. So it's kind of like a hit and miss. (YouTube creator #13) Consequently, creators, viewers, and advertisers alike seem to lack trust in the software and may opt to request human review of content to gain a comprehensive understanding of the context, "look at the specifics," and potentially prompt revisions in automated filtering mechanisms.
It's not necessarily that I don't trust the software, but as someone who deals with software in my personal life, and for work, there are grey areas within software, like there's, you know, things that the software doesn't necessarily take into consideration. Because it's not a person. (. . .) So that's what I feel like there needs to be a person at some point to look at that for the specificities. (YouTube consumer #15) In summary, the different stakeholders' engagement in judging and contextualizing feeds back into the algorithmic stakeholder governance efforts of the platform, given that these behaviors allow the platform to collect important information about the content preferences and aversions from their stakeholders. However, the efficacy of the directional effects of unreflective endorsing and critical reporting on algorithmic stakeholder governance is not flawless. The fact that unintended consequences prevail is in indicator that YouTube faces challenges to fully incorporate the constantly evolving and often conflicting perspectives of all diverse stakeholders. In the following, we synthetize and present our integrated model.
The model depicted in Figure 2 synthesizes our findings into an explanation of algorithmic stakeholder governance, that is, a process through which algorithms are designed and used to shape interactions and create forums "where conflicts among stakeholders can be addressed" [3:500], ultimately with the goal of bringing stakeholders' interests into the governance of the platform [3,9,29,32,42]. Our model explains the process by which platform stakeholders, i.e., creators, consumers, and advertisers, are algorithmically governed by policing, recommending, and monetizing content to mitigate stakeholder conflicts, including the freedom of speech, information diversity conflict, and content safety conflict. In line with the lead role governance form introduced in stakeholder governance theory [9], our model suggests that algorithmic stakeholder governance seeks to provide a forum [3] for resolving these stakeholder conflicts while creating, consuming, and advertising content in the three-way interactions between creators, consumers, and advertisers. We find that there are limits to how effectively the platform can perform its lead role in resolving the stakeholder conflicts algorithmically due to issues with accuracy and appropriateness in moderating content on the platform, reinforcing the idea from stakeholder governance literature that the voice of direct stakeholders needs to be directly incorporated into a firm's governance [3,9,42].
YouTube's algorithmic stakeholder governance processes produce multiple unintended consequences [36,41,49], including misrepresentation manipulation, and marginalization, to which platform stakeholders respond. The difficulty of synthesizing different stakeholders' interest in one algorithmic system, could, for instance, lead to filter bubbles and echo chambers that exacerbate further the content diverse conflict [36]. Our model suggests that securing the active involvement and engagement of platform stakeholders (e.g., [2,37]) to respond to unintended consequences in algorithmic stakeholder governance on the platform is contingent upon their behavior, ranging from critical reporting to unreflective endorsing. This stakeholder participation in algorithmic governance may create feedback loops. It can help to adjust the algorithmic practices (e.g., in the case of more active behaviors in form of judging) or have a reinforcing effect on the algorithmic systems (e.g., in the case of more passive behaviors in form of ignoring) which may not result in substantial process of resolving stakeholder conflicts.
The interplay between what is depicted in the model as algorithmic stakeholder governance, stakeholder conflicts, unintended consequences, and stakeholder participation manifests a type of interaction among human stakeholders and machines [40,44] involved in the platform's governance practices. Our model thus suggests that keeping the human stakeholders involved is critical for algorithmic stakeholder governance to function and meet its objective of resolving stakeholder conflicts and enabling the platform to perform its lead role effectively.
The interplay of platform stakeholders with their algorithmic governance is thus a double-edged sword. On the one hand, to the extent that stakeholders on the platform provide meaningful human interpretation and input that helps improve the accuracy and appropriateness of algorithmic stakeholder governance processes, stakeholders become comoderators of content on the platform, supporting the platform to perform its lead role and resolve the stakeholder conflicts discussed above. On the other hand, depending on their participation behaviors, platform stakeholders may exacerbate the stakeholder conflicts further if they do not learn how to effectively collaborate with the algorithms. Our observation in the findings that unintended consequences remain is an indication that YouTube faces challenges in fully incorporating the perspectives of diverse stakeholders. As a result, while the platform seeks to maintain appropriateness and accuracy in its algorithmic stakeholder governance and balance the conflicting interest of different stakeholders, and despite sharing their feedback, stakeholders are confronted with a spectrum of issues, challenges, and adverse outcomes.
We adopt stakeholder theory [3,9,42], focusing on the lead role form of stakeholder governance [9] and its framing as a forum for conflict resolution [3], to coin and conceptualize a novel form of platform governance, algorithmic stakeholder governance, which is our key contribution.
Algorithmic stakeholder governance takes a more holistic approach compared to concepts such as algorithmic management, matching, and control [6,19,39,50] that have been receiving growing interest by the IS research more recently. Unlike the focus of prior research on everyday operations and short-term decision-making where platform workers may be directed, incentivized, or penalized [13,34,39], algorithmic stakeholder governance is concerned with using algorithms to ultimately ensure the long-term alignment of stakeholder behaviors with platform principles and guidelines. This involves guiding interactions and the attempt of resolving conflicts among stakeholders. Adopting a stakeholder governance perspective (e.g., [3,9,42]), we recognize the importance of platforms in using algorithms to balancing diverse stakeholder interests, and by facilitating a forum for creating, consuming, and advertising content. The learning from stakeholder participation behavior and feedback further influences the interactions of the algorithms with and between these stakeholders [1,2,28], thereby resulting in the synthesis between algorithmic and stakeholder governance through combinations of human and machine learning.
This conceptualization and its elaboration into a model come with, at least, two significant implications for prior work on algorithmic governance in platform settings (e.g., [29,32,33]), and platform governance more generally (e.g., [12,31,46,45]).
Prior research in algorithmic platform governance suggests that advances in technologies, in particular artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning [29,32], allow platforms to execute low-cost governance, which enables them to maintain competitiveness [20,35]. Automating a platform's relevant decision making mechanisms, and executing no or very minimal human intervention, has been traded as a promising approach [6,39] to realize scalability through the use of external data resources and digital technologies [20], and to create user value [28]. Our research, guided by stakeholder theory (e.g., [3,9,42]), suggests that relying solely on algorithms to scale platform governance has its limitations. Fully automated governance systems may struggle to adequately address the real human needs, interests, and concerns of users-especially when those interests are in conflict and are difficult to reduce to binary, algorithmically enforced decisions that implement community guidelines in practice. Implementing algorithmic stakeholder governance, and allowing creators, consumers, and advertisers to engage with the algorithmic system of the platform through participation, interactions, and responses, presents a useful approach to overcome some of these challenges. To this end, we identify some sort of interaction between stakeholders and machines (i.e., the platform's algorithmic system) [40,44]. While debates and discussions among different stakeholders may typically be without material consequences, participation that allows to directly share feedback with the algorithmic system (e.g., by reporting content) turns each user into an active participant in algorithmic stakeholder governance. While our case study of YouTube highlights that unintended consequences such as misrepresentation, manipulation, and marginalization persist, human feedback from stakeholders can offer significant benefits for platforms that heavily rely on automation. For instance, our findings show that stakeholders can provide valuable context for certain content, potentially enabling the platform to reassess or reverse automated policing or monetization decisions, and to adjust their longterm strategy of how to moderate content. Thus, maintaining human involvement is essential for the effectiveness of algorithmic governance [44]. To develop a more sustainable relationship with users, our research suggests that they need to be viewed as stakeholders to be empowered by the machines and a more decentralized model of stakeholder participation [5,15,27] to get their interests reflected in the design of algorithmic governance.
Rather than governing users through an algorithm-enabled centralized control model [12,31,46,45] to get access to and monetize their personal data [1,51], our theorization suggests that creators, consumers, and advertisers are stakeholders that content platforms such as YouTube can actively incorporate into their overall governance framework. To this end, our theorization suggests that content platforms have implemented a more decentralized from of governance than accounted for in previous platform governance literature. We show that YouTube takes over a lead form of governance [3,9] through which algorithms are designed and implemented to facilitating a forum for its various stakeholders. While the platform remains in a dominant role, algorithmic stakeholder governance can be considered a type of community governance, which offers creators, consumers, and advertisers the opportunity to engage in multilateral, direct relations with other stakeholders. Viewing these stakeholders as active participants, rather than objects of governance, offers a fresh perspective and is a considerable departure from prior literature [12,31,46,45]. Our theorization provides a new view of more distributed stakeholder influence in platform governance in general and content moderation in particular. Highlighting the limitations of centralized platform governance encourages the exploration of more decentralized governance models [15], extending beyond the lead governance form discussed here. Thus, we believe it is crucial to assess and evaluate the adoption of alternative governance structures, such as the shared governance model [9], which is commonly adapted in blockchain contexts [5,27]. Shared governance diminishes even further the power and influence of the central platform, empowering stakeholders to fully self-govern their interactions and exert even greater control over the design and use of governing algorithms.
Our research also allows us to derive some practical implications. In theory, algorithmic stakeholder governance has the potential to limit the often-criticized dominance of big tech over its users [1,51], given that stakeholders are becoming more involved in governance. Yet it is important to note that the option for stakeholder participation is confined within the boundaries set by the platform, and thus, in some cases algorithmic stakeholder governance may just capture psychological ownership, or a sense of collective ownership, rather than authentic algorithmic stakeholder governance. Platforms need to reflect on the different ways by which they may involve stakeholders in their endeavors.
Furthermore, our study relates to the ongoing trend that business models increasingly rely on a synergistic combination of human and machine agency and capabilities [40,44]. An algorithmic stakeholder governance strategy that is well aligned with platforms' business requirements can contain operational costs and limit the use of internal, human resources for regulation of user content and behavior. It is important for governance systems relying on this combination to be designed with stakeholders, not without them. It is pivotal for the long-term survival of platforms to reflect on how to design these systems efficiently and effectively, to enable a form of algorithmic stakeholder governance that is both scalable and sustainable.
Our work on algorithmic stakeholder governance offers several directions for future research. First, we encourage future research to validate our model for different types of platforms employing machine learning algorithms. This could be social media platforms such as Facebook or X, information sharing platforms such as Reddit, or educational platforms such as Wikipedia. For example, some platforms may be more reliant on traced user data that is automatically fed into the algorithmic governance models, while others may be more reliant on qualitative, critical reporting of content by users (e.g., in form of making a case by providing more extensive explanations).
Furthermore, research should explore the merits of alternatives to the observed lead role algorithmic stakeholder governance form and investigate algorithmic stakeholder governance on platforms that exhibit varying degrees of centralization and decentralization. We encourage future research to investigate the a shared governance form [9] that reduces the power and influence of the focal firm or platform and instead empowers platform stakeholders to self-govern their interactions. One example for a platform that is substantially less centralized than YouTube is DTube 23 (Decentralized YouTube), which is built as an application on top of the blockchain-based social media platform Steemit. It will be interesting to research how algorithmic stakeholder governance unfolds once the platform organization moves even more to the background, potentially at some point removing itself completely as the central authority deciding on what tasks to delegate to the machine, and which norms, guidelines, and rules to implement.
In this paper, we examine algorithmic stakeholder governance in the context of content platforms. We develop a model that explains how interactions among three key platform stakeholders-creators, consumers, and advertisers-are algorithmically governed to address conflicts related to free speech, information diversity, and content safety. Our model suggests that algorithmic stakeholder governance provides a forum for resolving these conflicts while highlighting the interplay between the platform's governance approach and stakeholder participation. The paper contributes primarily to the literature on platform governance, and more specifically to algorithmic governance on platforms, and we hope that our study will spur further investigation in this important domain.
