See Figure 1.1 in the Online Supplemental Appendix 1 for an illustration of WT's timeline and a more complete history; whereby one year later (Oct-19) the original idea and solution was abandoned and transformed into a custom-built collaboratively editable social network called WT.Social.
Qualitative data were collected from current and historical versions of the WT platform using the Internet Archive to identify key phases of project development, WT project posts (n = 111) to identify project relevant information including policies, guidelines, and formal processes, WT Medium articles (n = 49) for pre-launch project information, WT mailing list e-mails (n = 162) from point of researcher registration (March 2018), WT Slack workspace messages (with 10k searchable messages available from a total of 29,680; used as an approximation of members and daily active users). The full qualitative dataset is detailed in Table 1.2 of the Online Supplemental Appendix 1.
Article information was initially gathered with Python scripts using the WT API. Revision history was collected using Python to extract data directly from WT using the Beautiful Soup package. Data was loaded into R/R Studio for full analysis. Data on 1,597 articles were extracted with 14 data points for each article: title text, story author, type (staff or volunteer), start date, publish date, last update date, total unique contributors, total contributions, total talk comments, primary category, article categories (official project-assigned topics), article tags (unofficial user-generated topics), total categories, and total tags. Staff were identified on the WT platform staff profiles and Slack workspace to help differentiate user contributions and better understand coordination and user activity [6]. We identified 28 staff members as active contributors on the platform out of about 46 (not all staff produced articles and staff joined/left the project at various stages).
The study collected qualitative and quantitative data to identify: (1) the project's public intentions (goals and objectives), (2) the project's public implementation (platform design and governance), and (3) the project's public outcomes (article production and community activity). We compared participation and contribution levels of paid professionals with unpaid volunteers across the project lifecycle, mapping changes to policy, platform, and activity. Applying Benkler's theory, the data was analyzed by identifying the factors affecting the advantages and challenges of CBPP. The analysis on the information processing and resource allocation advantages identified factors that related to the size and diversity of the user base and community resources, the design of the system, and any evidence of implementing concepts related to task modularity, granularity, and heterogeneity. Likewise, these factors were analyzed using the three challenges: motivation (user participation), coordination (processes for producing content), and integration (creating a high-quality final product). This was compared with project activity metrics to understand how the community evolved and was shaped by platform, policy, and user behavior.
WT had a total of 1,597 articles from May 2017 to the end of October 2018 (151 of which were drafts). Figure 2 displays the total articles created by staff, volunteers, and deleted users (excluding period 2 which had zero articles) and the growth of unique authors for each period. Overall, there were 204 unique article creators and during this time the size of the community on Slack went from 178 at pre-launch end (Nov-17), 477 at pilot launch end (May-18), to 558 at platform redesign end (Nov-18). An average of 10 unique authors (5.6 percent of Slack members) created articles each month pre-launch (25 total unique authors overall). This grew to 26 (5.5 percent of Slack members) following pilot launch (85 total unique authors overall), and 38 (6.8 percent of Slack members) after platform redesign (140 total unique authors overall). Staff were more likely to start an article from scratch, accounting for 72 percent (or 1146) of all articles. Volunteers created 26 percent (or 421) of all articles, with the remainder attributed to deleted users. This dynamic began to shift in the redesign period, with increasing numbers of articles created by volunteers, and a significant drop in the final month by staff creators, as well as overall production levels. In general, most of the broader WT community did not create an article on the WT platform and either represented consumers of the news articles or contributors (whether minor or major) to existing articles (Figure 1.2 in Online Supplemental Appendix 1 displays a comparison of article modifications undertaken by staff and volunteers). Figure 3 shows the rise and fall of the average of total categories, tags, and comments associated with each period. Comments begin to taper near the end of the timeline with a positive upswing in the final month, perhaps representing reengagement. The categories (system-based) and tags (user-generated) show an increase of topic coverage in the mid-project phase. Articles are centered around current affairs with a traditional newsworthy focus. A decline in topic coverage occurs near the end of the timeline as unique authors begin to fall and the project is restructured.
The Pre-Launch phase is characterized by a focus on professional journalists and editorial staff and their future role in the community, along with messages promoting community involvement in advance of pilot launch. The platform is not yet public and only limited members have access to the beta site for testing purposes (from mid-September 2017). The project is using an official "Medium" profile to promote the crowdfunding campaign and to inform and engage with donors about new project information. The Medium articles were coded as follows: crowdfunding campaign (updates, funding milestones, and donor information), staffing information (hiring of editor and journalists), feedback to users (addressing donor questions, supporter survey results, platform development updates), goals and objectives (clarification on evidence-based news production processes, the ad-free donation-based revenue model, and introduction of the pilot project), and finally, news agendas and news topics (promoting new articles and content planning/production by staff). The qualitative evidence can be found in Table 1.3 of the Online Supplemental Appendix 1, and the table row numbers will be referenced in the following sections to highlight supporting evidence.
Factors impacting motivation include the financial support provided by over 12,000 donors toward project development. These donors represent potential members that have already committed time and money toward project initiation, whether as future producers or consumers (by the end of the 18 months, 558 individuals have joined Slack, about 0.05 percent of project donors, and 204 individuals have created an article, about 0.02 percent of project donors). Monetary incentives are limited to the professional editorial staff. During this phase, 170 articles are created, 75 percent by staff and 25 percent by volunteers. Factors affecting coordination of the community include the hiring of the launch editor (Aug-17) in charge of managing the professional journalists and the daily news agenda. The launch editor clarifies how users can draw attention to news for coverage (see Online Supplemental Appendix Table 1.3 Row 1) and even though the open collaborative process is highlighted in promotional messages, there are clear distinctions between staff and volunteer members; for example, users are encouraged to discuss and engage with staff to direct content production.
An alternative public communication channel, the Slack workspace, is also created (Jun-17). This is distinct from the proposed project posts and associated talk pages on the official platform. Focusing activity on the platform keeps the conversations public and semantically linked to the content. Separate channels create less accessible and harder to find information, but alternatively enables synchronous and timely conversations for available group members. There are also email newsletters for registered users. These e-mails generally contain article highlights, information on the news agenda, and requests for participation.
The project posts on the beta platform are a first attempt at coordinating and integrating the work by both staff and volunteers, explicitly outlining the project procedures and guidelines (see project posts in Table 1.4 in Online Supplemental Appendix 1). The posts range in content from: specific news topics (Medicine, Global Affairs) and news agendas (the Daily News Agenda), WikiProjects (Translations, Podcasts), guidelines (how to write a piece of journalism), and several community policies, processes, and platform updates (Blocking, Conduct on WT). Project information and promotion is referenced, linked, or duplicated across communication channels (Medium articles, e-mail newsletters, project posts). Although some of the project communications are not yet available to a wider community, traces of a managerial hierarchy governing production are evident with a visible divide between the role of journalists and volunteers (see Online Supplemental Appendix Table 1.3 Row 2). This period represents the project's first steps toward building the community and launching the platform using various channels to coordinate and integrate the work. The messages created here carry over into the launch of the platform and evolution of the project's governance.
The official platform is launched to the public at the end of October 2018. During this period of growth, people begin registering and participating in a variety of ways, whether through article creation, revision, and commenting, or as subscribers and readers. The highest peak in article production is in the pilot's third month (Period 9 in Figure 2). Subsequently, production levels begin to drop, and staff remain the majority producers. A total of 728 articles are created in this period, 77 percent by staff. In fact, overall, just 10 editorial staff members represent the top 10 article creators (4.9 percent of unique authors), creating 62 percent of all articles and between 44-140 articles each.
An equal status between community members is promoted in project communications (see Online Supplemental Appendix Table 1.3 Row 3). However, new volunteers do not share the same permissions as staff members and are unable to set an article to a published status. All edits to a "Published" article are reviewed before going live (see Online Supplemental Appendix Table 1.3 Row 4). The professionals act as gatekeepers deciding what qualifies an article as ready to be published. They also influence the story agenda, by announcing daily news agendas and requesting user feedback through conversations (see Online Supplemental Appendix Table 1.3 Row 5). An e-mail newsletter announces that the use of these daily briefings with staff will cease at the end of this period (May-18) (news agendas continue in various formats for story promotion). Suggestions are provided to illustrate how volunteers can contribute to WT (see Online Supplemental Appendix Table 1.3 Row 6), namely, fixing typos, adding images, applying style guides, or starting a new story. The design of the platform centers on read-ability over edit-ability, displaying grids and sections that highlight specific articles (see Figure 1.3 in Online Supplemental Appendix 1), akin to an online commercial newspaper. This issue is highlighted in various communications by the founder in later months and is implicated in having a negative effect on participation levels (see Online Supplemental Appendix Table 1
There are seven core topics included on the home page (as a part of a larger and growing taxonomy of article categories). These topics are: Current Affairs, Politics, Culture, United States, Europe, Asia, and the Middle East. The focus of the articles in this period and the agenda set and promoted by the editor and news team is narrow in focus, limiting more diverse contributions. This is evident in the number and type of categories/tags used for articles and in communications by the founder who seeks to encourage more diversity (see Online Supplemental Appendix Table 1.3 Row 7). It is near the end of this period that certain updates to the project are announced (see project posts in Table 1.4 in Online Supplemental Appendix 1). For example, the launch editor leaves the project (Apr-18) with a fall in production in subsequent phases (Periods 13 and 14 in Figure 2), there are ongoing staffing changes, and WT start crowdfunding to expand into Spanish (accessing and serving more cultures and demographics). Certain community-driven initiatives are underway, including the formalization of a fact checking space to organize and coordinate related projects. Fact checking is recognized as valuable work suited to the WT model and the capabilities of a large community, as a more standardized and accessible task for amateurs (increased task granularity) and less complex than creating a new article or investigative journalism pieces.
The final phase in the study represents an opening up of the WT platform and community. A "radical redesign" to make the site "more wiki" is launched at the end of May 2018 (for new design see Figure 1.4 in Online Supplemental Appendix 1) with an official e-mail sent out to community members (see Online Supplemental Appendix Table 1.3 Row 9). The project begins to trust the community with more genuine control and the platform has been given a participatory design to help improve production levels. Initial results from this redesign are reported (Jun-18) with findings that show an increase in social actions, engagement, and visits (reflected in Periods 15 to 17 in Figure 2). However, the project is losing money and further redesigns are planned. In this period, 699 articles are produced, with an increase in volunteer created articles (44 percent). The following updates ensue (see project posts in Table 1.4 in Online Supplemental Appendix 1): the homepage algorithm is updated (Jun-18) to strike a balance between freshness and quality and better organize the articles for visitors; a new front-end editor is announced in the newsletter, moving away from the WordPress editor to make it easier to collaborate/contribute and for mobile devices (Jul-18); WikiTribune en Español is launched as a distinct platform, and a more extensive style guide is posted with style resources and guides for building stories (Sep-18).
At the end of this period (Oct-18), several significant changes are implemented. To improve inclusivity and participation levels, user publishing rights are updated (now a broader category of "trusted members") to speed up the publishing process due to evidence of bottlenecks and volunteer created articles remaining as drafts (see Online Supplemental Appendix Table 1.3 Row 10). There are also staffing changes, with staff journalists laid off at the end of the period with an aim to hire new journalists refocused on community support (see drop in production in period 18 in Figure 2). The announcement for this change seeks to rectify the perception that journalists are the gatekeepers of the community and address the early design/structure of the platform that limited community growth (see Online Supplemental Appendix Table 1.3 Row 11). With this change the community moves from Slack to Discord, a new communication platform (members drop from 558 to 329 in the first month of changeover). The project aims to create more granular and heterogeneous tasks for users (through "Subwikis" and a broader category of topics), a challenge outlined by the founder and addressed in planned future redesigns (see Online Supplemental Appendix Table 1.3 Row 12). This period includes new system features: article history log improvements (distinguishing system actions from revision edits), a follow article button to receive notifications, a new community portal for community-driven initiatives, a fact checking portal, and planned redesigns to increase resource allocation capabilities (see Online Supplemental Appendix Table 1.3 Row 13).
This section presents an analysis of the WT case across the project timeline to identify the factors that impact the advantages and challenges of hybrid peer production, as summarized in Table 1.
Table 1 summarizes the factors related to the advantages during the Pre-Launch period, as well as the potential challenges in terms of motivation (MC), coordination (CC), and integration (IC). This is a period of development, with a core set of paid professionals developing the software and platform content to begin creating value and attracting users. We describe this stage as having: (1) a limited community (of professional staff and select project donors), (2) a platform under development, and (3) a managerial hierarchy. Both the project resources and processes are closed in nature, and neither accessible nor transparent to a broader community.
The advantages include a large group of motivated donors as a potential pool of contributors (approximately 12,000 donors), a small group of skilled professional staff to initiate content creation and attract users, granular task setting with WT staff setting and promoting the news agenda, and modular articles that can be created independently (but not built collaboratively). For the challenges of motivation, the community only includes a limited contributor base with a small number of volunteers included in beta testing of the platform. As a result, the community lacks diversity with a limited number of paid staff members creating most of the content. The content produced is homogenous in nature with a limited topic focus based on a news agenda set and controlled by the editorial team (with a focus on current affairs). Challenges of coordination result from isolated article production and the limited collaborative capabilities due to a lack of a functioning technical platform. Resources are limited as the project starts the initial stages of content production. Likewise, a managerial hierarchy is at play with coordination occurring through insular communication channels. Integration challenges arise from the lack of a technical infrastructure for facilitating collaborative work. A private beta platform is tested with limited users and content with which to interact. In addition, the formalization of processes and social structures is internal in nature and not yet expanded to a larger community for knowledge sharing and widespread adoption.
Table 1 summarizes the factors related to the advantages and challenges emerging during the Pilot Launch. This is a period of growth in both community and content with an open call for the public to register and join. The way the community operates is still in flux with many issues remaining open to interpretation. The formalization of processes and community policies is under way. We describe this stage as having: (1) an expanded community, including paid staff and unpaid volunteers, (2) a platform with a non-participatory design and limited taxonomy of topics, and (3) a social structure of restricted community rights with limited resources for new volunteers.
The advantages include an expanding community of volunteers joining the platform (diversifying the community and expanding resources), modular news articles that can be built collaboratively on the new platform, the use of multiple channels of communication to provide for the needs of a diverse community and to create spaces for coordination, and formalization of spaces for accessing and discussing specific projects and topics. However, motivation challenges have increased with unequal incentives for community members (paid versus unpaid), the non-participatory design of the website limiting participation signals and accessibility of resources, user registration acting as a participation barrier, limited topic heterogeneity with the core of articles created by staff based on an agenda set by the editorial team, and finally, limited granularity of work, which requires skills and experience for greenfield production. Challenges of coordination include unequal power structures across community member roles for administrative and publishing rights, an expanded contributor base for more difficult coordination, fragmented coordination due to multiple channels of communication, and limited article filtering capabilities for resource allocation. Finally, integration is challenged by limited formalization of processes and social structures with which to improve overall integration and quality of articles. Quality of articles in this period is controlled by a small set of users, mainly the news editor and certain staff members, who oversee the publishing of articles and any changes to existing articles. This results in production bottlenecks, with many drafts and articles awaiting editor approval (unpaid volunteer drafts are less likely to receive timely feedback or publish approval).
Table 1 summarizes the factors related to both the advantages and challenges identified during Platform Redesign. This is a period of improvement to address issues that have arisen with the launch and implementation of the platform. We describe this stage as: (1) a community in flux with increasing unpaid volunteers and ultimately the removal of professionals, (2) a platform with a participatory design and expanded taxonomy of topics and filtering mechanisms, and (3) a social structure of expanded community rights and growing resources for new and existing members.
The advantages include a growing community of unique authors joining the platform and other formal channels (increasing community diversity), a large pool of modular news articles with more transparent and detailed revision histories, increased accessibility of resources and spaces that enhance coordination with new system features, the levelling of incentives between community members with less visible distinctions between paid and unpaid staff, a participatory design with increased participation signals and more accessible resources, and a more defined production process with the development of further project policies and guidelines. Motivation challenges resulted from limited granularity of modules, with only initial steps towards formalizing production processes and a still limited topic heterogeneity (decreasing topic coverage overall potentially reducing resource allocation opportunities). Paid journalists and editors are removed at the end of this period, impacting production levels and member roles. This represents a large divergence from the project's founding objectives and goals. The challenges of coordination include fragmented organization through multiple channels of communication with dispersed and disconnected messages, a period of adaptation due to the introduction of new communication channels and system design features, and limited filtering of article topics/projects for less modular spaces to allocate resources. Finally, integration is challenged with the expansion of rights for volunteers to publish articles and evaluate article quality. This requires an accommodation for expanding community skills and experience in this area. Multiple resources are provided to guide users in their new role and to help in the transition to a more communityled project.
The previous section presented an analysis of WT's hybrid model of production using the constructs in the study's conceptual framework of peer production (Figure 1). The findings suggest the aspects that disadvantaged the project and impacted levels of participation and production stem from the hybrid model. These included issues related to governance and coordination via member asymmetries and managerial hierarchies, the non-participatory design of the platform, and limited accessibility of resources in the developed solution. Each phase of community development has a unique set of characteristics ranging from closed to more open modes of production. For each of these representations certain advantages and challenges arose. As one challenge was met another subsequent challenge transpired with new community dynamics and manifestations. Building on Benkler's framework, we theorize that each of these design choices, or factors from the findings, produces a signal to the user that helps to reduce uncertainty and begin the process of leveraging the resource allocation and information processing advantages. However, these signals also have potential consequences that may or may not align with the project's strategic goals (e.g., increasing participation versus improving content quality).
We propose a social signaling model that deconstructs Benkler's [7] theory of CBPP by expanding the social signal construct in the original model (Figure 1) and identifying three sub-constructs. This expanded model, presented in Figure 4, includes three levels, or perceived barriers, that users encounter on project entry and further as they move through the internal workings of the community. These levels are: (1) System Signals, ( 2  based on perceived user identity. Internal users perceived identity clusters around the visibility of community roles (e.g., professional versus amateur), the reward system incentivizing them (e.g., monetary versus non-monetary), and the permissions granted to groups (e.g., trusted versus untrusted members).
Finally, behavioral signals at level three are embedded in the products and outcomes of the organization and its users. Where normative signals guide behavioral intentions, behavioral signals indicate the actual behaviors of the organization. In this study, they were embedded in the communication mode signals, or the way users chose to communicate with each other, the task formalization signals, or the way users formalized and coordinated the production of content, and the content heterogeneity signals, or the focus of content produced. These behavioral signals are informed by the system and normative signals and serve to further embed within the system as enacted by its' users.
We posit that these three levels represent the visibility and accessibility of (1) the system and its uses, (2) the community and its members, and (3) the project's resources and content. Each level provides signals that help to reduce uncertainty and either positively or negatively align with a project's strategy and influence a user's perception about the system and community. Thus, there are appropriate social signals, resulting in signalstrategy alignment, and inappropriate social signals, resulting in signal-strategy misalignment. Signal-strategy alignment helps to overcome the challenges and support the community towards realizing the advantages of CBPP. However, signal-strategy misalignment inhibits the advantages and fails to overcome the challenges. In addition, social signals impact on each other (i.e., system, normative, and behavioral) and either serve to reinforce or undermine the other signals. When the signals undermine each other or fail to reinforce the social norms and strategic goals of the project, disparity may occur, and the project may fail to realize the information processing and resource allocation advantages.
This study identified two system signals at the point of project entry: system design and system-level access. These signals are critical to technologically dependent communities that rely on the design of a platform to reinforce project goals and user capabilities. The system signals not only act as the external boundary to the community, either encouraging or discouraging participation, they also reinforce the normative and behavioral signals by supporting the visibility and accessibility of community information and activity.
In this study, the design of the system included participatory and non-participatory signals. These signals affect how users perceive the affordances of the platform and the action possibilities available to them (see Norman [43]). The non-participatory design in the original WT solution signaled a read functionality over a more wiki edit functionality when first exploring the website. In the context of iterative peer production, misalignment at this entry point may demotivate potential users from taking part, as they do not perceive participatory action possibilities or an invitation to contribute. A non-participatory design focuses on the potential consumers of a community. This type of design helps to address the integration challenge, by signaling a high-quality finished product. However, by indicating a finished product, the system deters potential contributions from external members. In addition, the functionality of a participatory design can be used to indicate granular tasks and better leverage the information processing and resource allocation advantages. The visibility of tasks and resources is essential for users to self-assign appropriate work and thus help to overcome the motivation and coordination challenges.
The system-level access signals in this study include membership and non-membership requirements in a community. A membership barrier was in place that required user registration for access to content production processes and a recommendation for the use of real names to enhance content credibility and traceability (i.e., quality control mechanisms). According to the literature, user registration facilitates a commitment from each individual to more explicitly create a sense of community identity and team environment [4]. This encourages a more transparent and credible community of people working together to leverage the non-monetary membership incentives of recognition, user status and peer rewards. Research on Wikipedia found that registered users contribute significantly more edits and more content per edit than anonymous users [4]. However, registration requires user investment up-front and limits the ease of access and potential opportunistic edits from casual visitors. This is in contrast with recommendations for attracting new users to online communities, which include: lowering entry barriers, encouraging engagement through conversation, and providing feedback [48]. Not including this signal has its own benefits, with research finding that anonymous users with fewer contributions are often more reliable than registered users [4]. In this project, certain tasks were minor or bounded in nature and did not require a serious time commitment (e.g., proofreading an article by correcting minor errors or approving an article for publishing). Tasks, such as article quality improvement, may have been restricted by requiring all users to register before contributing and not signaling to users that they could contribute in the first place. As anonymous users are more likely to contribute minor edits, a nonparticipatory design and registration requirement limited these potential actions.
The system signals in this case presented a barrier to user participation (motivation) by excluding users who wish to remain anonymous and limiting the potential for small contributions of fine-grained modular tasks (e.g., proofreading or fact-checking) from unregistered external users. The design also encouraged consumption over participation and may have discouraged less motivated individuals in making the decision to participate. We present the following propositions: Proposition 1a. Increasing the difficulty at project entry points with system signals that align with project strategy, positively incentivizes long-term engagement from highly motivated users to overcome the motivation challenge.
This signal could be further studied by measuring the difficulty of an entry point in other projects while investigating correlation with an empirical measure of motivation. Example hypotheses are mapped to the propositions in Table 1.5 in Online Supplemental Appendix 1.
Normative signals represent the intended behaviors based on the cultural and social norms of a community. In this case, identity perceptions form based on the visibility of different user roles (who you are), rewards (how you are motivated and rewarded), and permissions (what you are allowed to do). Misalignment in the signals about a user's role in the community impacts on the coordination challenge, and as a result the ability to appropriately assign resources and coordinate the work. Thus, misalignment between project intentions and the normative signals can impact on how the community evolves. Though the project intentions in WT indicated equal membership between professional and unprofessional users through egalitarian ideals, the normative signals interacted with each other to reinforce distinct divisions between user groups. These roles were further reinforced through system-level signals. For example, professional journalists and volunteers were promoted as equal members in the community from project initiation. However, the system was designed to limit volunteer member action possibilities and the community developed a culture that elevated professional journalists above community members. The professional staff remained the largest contributor-base until the signals were altered through numerous redesigns of policy and platform. The system-level signals did not match the intended normative signals, resulting in user behaviors (and behavioral signals) that further embedded signal-strategy misalignment.
This signal represents the boundary in visibility of different user roles. In this hybrid case, it encompasses the distinction between professional and unprofessional members. These groups are motivated and incentivized differently, and thus may not respond equally to the same social signals. The value of including professionals in a peer production community is to ensure standards-based and skilled work for both credible and reliable content creation. From a learning perspective, an advantage to this dynamic is that amateur members can leverage professional workers to enhance and refine their own skills [32], and likewise professionals can also benefit from these interactions for learning and skill enhancement [36]. However, the literature on professionalism and volunteerism acknowledge that tensions arise when these two social worlds meet [37]. For example, semantic boundary problems, like a lack of common vocabulary and shared meanings, may impact on interactions, as well as other issues such as a lack of common interests, motivations, and goals [37]. In crowdsourcing examples it has been found that visible hierarchical configurations can "erode team coordination and functioning by provoking conflicts and rivalries among team members" [10, p. 249]. This signal may act as a participation barrier, limiting inclusivity with mixed messages about the role of skilled professionals versus volunteer members. Moreover, the attachments formed by these groups, whether to the community as a whole (identity-based attachment) or to individual members (bond-based attachment) [48] may impact on community evolution. In WT, a key motivating factor for volunteer members was an identity-based attachment through a commitment to the objective of the project (i.e., evidence-based news) and not solely to the relationships formed within the community. However, the paid staff represented a high-density network of familiar partners (see Morgan et al. [40]) that benefitted from bond-based attachments (see van Osch and Bulgurcu [45], Ren et al. [48])-relationships often inaccessible to new members. This created imbalance between the professional staff and amateur volunteers and miscommunication in how the community should be designed to benefit both types of networks, whether the high-density network of familiar partners (staff) or the low-density network of multiple, often unfamiliar, partners (volunteers). This plays a role in shaping the behavioral signals. For example, bondbased attachments improve through private communications amongst identified participants while identity-based attachments improve when communication occurs in public forums accessible to a large number of participants [45,48]. Due to the hybrid model, both forms of communities developed, with a mix of characteristics and structures for coordinating the work. Throughout the WT lifecycle, professional journalists were identified as a key component in the hybrid model and undertook the bulk of the content creation, often in synchronous ways. Staff were identified on the website with a section introducing them and their roles in the project. This created an environment more akin to a traditional newspaper, whereby articles were produced by a professional journalist and approved by an editor, leaving little room for collaborative work between multiple members of the community. This did not match the promotion of the project during its crowdfunding phase with the premise that "community and journalists are equals" and would be working "side by side." There was evidence that some community members felt uncomfortable altering a professional's published product. This, in concert with the nonparticipatory design of the website, signaled consumption over collaboration. Creating visible boundaries between users through multiple normative signals (and reinforced by the system design) furthered project-signal misalignment. The inclusion of experienced or more skilled users alone is not a deterrent to users within other cases of social peer production [8]. However, when professionals are included in a process in which a community of volunteers are key to success, it is vital that volunteers are not diminished in the community and the signals are appropriate to their role. To benefit from the advantages, a diverse and global community must be supported to participate in a meaningful and valuable way in conjunction with the skilled professionals. The visibility of these divisions needs to be considered to ensure signal-strategy alignment, as clearly identified boundaries indicate to users what their role is, reducing uncertainty about how they can contribute, whether appropriate or not.
User incentives vary in peer production communities, with both monetary and non-monetary rewards used to motivate participation [7]. However, including paid incentives for some and not for others may create task divisions and member asymmetries that limit production processes. On a positive note, monetary incentives ensure an active paid user base generating content and value in the initial development of a community and beyond. This helps to counteract the startup paradox [62] and to produce enough content in initial phases to attract users to grow the community [31]. Paid staff members may shoulder the tasks that are unappealing to volunteer members. However, confusion in the role and status of unpaid volunteers may arise and result in a participation barrier. It is necessary to ensure that members are incentivized to contribute even if they are not a part of the paid community. In this case, the project focus (to create evidencebased news articles) may have attracted citizen journalists and other types of motivated individuals. However, clarity in a volunteer's role and the ways in which they can expect to contribute to a project may help to alleviate issues that transpire over time. For example, in the Pre-Launch and Pilot Launch periods, staff were encouraged to create as many articles as possible to generate a large set of resources for users. This was an advantage of the hybrid model, by having a core set of paid skilled staff members with planned time commitments for which to advance the community and to start generating value for donors. But this advantage turned into a disadvantage by focusing efforts on the paid professionals and creating perceptions about their elevated role in the community. In addition, reward mechanisms were not leveraged effectively for unpaid users. For example, an important reward mechanism is feedback [10,48,52]. Feedback in this case could have included setting volunteer-created articles to a published status, confirming the value of their contribution. However, due to production bottlenecks, many volunteer-created articles were left in a draft status for a long time. Volunteer articles received fewer talk comments and lower levels of engagement. A few factors that may explain this are the promotion of staff news agendas across communication platforms, the lack of filtering capabilities in the system design, and the option for gated and private communication spaces that decoupled articles from relevant conversations. There was an emphasis on a one-way feedback mechanism from volunteers to the project, while overlooking effective feedback to volunteer-led contributions. Another mechanism is trust [29]. Trusting volunteer members with the same permissions and capabilities creates recognitions for their contributions, instead of limiting their potential work. The reward system ties in with the other two normative signals in creating an internal user barrier between the paid professional staff and the unpaid volunteers, signaling a more limited role in the community. Given the evolving nature of this case, a more conscious evolution from a small bond-based community to a larger identity-based community could have been managed with a better understanding of the factors that would effectively incentivize participation.
Applying a hierarchy to membership rights may help to define the member roles and guide users to appropriate tasks to leverage the resource allocation advantages. Furthermore, limiting certain member's rights may help toward credibility and quality assurance measures and ensure task fulfilment for appropriate users. This may be necessary if skilled or technical experience is required in the process of creating the final product or if measures need to be taken to reduce vandalism or errors by malicious or incompetent users [7]. However, member asymmetries may occur leading to task exclusions that potentially slows down production or the allocation of resources, a negative impact of which is unrealized valuable contributions. It may also disincentivize certain members and create an ethos similar to a managerial hierarchy, without the benefits of managerial control for coordinating the work. In this case, not allowing certain members to set an article to a published status reduced the opportunity for a large and diverse user base to undertake the final quality check of an article that ensured it had reached a certain standard for publishing. This reduced a specific task to a small group of staff members with limited capacity to undertake the task alone, slowing down article production, as well as discouraging certain tasks (like quality checks) that may have benefitted from a large user base and a very defined and granular work task. Likewise, any additions to published articles were vetted by editors, regulating the actions of volunteer members. Overtime, this may have impacted on user contributions, as volunteer members were more likely to have articles left in a draft status for an extended period of time and were limited in their capacity to change an existing published article. This would have affected the non-monetary reward system, as this type of feedback would have signaled to a user that their contributions were valued (as opposed to invisible). Member permission hierarchies in combination with unequal user rewards and an identifiable professional user base may misrepresent the inclusive nature of an open peer production community. The literature identified the importance of trust as a mechanism for governance and collaboration in peer production communities, distinguishing collaborative communities from traditional organizations [29,40]. It is important not to impose unnecessary limitations to a motivated user base given their potential to provide valuable contributions.
Reinforcing identity-based distinctions creates a visible boundary between the internal members of a community, indicating their role and status. When aligned, the ability to perceive their roles and identify their status enables users to quickly find appropriate tasks and effectively participate in the community, helping to overcome the coordination challenges. When misaligned, users cannot benefit from the information processing and resource allocation advantages as they are not correctly perceiving appropriate action possibilities and are thus discouraged from undertaking certain tasks or roles in the community.
Proposition 2a. Increasing the visibility of identity groupings with normative signal that align with project strategy, positively reinforces the perceived role of community members to overcome the coordination challenge. Proposition 2b. Increasing the visibility of identity groupings with normative signal that are misaligned with project strategy, negatively reinforces the perceived role of community members and fails to overcome the coordination challenge.
This signal could be further studied by measuring the visibility of identity-based user groups in other projects while investigating correlation with an empirical measure of coordination. Example hypotheses are mapped to the propositions in Table 1.5 in the Online Supplemental Appendix 1.
Behavioral signals are indicators of how the project functions. User behavior is shaped by the system-level and normative-level signals and further embed these outcomes in the community, for better or worse. These behaviors shape how users produce content and engage with the community and result in further normative signals about the community and its practices. The signals include how the users communicate with each other in the project-reinforcing communication modes, how the tasks are divided and undertakenreinforcing the work practices and embedding them in the culture, and the type of content that is produced-refocusing potential user directions.
The use of multiple communication channels allows for focused and time sensitive coordination between active members in a community. Users choose appropriate platforms to communicate both publicly and privately with other members. Private communication between members is recommended for communities supported by bond-based attachments helping to create more high-density networks of familiar participants [40,48]. However, this may result in fragmented and less accessible information for new or less active members. In this study, though users were able to create semantically linked and focused conversations around the production of a specific news article, discussions were also occurring on a separate communication platform (e.g., Slack) or in separate project areas (e.g., project posts). Containing the dialogue on article production within the content management system facilitates members to accurately trace and access relevant information and previous exchanges of knowledge. The value of publicly available and semantically linked user conversations have been exalted in studies of Wikipedia, for both supporting article development and the continued improvement of article quality [9,33]. Likewise, for encouraging larger low-density networks and a community built on identity-based attachments, it is recommended that communications are conducted in public forums [48]. Due to the hybrid nature of this community, the tensions between the needs of a high-density network of paid professionals and the needs of a large low-density of unpaid volunteers were at odds with each other for ensuring a cohesive and transparent mode with which to coordinate and integrate production. Fragmented and decentralized discussions reduce the information gains necessary to integrate the efforts of a diverse user base.
Providing explicit information about tasks, as well as outlining formal policies and procedures, offers users granular detailed information about how to approach specific tasks and the skills required for task completion. This enhances resource allocation, so that users can self-select based on their own interests and capabilities [7,13]. However, by providing such specificities, certain input and innovative practices may be limited. The contribution range of users may be limited by incomplete or poorly delineated policies or processes suited to a more traditional organizational environment. In the case of WT, processes were poorly aggregated and hard to access unless specifically sought by a user. Due to the design of the technical platform, several articles and web pages were created over time for users to actively locate through platform exploration. However, clear guidance and instructions were kept separate from the direct actions of content production (e.g., process of creating a new article) and not easily accessible to users without knowledge of the structure of the community and how it evolved its operations. From the literature, transparent task structure, as well as an accessible resource commons, enhances the ability of users to self-assign tasks and thus make use of the resource allocation advantages [29]. Rules, like those identifying protocols for interaction, provide guiding principles with which to selforganize in a peer production community [29]. However, the rules enacted within the WT community initially mirrored traditional managerial hierarchies and were based on daily staff agendas and requests for community feedback from editors. These structures displaced motivated volunteers, incorrectly implying divisions between member types. Likewise, the initial non-participatory design of the website reduced signals for participation and did not clearly identify transparent task structures for users to begin contributing. This supports previous literature that states that information access is necessary to enable a flow of information to stimulate a user's desire to participate [13,16]. Overtime, community-driven initiatives helped to build more formal accessible spaces for coordinating and integrating work on specific tasks. This drive was non-hierarchical and emerged from the needs of the community. The initial constrictions placed on the community, through the factors described in the analysis section, hindered community participation and resource allocation. Potential solutions that emerged over time in this study included trusting the community to self-organize and create formal processes for specific tasks via community-driven initiatives (like the fact-checking project, a more defined and approachable task for newcomers) and the improvements in the design of the technical platform for more visible and accessible resources.
Imposing a narrow content focus encourages certain types of contributions and limits any potential divergence or confusion within a community. However, excessive restrictions on content act as a barrier to heterogeneous content production and may limit a more diverse user base or potential audience. A restricted set of resources, based on very specific types of content, limits the resource allocation for a large user base and thus may be suited to smaller more focused communities. As previous literature has found "the specific participation opportunities should encourage a wide range of contributions and knowledge sharing without any limits for content creation, even if it seems to be opposed to the original strategy endeavor" [16, p. 365]. Covering the "news" provides a broad and diverse set of topics for users to engage with. However, in the initial phases of the project, articles on "Current Affairs" and "Politics" were promoted over other topical issues. An editorial team employed a managerial hierarchy for setting the news agenda, potentially deterring certain contributions from external volunteers. Not only did this limit topic heterogeneity, it also may have impacted on challenges related to motivation and coordination in terms of the types of people and topics that were included in the community. The language around engagement between staff and volunteers denoted a hierarchy, whereby the staff elicited and evaluated ideas from the community. This may have discouraged volunteers from actively engaging in the project to create articles on topics beyond this discourse. In the news domain, articles solely on current affairs and politics may represent a complex task that requires professional reach, in terms of access to sources and specific experience for interpreting and reporting on specialist news. Signals promoting inclusivity should be considered when a project requires a large and diverse user base. While content focus is important to stay on topic, excessive restrictions (beyond off-topic conversations) will ultimately hinder participation. In the hybrid setting, both the types of content promoted for creation (content strategy inclusivity) as well as the ability to edit or revise the produced content (content production inclusivity) was limited affecting the final products of the community.
Behavioral signals embed the social norms and culture of the community further within the system. This is a positive or negative feedback loop that provides clues to members about how the community functions, the type of work that the community is focused on and the way in which the work is undertaken. Identifying the outcomes of the socially productive behaviors in a community, further signals appropriate or inappropriate behaviors to other users and influences user motivation, coordination, and integration. Proposition 3a. User behaviors that align with project strategy positively embed into the system and normative signals to overcome the integration challenge. Proposition 3b. User behaviors that are misaligned with project strategy negatively embed into the system and normative signals and fail to overcome the integration challenge.
This could be further studied in other projects by measuring the alignment of user behaviors with the intentions of a project (with factors related to communication practices, task management, or type of product/content) while investigating correlation with an empirical measure of integration. Example hypotheses are mapped to the propositions in Table 1.5 in Online Supplemental Appendix 1.
A further relationship between the social signals is proposed in this paper. For example, alignment between the system, normative, and behavioral signals is important for ensuring a healthy and sustainable community that communicates a consistent and appropriate message to all users. Misalignment may create disparity that miscommunicates project strategy and results in misdirected user behaviors that further embed negative signals into the community structure. These digital traces of user behaviors may be harder to remove than redesigning policy and platform. For example, applying the content heterogeneity signal, users that create specific news articles around current affairs signal to other users the focus of production, leading to more and more content that mirrors this signal further embedding perceptions about the appropriate products of production. In the relationships between social signals, the system may conflict with the norms, the norms may conflict with the system, and the behaviors may conflict with both. This raises the following questions: Has the system provided the right capabilities? Has the culture (norms) provided the right indicators for what users should be doing? This paper used empirical data from a collaborative journalism project to theorize the role of social signals in overcoming the motivation, coordination, and integration challenges of a hybrid CBPP. Though the study was limited by the single case study design, the findings present an extension of Benkler's [7] theorization of CBPP and contributes to our understanding of how communities can leverage the social signaling model to better meet the challenges of peer production. By extending the social signal construct, this study provides three further constructs with which to investigate the positive and negative consequences of social signaling for building and sustaining open peer production communities, especially in the increasingly prevalent hybrid context.
This study offers a number of contributions to our understanding of open forms of organizing. The core contribution is the extension of Benkler's construct of social signals into three constructs: system, normative, and behavioral signals. The study suggests that these signals individually impact (positively or negatively) on the motivation, coordination, and integration challenges, and collectively interact to affect community effectiveness. The study identified a complex relationship between signals that aligned or misaligned with each other and with a project's strategy. Alignment is important for overcoming the challenges in peer production and creating a healthy and sustainable community that positively reinforces the feedback loop of these social signals.
Additionally, the study characterizes a unique hybrid model of production, and distinguishes it from other forms of open production communities. The paper highlights the dynamic nature of such communities over time, presenting empirical findings and extending the theorization of CBPP by Benkler [7] to map the evolution of the WT project from a more closed traditional-style organization to a fully open community-driven platform. The study illustrates that hybrid and open peer production models behave in many similar ways and that both models face the advantages and challenges theorized to characterize peer production.
Finally, the study reveals that to leverage advantages and address challenges, WT became more open over time, expanding the rights of its user base and developing more transparent and accessible resources, relying on a variety of social signals to address this.
This study has characterized a specific case of hybrid peer production and presented a signaling system that shapes user participation and activity. In doing so, we have identified the tensions that arise when combining the social worlds of both paid professionals and unpaid volunteers in an open and collaborative wiki environment. Our signaling system highlights several areas for open organization research. As a first step, we recommend further research into other cases of hybrid peer production to understand if the three signals affect the challenges and advantages of other types of hybrid communities within different organizational contexts and domains. Furthermore, by mapping the dynamic nature of a hybrid community over time, we captured an evolutionary perspective of a community. Future research would benefit from more longitudinal research of other hybrid models of peer production to compare community evolution and existing and new signals (or combinations of signals) that emerge. Although we identified that WT behaves in ways similar to other open peer production communities, it is unclear how the advantages and challenges manifest in other contexts and under what conditions they arise. Likewise, deeper qualitative work into how signals are created and whether they always behave as intended (in both pure play communities and hybrid settings) would expand our understanding of the signaling model proposed in this study. Finally, in identifying the advantages/ challenges that emerged and evolved in this case, a more nuanced understanding of open organizing can be explored. For example, although WT included principles of transparency and inclusivity, the levels of transparency and inclusivity varied throughout the project timeline, depending on community governance factors and the design of the technical system. There was evidence of strategy (or decision making) transparency and content production transparency during project initiation, while at the same time measures were implemented to restrict inclusivity in the name of professionalism and information quality. This resistance to openness emerged from the traditional organizational structure, and the signals that resulted were key to understanding what stifled community participation and content production. To address the problems that arose from this manifestation of openness, measures were taken to increase signals of inclusivity and alter the dynamic between the paid professionals and unpaid volunteers and resolve residual tensions that had emerged as a result. This characterization presents an opportunity for further research into the inherent conflicts within openness and open communities. As different manifestations of openness impact on each other, we propose further research into understanding how to design an open community to best leverage the advantages of peer production and create the appropriate signals by which to realize project goals.
