Finally, because our pipeline breaks interviews into isolated QA pairs, MentalChat16K does not preserve multi-turn conversational flow (e.g., follow-up questions, clarifications). In real counseling, exchanges often span multiple turns. We plan to release a multi-turn subset in a future version to support dialog-flow research.
In this paper, we propose MentalChat16K, a benchmark dataset that significantly advances the field of AI-driven mental health support. By incorporating both synthetic counseling conversations and anonymized real-life intervention interview data, MentalChat16K addresses the critical need for domain-specific training data, facilitating the development of large language models capable of empathetic and personalized interactions. Our comprehensive evaluation framework, utilizing state-of-the-art models and advanced metrics, demonstrates the superior performance of LLMs fine-tuned on this dataset in delivering nuanced and compassionate mental health assistance. This work not only highlights the transformative potential of AI in augmenting mental health services but also establishes a new standard for ethical and effective AI development in this sensitive and vital domain.
To perform efficient fine-tuning by using only one GPU that is more affordable, we adopt Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation (QLoRA) [15]. QLoRA is a technique designed to optimize the fine-tuning process of LLMs, making it more efficient in terms of computational resources and time. QLoRA is based on Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) [26] which is a technique that compresses the update weight matrix Δ𝑊 ∈ R 𝑑 ×𝑘 (often termed adapters) of the pre-trained weight matrix 𝑊 ∈ R 𝑑 ×𝑘 by decomposing Δ𝑊 into two low-rank matrices, represented by Δ𝑊 = 𝐴𝐵, where 𝐴 ∈ R 𝑑 ×𝑟 follows the Gaussian distribution, 𝐵 ∈ R 𝑟 ×𝑘 is initialized to zero, and 𝑟 ≪ min(𝑑, 𝑘). Here 𝑟, 𝑑, 𝑘 refer to rank, input dimension and output dimension respectively. 𝐴 and 𝐵 containing the trainable parameters are updated through backpropagation during fine-tuning while 𝑊 remains frozen. The forward pass is then represented as:
LoRA reduces the number of trainable parameters and accelerates computation. QLoRA enhances the LoRA method via 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4) Quantization and Double Quantization. Quantization involves converting the precision of model's weights from higher precision representation (e.g. 32-bit floating-point number) to lower precision format (e.g. 8-bit fixed-point number). In QLoRA, model's pre-trained weight matrix 𝑊 is quantized and preserved in NF4 datatype. The trainable weights in the A and B are stored as 16-bit BrainFloat (BF16) datatype to perform computational operations. Double quantization further reduces memory usage by further quantizing the quantization constants. QLoRA stores the quantization constants 𝑐 in 8-bit floating-point numbers. The forward pass in Eq. ( 1) is then transformed to Eq.
(2) in QLoRA:
𝑌 𝐵𝐹 16 = 𝑋 𝐵𝐹 16 DDeq(𝑐 𝐹 𝑃 32 , 𝑐 𝐹 𝑃 8 ,𝑊 𝑁 𝐹 4 )
where DDeq(•) is the double dequantization that first dequantizes the quantization constants and then the pre-trained weight matrix into the computational datatype BF16. These techniques together reduce the memory footprint of LLMs, making it possible to fine-tune LLMs with billions of parameters on a single GPU.
Mental Health. The significance of mental health often receives less attention compared to physical health, despite its profound impact on individuals and societies globally. Mental health disorders, encompassing conditions such as depression and anxiety, lead to substantial challenges, affecting personal well-being and causing widespread socio-economic consequences. The global economy faces an estimated annual productivity loss of approximately $1 trillion due to these disorders, highlighting the urgent need for effective solutions and interventions [62]. The prevalence of depression among individuals aged 65 and older varies significantly, ranging from 7.2% to 49%, depending on various factors including living conditions [16]. Surprisingly, depression has been identified as more prevalent than dementia within this demographic, underscoring the critical need for addressing mental health issues among the elderly [1]. In this evolving landscape, the integration of AI in healthcare, particularly through the development of LLMs such as Alpaca, GPT, LLaMA, and BERT, offers promising prospects for groundbreaking research and the creation of innovative mental health solutions [21,72,75].
LLMs in Mental Health Care. In 2021, WHO highlighted depression as one of the primary causes of disability across the globe [63]. Moreover, a range of mental health disorders, including those stemming from depression, anxiety, acute panic, obsessive tendencies, paranoia, and hoarding, has significantly added to the worldwide disease burden [18]. The introduction of LLMs, notably OpenAI's GPT3.5 and GPT4, as well as Meta's LLaMA1 and LLaMA2, has brought transformative changes to several sectors, including mental health care. These advanced algorithms, built upon cutting-edge deep learning frameworks like transformer and self-attention, are trained on extensive text datasets. This training empowers them to grasp the nuanced semantic context of natural language and produce human-like textual outputs based on the given context [14]. As the application of LLMs in healthcare systems continues to grow, researchers are actively integrating the open-source LLMs into independent mental health chatbot, including Psy-LLM [34], Mental-LLM [72], ChatPsychiatrist [42], MentalBERT [29], etc.
Historically, AI applications, especially those involving NLP, have been around for several decades [71]. Since then, AI has been employed in various mental health tasks, such as: detecting suicide risk [6], assigning homework during psychotherapy sessions [52], and recognizing patient emotions during therapy [76]. The newer LLMs have demonstrated exceptional capabilities in diverse tasks, including reasoning, natural language comprehension and generation, and problem-solving [40]. For instance, LLMs like GPT3.5 have been instrumental in aiding non-professional counselors in delivering responses to patients [20], and depression diagnosis and treatment [69].
LLMs have also been evaluated for various mental health prediction tasks via online text data, showing that instruction fine-tuning can significantly boost the performance of LLMs for all tasks simultaneously [29,72,73]. Emotional support chatbots, on the other hand, provide on-demand, non-judgmental conversational support, acting as a supplementary resource to traditional therapy [45]. Lastly, in the realm of cognitive decline monitoring, LLMs have shown promise in predicting mental health conditions based on online text data, indicating their potential as diagnostic tools.
Benchmark Datasets in Mental Health. Several benchmark datasets have been developed to advance natural language processing (NLP) research in mental health, sourced from both text-based and live counseling conversations. From text-based counseling, Althoff et al. (2016) [2] conducted a large-scale analysis of the SNAP counseling conversation dataset, a foundational dataset for understanding language use and patterns in mental health discussions, though access is required. The PsyQA dataset [59] contains Chinese counseling conversations crawled from the web, and Na et al. [48] used CBT-centric prompts to guide OpenAI's GPT-3.5-turbo-16k model in providing CBT-informed responses to questions from this dataset. Additionally, [7] provides 3.6k questions and answers from online counseling platforms, covering a wide range of mental health topics with responses from licensed therapists. From live counseling conversations, the HOPE dataset [46] includes 12.9k annotated utterances from publicly available counseling session videos on YouTube, specifically for dialog-act classification. The MEMO dataset [58] further annotates these same utterances for the task of counseling conversation summarization. Additionally, ChatPsychiatrist's Psych8K dataset [42] comprises training data from 260 real English counseling recordings. The MentalChat16K dataset stands out from the SNAP dataset by being curated from face-to-face or video conference conversations, which encompass both verbal communication and various forms of non-verbal interaction, unlike text-based messaging. These datasets are instrumental in advancing NLP applications aimed at supporting mental health and well-being.
A.3.1 Demographic Statistics of Caregivers in the Anonymous Study. Demographic information was collected from 421 caregivers who completed the information survey. Specifically, the majority of caregivers are female. Among female caregivers, White Caucasians constitute the largest group, making up approximately 88%, with less than 1% identifying as Hispanic. Male caregivers are a small minority, totaling 6, with White Caucasians being the predominant group. Other racial categories include Asian American, Black/African American, Multi-racial, and others, each comprising smaller proportions of the caregiver population.
The data is skewed toward white female caregivers in hospice care but the skew is not entirely unexpected as the national hospice population itself is known to have a similar demographic trend. According to a systematic review by [10], 9 out of 14 articles had a 70% or greater female population, with 4 being above 80%. Additionally, 5 out of 8 US-based studies had white/Caucasian populations above the national census average of 75%. Similarly, another review by [9] found that in 25 studies, 19 had 76% or more female caregivers, and 11 US-based studies reported Caucasian populations above the national average of 72%. These findings suggest that the skew in our dataset aligns with broader trends in hospice care and research participation. A.3.2 Topic Distribution For Synthetic Data. The Synthetic Data covered 33 mental health topics, including Relationships, Anxiety, Depression, Intimacy, Family Conflict, etc. The proportion of each topic (Figure 3) that typically arises in a counseling session according to the CounselChat [7] platform was specified in the prompt. This method ensures the synthetic conversations authentically mimic the complexity and diversity of therapist-client interactions, thereby exposing our models to a wide spectrum of psychological conditions and therapeutic strategies.

To assess the alignment between LLM-based evaluations and human judgments, we conducted a correlation analysis using Pearson's correlation coefficients across seven key evaluation metrics (Table 10). This analysis, performed with GPT-4 Turbo and Gemini Pro, revealed several compelling findings. Holistic Approach exhibited the strongest correlation across both models (GPT-4: 0.489, Gemini: 0.489), followed by Empathy & Validation (GPT-4: 0.433, Gemini: 0.355) and Active Listening (GPT-4: 0.411, Gemini: 0.324). These metrics demonstrated particularly robust alignment with human evaluations, underscoring the capability of LLMs to reliably assess critical aspects of mental health interactions. Clarity & Encouragement also maintained strong correlations (GPT-4: 0.413, Gemini: 0.364), while Open-mindedness & Non-judgment (GPT-4: 0.328, Gemini: 0.338) and Safety & Trustworthiness (GPT-4: 0.272, Gemini: 0.291) displayed moderate alignment. Although Boundaries & Ethical Considerations showed comparatively lower correlations (GPT-4: 0.203, Gemini: 0.291), they were still meaningful and consistent with expectations for this dimension.
To contextualize these results, we compared them with benchmarks from recent work, such as the EMNLP 2023 paper "Towards Interpretable Mental Health Analysis with Large Language Models". That study reported correlations between human judgments and automated metrics primarily in the 0.10-0.40 range, with ChatGPT true achieving 0.15-0.35 and BART-Score exceeding 0.40 only for specific metrics. In contrast, our correlation coefficients (ranging from 0.20 to 0.49) not only align with these benchmarks but often exceed them. For instance, Holistic Approach (0.489) performs comparably to their best metric (BART-Score: 0.428), while several of our metrics outperform their BERT-based methods (0.172-0.373). Crucially, the consistent performance across both GPT-4 Turbo and Gemini Pro highlights the robustness and reliability of our evaluation framework.
These findings demonstrate that LLM-based evaluations can effectively represent human judgments, particularly for metrics such as Holistic Approach, Empathy & Validation, and Active Listening, where correlations are both strong and consistent with prior benchmarks. While some dimensions, such as Boundaries & Ethical Considerations, exhibit weaker correlations, the overall results suggest that LLM-based evaluation is highly reliable for assessing key aspects of response quality. This evidence supports the adoption of LLMs for targeted evaluation tasks in mental health contexts, bridging a critical gap in scalable, automated evaluation methodologies.

As we work together in this therapeutic process, I'd like to propose a few strategies to help you manage your anxiety and improve your overall well-being. First, we can explore cognitive-behavioral techniques to help you challenge and re-frame negative thoughts that contribute to your anxiety and panic attacks. Second, we can work on developing coping skills, such as deep breathing exercises, progressive muscle relaxation, and mindfulness meditation, to help you manage your symptoms in the moment. Lastly, we can explore the possibility of connecting you with support groups and other resources in your community to help you build a network of understanding and compassionate individuals who can provide you with the emotional support you need.

title: Attribution theory: An introduction to the special issue
abstract: This special issue of the Journal of Organizational Behavior was developed to further extend attribution theory and its application to the field of organizational behavior. In this introduction, we provide a brief overview of the motivation for this special issue, a concise summary of the papers included in it, a discussion about progress toward the field's goals, and suggestions for how future research can move the field forward. In doing so, we describe how applying attribution theory to studies that utilize a broad range of study designs, research contexts, and focal topics results in insights that enhance our understanding of how attributional processes predict and explain individuals' emotions and behaviors. We also provide suggestions for how to further develop attribution theory so we can more clearly describe the generalizability of relationships across a wide variety of organizational contexts.
full_text:
processes are also a central theme for an Australian Research Council Grant (Ashkanasy, Bennett, & Martinko, 2014-2017) to study the effects of high-performance work systems. Attribution processes play a similar role in a recent book for the Frontier Series sponsored by the Society for Industrial and Organizational Psychologists, which explores when high-performance work systems cross the line to become perceived as abusive (Ashkanasy, Bennett, & Martinko, 2016). In summary, the scope of application for attribution theory has expanded considerably in recent years. This special issue is designed to provide a forum for further development of our understanding of how attributional processes contribute to explaining some of the most critical issues in organizational behavior.
Two methods were used to generate the papers for this special issue. As usual, a call for papers was announced by the Journal of Organizational Behavior. In addition, a call for papers was issued for the Third International Symposium on Attribution Theory, which was held in March 2018 at the School of Business and Industry at Florida A&M University. Previous symposia on attribution theory were held in 1994 and 2004. Both were well attended and resulted in attribution theory papers published in books by St. Lucie Press (Martinko, 1995) and Information Age Publishing (Martinko, 2004). The 1995 book was cited by Shafritz and Ott (2001) as one of the two most important contributions to the organizational sciences in 1994.
There were 40 attendees at the Third International Symposium on Attribution Theory, which included scholars from 10 countries (i.e., Australia, Canada, China, France, Germany, Great Britain, Ireland, the Netherlands, Scotland, and the United States). Although presenting at the symposium was not a formal requirement for inclusion in this special issue, all of the papers included in this special issue were presented during the symposium. The symposium was intended to bring the worldwide community of attribution theory scholars together to share constructive developments in the attribution theory literature and identify opportunities to advance both theory and practice. All participants, including keynote speaker Bernard Weiner, were able to provide feedback on every presentation. All papers included in this special issue were also subject to the Journal of Organizational Behavior's standard review process. Ultimately, the study authors, feedback from the attendees of the Third International Symposium on Attribution Theory, and the excellent review team at the Journal of Organizational Behavior developed the five papers included in this special issue that advance our understanding of attribution theory.
In the first paper, Sun, Liden, and Ouyang (2019)   to provide nuanced insight into attributional dimensions and their application to contexts critical for understanding organizational behavior (e.g., leadership). Thus, the papers included in this special issue demonstrate some of the numerous opportunities available for scholars to investigate attribution theory from a wide range of research orientations.
Overall, the five papers in this special issue provide novel insight into attribution theory that we hope will move the field forward.
The goal of the special issue, the symposium, and the prior two symposia was to further extend and adapt attribution theory and its application to the field of organizational behavior. As we consider the articles in the special issue, as well as the articles published in the two books from the prior symposia, it is clear that significant progress has been made
regarding the application and generalizability of attribution theory to organizational contexts. In this special issue, attributional constructs are applied to and help explain servant leadership, the dynamics of leadersmember relations, how the relationships of coworkers affect organizational members, reactions of organizational members to human resource management practices, and consumer reactions to product recalls.
In the prior symposia, and in reviews of the general organizational behavior literature (e.g., Mackey et al., 2017;Martinko, Harvey, & Douglas, 2007), a wide variety of other applications have also been generated knowledge demonstrating the power of attribution theory to explain aspects of goal setting, abusive supervision, work attitudes, aggression, stress, conflict, group behavior, political behavior, organizational citizenship behavior, and emotions. Thus, significant progress has been made demonstrating the power of attribution theory to explain a wide variety of organizational phenomena. We expect further progress in many of these areas as the principles of attribution theory are generalized to explain the complex aspects of organizational behavior.
Significant progress has also been made in developing and adapting attribution theory to organizational contexts. In this special issue, three of the articles (Carson, 2019;Gardner et al., 2019;Sun et al., 2019) focused on variations of relationship attributions. This focus appeared to be, in part, as a response to the recent conceptual and empirical work by Eberly and her colleagues (Eberly et al., 2011;Eberly, Holley, Johnson, & Mitchell, 2017). During the symposium, there was considerable debate as to whether or not the types of relational attributions described by Eberly et al. (2011Eberly et al. ( , 2017) ) should be considered a new dimension or a causal explanation that can be related to the traditional dimensions described in the Kelley (1973) and Weiner (1985) models. This issue is important because the dimensions described by Kelley illuminate the types of information people use to make attributions, whereas the dimensions identified by Weiner help predict both behavioral and emotional responses. If relational attributions are considered causal explanations, then it increases the power and generalizability of this construct because it enables the explanations to be categorized along the dimensions of the Kelley and
Weiner models that explain how these attributions are formed and their resultant effects on individuals' emotions and behaviors. It also enables these more specific areas of research to enhance the general theoretical tenants of attribution theory. A clear consensus was not reached during the symposium, so this is an issue that deserves further research attention.
Another issue that emerged as a result of the development of this special issue was the level of understanding that was demonstrated regarding attribution theory. Many of the papers submitted for review failed to demonstrate knowledge of the basic tenets and principles that comprise attribution theory. As Weiner (1995) observed, there are many possible causal explanations for any outcome. Constructing a separate theory and body of research to explain every possible attributional explanation would be impossible. As a result, a classification system (i.e., causal dimensions) is necessary in order to develop a theory that can generalize across contexts and situations. Kelley's (1973) model describes the dimensions of information used to form attributions, whereas Weiner's (1985Weiner's ( , 1986) ) model demonstrates how causal explanations can be classified into dimensions that predict both behavioral and emotional reactions. These classification systems then allow researchers to understand how information is used to predict causal explanations and how highly divergent causal explanations can be generalized (i.e., placed into dimensions) to predict emotions and behaviors. The lack of appreciation and understanding of how attributions work resulted in many submissions that identified causal explanations but failed to demonstrate how information was used to develop these various explanations. This limitation restricted the description of how the various explanations related to emotions and behavior.
One of the key takeaways from the process of developing the special issue was a recognition of the need for researchers to be more mindful of the roots of their contributions so that their results can be generalized and contribute to both predicting and understanding  Kelley's (1973) and Weiner's (1985) seminal works, a synthesis of the Kelley and Weiner models provided by Martinko and Thomson (1998), and the early work that tested the validity of attributional models (Ashkanasy, 1989(Ashkanasy, , 1995;;Ashkanasy & Gallois, 1994;Mitchell & Wood, 1980). More can be done to directly test the validity of the current models in organizational contexts so we can extend attribution theory to more effectively predict and explain workplace behaviors.
We were also a bit concerned about the lack of progress in relating attributional processes to emotional processes. Although there has been an increasing awareness of the importance of emotions in leadership and organizational behavior (Ashkanasy & Daus, 2002), we did not see this attention reflected in our submissions or in the recent literature.
However, there are a few notable exceptions in the existing literature, particularly in the area of leader-member relations (Dasborough & Ashkanasy, 2002, 2004;Martinko, Moss, Douglas, & Borkowski, 2007), abusive supervision (Brees, Mackey, Martinko, & Harvey, 2014;Chan & McAllister, 2014;Dasborough & Ashkanasy, 2002, 2004;Martinko, Harvey, Sikora, & Douglas, 2011), deviant behavior (Harvey et al., 2017), and aggression (Douglas et al., 2008). Works by Weiner (1985Weiner ( , 1986Weiner ( , 2004Weiner ( , 2018) ) and the works cited above offer specific guidance on how particular types of attributions lead to specific emotions, including anger, shame, and gratitude. Again, more can be done here to understand how attributional processes influence emotions and the behaviors associated with those emotions in organizations.
Finally, some comment regarding the future of attribution theory in the organizational sciences is warranted. As Weiner (2018) observed, attribution theory is not simply a naïve or "grandmother" psychology.
It has resulted in findings that generalize, are replicable, and explain many aspects of human motivation and emotion. From an organizational perspective, the analysis of causation is fundamental to understanding both success (i.e., reinforcement) and failure (i.e., punishments) at both the individual and organizational levels. Because the analysis of causation is a critical organizational competency, we are confident that the interest in attributional processes will continue to develop and thrive. Weiner (2019) expands on the history and trajectory of attributional processes in his invited contribution for this special issue.
As the keynote speaker for the Third International Symposium on Attribution Theory, Weiner was highly influential in the evaluation and development of papers that ultimately contributed to this special issue. His recommendation to solve the dilemma of how to evaluate relational attributions identifies a way for attribution theory scholars to meaningfully advance the field and generate additional interest in efforts to extend attribution theory. We are hopeful that researchers will continue to seek to understand the dimensions of causation that can be generalized across different contexts and situations.
Our motivation for this special issue was to illuminate and extend the current conversation within attribution theory research in the areas of both theory and application. The numerous study designs, research contexts, and focal topics to which attribution theory was applied in this special issue demonstrates the immense amount of opportunities for attribution theory to enrich our understanding of organizational behavior phenomena. Nevertheless, there are still many fruitful areas of inquiry, particularly with respect to theory development and the relationships between attributions and emotional processes. We hope that the contributions from this special issue and our general discussion of the issues that became salient during the development of the special issue provide guidance and motivation to continue the process of moving the field forward.

title: Leveraging Platform Boundary Resources: The Role of Distributed Sensemaking
abstract: Although mobile platform ecosystems are highly competitive environments, they provide important entrepreneurial opportunities for app developer organizations. To facilitate app innovations, platform owners regularly release platform boundary resources (PBRs) by adding novel technologies at the platform level. App developer organizations, however, face high levels of technological uncertainty as they create app-level innovations based on PBRs. We examine the effectiveness of the level of distributed sensemaking about PBRs in a context of technological uncertainty arising from either PBR's technological unrelatedness with prior PBRs or app complexity. Using a dataset of 933 PBR-based app innovations, the findings significantly contribute to our understanding of the duality between competition and cooperation in a platform ecosystem. We demonstrate that distributed sensemaking among app developers, who potentially compete against each other, is crucial for enhancing app competitive performance, especially when technological uncertainty is high. Thus, we encourage greater cooperation among app developer organizations to leverage PBRs.
full_text:
Mobile platforms provide important markets for app developer organizations. Organizations that publish apps on mobile platforms are considered app developer organizations (e.g., British Airways, CIBC). The number of mobile platform users is considerably high providing significant entrepreneurial opportunities to app developer organizations. In January 2019, the iOS platform reached 1.4 billion active devices [30]. Moreover, mobile platforms are characterized by highly competitive environments, making it a challenge to achieve high levels of app performance [28,62]. Surviving in such environments makes it necessary for app developer organizations to continually evolve their apps by releasing new app services [15]. A growing strategy used by app developer organizations is to extend their app functionalities by creating app innovations that integrate platform boundary resources (PBRs) 1 (e.g., ARKIT, and SiriKit). These app innovations are PBR-based app innovations. They represent new app features (e.g., authentication features) that are created based on a given PBR and are released either as new apps or updates to existing apps [61]. PBRs play the dual role of resourcing and securing the platform by providing (1) the software tools (e.g., APIs, SDKs) to access new platform resources (e.g., new hardware features such as TouchID), and (2) the regulations to control interactions platform owners-app developers, respectively [19].
Creating PBR-based app innovations entails mitigating technological uncertainty (i.e., lack of declarative and procedural knowledge) arising from the integration between the app and the PBR. Uncertainty is defined as "the availability and reliability of the information that is relevant in a given situation." [37]. App developer organizations face a high level of technological uncertainty undermining their ability to leverage PBRs. For example, soon after the release of ARKIT, several implementations of ARKIT-based features released publicly such as distance measurement and furniture visualization suffered from various technological limitations as app developer organizations did not take into account environmental parameters including lighting, user's perspective, and user's balance creating suboptimal apps that suffered in the market [5]. Hence, an important practical question is to understand how app developer organizations can leverage PBRs and improve app performance by mitigating technological uncertainty. PBRs offer tremendous opportunities for app-level innovation, but if technology uncertainty results in poorly designed apps, then the highly competitive market could significantly erode the apps' performance.
A platform ecosystem consists of the platform owners and the collection of organizations (i.e., complementors or app developer organizations) that create apps on the platform [26]. It plays a significant role in explaining app-level outcomes such as innovation [15] and performance [34]. Prior literature focuses on competition dynamics in the platform ecosystem and the implications for app-level outcomes. Foerderer et al. [15] find that the entry of complements created by the platform owner itself in the complementary market increases the number of reviews of competing complements. For instance, the entry of Google's Photos app drove consumer attention on apps in the photography category. Moreover, Liang et al. [34] observe that featured apps benefit similar apps. Consumer awareness of featured apps spills over to similar apps. Finally, Li and Agarwal [32] highlight that the integration between Facebook and Instagram positively influenced the consumer demand of big competing third-party apps while negatively influencing the consumer demand of small competing third-party apps.
While competition dynamics play a major role in understanding organizational outcomes (see [7]), there is limited attention on cooperation dynamics in the platform ecosystem. Cooperation is equally prevalent to, if not more prevalent than, competition in markets [69]. Prior research supports the duality between competition and cooperation indicating that both are interdependent and complementary in such a way that cooperation attributes might impact competitive outcomes [21], and competitive attributes might impact cooperation outcomes [20]. Cooperation is an important aspect of the platform ecosystem [23]. Prior literature highlights cooperation between the platform owners and the complementors. The platform owners share the platform resources with complementors through APIs, facilitating the creation of third-party innovations [27]. The cooperation among complementors is less explored, limiting our understanding of the impact of cooperation dynamics on app-level outcomes.
Following prior studies that highlight the duality between competition and cooperation [38], we emphasize cooperation dynamics in the platform ecosystem. We examine distributed sensemaking about PBRs occurring as app developers interact with platform owners and app developers from different organizations to understand how to integrate PBRs with their apps. Distributed sensemaking about PBRs is not merely to understand how the changes fit into existing ideas of current apps, but it can also serve the purpose of providing new ideas for new types of functionalities within an existing app or indeed for a brand-new app-such that sensemaking is a major source of inspiration for further innovation. We distinguish distributed sensemaking 2 -happening at the ecosystem level-from situated sensemaking-occurring at the organizational level. We define the level of distributed sensemaking about PBRs as the degree to which app developers create and maintain meaning about PBRs among themselves through interactions with the platform owners and app developers from different organizations. While sensemaking is key to resolving uncertain situations [72], there is a dearth of research about the effectiveness of distributed sensemaking at enhancing app-level outcomes. It is unclear whether the level of distributed sensemaking about PBRs can influence app-level outcomes irrespective of whether the focal app developer organization participates in the distributed sensemaking process or not. Against this backdrop, we seek to examine the extent to which app developer organizations mitigate PBRs' technological uncertainty to improve app performance in a hypercompetitive environment by addressing the following research question: what is the effect of the level of distributed sensemaking about PBRs on app performance?
Sensemaking allows individuals and organizations to address uncertain situations [72]. To answer the research question, we follow prior research that highlights the existence of different sources of uncertainty [67]. We propose a research framework that examines the effect of the level of distributed sensemaking about PBRs on app performance across different sources of technological uncertainty. We identify two sources of uncertainty related to the developer task environment: one at the app level-app complexity 3 -and the other at the platform level-PBR's technological unrelatedness with prior PBRs. Indeed, technological uncertainty related to the integration between the PBR and the app can arise from the complexity of the app or the level of PBR's technological unrelatedness with prior PBRs.
We suggest that the level of distributed sensemaking about PBRs is crucial to leverage PBRs and realize high app performance. Whether a focal app developer organization participates or not directly in the distributed sensemaking process, we argue that it will benefit as long as other app developer organizations participate in the distributed sensemaking process. The level of distributed sensemaking about PBRs puts app developer organizations-irrespective of whether they participate in the distributed sensemaking process or not-at a better place to resolve technological uncertainty because the option of using shared external understanding exists, and they can forgo it if it is not beneficial for alleviating technological uncertainty. And having such flexibility is important because the distributed sensemaking process has unique characteristics regarding solving technological uncertainty when compared to the situated sensemaking process. Drawing on organizational information processing theory [17], we propose that the relationship between the level of distributed sensemaking about PBRs and app performance varies across different app and platform contexts. This is because the varying app and platform contexts influence technological uncertainty, creating different information processing needs that should require the flexibility offered by the level of distributed sensemaking about PBRs to differing extents. We posit that the effect of the level of distributed sensemaking about PBRs on app performance rises based on challenges encountered due to high PBR's technological unrelatedness with prior PBRs and app complexity.
We tested the research model by collecting data about PBR-based app innovations released from September 2014 to July 2018. We focus on the iOS platform, a highly dynamic platform, looking at the following PBRs: TouchID, Apple Pay, "Hey Siri," ARKIT, CoreML, and FaceID. Our findings corroborate our hypotheses, thereby providing guidance on how app developer organizations can leverage PBRs to achieve high app performance through the creation of PBR-based app innovations. We organize the rest of the paper into four sections. First, we present the theoretical background of the study in the second section. Following this, we provide the research model and develop the hypotheses. We describe the research design and report the results of the analyses in the next section. Finally, we discuss the contributions, implications, and limitations of the study.
According to organizational information processing theory (OIPT)-also known as the information processing view of organizations-an organization, to achieve greater performance, must either increase its capacity to process information or reduce the need for information processing in such a way that information processing capabilities meet information processing needs [17]. Uncertainty is a problem that organizations must overcome to increase performance. Galbraith [16, p.5] defines uncertainty as the "difference between the amount of information required to perform a task and the amount of information already possessed by the organization." Thus, uncertainty increases an organization's information processing needs (i.e., the amount of information the organization needs to gather and process to execute a task). When an organization faces uncertainty, matching information processing capabilities (i.e., capacity to handle more information and make decisions to improve the execution of a task) with information processing needs enhances its performance [67].
In this study, we focus on technological uncertainty, that is, the uncertainty that app developer organizations face during the integration of PBRs into their apps. Technological uncertainty stems from the app (e.g., app complexity) and the PBR (e.g., PBR's technological unrelatedness). We use app complexity and PBR's technological unrelatedness to capture increased information processing needs (e.g., questions about how to solve some coding problems) during the integration of PBRs into apps. Information processing capabilities help organizations cope with technological uncertainty and increased information needs during the integration of PBRs into apps. We use distributed sensemaking as a source of information processing capability that helps organizations access shared understanding about the integration of PBRs into apps. Distributed sensemaking operates as a source of information processing capability because it supports interactions between individuals addressing uncertainty about the integration of PBRs into apps. Moreover, it increases an organization's capacity to handle more information. For example, it indicates solutions to problems avoiding that organizations rely on trial and error to find a solution.
We propose the level of distributed sensemaking about PBRs in an online community is effective at increasing the flexibility of app developer organizations to address such technological uncertainty. In different app and platform contexts, technological uncertainty changes as the app developer organizations' information processing needs either increase or decrease, hence moderating the effect of the level of distributed sensemaking about PBRs. We describe sensemaking, technological relatedness, and software complexity to lay out the theoretical foundation of the study. This section provides important insights into how app developer organizations mitigate technological uncertainty regarding PBRs (Online Supplemental Appendix T provides additional content on the theoretical background).
In mobile platform ecosystems, sensemaking happens at two levels: (1) internally at the organizational level (i.e., situated sensemaking), and (2) externally at the ecosystem level (i.e., distributed sensemaking). A platform ecosystem includes the platform owners and the collection of organizations that create apps on the platform [54]. Situated sensemaking refers to app developers of the same organization interacting to address uncertainty to maintain common beliefs towards PBRs and integration issues. Distributed sensemaking characterizes app developers of different organizations interacting among themselves as well as with the platform owners to create and maintain common beliefs regarding PBR integration. Although app developers create competing apps, their collective interest in resolving uncertainty regarding PBRs translates into greater distributed sensemaking through online forums. Technological uncertainty manifests as app developer organizations collectively seek procedural 4 and declarative 5 knowledge (See Online Supplemental Appendix A). This collective knowledge-seeking enables app developer organizations to address technological uncertainty by increasing the level of distributed sensemaking or shared understanding of PBRs.
Distributed sensemaking occurs through dynamic communicational interactions among heterogeneous app developer organizations of diverse backgrounds. The objective of the dynamic communicational interactions is to collectively seek solutions to solve common problems, hence increasing shared understanding of PBRs (See Online Supplemental Appendix A). These dynamic communicational interactions characterize the "milling" and "keynoting" processes [66]. Distributed sensemaking arises as app developer organizations' dynamic communicational interactions evolve from chaotic milling interactions into organized keynoting interactions.
Knowledge seeking about PBRs resembles milling as app developer organizations turn to others looking for cues. Milling involves many different app developer organizations of diverse backgrounds who interact in a chaotic manner by writing posts to resolve problems. Keynoting replaces milling enabling the creation of a shared understanding of PBRs. Keynoting occurs as solutions emerge overriding the divergent and chaotic opinions of app developer organizations about how to resolve problems about integrating PBRs. In the context of the creation of PBR-based app innovations, milling and keynoting can be detected through the reporting of problems and identification of solutions to problems about integrating PBRs. Hence, we focus on problem-solution pairs to assess the level of distributed sensemaking about PBRs. In the Online Supplemental Appendix B.1, we map the seven properties of distributed sensemaking to our context.
The digital innovation literature indicates that socio-cognitive sensemaking-the same as distributed sensemaking-is a critical element of digital innovation processes and outcomes [43]. This occurs as a result of the fluid innovation boundaries, dynamic pairing of problems and solutions, and heterogeneous innovation actors [43]. As PBRs span multiple app categories, any single app developer organization may not be able to understand the scope of PBRs. Moreover, distinct app developer organizations may assign different cognitive frames to PBRs. As a result, an app developer organization's cognition needs to be expanded beyond traditional product features to integrate PBRs. Communicational interactions among app developer organizations with different frames increase app developer organizations' awareness of new cognitive frames. Adopting new cognitive frames enables app developer organizations to pursue new ways to integrate PBRs, creating new PBR-based app innovation opportunities.
Two behaviors contribute to distributed sensemaking. First, app developer organizations seek knowledge in the community of heterogeneous app developer organizations by writing about the problems they encounter. Second, app developer organizations share knowledge in the community of heterogeneous app developer organizations by writing about solutions in response to the described problems. Knowledge seeking and knowledge sharing reduce technological uncertainty about integrating PBRs and creating PBR-based app innovations. This explains why the release of new PBRs generates high traffic of new posting. Digital technologies (e.g., online forums and social media) accelerate distributed sensemaking by facilitating knowledge seeking and sharing [46]. In this study, we examine whether the level of distributed sensemaking about PBRs mitigates technological uncertainty about the integration app-PBR, hence increasing app performance.
Technological relatedness has been used in various contexts including business diversification [58], product portfolio diversification [73], and IT relatedness [65]. In these different contexts, technological relatedness represents the degree of similar technological knowledge across firms' businesses, or products. Through acquisitions and divestitures of businesses, firms can modify the level of technological relatedness within their business portfolio [1]. Researchers have extensively examined the impact of technological relatedness on organizational performance. Previous studies indicate that the level of technological relatedness across business units has a positive effect on corporate performance [64] and joint venture performance [73]. Technological relatedness is important for organizational performance as it facilitates the creation and exploitation of cross-unit synergies [64]. Moreover, it enhances cross-unit knowledge sharing as it increases the similarity of technological knowledge across units [73]. Finally, prior literature indicates that technological relatedness facilitates coordination across units [65] leading to the centralization of business activities such as R&D [4] and IT governance [24] to leverage economies of scope. In this study, we suggest that PBR's technological unrelatedness with prior PBRs-a platform-related characteristic -is important to understand the impact of the level of distributed sensemaking about PBRs on app performance.
Following previous research [58], we define a PBR's technological unrelatedness with prior PBRs as the extent to which a given PBR demands technological knowledge distinct from that of previous PBRs. On the one hand, the level of PBR's technological unrelatedness with prior PBRs increases technological uncertainty related to the integration between PBR and the app since app developer organizations cannot reuse knowledge about prior PBRs, limiting their information processing capabilities. On the other hand, the level of PBR's technological relatedness with prior PBRs reduces technological uncertainty related to the integration between PBR and the app as app developer organizations who have experience with prior PBRs can rely on that experience, and those who do not have experience can rely on the level of distributed sensemaking about prior PBRs. Examining PBR's technological unrelatedness with prior PBRs enables us to unravel the role of the platform context on the effect of the level of distributed sensemaking about PBRs.
Software complexity is an important element of software design [11]. A software is a system composed of distinct subsystems that interact. Complexity arises as the number of subsystems increases as well as the interactions among the subsystems [70]. Complexity is defined as "the amount of relevant information that is available in a given situation" [37, p.172]. Moreover, Singh [60, p.340] defines a complex technology as "an applied system whose components have multiple interactions and constitute a non-decomposable whole." Complexity emphasizes the number of parts of a system and their interconnections making the whole system difficult to understand [70]. The number of parts of the system is highly correlated with the number of interconnections. A system with a high count of parts has a high number of interconnections [70]. As a result, prior research often defines complexity as the number of distinct parts in a given system [75].
Complexity has the advantage of rendering a product difficult to imitate. However, it also makes the design and implementation of the software challenging [70] and increases the uncertainty in the time and effort required to create and maintain the software [14]. Prior research indicates that high product complexity might even reduce product quality [10]. Furthermore, previous studies demonstrate that technological complexity increases the risk of technological failure as organizations face high costs and competency limitations [60]. The creation of a complex product requires a large amount of information to build each part of the product and the connections to other parts of the product. The amount of information required can often exceed the organization's processing capability as organizations have bounded rationality [59]. Hence, complexity can hinder an organization's ability to make a rational decision. As software complexity increases, app developer organizations' information processing capabilities might reach their limits creating uncertainty during the integration between PBR and the app. Following the concept of bounded rationality, there are limits to the app developer organizations' information processing capabilities, and the app developer organizations' ability to extend the app is reduced as app complexity increases.
Building on OIPT, we suggest the following research model (See Figure 1) to understand how PBR-based app innovations increase app performance. We consider the role of the level of distributed sensemaking 6 about PBRs. Consistent with OIPT, we argue that the effect of the level of distributed sensemaking about PBRs-a source of information processing capability-is contingent on two sources of technological uncertainty: the level of PBR's technological unrelatedness with prior PBRs and app complexity. Our hypotheses build on the concept of duality between competition and cooperation. Studies increasingly support the existence of duality between competition and cooperation indicating that both are interdependent and complementary [38]. Markets are characterized by competition and cooperation, and considering the duality between both is crucial to understanding market dynamics [38]. Competition and cooperation simultaneously exist as relationships between cooperators may also be open to competition [22]. Achieving competition outcomes often requires exploring cooperation-related variables [21], and achieving cooperation outcomes often requires examining competitive attributes [20]. A growing number of studies highlight such interactions between competition and cooperation by adopting coopetition and business network perspectives (see [38]). For example, scholars suggest that cooperation may enhance a firm's ability to compete in markets [63]. Also, in unstable situations, actors might prefer cooperation to reduce uncertainty (e.g. [68]) without ignoring competition [49]. Chen [6] categorizes studies on the competition-cooperation relationship into three groups including co-opetition, competition-oriented cooperation, and cooperation-oriented competition studies. Our research belongs to the last group as it examines the impact of cooperation through distributed sensemaking on competitive outcomes (i.e., ranking). 7

Technological uncertainty represents a lack of declarative and procedural knowledge related to the adoption of PBRs. 8 Moreover, app developer organizations must experiment with different use cases wherein PBRs can provide value to customers. The success of the exploration stage is dependent upon the degree to which app developer organizations understand PBRs. An adequate level of understanding of PBRs enables app developer organizations to develop app services with high quality and select use cases with high utility for the users. For example, HomeCourt is an example of such apps developed by engineers with a great understanding of the CoreML [29].
An important argument of OIPT is that greater information processing capability generates greater organizational performance [16]. The level of distributed sensemaking about PBRs-a source of information processing capability-is crucial as app developer organizations seek to leverage PBRs by developing new app services with high quality and utility. It increases the flexibility of app developer organizations, irrespective of whether they participate in the process of distributed sensemaking or not, to address uncertainties related to PBRs as these organizations can choose to rely solely on the level of situated sensemaking about PBRs or leverage the level of distributed sensemaking about PBRs. Notably, app developers with a superior level of situated sensemaking about PBRs when compared to the level of distributed sensemaking about PBRs might choose to rely on the level of situated sensemaking about PBRs while others with an inferior level of situated sensemaking about PBRs might opt for using the level of distributed sensemaking about PBRs. Generally, external knowledge is considered valuable when it is unique, that is, distinct from internal knowledge [40]. App developers with an inferior level of situated sensemaking about PBRs are likely to rely on distributed sensemaking to access unique external knowledge that might extend their internal knowledge. With low levels of distributed sensemaking about PBRs, app developers are limited to the level of situated sensemaking about PBRs. This could cause them to miss the collective wisdom of the ecosystem that could alleviate technological uncertainty about PBRs.
As app developer organizations in the ecosystems have distinct interpretive schemes, the level of distributed sensemaking about PBRs facilitates the construction of meaning and interpretation about PBRs. Prior literature illustrates the similar benefits of distributed sensemaking in product development [9]. Hence, the level of distributed sensemaking about PBRs enables app developer organizations to face technological uncertainty by enhancing app developer organizations' understanding of the technological capabilities of PBRs. For example, on online forums, app developer organizations can seek knowledge from the ecosystem regarding the working of PBRs by asking questions. Moreover, distributed sensemaking increases the amount of information that organizations can access, thus reducing uncertainty and facilitating rational decision-making [8]. The level of distributed sensemaking about PBRs might enable app developer organizations to detect feasible and optimal actions to leverage PBRs. Also, it facilitates the discovery of meaningful applications of PBRs, enabling the creation of high-quality and utility app services. It enables app developer organizations to respond to novel problems during the development of app services. Prior work associates sensemaking with product innovation [57]. Thus, we hypothesize that. .
The level of distributed sensemaking about a PBR has a positive effect on the performance of apps integrating that PBR.
Any given PBR introduces a level of technological uncertainty that app developer organizations must resolve to create app services with high quality and utility. It is critical app developer organizations acquire technological knowledge about the general working of PBRs and how PBRs can be used to create new app services. The existence of prior PBRs that are related to a given PBR facilitates sensemaking about the PBR as app developer organizations can benefit from their experience if they have used the prior PBRs or other app developer organizations' experience through the level of distributed sensemaking about the prior PBRs: shared external understanding. However, a PBR that is technologically unrelated to previous PBRs necessitates more learning -acquisition of new knowledge. As app developer organizations explore the PBR and experiment with different use cases, they cannot build upon prior experience as the PBR is not similar to any previous PBRs. The level of technological unrelatedness with prior PBRs does not facilitate the creation of synergies among PBRs as it increases the need for app developer organizations to generate new meanings and interpretations. Prior research identifies performance benefits of Information Technology (IT) relatedness [64] and product relatedness [73] to be mainly driven by synergies across business units [64] and knowledge sharing between firms [73]. As a result, app developer organizations are more likely to exploit the level of distributed sensemaking about the focal PBRs, which is a source of information processing capability, to understand PBRs that are technologically unrelated to previous PBRs. Moreover, app developer organizations are more likely to rely on the level of situated sensemaking and not on the level of distributed sensemaking about the focal PBRs when PBRs are technologically related to previous PBRs due to similarities across PBRs in terms of understanding. Hence, consistent with OIPT (i.e., information processing capability is a remedy for uncertainty), the flexibility offered by the level of distributed sensemaking about PBRs to address technological uncertainty matters more when PBRs are not technologically related to prior PBRs. We hypothesize that: Hypothesis 2 (H2): The effect of the level of distributed sensemaking about a PBR on the performance of apps integrating that PBR is greater when PBR's technological unrelatedness with prior PBRs is high.
The creation of app services with high quality and utility is particularly challenging when an app is complex. It is easier to understand how parts of an app affect each other when the app is less complex. However, as software complexity rises, developers are increasingly challenged to capture all interdependencies in the software logic [11]. When working with complex apps, app developer organizations face more difficulty trying to understand and resolve app issues that result from interactions among app parts. Large amounts of information are necessary to address app complexity. In situations where software complexity is high, it is strenuous cognitively for developers to understand (1) how software parts are assembled, (2) how the software parts are interrelated, and (3) how such interactions affect the software behavior and performance []. Adding a PBR requires the creation of additional app parts and interactions or the update of existing app parts and interactions.
Complex systems are difficult to manage (See [55]). Maintaining a high degree of reliability in the app behavior is particularly challenging for app developer organizations with complex apps. When adding a PBR in a complex app, app developer organizations are likely to face significantly greater challenges due to competency limitations, thus increasing the risk of app failures and reducing app quality. For example, complex apps are more likely to crash [53]. This follows prior research associating technology complexity with organizational failures (see [60]). The level of distributed sensemaking about PBRs-a source of information processing capability-enhances app developer organizations' ability to manage complex apps and mitigate technological uncertainty as they can access additional competencies from app developer organizations of different organizations. Hence, consistent with OIPT (i.e., information processing capability is a remedy for uncertainty), the level of distributed sensemaking about PBRs-by providing more flexibility to address uncertainty related to integrating PBRs-matters more when apps have high complexity. We hypothesize that:
The effect of the level of distributed sensemaking about a PBR on the performance of apps integrating that PBR is greater when app complexity is high.
We observe PBR-based app innovations released on the iOS mobile platform within the U.S. market. We select the iOS mobile platform over other mobile platforms (e.g., Android, and Windows Phone) because, in a given year, the diffusion rate of the latest generation of the iOS mobile operating system is high. For example, a year after the release of iOS 11 -the latest generation of iOS in 2017-, the adoption rate passed 85 percent of compatible devices [48]. On the other hand, the adoption rate of Oreo 8.0 (the latest generation of Android in 2017), was less than 15 percent of compatible devices a year after the release date [25]. Since PBR-based app innovations mostly require devices to operate the latest generation of the mobile operating system, it is important to choose a mobile platform whose latest generation diffuses quickly. Even though PBR-based app innovations can operate on older generations of some mobile platforms (e.g., Android), it is not appropriate to select these mobile platforms because they are highly fragmented. The iOS mobile platform by far is the least fragmented mobile platform [41].
We observe PBR-based app innovations supporting at least one of the following PBRs: TouchID, Apple Pay, "Hey Siri," ARKIT, CoreML, and FaceID. The six PBRs were released at different times: FaceID, CoreML, and ARKIT in 2017 with iOS 11; "Hey Siri" in 2016 with iOS 10; ApplePay and TouchID in 2014 with iOS 8. We select these six PBRs because they are major technologies that have attracted considerable attention from both iOS developers and users (see [61]). For example, the number of downloads of ARKIT-only apps passed 13 million six months after the release of iOS 11 [44]. Moreover, app developer organizations are more likely to mention the six PBRs in their PBR-based app innovations description and release notes. Thus, we can identify PBR-based app innovations by reading the description and release notes. We apply a keyword search mechanism to identify PBR-based app innovations. We use the following keywords adjusting for the letter case: "touch id," "touched," "applepay," "apple pay," "siri," "ARKIT," "ar kit," "coreml," "core ml," "faceid," and "face id." We search through all the release notes starting at the release date of the PBR.
We collected data from several sources including Apple developer documentation, 9 Apple developer Forum, 10 , appfigures, 11 and App Annie. 12 The Apple developer documentation provides guidance (e.g., API reference, articles, and sample code) about PBRs. The Apple developer forum facilitates discussion on PBRs among app developer organizations. Appfigures and App Annie are leading companies in app data and analytics. Moreover, they are reliable data sources that have been used in prior literature (e.g., [28]). App developer organizations and analysts use extensively Appfigures and App Annie to analyze the iOS app market. The Appfigures and App Annie databases contain data on iOS apps retrieved from Apple iTunes since 2009.
We use Appfigures's keyword search engine to identify all iOS apps that support at least one of the following PBRs: TouchID, Apple Pay, "Hey Siri," ARKIT, CoreML, and FaceID. The search engine goes through apps' descriptions and release notes to locate the given keywords. Additionally, we collect data about app ranking using the appfigures application programming interface (API). Furthermore, we use the Apple developer forum to gather data about iOS app developer organizations' discussions on PBRs. The Apple developer documentation provides information about the level of technological unrelatedness of PBRs with prior PBRs. Finally, we collect iOS apps' descriptions and release notes using App Annie. We use App Annie data to identify the release date of PBR-based app innovations.
Apple provides three major ranking lists including the top 1,000 free apps, the top 1,000 paid apps, and the top 1,000 grossing apps. 13 Considering that there are millions of apps available on the iOS app market, the ranking of an iOS app on any of these three lists provides a clear indication of app performance. App ranking is commonly used to understand app performance [28]. We access iOS apps ranking daily to capture the performance effects of PBR-based app innovations. We later aggregate daily app ranking over 28 days maximum after the release of PBR-based app innovations. We do not go beyond 28 days because app developer organizations in top lists mostly release their app innovations at intervals of one month. In this case, it is important to use periods shorter than 28 days.
We collect data about the Apple developer forum from the release date of the PBRs to app developer organizations till one year later (i.e., from June 2014 to May 2015 for ApplePay and TouchID, from June 2016 to May 2017 for "Hey Siri," and from June 2017 to May 2018 for CoreML, ARKIT, and FaceID) because the Apple developer forum does not differentiate between the original (i.e., the 1 st version) PBR and the subsequent updates (i.e., later versions). For example, as Apple updates ARKIT (ARKIT in 2017, ARKIT 2 in 2018, ARKIT 3 in 2019, and ARKIT 4 in 2020), the Apple developer forum does differentiate between all the versions. Hence, it becomes difficult to identify the posts about ARKIT after ARKIT 2 or another later version is released.
Moreover, we focus on PBR-based app innovations released not more than one year after the date when the PBRs are released to app developer organizations to ensure that the PBRbased app innovations are not integrating later versions of the PBRs. The earliest PBR-based app innovations are released the following September after the release of the PBRs to app developer organizations. Hence, PBR-based app innovations supporting ApplePay and TouchID are identified from September 2014 to May 2015, those supporting "Hey Siri" are identified from September 2016 to May 2017, and those supporting CoreML, ARKIT, and FaceID are identified from September 2017 to May 2018.
The final dataset comprises 933 PBR-based app innovations for which we can have complete data on key variables of interest (e.g., ranking, distributed sensemaking, PBR's technological unrelatedness, and app complexity). 14 We do not include new apps as we cannot measure prior-release ranking. The number of observations with TouchID, Apple Pay, "Hey Siri," ARKIT, CoreML, and FaceID is 257, 31, 29, 62, 10, and 544, respectively.
We use a pre-post design to measure the performance of iOS apps (See Online Supplemental Appendix C). We compute the average app ranking before and after the release date of the PBR-based app innovation. We calculate the average post-release ranking over 28 days after the release date of the PBR-based app innovation. Moreover, we assess the average pre-release ranking throughout 7 days before the release date of the PBR-based app innovation. 15 We measure app performance by calculating the difference between the average post-release app ranking and the average pre-release app ranking. Furthermore, we use different periods as robustness checks. The results remain consistent across these periods (See Robustness Checks Section). Since we are using a pre-post design, our sample of PBR-based app innovations does not include new apps as these apps do not have app ranking before the release date.
Sensemaking has been extensively used in the management literature [57,72]. However, there are few objective measures of sensemaking in prior literature. We propose an innovative approach to objectively measure the level of distributed sensemaking about PBRs. Prior research suggests text-based analyses (e.g., word count analysis) of conversations among individuals can reveal patterns of social interactions [50]. Text-based analyses can offer insights independently of the semantic context or the literal meaning [51]. For example, patterns of words usage can be used to identify cognition [46]. Following Pennebaker's work, prior research suggests a word-based analysis can provide a highlevel picture of distributed sensemaking in uncertain situations [47].
In the Online Supplemental Appendix P, we discuss why activities on the Apple developer forum can be qualified as distributed sensemaking. The level of distributed sensemaking about PBRs represents the shared understanding about PBRs among app developer organizations and occurs through the pairing of problem-solution. New problems-defined as problems that are not similar to prior resolved problems-indicate a lack of shared understanding. The level of distributed sensemaking about PBRs flattens when there are (1) no additional problems posted, (2) additional problems but with no solution given, or (3) solutions to additional problems that are not new problems. We use a text similarity measure based on words usage across different texts to measure similarity among problems reported through posts. More specifically, we use the text-similarity score among posts to assess the evolution of the level of distributed sensemaking about PBRs over the period following the release of the PBRs. Our text similarity score measures how text similarity among posts evolves as new posts come out. As a result, we can measure the level of distributed sensemaking about PBRs over time starting at the release date of the PBRs (See Online Supplemental Appendix B). Our measure is particularly robust as it can capture subcomponents of distributed sensemaking called milling and keynoting (see [66]). 16  Distributed sensemaking evolves from a chaotic milling phase into a stable keynoting phase. In our study, milling is reflected early after the release of PBRs through new unresolved problems (i.e., problems with low similarity and no solution). As distributed sensemaking evolves into the keynoting phase, solutions to problems emerge, and the newness of problems decreases.
We use the posts written by app developer organizations on the Apple developer forums (See Online Supplemental Appendix A). App developer organizations engaging in distributed sensemaking first search the forums looking for a post similar to their concern. Second, if they cannot find a post that might address their concern, then they will write a new post. Also, it can happen that app developer organizations write posts that are similar to prior answered posts (i.e., posts with solutions). Hence, there are two key indicators of the level of distributed sensemaking about PBRs. The first indicator is the number of resolved problems (i.e., helpful 17 posts) relative to each PBR at a specific point in time (Eq. 1). The second indicator is the newness of resolved problems (i.e., the distance between a resolved problem and prior resolved problems) relative to each PBR at a specific point in time (Eq. 2). For each PBR-based app innovation, we measure the level of distributed sensemaking about the PBR at a specific time corresponding to the release date of the PBR-based app innovation. For the first indicator, we count the number of resolved problems relative to the PBR before the release date of the PBR-based app innovation. And regarding the second indicator, we calculate the average newness of resolved problems relative to the PBR before the release date of the PBR-based app innovation. Specifically, first, we weight each resolved problem appearing before the release date of the PBR-based app innovation using a newness index. The weight corresponds to 1 minus the similarity index representing the highest cosine similarity score 18 between a given resolved problem and all previously resolved problems. Second, for aggregation purposes, we sum all the resolved problems with their respective weights. Third, we divide the weighted sum by the total number of resolved problems relative to the PBR before the release date of the PBR-based app innovation to calculate the second indicator of the level of distributed sensemaking about PBRs (See Online Supplemental Appendix Q for more details).
In the aforementioned equation, i represents PBR, t refers to the release date of PBR-based app innovation. Furthermore, we use a dummy variable to measure the level of PBR's technological unrelatedness with prior PBRs. The dummy variable takes a value of 1 if the PBR has a high level of technological unrelatedness with prior PBRs, and a value of 0 otherwise. We determine the value of the dummy following a two-step approach. First, based on Apple developer documentation [3], we create a list of frameworks (See Online Supplemental Appendix D). Second, we determine the frameworks that contain each of the 6 PBRs studied in this paper. For example, we found that FaceID and TouchID belong to the Local Authentication framework. In total, we identify 5 frameworks. Third, for each PBR, we identify whether the framework was created at the same time as the PBR or not. We code 1 if that is the case or 0 otherwise. When the PBR and framework are created at the same time, it means that the PBR is the first in the framework, thus there is not a technologically related prior PBR. However, when the PBR is created after the framework, meaning that the PBR joins an existing framework, it signifies that there is(are) already existing PBR(s) in the framework, hence there is a technologically related prior PBR. Because the PBRs that belong to the same framework have a similar implementation, we consider them to be technologically related. We use the dummy code to represent the level of PBR's technological unrelatedness with prior PBRs. Hence, FaceID and Apple Pay have a low level of technological unrelatedness with prior PBRs because they joined existing frameworks (i.e., the Local Authentication and the PassKit frameworks respectively) and are technologically related to prior PBRs (i.e., TouchID and Apple Passbook respectively). Moreover, ARKIT, CoreML, "Hey Siri," and TouchID have a high level of technological unrelatedness with prior PBRs since they were created at the same time as their respective frameworks. In our sample, the numbers of PBR-based app innovations integrating PBRs with low and high levels of technological unrelatedness with prior PBRs are 575 and 358, respectively.
Finally, we use a composite measure to determine app complexity. Since we do not have access to the code of the iOS apps, we conduct an exploratory factor analysis including various metrics that could explain app complexity. We find that the size of the code file, the number of SDKs used by the app, the number of permissions requested by the app load on the same factor. As a composite factor, they collectively represent app complexity (the number of parts of the app and their interactions). The results of the exploratory factor analysis indicating the factors, the eigenvalues, and the factor loadings are illustrated in Online Supplemental Appendix E. We estimate the composite factor which we consider to be a measure of app complexity. We assess app complexity as of July 2018. 19
We control for variables that may influence app performance. Since PBRs are heterogeneous, the type of PBR can explain some variance in the app performance. The extent to which a PBR-based app innovation attracts users depends on the users' interest in the PBR. For example, if users are more interested in "FaceID" compared to "ARKIT," we expect FaceID-based app innovations to have a greater effect on app performance than ARKITbased app innovations. Hence, we control for each type of PBRs including TouchID, Apple Pay, "Hey Siri," ARKIT, CoreML, and FaceID. Also, we use several app-level control variables. We measure the number of categories, languages, and countries per app. These variables affect the discoverability of the app, hence influencing app performance. It is easier for iOS users to discover apps that span different categories, support multiple languages, and are accessible in different countries. Moreover, we include the app's entry timing as prior research argues that entry timing is critical for performance [18]. Furthermore, we measure the number of and the average app ratings controlling for the effect of app popularity, app usability, and app quality on app performance as apps with high popularity, usability and quality are more likely to attract iOS users. We consider the effect of app seniority on app performance by calculating the number of days between the first release date of the app and the release date of the PBR-based app innovation. iOS users are more likely to use senior apps because they are more familiar with senior apps than recent apps. Also, app seniority has been used to characterize app development superiority, marketing capabilities, and brand strength [28]. Additionally, we control for the effect of app price on app performance as low app prices attract more iOS users. We measure the price, the number of categories, languages, and countries per app as of July 2018. 20 Finally, we use dummy variables to control for the types of ranking (i.e., handheld versus tablet, and top free versus top paid versus top grossing), year-specific effects, app category-specific effects.
