We report the descriptive statistics and the correlation matrix in Table 3. Moreover, we present the results of the analyses in Table 4. We correct for heteroscedasticity and autocorrelation using robust standard errors. Apps with high performance have low app ranking. Hence, a negative estimated coefficient represents an increase in app performance. Model 1 is the base model assessing the effects of the control variables on app performance. Model 2 tests the effect of the level of distributed sensemaking about PBRs on app performance. Model 3 examines the interaction effects between the level of distributed sensemaking about PBRs and both the level of PBR's technological unrelatedness with prior PBRs and app complexity while predicting app performance. We use models 2 and 3 to test the hypotheses H1, H2, and H3, respectively. In H1, we argue that the level of distributed sensemaking about PBRs has a positive effect on app performance. The results of model 2 (See Table 4) indicate that the level of distributed sensemaking about PBRs has a positive and statistically significant effect on app performance. The two indicators of the level of distributed sensemaking about PBRs (i.e., the number of resolved problems and newness of resolved problems) predict app performance (-12.6, p < .001; and -2113, p < .01 for the number of resolved problems and newness of resolved problems, respectively). An increase of one standard deviation in the number of resolved problems is associated with a gain in the app ranking corresponding to 150 positions. Additionally, one standard deviation growth in the newness of resolved problems is associated with a gain in the app ranking corresponding to 85 positions. Hence, the first hypothesis is supported, showing that irrespective of the participation of the focal app developer organization in the process of distributed sensemaking, the level of distributed sensemaking about a PBR has a positive impact on the performance of the app integrating that PBR. In H2, we posit that the effect of the level of distributed sensemaking about PBRs on app performance is positively higher as the level of PBR's technological unrelatedness with prior PBRs increases. Based on Model 3 of Table 4, we can conclude that H2 is supported as the coefficients of the interaction terms between the level of distributed sensemaking about PBRs and PBR's technological unrelatedness with prior PBRs are negative and statistically significant (-167, p < .001; and -14930, p < .001 for the interactions with the number of resolved problems and newness of resolved problems, respectively). The results, as well as Online Supplemental Appendix G, indicate that the level of distributed sensemaking about PBRs is important for PBRs with high technological unrelatedness with prior PBRs. When the PBR's technological unrelatedness with prior PBRs is low, a standard deviation increase in the number of resolved problems and newness of resolved problems are associated with a loss of over 1, 000, and 560 positions, respectively in the ranking. However, for a PBR with high technological unrelatedness with prior PBRs, a standard deviation increase in the number of resolved problems and newness of resolved problems are associated with a gain of 130, and 40 positions, respectively in the ranking.
In H3, we suggest that the effect of the level of distributed sensemaking about PBRs on app performance is positively higher as app complexity increases. According to Model 3 (see Table 4), the H3 is supported since the coefficients of the interaction terms between the level of distributed sensemaking about PBRs and app complexity are negative and statistically significant (-157, p < .05; and -40861, p < .05 for the interactions with the number of resolved problems and newness of resolved problems, respectively). The results as well as the Online Supplemental Appendix G indicate that the level of distributed sensemaking about PBRs is critical for complex apps. On the one hand, for less complex apps (1 standard deviation below the mean value), a standard deviation increase in the number of resolved problems and newness of resolved problems are associated with a loss of over 1, 000 positions in the ranking. On the other hand, for more complex apps (4 standard deviations above the mean value), a standard deviation increase in the number of resolved problems and newness of resolved problems are associated with a gain of 235, and over 1, 000 positions, respectively in the ranking. Online Supplemental Appendix G illustrates the moderation effects. 22
Our study provides important research contributions. First, we contribute to the literature on intra-platform competition which examines factors that determine app performance (e.g., [75]). The service ecosystem plays an important role in service delivery, but there is a lack of understanding of the specificities of such a role. While prior literature on platforms focuses on institutional logics in service ecosystems [52], there is a minimal amount of emphasis on the interactions among service actors. The interactive aspect of the service ecosystem is particularly important as it supports information seeking, offering, and sharing [47]. We unravel the role of the platform ecosystem in a mobile platform context by emphasizing distributed sensemaking occurring through interactions among the app developer organizations and platform owners (i.e., service actors). We highlight cooperative dynamics in the service ecosystem. While service actors (e.g., app developer organizations) are naturally competitors, we unveil how they collaborate through distributed sensemaking to mitigate technological uncertainty when leveraging PBRs.
Our findings indicate that such a type of collaboration is critical to explain app performance and understand how app developer organizations leverage PBRs. We support the existence of duality between competition and cooperation confirming that both are crucial to understanding market dynamics. A rich means of interaction is not necessary for distributed sensemaking. Despite the limitations of lean text-based interactions [12], the existing shared context among app developers makes it possible to rely on these lean interactions to facilitate distributed sensemaking (see [45]). Hence, we contribute to the literature on intra-platform competition by shedding light on cooperation at the ecosystem level on app performance. By emphasizing sensemaking on iOS developer forums, we unveil the role of the community of developers on app performance through their contributions to sensemaking. Theoretically and empirically, we highlight the influence of the level of distributed sensemaking about PBRs on the performance of apps integrating PBRs through PBR-based app innovations. Our study provides a significant contribution to the literature on app performance as app developer organizations face growing competition in mobile platform ecosystems, struggling to survive [13].
Second, we contribute to the literature that investigates the role of PBRs on app performance [27,35]. This line of research indicates PBRs have both positive [27], and negative [35] effects on app performance. Prior research suggests that platform transitions from one generation to a newer generation negatively influence app performance due to platform APIs creating interdependencies between the apps and the core platform [35]. Changes in platform APIs caused by platform transitions deteriorate app developers' ability to sustain their performance [28]. Similarly, the app's average rating diminishes as a result of API change proneness and API fault proneness [35]. Moreover, prior research finds a positive impact of PBRs on complementary innovation. Platforms APIs impact app novelty by influencing imitation and innovation [74]. Also, platform toolkits increase app developers' intention to innovate and the quantity of innovation [27]. We extend prior literature about the role of PBRs on app performance by proposing a theoretical framework about the effect of the level of distributed sensemaking about PBRs. By doing so, we provide an interesting perspective about how app developer organizations leverage PBRs (i.e., toolkits) and increase app performance. Our research unveils that whether platform innovations exert a positive or negative effect on app performance might depend on the level of distributed sensemaking about PBRs.
Third, we contribute to the literature on sensemaking which examines the effect of sensemaking on organizational performance [57]. Sensemaking is important as shared meaning about uncertain situations affects individuals' interpretations of actions and events [72]. Previous studies indicate sensemaking is a source of competitive advantage highlighting it is an internal resource (i.e., organizational sensemaking) that is critical to cope with complex and turbulent environments [57]. We study sensemaking as an external resource (i.e., distributed sensemaking) occurring in an online community of app developer organizations who work together toward a shared understanding of the integration between PBRs and apps (See Online Supplemental Appendix P). Our paper extends prior studies that describe distributed sensemaking in online communities [36,42]. We demonstrate that distributed sensemaking (i.e., cooperation) matters in an environment characterized by high competition (i.e., entities potentially preferring to rely on situated sensemaking). Also, we propose a way to quantitatively evaluate distributed sensemaking in online communities.
Finally, since we anchor our research model on OIPT, we contribute to that theory by showing that distributed sensemaking can be an effective information processing capability leading to greater app performance when information processing needs increase due to technology uncertainty about the integration of PBRs. Furthermore, we unveil the role of the level of distributed sensemaking about PBRs considering different sources of technological uncertainty. Our contribution is to demonstrate theoretically and empirically that distributed sensemaking is important besides the effect of organizational sensemaking shown in previous studies [57]. Unraveling the role of distributed sensemaking provides an adequate picture of the impact of sensemaking as it complements previous studies that focus on the effect of organizational sensemaking [57].
Mobile platform ecosystems are hypercompetitive environments requiring app developer organizations to innovate to remain relevant to app users [56]. While app developer organizations can innovate using only internal resources (i.e., proprietary toolkits), they are increasingly using PBRs to create new app services. Mitigating the risks surrounding the implementation of PBRs is critical to ensure app performance. Our study provides important practical implications about how app developer organizations can leverage PBRs to realize higher app performance.
First, our findings inform the allocation of resources suggesting an approach to overcome the limitations of internal resources (i.e., proprietary toolkits) to cope with technological uncertainty about the integration app -PBR. App developer organizations on mobile platform ecosystems are mostly small organizations. They are limited in the resources they can assign to the development of apps. As a result, they are more and more dependent on external resources (e.g., third-party toolkits). We suggest that app developer organizations must utilize knowledge shared on online forums about PBRs to complement their internal knowledge. App developer organizations tend to release their app upgrades early, soon after the release of PBRs, with the intent of benefiting from first-mover advantages. As this strategy might seem profitable, it requires app developer organizations to rely mostly on organizational sensemaking about PBRs. As a result, there is a risk that app developer organizations create app innovations with low quality because they do not have a clear understanding of PBRs. Our findings indicate that app developer organizations do not benefit from taking that risk. Hence, we recommend app developer organizations make decisions about entry timing based on the level of distributed sensemaking about PBRs. App developer organizations should release app innovations when they are not facing high technological uncertainty resulting from high app complexity or high PBR's technological unrelatedness with prior PBRs, or the level of distributed sensemaking about PBRs is acceptable. We encourage app developer organizations to include online communities of app developer organizations in their innovation strategy by monitoring exchanges about specific PBRs. This is particularly important for small teams of developers as they are more likely to have limited resources.
Second, our findings inform app developer organizations about optimal product strategies to leverage PBRs. Mobile platform owners release yearly various types of PBRs such as machine learning (e.g., CoreML by Apple, ML Kit by Google), AR (e.g., ARKIT by Apple, ARCore by Google), and voice assistant (e.g., SiriKit by Apple, voice interaction API by Google). Moreover, these PBRs have different levels of technological unrelatedness with previous PBRs. Our research suggests that the level of distributed sensemaking about PBRs is less effective when PBRs have low technological unrelatedness with prior PBRs. Hence, app developer organizations that plan to release app upgrades early should choose PBRs with low technological unrelatedness with prior PBRs (e.g., FaceID). They should delay their app upgrades release plans in case they select PBRs with high technological unrelatedness with prior PBRs (e.g., TouchID). Furthermore, our findings inform app design choices to leverage PBRs. App developer organizations follow different app design approaches. Some app developer organizations prefer creating single-purpose apps (e.g., WhatsApp) while others opt for building multi-purpose apps (e.g., WeChat). App complexity increases as app developer organizations create apps supporting more purposes and features. Our research indicates that the level of distributed sensemaking about PBRs is less effective when app complexity is low. Thus, we encourage app developer organizations with complex apps (e.g., multi-purpose apps, apps with a high number of features) to rely on the level of distributed sensemaking about PBRs, even if they might not participate directly in the process of distributed sensemaking -and release app upgrades late when the level of distributed sensemaking about PBRs is at an adequate level. App developer organizations whose strategy is to release app upgrades early must reduce app complexity by diminishing the number of purposes and features supported by the app.
Our study has several empirical limitations that can inform future research. First, we limited our sample to apps that explicitly mention the PBRs they support in their release notes. We reviewed the release notes of app upgrades, and we identified several PBRs including "Hey Siri," CoreML, ARKIT, TouchID, FaceID, and Apple Pay. Then, we collected apps that support the six PBRs. We are unable to observe additional PBRs that are less likely to be mentioned in the app upgrade release notes. Hence, future research might extract all PBRs supported by the app directly via the code if the researchers have access to the app code.
Another approach could be to survey app developer organizations even though it is not certain they are willing to disclose the PBRs they support. Despite our reduced sample size of PBRs, our findings are robust as we control for the type of PBRs.
Second, we measure the short-term impact of the level of distributed sensemaking about PBRs by observing app performance 1 week before and 4 weeks after the app innovation release date. Since app ranking is very volatile [28], we aggregate the daily app ranking per week(s) up to one week before and one month after the app innovation release date. We choose to limit this study to the short-term impact of the level of distributed sensemaking about PBRs because there are additional factors over time that create noise in the assessment of the long-term impact. For example, some app developer organizations release app upgrade once per month, thus increasing the identification problem. Future research could tackle the challenge of assessing the long-term impact of the level of distributed sensemaking about PBRs by conducting experiments wherein researchers can control the environment.
Third, even though our measures of app performance, app complexity, and technological unrelatedness have some theoretical [10,28], and practical [3] basis, they could benefit from a more fine-grained measurement. We offer some suggestions for future research. We propose that future measures of app performance may capture the costs of app innovations, the revenues, and profits generated by app innovations. Even though app ranking reflects the performance of an app relative to other apps, it excludes unpopular or low-performing apps and does not capture costs incurred by apps. Future studies may also explore outcomes related to the labor market [33].
Fourth, our study is not assessing integration issues between PBRs and non-iOS APIs within apps. Our data collection focuses on PBRs and iOS APIs. We consider the significance of non-iOS APIs by including the number of SDKs installed in the calculation of app complexity. Future studies might attempt to directly account for integration issues between PBRs and non-iOS APIs by collecting additional data on different online developer forums. Fifth, future research might extend our findings by measuring the extent to which each app developer organization consumes distributed sensemaking. This might require surveying app developer organizations about the level of use of distributed sensemaking (e.g., Apple developer forum). The survey might collect data about the extent to which app developer organizations implement the recommended solutions-found in the Apple developer forum-in their apps. Our study will benefit from such findings as we focus on the flexibility-to use or not use distributed sensemaking-that app developer organizations have when the level of distributed sensemaking is high.
Finally, we suggest researchers who have access to the app code should measure app complexity instead of relying on the composite measure of app complexity. For example, McCabe's cyclomatic complexity factor measures the understandability and intricacy of software projects [39] and has been used in studies on open-source projects to assess the code's structural complexity [11]. Additionally, measuring the level of coupling and modularity of the app code will help evaluate app complexity. Regarding PBR's technological unrelatedness with prior PBRs, future research can develop a different measure using a continuous scale. Our measure of technological unrelatedness is a categorical variable based on the platform owner's classification. Future measures can assess the level of reusability of the code from previous PBRs. They can also evaluate the level of similarity with previous PBRs code.
In the highly competitive complementor market, how app developer organizations can effectively innovate by leveraging PBRs can make the difference between success and failure. We bring to researchers' attention the risks app developer organizations face when they choose to support PBRs. We propose that the level of distributed sensemaking about PBRs, regardless of whether the focal app developer organization participates in the distributed sensemaking process or not, is effective at reducing technological uncertainty regarding the app-PBR integration, hence increasing the performance of apps integrating the PBRs. By focusing on cooperation dynamics in the platform ecosystem, our research extends prior literature which mainly considers sensemaking to be an internal resource. We demonstrate that the effect of the level of distributed sensemaking about PBRs is contingent on two sources of technological uncertainty including the level of PBR's technological unrelatedness with prior PBRs and app complexity. Our study provides both theoretical and practical implications for how complementors can effectively leverage PBRs.

An app developer raising the issue is likely engaging in sensemaking with team members (or colleagues) internally. However, our focus is distributed sensemaking happening externally with peers from other organizations. 3 In our conceptual model, we follow OIPT by suggesting that app complexity is a source of technological uncertainty about the integration of PBRs (See Figure 1 in the manuscript). We use technology uncertainty to emphasize the lack of procedural and declarative knowledge regarding the integration of PBRs. The level of distributed sensemaking about PBRs changes over time following an S learning curve. The shape of the S curve depends on the learning rate of app developer organizations regarding the PBR. Hence, the level of distributed sensemaking about PBRs differs depending on the PBR and can be obtained for each release date of PBR-based app innovations (see Online Supplemental Appendix B). 7 There are several reasons that could explain the behaviors of app developers to cooperate with potential competitors. For example, by providing solutions, the overall quality of PBR-based app innovation increases, potentially leading to a greater market size. Moreover, by providing solutions, the number of PBR-based app innovations increases, and due to two-sided network effects, the market size rises. A greater market size may benefit competitors as they can target more people and benefit from spillover effects.

title: Managing Digital Platforms with Robust Multi-Sided Recommender Systems
abstract: Digital platforms have replaced traditional markets in most industries and orchestrate socioeconomic aspects of our lives. We address the problem of negative direct side network effects that arise with an increased number of agents on one side of the platform. Negative effects, if unaddressed, lead to undesired long-term consequences for the platform by developing a positive vicious cycle. Addressing negative effects require dynamic solution mechanisms that adapt to the changing landscape of platforms. The recommender systems literature has proposed multi-sided recommender systems (MSR) as a dynamic solution to many problems on platforms. However, current state-ofthe-art MSRs do not consider uncertainty in predicting agents' choices, resulting in limited efficacy. We present a robust multi-sided recommender system that considers estimation errors in agents' choice to address this concern. Extensive experiments with agent-based models -ride-pooling and education platform-provide support for the efficacy and generalizability of the robust MSR to address negative effects.
full_text:
Digital platforms orchestrate many socioeconomic aspects in our lives. The network effect is a key mechanism driving and sustaining these digital platforms [25,40]. In this paper, we consider the dynamic problem of negative direct (or same-side) network effects on digital multi-sided platforms (hereafter, simply "platforms"). The direct side network effect on platforms is "the impact of users from one side of the market on other users from the same side of the market" [40, p. 29]. These effects can be negative or positive. 1 A negative direct side network effect (hereafter, simply "negative effects") is the "downside to the numbers growth on one side of a platform" [40, p. 30]. Specifically, as agents vie for limited resources on a platform, the activity leads to congestion [22,37], which impacts transactions and the overall experiences of the agents from multiple sides of the platform. For example, in ridepooling platforms, demand from riders may significantly exceed the supply of rides due to challenges in alternative modes of transportation and/or seasonality [16]. In education (university course registration) platforms, students can register for courses that they deem appropriate for their objectives. This could lead to overcrowding in popular courses, creating enrollment issues that ultimately delay graduation, along with unused capacity for regular courses [24]. For ride-hailing platforms, drivers often identify and crowd "hot" areas where consumers (riders) are most likely to be found [36].
Negative effects, if unaddressed, can lead to undesired long-term consequences for the platform by developing a positive vicious cycle instead of a positive virtuous cycle [44]. Addressing negative effects requires solutions that (a) concurrently consider the objectives of different sides on a platform, (b) do not control agents because the platform cannot direct agents' actions, and (c) do not prioritize performance of agents on one side at the expense of agents on the other side of the platform. Recommender systems are therefore an appropriate choice given their ability to influence agents on the platform without controlling agents' actions.
Multi-sided recommender systems (MSR) (extends the substantial work on one-sided recommender systems that has been developed for over two decades) concurrently consider the objectives and constraints of heterogeneous agents on digital platforms [27,39,42,48]. However, traditional formulations of multi-stakeholder recommender systems do not serve recommendations to agents on multiple sides of the platform. Consequently, their impact in addressing important problems on digital platforms is limited. To address this issue, recent work in information systems has led to multi-sided recommenders that serve recommendations to multiple sides of the platform [35].
Existing multi-sided recommender system (MSR) approaches have embraced optimization models 2 to serve recommendations [27,39,42,48] because (a) existing recommender approaches can be used to predict preferences, (b) the objectives and constraints of different stakeholders (buyers, sellers, platform, and platform owner(s)) can be modeled, (c) userdefined parameters (context specific) can be incorporated, and (d) platform-level transaction data can be used to refine recommendations. Despite their relevance to digital platforms, existing MSRs with optimization models have a critical problem in terms of optimizing digital platforms -namely the way they (do not) model uncertainty in data. Specifically:
• In any optimization formulation, the solution depends on parameter values.
• For MSRs, one of the most important parameters is the predicted rating.
• There is uncertainty in predicting this rating, and • This uncertainty can lead to sub-optimal solutions and/or constraint violations.
Note that this problem of optimization methods is not specific to MSRs but occurs when there exists uncertainty in data [10]. This is important and timely here because (a) MSRs are gaining popularity in optimizing recommendations on platforms [28,29], and (b) optimization frameworks are common approaches for MSRs [39,48]. One possible solution is to use MSR frameworks that do not consider optimization-based approaches. Another approach is to keep the optimization framework for MSR but develop solutions to address this problem. This paper takes the second approach and presents a robust optimization framework for MSRs.
This research contributes to the discourse on digital platforms and recommender systems. For the practice and management of the digital platforms, the research has (a) highlighted the severity and challenges of negative direct side effects [5,26], and (b) called for dynamic solution mechanisms to address these negative direct side effects [18,49]. For the recommender systems literature, optimization-based MSR do not consider uncertainty in data. Consequently, their efficacy on digital platforms is limited due to buyers' and sellers' heterogeneity on digital platforms.
This paper contributes a novel robust MSR framework to address the negative effects and manage multi-sided platforms efficiently using recommendations. The applications are broad given the wide range of digital multi-sided platforms today (most of which still use single-sided recommendations and suffer from negative direct side effects). To illustrate the efficacy of the proposed framework and generalizability of these contributions, we present two detailed case studies (ride-pooling and an education platform) using agent-based simulation models. The results clearly demonstrate that a robust MSR outperforms common recommender systems in terms of addressing negative direct side effects by explicitly modeling uncertainty in data. The problem of developing robust multi-sided recommendations that consider uncertainty, as well as our specific solution method are novel and significant contributions to the nascent yet growing literature on MSR. Next, we will illustrate the challenges introduced by uncertainty in agents' choice and its effects on existing recommender systems.

To illustrate the problem of uncertainty in data, we consider the following representative setting (Eq. 1 and 2). Let U ¼ 1; . . . ; m be the set of users, I ¼ 1; . . . ; n be the set of items, R u,i be the actual rating provided by user u for item i, and Ru;i be the predicted rating for user u and item i. Model 1 provides a representative recommender system that considers the constraints of users and sellers. x u,i = 1 if user u is recommended item i. The objective function (1a) identifies items with higher predicted ratings across all users. Constraint (1b) requires that each user be recommended k items (typically, k is determined by the analyst). Constraint (1c) requires that the average rating of all recommended items across all users be at least β (the threshold quality parameter). In other words, the platform owner(s) can control the quality of the recommendations by specifying that the average predicted rating across all recommendations should be at least 3.5 out of 5. Finally, constraint (1d) reserves some recommender capacity for each item (α i , determined by the analyst, could be the fraction of total users on the platform or the current capacity of the item). If we do not include constraint (1d) in the model, the recommender may identify same product for many users, leading to unavailability of the item or underutilized capacity for the focal item.
Ideally, we would expect the MSR to identify an optimal solution that satisfies all constraints. However, uncertainty in data (the predicted rating is a random variable that takes values between � R

For example, consider that the average predicted rating across top k items for all users at period t is 3.65; this would satisfy constraint (1c) for β of 3.5. Then, at period t+1, if the average predicted rating across the top k items for all users is 3.49, the MSR would substitute the item(s) for the user(s) in the top k to satisfy the constraint. If no item(s) can be substituted, the MSR may output no solution or the analyst must reduce β to match the maximum possible average predicted rating, which will still be below 3.5. Similar challenges may arise when we concurrently consider multiple constraints. For example, there may not be items that satisfy the average recommendation quality across all users (constraint 1c) while satisfying the requirements of the capacity (constraint 1d) and the top k recommendations (constraint 1b). Also, the model may be infeasible due to competing constraints (1b, 1c, 1d), as the MSR must at least recommend k items to each user, where the average predicted rating across all items satisfies a threshold (β) without exceeding the reserve capacity for each item. In summary, an optimization approach in traditional MSRs aims to identify the optimal solution based on the data. However, we need a mechanism that will provide a robust solution (feasible and may be close to optimal solution) in the face of uncertain data.
To address the challenge stemming from the uncertainty of data in optimization-based MSRs, this paper presents a robust MSR to the recommender systems domain. A robust counterpart of an optimization problem introduces a parameter for each constraint to adjust the problem such that the constraint is not violated, and the solution is feasible (model 2 is the robust counterpart 3 of model 1 where constraints (2c) and (2e) are the robust counterparts of constraints (1c) and (1d), respectively). Specifically, the robust counterpart of model 1 will include a parameter for each constraint with potential data uncertainty variables (y u;i in constraint 2c and z u;i in constraint 2e). In the case of (2c), the worst-case scenario is the minimum value of the left-hand side [and is equal to the left-hand side of Eq. (1c)], which needs to be greater than or equal to the recommender quality threshold. Similarly, the worst-case scenario for constraint (1d) is its maximum value [and is equal to the left-hand side of Eq. (1d)], which needs to be less than or equal to α. Due to the uncertainty of the predicted ratings, these constraints may be violated. To address this issue, the term ε u;i y u;i (y u;i is continuous; ε u;i is the prediction error in R u;i ) provides the necessary gap between
In other words, the robust term (continuous value) increases or decreases, in response to the value of the predicted ratings, to a solution that is feasible and close to optimal, whenever possible. In addition to addressing these challenges, robust MSRs have additional properties that make them attractive: (a) existing approaches to predicting preferences can be easily integrated, (b) user-defined parameters can be incorporated, and (c) robust MSRs are mixed integer programs that can be solved in a reasonable amount of time.
The traditional approach to evaluate a recommender system's efficacy has been to use a hold-out sample and measure candidate algorithms on chosen metrics [43]. There are two issues in using the traditional approach to evaluate MSRs: (a) a hold-out sample represents a snapshot of the dynamic system; a champion algorithm based on experiments with a holdout sample may not lead to better outcomes on the platform [35], and (b) traditional measures of recommender efficacy may not translate to settings where MSRs are applicable [28]. To address these issues, we present an Agent-Based Modeling (ABM) framework to evaluate MSRs. Agent-based models have been used in the recommender systems literature [35,53] to (a) incorporate platform-level data, (b) address limitations in accessing realworld platforms, data, and experiments, and (c) develop forward-looking simulations to understand the long-term effects of MSRs on the platform.
The problem of negative direct effects on platforms has been identified in different contexts such as ride-pooling platforms [16], peer-to-peer networks [5], email-based social networks [15], shared online spaces [30], broadcasting [4], ride-hailing platforms [49], and energy markets [32], among others. However, the research on addressing the negative direct side effects on platforms has been limited. Multiple management tools are employed [12,13,40] digital platform owner(s) such as legal, pricing [6,52], analytics, and curation mechanisms. However, some of these approaches require constant monitoring by the platform owner(s) to address negative effects. Constantinides et al. [18] highlight the need for mechanisms that can help the platform owner(s) to address these negative effects.
Recent work in the recommender systems literature has considered the heterogeneity of agents and the need to consider the diverse objectives and preferences of heterogeneous agents. MSR are developed to consider the heterogeneity of agents and their objectives and preferences. In their commentary, Jannach and Adomavicius [28] highlight the need to consider multiple stakeholders with diverse objectives. Adomavicius and Tuzhilin [3] and Adomavicius et al. [2] discuss the use of multiple criteria to develop recommendations. Chen et al. [17] discuss the use of recommender systems to improve sellers' profitability and consumer welfare. In the context of job candidate recommendation, Rodriguez et al. [42] develop a constrained optimization problem with competing objectives. Burke and Abdollahpouri [14] discuss the applicability of MSR in recommending educational programs to students. Jannach and Adomavicius [29] simulate a price and profit aware recommender system to show the trade-off between accuracy and profitability for users and sellers, respectively. Jambor and Wang [27] use simulation experiments to show the benefit of optimizing multiple objectives such as promoting long tail items or resource constraints in a collaborative filtering approach, in addition to the standard objective of recommendation accuracy. In the context of Expedia platform, Nguyen et al. [39] develop a recommender system that addresses the problem of multiple stakeholders (consumers, sellers, and platform intermediaries) having different criteria and objectives. They propose a re-ranking approach of recommendations such that multiple objectives are optimized. In a similar vein, Sürer et al. [48] propose a constraint-based integer programming optimization model with constraints representing different goals of various stakeholders (buyers, sellers, and platform owner(s)). Similar related work can be seen in the area of information retrieval, where the search results are re-ranked based on multiple competing criteria [31,51]. Finally, Malgonde et al. [35] consider recommendations to multiple sides to address search complexities on a digital platform.
As noted above, while there is increasing interest in using MSRs to improve platform dynamics, existing approaches do not deal with the uncertainty of data and associated challenges. In this paper, we introduce robust optimization 4 to address these issues to make MSRs significantly more useful in managing digital platforms.
Before we discuss the robust MSR, this section presents a general model of MSRs with objective and constraints that can be adapted for a specific platform. We assume that the platform has a set of buyers (I) who transact with a set of sellers (S) on the platform for a set of items (J). Each seller offers a set of items (J s ) on the platform. The platform allows buyers to view seller-provided information about an item such as the description, price, seller information, and shipping cost and duration, among others. There are no preferred agents on the platform based on characteristics such as the status, preferences, location, or transaction history. Finally, owing to heterogeneity in the definition, operationalization, and business rules, we present each constraint of the general model separately and discuss its applicability using specific examples. It is important to note that applying this general model to a platform may require the adaptation, addition, and/or deletion of constraints and objectives. Figure 1 illustrates the design considerations for MSRs using platform-level data to learn buyers and sellers' preferences, constraints, and objectives, to serve heterogeneous recommendations.
When buyer i buys item j from seller s on the platform, let u i js and u s ij denote the utility for buyer i and seller s, respectively. We define x ijs as a recommendation by the MSR to buyer i about item j offered by seller s; if so, x ijs = 1; otherwise, x ijs = 0. The objective function of the MSR can be given by: maximize
//maximize the utility of sellers and buyers on the platform// Defining and operationalizing the utility for buyers and sellers is platform specific and may include multiple objectives. For example, in the case of the ride-pooling platform, a focal buyer's utility may consist of the ride acceptance, price, and driver's ratings (proxy for ride quality), whereas for the seller, the utility may consist of the profit, rider's ratings, and capacity utilization. Similarly, in the case of lodging rental platforms such as Airbnb, the buyers' utility may consist of the rental location's ratings and price, whereas the sellers' utility may consist of the duration of stay, profit, and buyer characteristics. The objective implicitly considers the platform and its owner(s)' utility because the platform and its owner(s) extract value from utility maximizing transactions between buyers and sellers. However, platform-specific adaptation of this objective function may need to explicitly include platform and its owner(s)' utility.

The value of the service-level constraints is evident on digital platforms. For example, on ride-pooling and ride-hailing platforms, 100 percent utilization may be challenging due to competing drivers. In the case of lodging platforms, a focal seller would seek to maximize utilization of her offerings (one or many lodges). Initially, the minimum service level capacity usage (λ 1j and λ 1s ) could be derived from platform data. Over time, it can be adjusted based on the seller preferences, platform's service-level guarantees, or demand.
Demand for an item may arise from recommendations served by the recommender system or organically. If the demand generated by the recommender system exceeds the existing capacity of an item and seller, organically generated demand is unmet. We add a capacity buffer constraint to address balancing the demand:
//For each item in J, its recommendations to buyers should not exceed the item's recommendation service level λ 2j //
//For each seller in S, recommendations to buyers across its items should not exceed the seller's recommendation service level (λ 2s )//
In the case of lodging rental platforms, the recommended demand can be limited for a rental location to allow for organic and direct demand to rental locations with low demand. Such constraints may seem unfair to buyers who are not recommended the focal location. However, other constraints consider specific matching constraints such as reviews and the price to recommend other locations. In the case of education platforms, the demand for popular courses can be managed by recommending other courses and allowing buffer capacity for priority students.
Recommendations to the seller-side are focused on incrementing capacity, which has associated costs for the focal seller. Therefore, any recommendation to increment capacity needs to be limited and only one policy to increment the capacity should be recommended. The following constraints incorporate this logic:
//For each seller, total capacity increment should not exceed αs% of existing total capacity for the focal seller// X s2S j
//For each item in J, only one policy of capacity increment should be recommended// Limits on capacity increments are relevant in many digital platforms. For example, in the case of an education platform, recommending additional course capacity for courses (in anticipation of increased demand) as a fraction of the existing course capacity is acceptable. In the case of lodging rental platforms, recommending additional days for a rental location (capacity) is limited to a fraction of the existing number of days that the focal rental location is available for rent.
In recommending to multiple sides on the platform, the multi-sided recommender system needs to consider the objectives and constraints of these sides. On the buyer-side of the platform, the quality of recommendations (the predicted probability of the buyer's preference) is important. In other words, buyers will like to see recommendations of items that are relevant to them (including the serendipity of these recommended items) [43]. In addition, the number of recommendations served to each buyer is limited by the user interface design. We assume that r recommendations are served (all seen at once or via a scrollable interface).

In the case of lodging rental platforms, the platform may seek to provide 4 recommendations (r = 4) where the probability of the buyer selecting each recommended rental is at least 0.6 (β= 0.6). Similarly, an education platform may recommend 10 courses (r = 10) to each student where the probability of the focal student selecting each recommended course is at least 0.55 (β= 0.55). In this section, we present the robust counterpart of a general MSR (discussed in earlier section) and illustrate how future research in MSRs can build on this approach. Before we discuss the robust approach for MSR, it is important to acknowledge the flexibility afforded by this approach. For a given choice prediction approach, we see a continuum of prediction confidence for user-item pairs due to available data. In cases where the prediction confidence is high (negligible perturbation in estimation), the modeler may choose to use the non-robust version of the constraint. For user-item pairs with low prediction confidence (significant perturbation in estimation), the robust version of the constraint can be incorporated. This will lead to a mixed robust optimization model that may be simpler to program and solve as compared to a purely robust optimization model. As a general approach to develop a robust MSR, the modeler will derive a robust constraint for each nonrobust constraint that includes random variables, which may introduce error. Then, the modeler will transform the min and max constraints to the regular constraints. Finally, the constraints are combined to develop a robust integer program. In instances where MSR do not converge, we use an approach similar to the one-sided recommender system. Before we discuss the key areas of robust MSRs to incorporate robust formulations in recommender systems, we outline the general steps (Figure 2) that can be adopted for future research.

Evaluating MSRs is particularly challenging to do with historical data only, given that the past may have reflected the behavior of the different agents when there was no MSR in place.
Extrapolating from that to guess what might happen with an MSR in place is fraught with challenges. One possibility is to run controlled field experiments, but that requires access to a platform that is willing to run controlled MSR tests, which might be challenging for all researchers in terms of having access to build a body of work around this area. In our work, we advocate the use of agent-based models to evaluate MSRs. Such models can simulate competing approaches in parallel (i.e., run parallel universes) and do so under different managerial tools -with no recommender, with traditional single-side recommenders, with an MSR, and with a robust MSR. Figure 3 illustrates this generic approach in which the parallel paths simultaneously test different universes and operate much like groups in a controlled experiment. We perform multiple experiments with the agent-based model to generate platform-level data, which are used in statistical tests to compare different universes. Agents' preferences can be modeled based on assumptions, aggregate patterns identified from anecdotal evidence, and/or real data, if available [19]. Finally, we perform multiple sensitivity tests to establish the robustness of the simulation model and results. In what follows, we instantiate this generic approach in an empirical case study from the ridepooling platform to discuss the efficacy of a robust MSR in addressing negative effects. In Online Supplemental Appendix 2, we discuss another empirical case study from the education platform.
Ride-pooling platforms 5 facilitate matches between drivers and riders. For example, driver A may offer a ride from Dallas to Austin on Friday. Riders seeking similar rides (parameters may include the start and end time, source and destination, and ratings, among others) make ride requests. Based on her vehicle's capacity and preferences, driver A accepts certain riders' offers, whereas other offers (if any) are rejected. A focal rider may submit multiple offers on the platform. Agents participate on ride-pooling platforms for various reasons such as the ability to use high occupancy vehicle lanes, cost, traveling with others, environmental concerns, and saving time, among others [33], and follow the platform's rules to enter and complete transactions. A ride-pooling platform 6 is an appropriate choice to test the efficacy of a robust MSR for several reasons: (a) agents have choice in determining their actions (drivers can choose which offers to accept, and riders can choose which rides to make offers on); (b) there is uncertainty in agents' choice (uncertainty about preferences); (c) agents actions can be influenced with recommendations; (d) the platform and its owner(s) do not match 7 agents on the platform; (e) recommendations can be served to both sides of the platform; and (f) negative effects arise when multiple riders seek similar rides on the platform [16].
On a ride-pooling platform, drivers' and riders' transactions may be driven by different objectives. For example, objectives such as capacity usage and price may be important to drivers, whereas price, ride availability, and match quality may be important to riders. This introduces the challenge of identifying an appropriate metric to measure agents' performance on each side of the platform. To address this issue, we introduce fitness 8 as a composite measure of agents' performance on the platform. We define an agent's fitness as an aggregate measure of an agent's willingness to continue transactions on the platform. As a composite measure, an agent's fitness may comprise one or more metrics that are of interest to the modeler. At any time, the fitness of an agent takes a value between 0 and 1. For each new rider and driver entering the simulation, we assign a fitness score (random value between 0 and 1 drawn from a uniform distribution).
For each new agent entering the simulation environment, a copy of the driver or rider enters the other universes simulated in parallel. This ensures that the fitness of new entrants across parallel universes is the same, allowing us to see the effect of different recommender systems on agents' fitness. Assigning an initial fitness value to each agent also allows us to simulate the variation in agents' commitment toward transacting on the platform. Specifically, some agents participate on a platform with little to no intention of making recurring transactions whereas some agents may view the platform as their primary transacting mechanism. Finally, it is important to note that an agent's fitness is an intrinsic property that cannot be accessed or manipulated by the recommender system active in the universe.
In our agent-based model, the drivers' fitness consists of two metrics: (a) minimizing the unused capacity, and (b) the quality of matched riders. Minimizing the unused capacity for every ride offered by a focal driver has direct implications for the driver's profitability and sustainability on the platform, as well as environmental implications. Also, it is important for the driver to be matched with preferred riders (we discuss preference computations in later sections). In the case of riders, fitness consists of two metrics: (a) accepted offers and (b) the quality of matched drivers. It is important that at least a fraction of the offers made on the platform be accepted. In addition, preferred matched drivers are desirable from the riders' perspective.
While other metrics of interest for agents on the ride-pooling platform exist, our choice of metrics here is driven by three reasons. First, our chosen metrics are clearly important for the agents themselves and can be quantified and measured for each agent. Related work in the ride-pooling literature has adopted some of these metrics [11,47]. Second, the chosen metrics are affected by the recommender system on the platform. Finally, the problem of negative effects has severe and direct implications for the chosen metrics.
We now discuss the overall flow (Online Supplemental Appendix Figure 1.1) of our agent-based model (ABM) for the ride-pooling platform along these points: (a) initialize agents' preferences, (b) agents' decision logic and recommendations, (c) update agents' fitness, and (d) simulation experiments. First, consider the agents' preferences. Agents (drivers and riders) on a ride-pooling platform have heterogeneous preferences that could be along several intrinsic and extrinsic dimensions such as the start and end time, origin and destination, vehicle, gender, and route, among others. The challenge of modeling such heterogeneous preferences is twofold: (i) identifying the preferences to model and (ii) initializing agents with values for each of these preferences. Clearly, enumerating all preferences and initializing agents for these preferences not only leads to an exponential rise in the number of scenarios to consider, but also takes away from the value of such approaches, which is often a study of likely scenarios of interest. Anecdotal evidence from ride-pooling and related platforms suggests that certain behaviors 9 of drivers 10 , 11 (politeness, responsible driving behavior, and cleanliness, among others) may be preferred by most riders 12 , 13 (politeness, punctuality, and cleanliness, among others), and vice versa. Thus, we use a left-skewed normal distribution 14 (in our experiments, we vary the mean of this distribution) to draw preference scores. Specifically, we draw from the distribution to initialize (i) a focal rider's preference toward a driver, (ii) a focal rider's preference for a ride, and (iii) a focal driver's preference for a rider. Consequently, we can experiment with individual heterogeneity while retaining the platform-level characteristics for agents' preferences. For example, sampling from a left-skewed distribution with a 0.98 mean, 15 we note that the drivers' ratings (average preference across all riders on the platform toward a focal driver) are between [0.898, 1]. Unsurprisingly, when all drivers are considered, the mean rating is 0.977. Thus, our model aligns with anecdotal evidence from ride-pooling platforms: (i) all drivers have a relatively high average preference score on the platform, (ii) although most drivers are acceptable, certain drivers are preferred over others by most riders, and (iii) drivers' ratings show heterogeneity (not all drivers' ratings are close to the mean of the distribution used to generate preferences).
Second, consider agents' decision logic and recommendations. During each period, riders are seeking rides whereas drivers are offering rides. In their universe, recommender systems serve recommendations to riders and drivers. ( 1) Consider a one-sided recommender system. The recommender computes a preference score for each rider-driver-ride triad. Across all driver-ride combinations, the one-sided recommender system recommends the top n rides to a focal rider. For each driver-ride pair, the one-sided recommender system recommends the top m riders. ( 2) Consider the multi-sided recommender system (technical details of the model such as the objective function and constraints are presented in Online Supplemental Appendix Section 1.1). We consider each rider, driver, and ride to formulate the model. The model considers objectives, preferences, and constraints of both sides of the platform. Based on the model's output, we recommend n rides to each rider and m riders to each driver-ride pair. (3) Consider the robust multi-sided recommender system (technical details of the model such as the objective function and constraints are presented in the Online Supplemental Appendix 1). We extend the multi-sided model to consider the uncertainty in predicted preferences. Thus far, we have assumed that the computed preference score represents the true score of a rider liking a ride offered by a driver. However, in practice, this true score is unknown and can only be predicted; moreover, it is the source of uncertainty in choice. To simulate this uncertainty, we introduce perturbation (a random value drawn from a uniform distribution) to certain agents on the platform (agents are chosen at random; the total number of agents with perturbations is a fraction of the total population determined by a random value drawn from a uniform distribution). Such perturbations are introduced in each simulation universe to simulate uncertainty in choice in addition to the negative effects. Similar to the MSR, the robust variant recommends n rides to each rider and m riders to each driver-ride pair.
After the recommendations are served to the riders and drivers, riders make offers to preferred driver-ride pairs. On a ride-pooling platform, multiple rides may satisfy the search criteria specified by a focal rider. To simulate the challenge of identifying rides to make offers, we randomize the order of evaluating rides to make offers. In other words, if 10 rides are offered on the platform, a rider randomly picks a ride, evaluates whether an offer is to be made, and continues to the next randomly chosen ride unless a maximum limit of offers is reached. If the randomly chosen ride has been recommended by the recommender system in the universe, the focal rider will accept the recommendation if her fitness is greater than a random value drawn from a uniform distribution; otherwise, she will reject the recommendation.
After offers are made on the platform, each driver evaluates the received offers. Similar to riders accepting recommendations, drivers probabilistically accept recommendations and accept offers if the capacity for the focal ride has not been met. An offer may be rejected based on the rejection of a recommendation or when the ride's capacity has been met.
A focal driver will select an offer for its ride at random from the pool of offers for the focal ride.
Third, we update agents' fitness at the end of each period as follows. (1) Consider drivers whose fitness consists of minimizing the unused capacity and increasing the match quality. We compute the average capacity usage and average quality of the matches for the focal driver across past time periods in the simulation. For a focal driver, if the average capacity utilization is greater than a specific value 16 and the average quality of the matches is greater than a specific value xv , we increment the focal driver's fitness by some percentage xvi of her current fitness value; otherwise, we decrement the focal driver's fitness by some percent 17 of the current fitness value. 18 A driver is considered for a fitness update only when she has at least one match during the period. Otherwise, the focal driver is considered inactive for the period. (2) Consider riders whose fitness consists of accepted offers and match quality. We compute the average ratio of offers accepted/made and the average quality of matches for the focal rider across past time periods in the simulation. For a focal rider, if the average ratio of the accepted offers is greater than a specific value xv and the average quality of the matches is greater than a specific value xv , we increment the focal rider's fitness by some percent xvi of her current fitness value; otherwise, we decrement the focal driver's fitness by some percentage xvi of the current fitness value. A rider is considered for a fitness update only when she has made at least one offer during the period. Otherwise, the focal rider is considered inactive for the period.
Finally, we record all metrics of interest (agents' fitness, capacity usage, and accepted and rejected offers) for each simulation universe. Also, existing riders on the ride-pooling platforms may change their role and offer rides. To model this possibility, we allow a fraction (a random percentage between 0 and 5 percent) of existing riders to change their role and offer rides on the platform.
We use Python programming language to implement the agent-based simulation. Multisided and its robust variant model is dynamically solved using IBM ILOG CPLEX and interfaces with the Python code. To simulate the negative effects, we manipulate the ratio of riders to drivers in our simulation experiments. In these experiments, we introduce 20 riders 19 for every driver added to the simulation. For the main analyses, we limit our simulation setup to 5 periods due to computational limitations, but the framework is indeed general (Online Supplemental Appendix Table 1.4 provides the default parameters of the model). At the end of the last period, we record the platform-level metrics of interest. We perform 100 runs of the simulation model to record the systems' performance. The data from these experiments are used to statistically test the efficacy of different recommender systems.
We use the Wilcoxon signed-rank test to compare agents' fitness across the different universes. We find that the riders' and drivers' fitness is greater for the simulation universe where the Robust Multi-sided Recommender System is in use and that the difference is statistically significant 20 (Tables 3 and4), in comparison to simulation universes where there is no recommender system, a one-sided recommender system, or a multi-sided recommender system. The robust approach improves riders' fitness by 11.62 percent, 13.75 percent, and 14.04 percent, in comparison to no recommender, a one-sided, and a multi-sided recommender system, respectively. Similarly, the robust approach improves drivers' fitness by 25.37 percent, 1.69 percent, and 2.02 percent, in comparison to no recommender, a one-sided, and a multi-sided recommender system, respectively.
We also compute the effect size 21 [46] to quantify the differences in the systems' performances. In the case of riders (Table 5), we note that the robust variant has a large effect size in comparison to other approaches. However, in the case of drivers (Table 6), we see a large (no recommender) or a small (one-sided and multi-sided) effect size for the robust variant. Qualitatively, we interpret (the probability of superiority) the effect size as follows [34]. (1) There is an 83 percent, 85.6 percent, and 86.3 percent chance that a rider picked at random from the robust multi-sided recommender system will have a higher fitness score than a rider picked at random from no recommender, a one-sided, or a multisided recommender system, respectively. Based on results from the statistical tests, quantitative increase in fitness, effect size, and probability of superiority, we note the following points. (1) Riders' fitness in the robust system is greater, statistically significant, and shows a large effect size and a high probability of superiority, in comparison to the other systems. (2) Riders' performance in the robust system is not at the expense of drivers' performance, as compared to other systems. In other words, the superiority of the robust approach on riders' performance is not at the expense of drivers' performance. (3) Although drivers' fitness in the robust system is greater and statistically significant, the effect size is small and the probability of superiority is comparable. However, negative effects due to an increase in riders have severe implications for riders. Hence, the champion solution approach should improve riders' fitness while maintaining their fitness, in comparison to the other competing approaches.
Thus, these results provide compelling evidence that the robust approach can outperform other approaches under negative effects on the ride-pooling platform.
There are indeed limitations to our work, which we will highlight here in the spirit of transparency; we also suggest future work that can address these points. First, our results are limited to the market intermediary stream of platforms [50], where capacity constraints create negative effects. Second, we assume certain preferences and decision behaviors of agents (a skewed distribution to initialize the preferences, maximum number of offers, maximum number of recommendations, and maximum rides offered by a driver). To assuage concerns related to the effect of such assumptions and the variables' values on our results, we (a) inform our simulation design using available evidence, (b) simulate the system multiple times, and (c) perform multiple sensitivity tests. Third, other metrics may be considered in computing agents' fitness. We recognize that identifying additional metrics for inclusion would depend on the platform's domain and would identify this as a future research direction. Fourth, prior work has considered the impact of recommender systems on platforms [23]; further research is required to understand the impact of MSR and its robust variant on the management of platforms. Fifth, this research does not model price ix differences on the platform. The driver's price setting and the rider's willingness to pay have the potential to partially address the negative effects on the platform. For example, consider two offered rides-A and B. Of the two rides, if the price requested by the driver of ride A is substantially higher (above the willingness to pay threshold) than the price requested by the driver of ride B, riders will self-select and make offers to drivers whose price for a ride is at or below the willingness to pay threshold. However, as the severity of negative effects increases, the effectiveness of price-based mechanism decreases as many riders may selfselect and make offers to drivers whose price is at or below their willingness to pay threshold. Finally, we acknowledge the methodological limitations of agent-based simulation models that have been discussed in the management science literature [19,20]. Within the boundaries of these limitations, we believe that our results are conclusive given the realism incorporated from existing platforms, additional analyses to identify the boundary conditions, and sensitivity tests to understand the impact of the simulation parameters.
For the ride-pooling empirical case study, we identify preferences, constraints, and objectives that are relevant for the context. It is important that the framework contributed by this study is generalizable to other contexts and can be adapted by future studies in the recommender systems domain and beyond. Towards this goal, we present (Online Supplemental Appendix 2) another empirical study of an education platform.
In the education platform study, students (buyers) seek courses offered on the platform. Courses (sellers) have limited capacity to serve the students. As the number of students increase on the platform, negative effects arise (popular and/or required courses are unavailable to students). Students' fitness is determined by (a) success in registering for courses and (b) the match quality, whereas fitness for courses is determined by the (a) unused capacity and (b) severity of capacity increments. We find that the robust MSR outperforms other recommender approaches in terms of addressing the negative effects on the education platform.
Together, the two case studies show that the framework presented in this study (Figure 2) can be adapted to multiple domains with suitable adjustments to the agents' objectives, preferences, and recommendations. The two empirical case studies discussed in this paper provide examples of such operationalization. Also, our study is generalizable to the onesided recommender literature, which has been dominant for the past two decades because it too suffers from uncertainty in data.
We attribute the robust MSR's performance to three points. First, the robust MSR collectively considers agents' objectives, constraints, and preferences to serve recommendations. In doing so, the robust MSR can identify globally optimal solutions rather than agentspecific optimal solutions that may exacerbate the problem of negative effects. Second, as the severity of the negative effects increases, the robust MSR can spread the demand to less popular supply sources while retaining the recommendation quality specified by the modeler. Such modeling flexibility is a desirable property to the platform owner(s) perspective. Finally, the robust MSR considers uncertainty in choice estimations. Consequently, the robust MSR can serve better recommendations (toward the modeled objectives), in comparison to other recommender systems. In summary, although onesided, multi-sided, and robust MSRs use platform-level data, the robust MSR better addresses the negative effects that arise with an increasing number of agents on the platform.
From additional analyses (Online Supplemental Appendix 1), we note six important points for the management of digital platforms. First, as the severity of the negative direct side increases, the platform's side that is responsible for the negative effects will experience a drop in agents' fitness (riders' fitness decreases with an increased number of riders on the platform). Second, as the severity of the negative direct side increases, the platform's side that is not responsible for the negative effects may experience an increase in the agents' fitness (the drivers' fitness increases with an increased number of riders on the platform). Third, in comparing multiple solution mechanisms for complex systems such as digital platforms, the systems' designers/managers need to consider the performance of the candidate approaches across multiple measures. From our analyses, we find that although there may not be significant differences for a composite measure, candidate approaches may differ in their efficacy across other measures of interest. Fourth, solution mechanisms proposed to address platform-level issues may be subject to performance thresholds, as identified by the platform owner(s). Specifically, further research is needed to inform platform owner(s) on the thresholds beyond which one may deem an approach superior to the existing state of the art. Fifth, we observe that a competing approach may lose competence on one side of the platform while gaining competence on the other side of the platform (e.g., drivers' fitness decreases while riders' fitness increases). This points to the competing objectives at play on platforms and highlights the need for dynamic solution mechanisms to orchestrate the platform. Finally, the framework proposed in this research, which can be adapted to other platforms by adding, editing, or deleting, illustrates the constraints. Managers of digital platforms need such flexible solution mechanisms to address issues that arise organically.
In the platform context, self-organizing agents vie for limited resources, resulting in negative direct side effects that may lead to a vicious cycle for the platform. To address the negative direct side effects, we introduced adaptive intelligence to the platform in the form of a robust MSR that can handle uncertainty in data. To evaluate the efficacy of a robust MSR, we presented two agent-based simulation models-a ride-pooling platform and an education platform. Experiments with agent-based simulation show that a robust MSR can better address the negative effects on digital platforms. This research has two main contributions to the literature on the management of digital platforms and recommender systems. First, this research demonstrates an approach to incorporate data, choice, and optimization models, to develop an analytics framework that addresses the negative direct side effects on digital platforms. The framework presented in this research is generalizable to multiple platforms and contributes an important managerial tool to the management of the digital platform literature. Second, we present a robust model of the multi-sided recommender system that considers error in the computation of choice probabilities. This represents an important methodological contribution to the recommender systems research domain and specifically to the growing MSR literature.
Our research has three implications for practice on platforms. First, managing digital platforms require dynamic solution mechanisms that can adapt to changes in agents' preferences. Such dynamic mechanisms can use platform-level data to nudge agents and optimize the platform owner(s)' objectives, which may extend beyond profitability (such as fairness and bias). Recommender systems are an important tool among the portfolio of tools used to manage a digital platform. Second, robust MSRs are a dynamic solution mechanism that can consider uncertainty in agents' choice. Not only is considering uncertainty in agents' choice important from a technical standpoint, but it is also important for a platform's competitiveness. For example, a platform with a robust recommender system could be more adaptive to changes/uncertainty in agents' choices and preferences, in comparison to a competing platform without a robust MSR. Finally, a platform and its owner(s) may seek hybrid and/or dynamic solution mechanisms that morph recommendations based on the challenges faced by the agents on the platform. For example, a platform may be subjected to multiple challenges at the same time. Platform management tools which can identify challenges and intervene as required, are key tools for managing digital platforms.
There are many opportunities for future work as this methodology is applied to specific large-scale platforms, and there are likely platform-specific idiosyncrasies that might suggest novel extensions of this approach. Facebook for instance, has individual users, news organizations who place articles in feeds, and advertisers, making it an attractive platform to model using this methodology. Upwork has individuals who sign up for e-lancing and companies who provide jobs or tasks. This setting is quite different from Facebook and may offer other unique abilities to customize the ABM and/or framework. In all these cases, managing the platform is important and challenging. However, the results presented here provide some reason to believe that the design of effective MSR can be a particularly promising area for information systems research.
