title: Chilling Effect of the Enforcement of Computer Misuse Act: Evidence from Publicly Accessible Hack Forums
abstract: To reduce the availability of hacking tools for use in cybersecurity offenses, many countries have enacted computer misuse acts (CMAs) that criminalize the production, distribution, and possession of such tools with criminal intent. However, the dual-use nature of cybersecurity technology complicates the legal process of recognizing such computer misuse tools and of predicting harmful intent based on mere possession. This predicament introduces the possibility of unfounded prosecution that may produce a chilling effect on the provision of techniques otherwise valuable in maintaining cybersecurity and defending against hackers. This study establishes a theoretical foundation for the potentially chilling effect of such legal enforcement by adopting theories about choice under uncertainty. Leveraging an external shock in publicly accessible online hack forums, we examined the impact of CMA enforcement on users' contributions to cybersecurityrelevant topics that are not targeted by the law. We found that CMA enforcement reduces the quantity and the extent of relevance to cybersecurity in discussions in hack forums. We further identified the mechanisms of this chilling effect by delving into users' heterogeneity in responding to the uncertainty of false prosecution imposed by CMA enforcement as well as users' proactivity undertaken to alleviate such uncertainty. Our study reveals this chilling effect is not just about restraining individuals from lawful acts but also about how they refrain from acts not intended as targets of the law.
full_text:
Information technology-enabled digitization has enlarged the areas of the physical world vulnerable to cyberattacks and created substantial cost advantages for cybercriminals. From these perpetrators' perspective, automation and the accessibility brought about by computers and the Internet have made it much cheaper to commit crimes in cyberspace than to commit real-world crimes such as theft, burglary, or murder (Katyal 2001). Because the widely available online hacker communities, including those in the surface network and darknet, lower the knowledge barrier and provide markets for hacking tools, even a novice can leverage advanced hacking techniques to execute sophisticated cyberattacks (Pastrana et al. 2018). Contrary to the low costs of cybercrime, defending against them remains costly. The Internet confers anonymity on cybercriminals, enabling them to escape detection and apprehension (Katyal 2001). Jurisdictional boundaries further complicate efforts to penalize cybercriminals whose criminality involves multiple countries (Png et al. 2008, Wang and Kim 2009, Kim et al. 2012, Hui et al. 2017).
In view of the challenges in prosecuting cybercrimes ex post, many countries, including Australia, China, France, Germany, Singapore, the United States, and the United Kingdom, have enacted legislation to criminalize the production, distribution, and possession of hacking tools with an intent to commit offenses against the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of computer data and systems. 1 The purpose of the enforcement of computer misuse act (CMA enforcement) is to increase the cost of committing criminal offenses ex ante. In pursuing CMA enforcement, the legal system needs to consider ex ante adjudication of the malice and severity of the misuse of cybersecurity tools.
However, uncertainty and unpredictability complicate the process of prosecution for CMA enforcement for two fundamental reasons. First, government enforcement agencies often lack sufficient resources to keep pace with assessing the potential cybersecurity risks associated with new technology or new uses of existing technology (Katyal 2001, Yue et al. 2019). Although the legal process is inherently surrounded by fallibility and uncertainty (Schauer 1978), the innovation-and technologyintensive nature of cybersecurity further increases the difficulty of distinguishing between the positive and negative variants of cybersecurity-relevant acts in different instances (Katyal 2001). Second, and more importantly, the dual-use nature of cybersecurity technology further contributes to this uncertainty in recognizing and evaluating computer misuse tools (Yue et al. 2019). The tools cybercriminals exploit to crack computer systems (e.g., tools for penetration tests) can be easily used by cybersecurity researchers or professionals to assess system vulnerabilities. Similarly, the tools used to secure legitimate systems and networks (e.g., encryption) can be adapted by cybercriminals to conceal their criminal activities (Chen andHe 2013, Yue et al. 2019). 2 This dualuse nature makes it difficult for legal concepts to precisely define what conduct and what kinds of computer misuse tools should be regulated (Schauer 1978), increasing the ambiguity involved in imposing sanctions on conduct closest to the line separating lawful and unlawful activities (Schauer 1978).
Unlike the deterrent effect, which posits that the threat of punishment prevents people from committing criminal activities, the chilling effect arises when people, fearful of false prosecution, avoid lawful activities that the law did not intend to target, including socially desirable ones such as well-intentioned efforts for cybersecurity protection (Stoycheff et al. 2019). The design of any legal system applicable to cybercrimes needs to balance between the intended outcome of increasing perpetrators' costs of committing cybercrimes and the unintended outcome of shrinking legitimate research and development on cybersecurity. On the one hand, such uncertainty and unpredictability surrounding the legal processes for CMA enforcement may eventually lead to an unexpected chilling effect on well-intentioned efforts to understand cybercriminals' hacking techniques and exploit their vulnerabilities through the hacking communities. On the other hand, despite the increased uncertainty because of CMA enforcement, the chilling effect on legitimate content may not be realized if the cybersecurity communities maintain a high level of anonymity. It is well known that law enforcement may even trigger defiant behaviors (Sherman 1993), making it difficult to predict the net effect of CMA enforcement. Therefore, it is important to examine empirically whether and how CMA enforcement may suppress legitimate provision and communication of cybersecurity technology. For example, in May 2021, the UK Home Office opened a "Call for Information on the Computer Misuse Act 1990," posting key questions about whether the offenses set out in the CMA adequately cover cyber-dependent harm on one side and whether the CMA provides adequate cover to the protection of legitimate cybersecurity activity on the other side (Government 2021). This aligns with Senator Sheldon Whitehouse's query on enhancing the legislation's clarity regarding the protection of information security researchers from unjust federal prosecution, ensuring they are not mistaken for cybercriminals.
Given this backdrop, this paper attempts to empirically investigate the potential chilling effect of CMA enforcement on legitimate activities on publicly accessible hack forums, where anonymity is relatively high. Our understanding of the chilling effect is grounded in theories of law and economics about rational choice as well as theories of psychology about how individuals deal with uncertainty about their contemplated conduct. According to Roloff and Cloven (1990), fear of negative outcomes is a key mechanism of the chilling effect, and people may adjust their behavior to reduce the risk of erroneous judgment. From a utilitarianism perspective, rational choice theory (RCT) argues that an individual will refrain from even lawful acts to reduce the potential cost associated with the uncertainty about prosecution imposed by CMA enforcement, which served as the theoretical foundation in prior studies on the chilling effect (Schauer 1978, Katyal 2001, Kaplow 2011, Kirsch 2014, Guinchard 2018). However, because the probability of false penalization by CMA enforcement is unknown, so is the potential cost an individual may incur because of contemplated activities. Therefore, RCT is limited in understanding how different individuals would react differently under uncertainty. We suggest the different perceptions of uncertainty as a main mechanism that helps refine the heterogenous effect. That is, people's decisions are affected by their heterogeneity in perceiving and reacting to uncertainty-issues addressed by social learning theory (FeldmanHall and Shenhav 2019) and Knightian decision theory (Bewley 2002(Bewley , 2011;;Alvarez and Christensen 2021). Similarly, uncertainty-identity theory (Hogg 2012) can be applied to the conformity they undertake to alleviate their uncertainty. Therefore, these three theories complement RCT to provide a comprehensive and nuanced understanding of the chilling effect.
We exploited a quasi-natural experiment to investigate the chilling effects of CMA enforcement, the heterogeneous effects, and the underlying mechanism rooted in the increased uncertainty of false prosecution as explained by RCT and the three uncertainty-related social psychology theories mentioned previously. The exogenous shock is CMA enforcement, especially the Amendment of Article 285 in the Criminal Law, enacted on February 28, 2009, in China. The treatment group consists of content contributors from May 2007 to March 2011 in the two dominant publicly accessible Chinese hack forums that were officially licensed to operate only in China and consisted of anonymized content contributors located within its judicial boundary of CMA enforcement. The control group consists of users of one of the most popular and publicly accessible Englishlanguage hack forums, Hackforums.net. Conventionally known as "hack" forums, the three Internet forums studied in this paper are not specifically for black hats like those in the darknet. 3  These cybersecurity communities bring together individuals interested in hacking and facilitate their communication and exchange of skills and experiences related to cybersecurity. Because the acquisition of cybersecurity capability against ubiquitous attacks requires organizations to understand their adversaries' technology and mindsets (Grimes 2017), these publicly accessible forums on cybersecurity techniques serve as vantage points for professionals and as schools for students and junior hackers to exchange knowledge and learn from their counterparts (Pastrana et al. 2018). Therefore, it is important to examine the chilling effects of CMA enforcement on publicly accessible hack forums in which users' contributions are not directly targeted by CMA enforcement.
Our data set includes 43,322 active users from the treatment group and 6,728 active users from the control group who contributed at least one thread after May 2007 and before the CMA enforcement. Then, we apply multiple machine learning approaches (i) to label each post as cybersecurity-relevant or irrelevant; (ii) to count the number of cybersecurity keywords mentioned in each post; and (iii) to measure the similarity of each post compared with contemporaneous content generated by cybersecurity professionals. By adopting a difference-indifferences (DID) approach, we found that CMA enforcement generated significant chilling effects on users' contributions to cybersecurity-relevant topics in publicly accessible hack forums. That is, after CMA enforcement, users in the treatment group refrained from contributing to cybersecurity-relevant topics in both quantity and the extent of relevance.
Our empirical results substantiate the role of uncertainty as a key mechanism of the chilling effect. Our findings support that the different perception of uncertainty leads to a heterogeneous chilling effect among users. As Knightian decision theory suggests, those users with more past contributions and inertia to cybersecurityrelevant topics were less influenced by CMA enforcement than those with fewer past contributions. This lessened influence was also true of users whose historical contributions had higher intensive use of cybersecurity keywords. We further found the chilling effect was attenuated when they received more cybersecurityrelevant feedback from their peers in response to their own cybersecurity-relevant topics, suggesting a moderating effect of social learning. Furthermore, in response to increased uncertainty, users under CMA enforcement altered how they framed their posts by conforming with the contemporaneous content generated by cybersecurity professionals in online social and public media, by their self-categorization process, as explained by uncertaintyidentity theory. Interestingly, in facing increased uncertainty, although both knowledge acquisition and provision activities were chilled by the CMA enforcement in terms of both leading posts and replies, the effect was slightly greater on acquisition than on provision.
Our study makes important theoretical and empirical contributions to the literature of law enforcement and cybersecurity policy. Departing from the literature that focused on a cost-benefit perspective to qualitatively address the chilling effect in terms of the fear of privacy harm and at an aggregate level (Marthews and Tucker 2017), we empirically confirmed the presence of the chilling effect as the fear of legal harm and established a theoretical foundation to understand its additional mechanisms based on theories of psychology about the uncertainty of false prosecution. We provide new knowledge about how ambiguous legal enforcement and its associated uncertainty could suppress lawful or even socially desirable acts by considering heterogeneity across individuals and the dynamics of their social categorization. We are among the first to empirically address this chilling effect at an individual level, characterize the heterogeneity of the chilling effect, and identify the increasing similarity in online content generation. These findings reveal informational and normative influences on individuals tackling the uncertainty of false prosecution imposed by CMA enforcement. For policymakers in cybersecurity, our study provides empirical evidence of the chilling effect on the lawful activities that may be desirable for cybersecurity research amid an ongoing debate on how the current CMA can ameliorate its possible chilling effect on such activities.
The phrase chilling effect was first introduced in free speech adjudication in which individuals could be deterred by the fear of punishment and consequently refrain from speaking or publishing something that they lawfully could or even should (Schauer 1978). Unlike a deterrent effect, which is an intended outcome of legal enforcement against criminal acts, a chilling effect is considered unintended overdeterrence that disincentivizes activities not targeted by the law (Schauer 1978). Since the original legal and policy studies on the chilling effect of enforcement against defamation, obscenity, and incitement (Schauer 1978, Solove 2007), the academic interest in the chilling effect has moved to restrictions on Wang, Geng, and Kim: The Chilling Effect of Enforcement Information Systems Research, 2024, vol. 35, no. 3, pp. 1195-1215, © 2023 INFORMS online social media speech (Bedi 2021) and further extended into two separate fields: the fear of privacy harm caused by surveillance and data collection on the Internet (Kendrick 2012, Richards 2012, Stoycheff et al. 2019) and the fear of legal harm, the focus of our paper, caused by legislation (Katyal 2001, Kirsch 2014, Guinchard 2018). Schauer (1978) decomposes the uncertainty of the erroneous imposition of legal sanctions into two components. One is the fallibility and consequential uncertainty inherent in the legal process in judicially distinguishing between licit and illicit acts. The other is the formulation of legal rules according to the principle of comparative harm. Because the design of the legal system must balance between the two errors of wrongful conviction of the innocent and wrongful acquittal of the guilty, the principle of comparative harm means higher weightage will be given to the error considered most harmful. In the context of cybercrime, cybersecurity technology is characterized by fast innovation and its dual-use nature, which makes it difficult and costly to distinguish between the positive and negative variants of cybersecurity-relevant acts and to recognize and evaluate computer misuse tools in different circumstances (Katyal 2001). However, given the surging costs caused by the threats of cybercrimes and the deterrence's difficulty in prosecuting cybercriminals, many countries have enacted laws to criminalize the production, distribution, and possession of computer misuse tools (see Table B1 in Online Appendix B for a list of countries with CMA enforcement). With the rise of CMA enforcement as a major rule of law exercised by courts in cybersecurity related lawsuits, the decades-long concerns of policymakers are about its invidious chilling effect on preferred societal values. Recognition of CMA enforcement as a double-edged sword can be traced back to the United Kingdom's failed attempts to gain recognition of vulnerability research as a legal activity before the Computer Misuse Bill of 1990 (Guinchard 2018). Such concerns remain significant and echoed in many countries, including the United Kingdom and United States in recent years (Government 2021). 4  Despite its importance and implications for policymakers in cyber criminology (Kirsch 2014, Guinchard 2018), no chilling effect of CMA enforcement has ever been empirically substantiated. Most empirical evidence of chilling effects is associated with the fear of privacy harm caused by government surveillance and online data collection (Kendrick 2012, Richards 2012, Stoycheff et al. 2019) rather than the fear of legal harm caused by legislation (Penney 2022). Probably because of the challenge of finding suitable control groups, existing empirical studies either investigated the chilling effect at an aggregate level (Marthews and Tucker 2017) or collected evidence through surveys (Gamero-Garrido et al. 2017) or laboratory experiments with hypothetical restrictions (Bedi 2021). Instead of using a traditional DID approach, they created a hypothetical control group that included acts (not individual users) of no legal or policy concern. Therefore, the chilling effects were identified through significant changes in the acts that were related but not targeted by the law, relative to irrelevant acts marked as a hypothetical control group. As mentioned by Bedi (2021, p. 270), the existence of chilling effect as the fear of legal harm has "gone unanswered for over seventy years." Therefore, our study takes a DID approach and aims to substantiate the chilling effect more precisely at the user level by incorporating forums in the same category, but in different jurisdictional locations, as treatment and control groups, respectively.
As for the theoretical foundation, most previous studies on the chilling effect are rooted in RCT and incorporate the uncertainty of false prosecution as a potential cost into individuals' rational decisions on lawful acts (Katyal 1996(Katyal , 2001;;Marthews and Tucker 2017). Consistent with the literature, we expected CMA enforcement to reduce users' contributions on cybersecurity-relevant topics in publicly accessible hack forums because the possibility of being falsely penalized will translate into a potential cost that offsets any benefit from contributing knowledge and techniques. However, the prediction of a chilling effect solely based on RCT is limited in providing policy insights because we do not know to what extent the uncertainty of being falsely prosecuted will translate into a potential cost in an individual's utility function. As Penney (2022Penney ( , p. 1462) noted, "perhaps due to the multi-disciplinary nature of the phenomena and difficulties of exploring it empirically, there still remains a clear dearth in systematic theoretical and empirical work on" its existence and a comprehensive understanding of it. Hence, we have extended the theoretical foundation for substantiating the chilling effect by applying theories in psychology that have long established that the more uncertain a person is about a situation, decision, or other course of action, the likelier that person will seek out informational and normative influences to decide how to act or behave and conform her or his behavior accordingly (Penney 2022). Specifically, we adopted Knightian decision theory and social learning theory to address individuals' heterogeneous responses to the uncertainty of false sanction and applied uncertainty-identity theory to address individuals' conformity undertaken to reduce this uncertainty.
In economics, Knightian uncertainty, which is distinct from risk, refers to a lack of quantifiable knowledge about a possible occurrence in contrast to the presence of quantifiable risk (e.g., with known probability distribution; Knight 1921). Knightian decision theory (KDT) is a rigorous formulation developed by Bewley (2002) based on a stream of research on Knightian uncertainty (Anscombe andAumann 1963, Williams 1976). In the presence of Knightian uncertainty, people are repelled by the vagueness of probabilities (Ellsberg 1961) and may obtain a set of subjective probabilities (Bewley 2002). KDT predicts individuals will choose the status quo option if they do not know the probability distributions over the outcomes of their contemplated conduct (Bewley 2002). Therefore, if there is any change in an external environment that induces uncertainty about the outcomes of their alternatives, an uncertainty averse Knightian decision maker would choose something other than the status quo only if an alternative action increases the expected payoff according to all the distributions (Bewley 2011). Otherwise, Knightian decision makers under increased uncertainty and ambiguous probabilities become indecisive and exhibit inertia (Bewley 2002, Sautua 2017) instead of taking action in response to the environmental change.
The assumption of uncertainty aversion and inertia implied in KDT has been evidenced by scientific experiments (Ellsberg 1961, Sautua 2017) and widely used in explaining puzzling economic phenomena (Bewley 2002), investor behavior during financial panic (Basili 2001, Caballero 2010), and the unintended misjudgments in entrepreneurial activities (Bhide 2021). For example, when information is ambiguous and imprecise, market agents face Knightian uncertainty instead of risk, and their aversion to such uncertainty can lead to portfolio inertia (Basili 2001, Caballero 2010).
We applied KDT to address users' heterogeneity in dealing with the chilling effect induced by CMA enforcement in publicly accessible hack forums. In our research context, CMA enforcement is an incident that changes the probability distribution of outcomes for users' contributions, but with uncertainty and ambiguity in being falsely penalized for legitimate cybersecurity-relevant posts. Although the rational response to CMA enforcement based on RCT is to reduce their contributions and to avoid a chance of false prosecution in general, because the probability distribution of outcomes is unknown and ambiguous, Knightian decision makers may exhibit inertia by which they have a tendency of choosing a status quo option by taking no action in response to CMA enforcement. Thus, although the CMA enforcement as an outside incident reduces contributions because of its chilling effect, the opposing force will be inertia because of the uncertainty in outcomes of their changed actions. Users in publicly accessible hack forums are characterized by histories of different contributions on cybersecurityrelevant topics in terms of quantity and intensive use of cybersecurity keywords. Heavy contributors, with stronger inertia in terms of the quantity and intensive use of cybersecurity keywords, tend to continue their contributive behaviors as before. By contrast, light contributors, less influenced by inertia, would reduce their contributions more. 5
CMA enforcement implies individuals must make inferences about the uncertainty of false penalization based on private (only available to an individual) and public (available to all individuals) information. Social learning theory (SLT) provides insights on how hack forum users tackle a sense of fear and the uncertainty resulting from false punishment based on informational cascades from the public. According to SLT, individuals can directly observe how a person or group behaves in different situations or in response to actions they take, and in turn update their predictions about the uncertainty of outcomes resulting from their contemplated acts. Specifically, they tend to narrow the distribution of subsequent expectations about their motives and likely actions if the newly collected evidence is consistent with their prior experience (FeldmanHall and Shenhav 2019).
In our research context, forum users received various replies from their peers in response to their cybersecurityrelevant topics. As these users received more cybersecurityrelevant comments, both positive and negative, on their contributions, they would be able to learn more about what is considered more or less legitimate. This observational social learning through interactions with other members reinforces the authors' confidence in their assessments of the legitimacy of their contributions and hence alleviates their perceived uncertainty of false penalization. Their uncertainty may be further attenuated by observing other hack forum users' active contributions to cybersecurityrelevant discussions. Therefore, we expect the chilling effect of CMA enforcement will weaken when individuals receive more cybersecurity-relevant replies on their own cybersecurity topics or when they observe increasing quantity and relevance of cybersecurity-related discussions.
Uncertainty-identity theory (UIT) (Hogg 2007(Hogg , 2012) ) concerns how individuals under feelings of self-uncertainty reduce their perceived uncertainty through group identification, "the process of identifying with a group that a person imitates its features and objectives" in social psychology (Sam 2013). It posits that individuals are motivated to reduce uncertainty and protect themselves. Identifying with a "entitative" group, via social categorization process of self and others, is an effective way of uncertainty reduction through cognitive internalization of the group as a prototype of how one should behave (Hogg 2012). This process becomes more effective when the group has high entitativity with distinctiveness and clear structure (Hogg 2012). UIT has been applied to various decision-making processes, including the context of individuals' compliance behaviors with legal enforcement under uncertainty (Bradford et al. 2015).
In the context of cybersecurity, group identification in publicly accessible hacker forums would be achieved by categorizing themselves as a certain type of hackers. If
Wang, Geng, and Kim: The Chilling Effect of Enforcement Information Systems Research, 2024, vol. 35, no. 3, pp. 1195-1215, © 2023 INFORMS they are associated with legitimate users who wish to comply with CMA enforcement, they are likely to identify with the prototype of cybersecurity professionals. Such prototypical members are usually those in leadership and function as a reliable source of information (Hogg 2012). Following UIT, industry-or governmentsponsored cybersecurity professionals and researchers often collaborate with the government and are recognized as an important workforce to protect network and information systems from cyberattacks; with its high entitativity as the white hat, contrary to the gray or black hats who are considered the perpetrators of cybersecurity. Thus, the group identification process in the context of hack forums is a process of conforming with the positive expectations of the authorities, as represented by the content generated by the white hats. When cybersecurity professionals share with the public the most recent cybersecurity threats and hacking techniques, they are more likely to be considered protection oriented, and thus their acts have legal protection. Therefore, for forum users who still choose to contribute to cybersecurityrelevant topics after CMA enforcement, they are likely to purposely write in a way similar to the content published by cybersecurity professionals to increase their chances of being identified as members of the group and consequently reduce their uncertainty over false sanctions. Thus, we expect, after CMA enforcement, cybersecurityrelevant contributions on hack forums to be written to resemble the content published by cybersecurity professionals.
in China On February 28, 2009, the government of China enacted Amended Article 285 in the criminal law. It states, "Any person who provides programs or instruments used specially for invading or illegally controlling computer information systems, or knowingly provides programs or instruments to another person for committing illegal or criminal acts of invading or illegally controlling computer information systems shall, if the circumstances are serious, be punished in accordance with the provisions of the preceding paragraph." Enforcement of this amendment had a widespread and substantial impact on publicly accessible hack forums in China. Internet security agencies there monitored online hack forums and arrested some forum administrators for alleged violations.
The most difficult challenge faced under CMA enforcement by hack forum users who tried to participate in forums within the scope of the act was the failure of the act to distinguish between criminal and ethical hacking. Because an effective defense against cyberattacks relies on a thorough understanding of perpetrators' techniques and mindsets (Grimes 2017), hack forum users often discuss cybersecurity-relevant exploits and techniques. However, the rapid advancement of new techniques and the dual-use nature of cybersecurity technology, makes it hard to distinguish between malicious and protection-oriented intent and predict potential cybersecurity threats associated with these discussions. Thus, many in the industry believe that "the hacking offenses under the Computer Misuse Act are too 'broad brush'," making it technically impossible to perform ethical hacking against cybercriminals (McCallion 2021). Because CMA enforcement imposes the uncertainty of false prosecution on any cybersecurity-related discussions, we are concerned about its chilling effect on the contributions of cybersecurity-relevant content-specifically, those contributions that were not the intended targets of these cybersecurity laws.
To investigate the chilling effect of CMA enforcement at an individual level, we chose users from two representative publicly accessible hack forums (called Hackbase and 2cto 6 hereafter) in China as the treatment group. As our control group, we chose users from hackforums.net 7 , one of the most visited English language hack forums on the Internet. We selected these three forums because other higher-ranked forums are less focused on hacking or cybersecurity or began operating much later, rendering them incapable of providing a balanced longitudinal data set with sufficiently long intervals before and after enforcement of the Amended Article 285.
We collected all the posts created in the three forums from May 2007 8 to March 2011 (205 weeks). 9 During that period, 50,050 users who created at least one thread before CMA enforcement were selected as target users for DID analysis. We measured two aspects of cybersecurityrelevant discussions on these forums: (1) whether a post contains explicit or implicit references to, or discussion about, cybersecurity techniques; and (2) the extent of cybersecurity relevance as measured by the number of cybersecurity-relevant keywords. Thus, we could examine whether a chilling effect existed by comparing the legitimate discussions on hack forums with respect to the quantity of cybersecurity-relevant leading posts and the extent of their relevance to cybersecurity techniques before and after CMA enforcement. To ensure the two Chinese forums and the one English forum are eligible for a DID-based study of a chilling effect, they had to satisfy the following conditions.
First, the user-generated content shared in the two Chinese forums must be legitimate and thus should not be targeted by CMA enforcement. Indeed, the two Chinese forums remained active during our study period while legal authorities had suspended similar forums because of violations of the CMA. 10 According to news reports, as of September 22, 2009, and May 8, 2010, respectively, Hackbase and 2cto removed any posts (including those posted before February 28, 2009) that might be considered illegal under the CMA. To further demonstrate their thorough compliance with the CMA, both forums have formal policies that ban any usergenerated content that violates the law.
However, because of the inherent challenge of ex ante adjudication of the malice and severity of hacking tools pertaining to CMA enforcement, it is impossible for even legal agencies or forum administrators to accurately define a clear-cut demarcation between legal and illegal posts. Nevertheless, a safe inference derived from the posts we crawled from the two Chinese forums at the end of 2014 is that they are not targeted by the CMA, given the substantial implementation by legal agencies and the active compliance undertaken at the forum level. Although the self-screening imposed at the forum level may interfere with the measurement of individuals' initial contributions on the two forums, the interference was randomly imposed on content contributed either before or after CMA enforcement. Furthermore, by examining the average extent of relevance to cybersecurity and the quantity, we can reduce the bias resulting from any possible systematic difference imposed on content by forum administrators before and after the CMA enforcement because the extent of relevance is unlikely to be affected by any self-screening. Overall, the nature of content in both forums ensures our study investigates content not directly targeted by the government, and any reduction in contributions after the CMA enforcement could be attributed to the chilling effect.
Second, the English forum should be similar to the two Chinese forums in every aspect except CMA enforcement. Hackforums.net, which is owned by a U.S. citizen, is one of the largest English forums dedicated to hacking discussions on the Internet. It has servers hosted in India and has contributors from more than 38 countries. The English forum was beyond the radar of any domestic CMA enforcement because of its server location. Any user from anywhere (except China) could freely access the English forum. This is contrary to the situation of users in the treatment group in China who were limited by a language barrier and the government-sponsored Internet filter-the Great Firewall-from joining overseas hacking communities or the darknet. Those same barriers made it difficult for foreign users to join these forums. 11 This ensures that most users in Chinese forums, unlike in the English forum, were within the jurisdictional scope of CMA enforcement. However, the three forums are similar in that they remained active during our study period and were classified into the hacking subcategory under Computers/Security by Alexa.com, making the English forum a reasonable control group.
To measure the quantity and the extent of relevance to cybersecurity in hack forum discussions, we first trained a convolutional neural network (CNN) model and a long short-term memory (LSTM) model to identify cybersecurity-relevant posts that are presumed to be affected after CMA enforcement. We manually labeled about 20% of all leading posts along four dimensions: cybersecurity-relevant or not; knowledge acquisition or not; knowledge provision or not; money-involved or not. The classifier was trained on the training data set (80% of the coded posts) and the classification performance was evaluated based on 10-fold cross-validation from the testing data set (the remaining 20%). 12 The two validated classifiers were then applied to automatically classify all the posts. We aggregated the prediction results of the LSTM and CNN models and resolved the inconsistencies with manual screening, which resulted in final labels for all posts in the hack forums.
To enhance the specificity of our analysis, we further extracted keywords and measured the extent of intensive use of cybersecurity keywords in each post based on multiple glossaries of cybersecurity terminology. For all the posts in the full data set, the stop words, underlinings, punctuation, numbers, and spaces in the content were first removed. Then the N-gram stemming procedure was performed on each post's content, in which n � {1, 2, 3}. All the stemmed words were reassembled as a spacedelimited text for keyword extraction (Porter 1980). We adopted a knowledge-based approach to extract cybersecurity keywords in each post based on the following three collections of keywords commonly used in the cybersecurity industry. The first source (noted as "src1") is the glossary of cybersecurity terms published by Sys-Admin, Audit, Network, and Security (SANS), 13 a cybersecurity training institute, and by National Initiative for Cybersecurity Careers and Studies, 14 a cybersecurity agency. The second source (noted as "src2") is a dictionary of information security terms, abbreviations, and acronyms by Calder and Watkins (2007). The third source (noted as "src3") is a database of publicly disclosed cybersecurity vulnerabilities compiled since 1999 by a common vulnerabilities and exposures (CVE) program.
All the terminologies from the three sources were translated into Chinese by senior cybersecurity professionals to accommodate keyword extraction from the Chinese forums. 15 The three terminology dictionaries capture the different aspects of emerging cybersecurity techniques and threats. Each word in the posts was compared with the three dictionary files, and the count of keywords in each post corresponding to each terminology source was calculated to measure the extent of relevance to cybersecurity in hack forum discussions. The details of the supervised classification scheme, keyword extraction steps, and theoretical justifications are reported in Online Appendix A.
To investigate a chilling effect of CMA enforcement on cybersecurity-relevant discussions in hack forums, we constructed a panel data set at the user-week level between May 2007 and March 2011. We included only authors who created at least one thread before the start of CMA enforcement on February 28, 2009, and further trimmed the data set to include balanced observation periods before and after the event for each author. 16  Within each thread, we distinguished between leading posts and replies to it. For each post, we collected information on the date it was posted, the number of replies from viewers (i.e., num_replies); content classification based on the four dimensions (i.e., is_cybersecurityrelevant, is_knowledge_acquisition, is_knowledge_ provision, and is_money-involved); and the number of cybersecurity keywords matched with the three glossary sources (i.e., src1_keyword_counts_per_post, src2_key-word_counts_per_post, and src3_keyword_counts_per_ post). From May 2007 to March 2011, the users in our data set composed 252,742 threads. Users in the Chinese and English hack forums contributed 151,082 (59.78%) and 101,660 (40.22%) threads, respectively (see Table B2 in Online Appendix B for summary statistics of content features at the leading post level for each forum).
All the post-level features were aggregated to the user-week level to construct a panel data set. We constructed two groups of outcome variables per user per week to measure the quantity of cybersecurity-relevant leading posts and the extent of relevance to cybersecurity among leading posts contributed weekly by each user. The first group involved the number of cybersecurity-relevant leading posts generated by each user per week (i.e., num_security_posts), and the proportion of such overall leading posts generated by each user per week (i.e., perc_secpost 17 ). The second group measured the extent of relevance to cybersecurity in hack forum discussions based on the three terminology dictionaries discussed above. Referring to each terminology dictionary, we calculated the average number of cybersecurity keywords contained in each leading post over all leading posts contributed by each user and then used its logarithm transformation as a dependent variable in regression (i.e., src1_keyword_counts, src2_keyword_ counts, and src3_keyword_counts). Then, we compared the change in the mean value of each output variable before and after CMA enforcement for all forums, as reported in Table B3 in Online Appendix B. It shows generally decreasing time trends in the quantity of cybersecurity-relevant contributions and in the extent of cybersecurity relevance in all forums. However, the Chinese forums consistently exhibit 27%-34% steeper drop across all the output variables compared with the English forum, which implies a potentially systematic impact after CMA enforcement. The correlations among outcome variables are reported in Table B4 in Online Appendix B for Chinese and English forums, respectively. The withingroup correlation is much higher than the between-group correlation (i.e., quantity versus relevance), indicating the two groups of variables measure relatively distinct dimensions.
Figure 1 provides model-free evidence of the chilling effect via the monthly trends of the number of cybersecurity-relevant leading posts and the number of cybersecurity keywords (referring to Source 1) contributed by users in the control and treatment groups. It shows that the preintervention trends are very similar between the treatment and control groups, but the trends of the treatment group drop significantly after CMA enforcement. Similar trends can be found by referring to a cybersecurity dictionary from Source 2 or Source 3.
To control for general trends in the content-generation behavior of hack forum users, we added into our model a list of control variables at the per user and the per week levels. We measured weekly for each user the number of weeks since the user posted her first leading post in a forum (i.e., auth_life); her contributions (as measured by the cumulative number of leading posts with respect to each category; the cumulative number of cybersecurity keywords referring to each source of dictionaries); the feedback she received from her peers in response to their own cybersecurity-relevant leading posts (as measured by the cumulative number of replies control treatment with respect to each category; and by the cumulative number of cybersecurity keywords contained in replies). Similar contribution and feedback variables were also generated weekly at the forum level. Tables B5a-B5d in Online Appendix B present the description and summary statistics of all variables derived from the panel data.
We relied on a DID model to estimate the impact of CMA enforcement on the quantity of cybersecurityrelevant leading posts and the extent of relevance to cybersecurity. We adopted the two categories of dependent variables to provide a full picture of the chilling effect of CMA enforcement in different dimensions. Table 1 shows the estimation results. Across columns (1)-( 5) of Table 1, all DID estimators are negative and significant. These results indicate the number of cybersecurity-relevant discussions, the percentage of cybersecurity-relevant discussions, and the average weekly count of cybersecurity keywords per post decreased significantly after the CMA enforcement in the treatment group compared with those in the control group. These decreases in the treatment group in both the quantity and the extent of relevance of cybersecurity topics imply the presence of a significant chilling effect among hack forum users after CMA enforcement. 18
We performed a set of robustness checks, including alternative explanations of the decreases in cybersecurityrelevant discussions because of an environmental disturbance, selection bias, confounding effect of other cybersecurity-relevant events, the parallel trends assumption, and the survival bias because of possible censorship by forum administrators after CMA enforcement.
To measure the policy's effects, it is necessary to control for other environmental disturbances that may have affected the discussion of cybersecurity issues. Because cyberattacks are borderless, discussions in Chinese and English hack Next, it is also possible that CMA legislative efforts by other governments might have driven users to migrate to Hackforums.net. To account for this possibility, we collected CMA enforcement efforts in countries that were sources of the traffic on the English hack forum as reported by Alexa (see Table B1 in Online Appendix B for a summary of CMA enforcement actions during our observation period). We compiled an integrated enforcement effort index by linearly combining the list of CMA enforcement indicators in each country and applying the traffic originating from each country over the total traffic to Hackforums.net as weightage (see the traffic statistics reported in Table B13 in Online Appendix B). Then, we added the integrated enforcement effort index and its interaction with the control group indicator (denoted as Eng × Effort). Our results in Table B14 show that the chilling effect of CMA enforcement remains negative and significant after controlling for the legislative efforts by other countries. The coefficient for Eng × Effort is insignificant, implying that our results were not affected by the CMA enforcement efforts occurring in other countries. 23
As a fundamental identification assumption of the DID approach, the treatment and comparison groups should share the same trends but possibly different levels of pretreatment outcomes (Angrist and Pischke 2008). Violation of this assumption implies the untreated group is not a valid control, leading to a biased estimate. We used a relative time model (Autor 2003) extensively used in the literature (Chan and Ghose 2014, Bapna and Umyarov 2015, Greenwood and Wattal 2017). This model allowed us to evaluate the parallel trends assumption and to ascertain how long it takes for any effect of CMA enforcement to manifest. The relative time model replaces the vector of CMA t with a series of time dummies that denote the chronological distance between our observation period, t, and the date of CMA enforcement. To alleviate the many confounding effects over a long time period, we collapsed the leads or lags of CMA enforcement beyond seven months into a single dummy.
Using this procedure, we estimated the coefficients for the leads and lags of the treatment effect on all outcome variables based on the full sample (column (1) in Figure 2) along with the PSM matched sample (column (2) in Figure 2). 24 Although one pretreatment term is significant (t � 7) based on the full sample, they are few and far from the start of treatment. Additionally, the coefficients of pretreatment periods based on the PSM matched sample do not differ statistically from zero, which indicates parallel trends. This test indicates that the parallel trends assumption is satisfied and the DID approach is likely valid. In addition, the coefficients in the postshock period are negative and significant, which signifies that the impact of CMA enforcement occurs after the shock. Even more revealing, the figure shows the negative effect based on the PSM-matched sample has not shrunk in magnitude over time, suggesting that the persistent chilling effect. 25 4.2.5. Moderation by Users and Forums. Because our data set was collected in 2014, some posts might have been removed by users and forum administrators in the Chinese forums. However, we believe this does not harm our estimation unless the Chinese forums more arduously removed their posts contributed after the CMA enforcement than those contributed before it. This is unlikely because the posts contributed before the CMA enforcement are also subject to the CMA enforcement if they are publicly accessible. Furthermore, this feature of the data set, if it exists, actually helps us focus on the contributions not directly targeted by the law enforcement and measure the chilling effect. Nevertheless, we performed a robustness check. In both the Chinese and English forums, we noted that the content in some leading posts were emptied by forum administrators because of violation of the forums' moderation rules. Although we cannot be sure all the "censored" leading posts were moderated because of concerns for CMA prosecution, we used these empty

Specifically, based on a DID approach, we checked (1) whether the censorship on Chinese forums has significantly shifted before and after CMA, compared with the English forum at both the forum and user levels, and (2) whether our results might change if we included these censored posts into our main dependent variable, cybersecurityrelevant leading posts. We confirmed that the possible censorship by administrators after CMA did not introduce bias and that the chilling effect remains significant when the censored posts are included (see Online Appendix D for more details).
Given the large data set used for our main analysis, one possible concern is that the significance might have been driven by a large sample size. Therefore, we report the coefficient/p-value/ sample-size (CPS) charts, as suggested by Lin et al. (2013), in Figures B3 andB4 of Online Appendix B, displaying the two-sided 95% confidence intervals of the net chilling effects alongside the increasing sample size. For instance, the net chilling effect at individual and weekly level remains significant even when the sample size is reduced to 20% of the full sample.
We conducted three falsification tests to assess any spurious correlations in our analysis. First, we replaced the number of cybersecurity-relevant leading posts with the number of cybersecurity-irrelevant leading posts. If our results were driven by other unobserved contemporaneous events, we would observe the same results for this alternative dependent variable. As shown in Table B15 in Online Appendix B, CMA enforcement had no influence on cybersecurity-irrelevant leading posts.
Second, we repeated the main tests using the number of money-involved discussions as an alternative dependent variable. Hacking-related transactions are recognized as the most salient offenses against CMA because of their monetary intent for hacking; hence, they have been banned in Chinese forums. Thus, the remaining money-involved discussions in Chinese forums were general transactions for information technology-related products or services. Furthermore, with money-involved posts, contributors' intent is easier to judge. When the posts involve suspicious activities with monetary incentives, they will be easily distinguished as to whether they are a direct infringement of CMA, thus leading to a relatively lower "uncertainty" of false penalization. Therefore, because increased uncertainty of false prosecution under CMA enforcement is the key mechanism of the chilling effect, money-involved lawful posts are less likely to be chilled by CMA enforcement. 26 Specifically, we tried the number and percentage of money-involved leading posts generated per user in each week as dependent variables. The results show CMA enforcement had no impact on money-involved discussions, unlike its impact on cybersecurity-relevant discussions (see Table B16 in Online Appendix B).
Third, we performed a placebo test by randomly assigning users from the three hack forums as treated users. Specifically, we randomly applied our treatment to 43,322 users in our data, which corresponds to the number of actual treated observations, to create a pseudo-treatment for a placebo test. We regressed the same dependent variables as in Equation ( 1) on the constructed pseudotreatment indicator. We then stored the estimated coefficient of this pseudo-treatment and replicated this procedure 1,000 times. This placebo test helps us assess the potential spuriousness of any significant results that arise from autocorrelations in the dependent variable (Bertrand et al. 2004). Moreover, it provides a reliability check against outliers (Burtch et al. 2018). We visualized the kernel density estimate (Jones 1993, Jann 2005) of the regression t value of the pseudo-treatment variable in Figure B2 in Online Appendix B. If the distribution is a symmetrically inverted U-shape with zero as the axis, it indicates the pseudo-treatment variable has no treatment effect on outcome variables. The results are presented in Table B17 in Online Appendix B. It shows the estimated average β associated with the randomly assigned treatment does not differ significantly from zero. Therefore, our main results are reliably estimated, and the estimated β is not driven by serial correlation in the standard errors.
We further conducted three tests that delve into the different perceptions of uncertainty as a main mechanism that helps refine the heterogenous effect and the nature of the chilling effect. In the first test, we considered the moderating effect of behavioral inertia in the presence of Knightian uncertainty by examining whether the inertia of choosing the status quo may partially offset the chilling effect of CMA enforcement. In the second test, we applied SLT to verify whether peers' feedback in cybersecurity-relevant discussions reduces a focal user's perceived uncertainty and then mitigates the chilling effect. In the third test, we examined whether CMA enforcement may lead hack forum users to create content more similar to content generated by cybersecurity professionals. Such behavior, according to UIT, is regarded as individuals' conforming efforts to reduce uncertainty. In addition to these tests, we examined what types of contributions are chilled, which helps gain a comprehensive understanding of the chilling effect in hack forums.
Although the rational response to CMA enforcement based on RCT is to reduce users' contributions and avoid a chance of false prosecution, because the probability distribution of outcomes is unknown and ambiguous, KDT (Bewley 2002(Bewley , 2011;;Alvarez and Christensen 2021) suggests users are likely to exhibit inertia through a tendency to choose the status quo. We created four variables (Z it ) that measure the status quo (or prior experience) of each user regarding content contributions in terms of quantity and relevance-that is, the cumulative number of cybersecurity-relevant leading posts as of t � 1 and the cumulative number of cybersecurity keywords referring to Sources 1-3 as of t � 1 (see Table B18 in Online Appendix B for the descriptive statistics of all variables introduced in this section). We reran the main DID model with one of the four variables used as a moderator for a three-way interaction with the chilling effect indicator Treat i × CMA t (Meyer 1995). The moderating variables took a logarithmic form to eliminate the distraction of the heterogeneous frequency of content contribution. The coefficients for the DID estimator (β 6 ) and three-way interaction term (β 7 ) from each regression are reported in Table 2. The results suggest users' experiences with cybersecurity-relevant contributions exhibited inertia in their corresponding content contributions. Taking as an example the moderating effect of the cumulative number of cybersecurity-relevant leading posts, users in the treatment group who created relatively more cybersecurity-relevant leading posts before CMA enforcement also contributed more of them after enforcement (Table 2, Panel A), whereas the main chilling effect remains significant, exhibiting a prominent effect size of 1.9%, which is considerably larger compared with the net effect reported in column (1) of Table 1. We observed similar patterns for the percentage of cybersecurityrelevant leading posts and the extent of relevance to cybersecurity (Table 2, Panels B-D). These results offer support for the presence of behavioral inertia in contributions, which mitigates the chilling effect of CMA enforcement. Such differential effects among users also explain the smaller net chilling effect size as observed in our main models.
In addition to their adopting the status quo, indecisive users in hack forums may make inferences about the possibility of false penalization under CMA enforcement by learning from their peers. Applying SLT to the context of hack forums, users' perceived uncertainty of false  , 2024, , vol. 35, no. 3, pp. 1195, -1215, , © 2023 INFORMS INFORMS punishment could be affected by information cascades from the public. Specifically, the concern about such uncertainty could be alleviated through social learning processes in which users receive cybersecurity-relevant replies to their own cybersecurity-relevant topics from other forum users (i.e., feedback from peers). We aggregated the cumulative cybersecurity-relevant replies until week t � 1, which responded to a user's cybersecurityrelevant leading posts generated as of week t � 1, and created four variables that measure the social learning effect received by this user in terms of quantity and relevance (i.e., the number of cybersecurity-relevant replies 27 and the total number of cybersecurity keywords (referring to src1, src2, and src3) mentioned in these replies), relative to the cumulative number of cybersecurityrelevant leading posts the user created as of week t � 1.
The newly created four variables took a logarithmic form to eliminate the distraction of heterogeneous user activity and were used as a moderator for the threeway interaction with the chilling effect indicator.
As for the moderating effect of peer feedback, most coefficients for the three-way interaction term are positive and significant in Table 3, indicating the chilling effect of CMA enforcement was attenuated when users received more cybersecurity-relevant replies or replies with intensive use of cybersecurity keywords to their cybersecurity-relevant leading posts. Moreover, we observed that such a moderating effect is consistent for dependent variables about quantity and the relevance of cybersecurity contributions. This indicates the moderating effect is driven by a decrease in perceived uncertainty about the outcomes of users' various forms of contributions on cybersecurity-relevant topics. 28 In summary, social learning by peer users' feedback alleviated a user's perceived uncertainty about the erroneous imposition of legal sanctions, which in turn partially offset the chilling effect.
An alternative option to remaining silent is for hack forum users to reduce their uncertainty of being falsely penalized by conforming their behavior with the positive expectations from the authorities (Penney 2022). Such a normative influence is consistent with UIT that suggests users may boost their confidence about avoiding spurious prosecution if they make their contemplated cybersecurity discussions resemble content created by government-or industry-sponsored cybersecurity professionals whose mission is to protect information systems from cyberattacks (Guinchard 2018).
To measure the similarity of each leading post to contemporaneous content generated by cybersecurity professionals, we referred to reputational cybersecurity archives generated by cybersecurity professionals from two sources, the Diary Archive provided by SANS Internet Storm Center (ISC) 29 and the Internet Security Threat Reports provided by Symantec. 30 The SANS ISC, which is considered one of the largest and most-trusted resources for security training and research, provides a daily Handler Diary that summarizes and analyzes Internet security events and updates professionals and businesses about the latest and most pressing threats. Symantec publishes its annual reports of Internet security threats that have become vital resources for industry professionals and researchers in understanding trends in cybersecurity threats on the Internet. It is reasonable to compare the leading posts in Chinese hack forums to contemporaneous content generated by cybersecurity professionals published by English authorities, because in China the normative cybersecurity education, professional training, and sharing of cybersecurity information at the national level are highly synchronized with the oversea English communities. 31 We calculated the cosine similarity scores (called ISC_similarity and Symantec_similarity) by comparing, respectively, the content of each leading post with the pool of ISC diaries published within the same month and with the Symantec threat reports published in the same year. Cosine similarity scores have been widely used in text analysis to measure document similarity (Han et al. 2012).
Unlike the measurement using the number of cybersecurity keywords, cosine similarity measures the cosine of the angle between the term-frequency vectors of two documents in an inner product space. This measurement determines whether the two vectors are pointing in roughly the same direction. We reran the main DID tests using the similarity scores as dependent variables. The results reported in Table 4 indicate a positive and significant effect of CMA enforcement on content similarity with these cybersecurity professional archives. The CMA enforcement induces on average an increase of 0.000161 and 0.000127 in the similarity with ISC dairies for each user per week (column (1)) and Symantec threat reports for each user per week (column (2)) in Table 4, respectively. Given that the average ISC and Symantec similarities before CMA enforcement were 0.000482 and 0.000220, respectively, the content similarity with the two cybersecurity professional archives increased by 33.4% and by 57.7%, respectively. This is consistent with our presumption that individuals may adapt their behavior to conform more closely with the information of beliefs provided by or inferred from legal or government authorities (i.e., examples from cybersecurity professionals). The shift in content similarity supports a strong argument that the underlying mechanism of the chilling effect stems not just from a fear of erroneous judgment but more about its uncertainty. The uncertainty and ambiguity associated with the legal standards would lead people to interpret legal standards in light of what is recognized by legal or government authorities (Penney 2022). Hence, the chilling effect is not simply selfcensoring to avoid a legal harm but also involves making efforts to conform to reduce the uncertainty of false prosecution.
To gain a more comprehensive understanding of the chilling effect on hack forum users, we further investigated what types of contributions are being chilled. Based on our classification scheme, leading posts can be related to knowledge acquisition, knowledge provision, both, or neither. By applying the same algorithms, we also classified users' replies to cybersecurity-relevant leading posts and tried alternative dependent variables, including the number of cybersecurity-relevant leading posts for knowledge acquisition or knowledge provision and the number of replies to cybersecurity-relevant posts, the number of cybersecurity-relevant replies for knowledge acquisition or knowledge provision. Our results in Table 5 show CMA enforcement had a chilling effect on both knowledge acquisition and provision in terms of leading posts (columns (1) and ( 2)) and replies (columns (3) and ( 4)), implying a broad impact on legitimate knowledge-sharing activities. The effect was slightly greater on acquisition than on knowledge provision behavior, regardless of leading posts or replies. The possible explanation is that users who posted for knowledge acquisition are more likely to be junior hackers with less expertise on cybersecurity and hence higher perceived uncertainty about the malice of their contributing content, and thus were chilled to a greater extent. Such a difference confirms again the different perceptions of uncertainty as a main mechanism that leads to the heterogeneity of chilling effects among individuals.
Our study, through a quasi-experiment, aimed to overcome the challenges faced by existing research on measuring any chilling effects of CMA enforcement and its mechanisms from the perspective of individuals' perceptions of uncertainty. First, our study used publicly accessible hack forums as a vantage point to observe users' subtle changes in cybersecurity-relevant knowledge sharing after CMA enforcement. The mobility of users of Chinese hack forums was constrained by language and architectural barriers. This was harder to achieve in studying the chilling effect of the U.S. government's surveillance (Marthews and Tucker 2017) of Internet users' search activities that are fluid and not trackable. Second, our study measured acts that were not targeted by the law in China but are nevertheless subjected to the uncertainty of being falsely penalized because of the dual-use nature of most cybersecurity technologies. Obviously, content hosted on the darknet or discussed via the Internet Relay Chat that has been studied in the literature (Benjamin et al. 2019, Li and Chen 2022, Samtani et al. 2022, Chan et al. 2023) is likelier to be targeted by law enforcement and hence is outside the scope of a chilling effect. Last, our study overcomes a lack of a valid control group by using an English hack forum. Probably because of the technology-focused interest across hacker communities and the highly synchronized knowledge base on cybersecurity, the Chinese and the English hack forums in this study share similar trends in their participants' contributions to cybersecurity-relevant topics before the CMA enforcement, thus legitimizing a DID approach.
We found that CMA enforcement provokes a significant chilling effect not only in the quantity of cybersecurity-relevant leading posts but also in terms of the extent of relevance to cybersecurity in publicly accessible hack forums. Although the scale of the chilling effect at an individual level is not as substantial as what has concerned researchers and policymakers (ENISA 2016), its aggregate impact on the provision and communication of cybersecurity techniques in online communities nevertheless warrants attention. Furthermore, the relatively small magnitude of the chilling effect on average is well explained by its heterogeneous impact across users, depending on how they perceive and address the uncertainty of the CMA enforcement. Interestingly, we also found that the chilling effect may have a broad impact on legitimate knowledge sharing because it tends to shrink both knowledge acquisition and provision in terms of leading posts and replies.
Departing from the literature that has taken a costbenefit perspective in addressing this potential chilling effect (Katyal 2001, Marthews andTucker 2017), we recognized that the essential difference of the chilling effect on lawful acts compared with its deterrent effect on illicit acts lies in the uncertainty of false prosecution (Roloff and Cloven 1990). If the chilling effect is driven by the uncertainty imposed by CMA enforcement, we should expect the chilling effect to differ in individuals' status quo as predicted by KDT (Bewley 2002(Bewley , 2011;;Alvarez and Christensen 2021) and differ in their interactions with peers on cybersecurity-relevant discussions as predicted by SLT (FeldmanHall and Shenhav 2019). Indeed, we found that for individuals with more historical contributions on cybersecurity-relevant topics, they remained with the status quo because of inertia, which partially offset the chilling effect of CMA enforcement. Similarly, for individuals who received more cybersecurity-relevant replies from their peers in response to their own cybersecurityrelevant leading posts, this very relevant feedback counteracted the chilling effect of CMA enforcement. If the chilling effect is driven by the uncertainty imposed by CMA enforcement, it will also affect how users contribute. We found that individuals who still chose to contribute to cybersecurity-relevant topics after CMA enforcement tried by 45.6% on average to write their posts in ways to increase their semantic similarity with the online content contributed by industry-or government-sponsored cybersecurity professionals. This is a social categorization process predicted by UIT. Behind such social categorization is the fear of false penalization if their framing and phrases do not fit the expectations of law enforcement or government authorities. This rising normativism in cybersecurity knowledge sharing has not been identified and formally addressed in the literature on the chilling effect. In addition, although CMA enforcement had a chilling effect on both knowledge acquisition and provision, the effect was slightly greater on acquisition than on provision, possibly because those who ask for knowledge perceive higher uncertainty about the malice of their content.
Our study provides important theoretical and empirical contributions to the literature of law enforcement and cybersecurity policy. We established a theoretical foundation to understand the mechanisms of a chilling effect at the individual level by applying theories about choice under uncertainty. Via this framework, we can break through the limitation of a cost-benefit perspective in tackling risks with unknown probability distributions of false penalization and, by considering the heterogeneity across individuals and the dynamics of their social categorization, derive new knowledge about how law enforcement could suppress lawful acts. Therefore, our study can help gain more granular insights by complementing RCT in understanding users' behavior in publicly accessible hack forums. These theoretical considerations also open new windows for research into the chilling effect by considering what aspects can be chilled and which factors affect the chilling effect.
We also believe our findings can contribute to the burgeoning empirical literature on the chilling effect. Compared with prior studies that tested for the chilling effect only at an aggregate level and with a focus on the fear of privacy harm rather than legal harm (Penney 2016, Marthews andTucker 2017), this study is, to the best of our knowledge, the first to examine the chilling effect in terms of the fear of legal harm at an individual level and in a context in which anonymity is relatively high. It delivers the initial empirical evidence of the chilling effect of CMA enforcement and of its mechanisms as driven by the uncertainty of false prosecution. Our findings suggest that CMA enforcement may deprive users of hack forums of incentives to communicate cybersecurity techniques and that such a chilling effect can affect the members of online communities differently. Our analysis also reveals the trend of social categorization in online communities toward cybersecurity professionals as an alternative way for individuals to reduce the uncertainty of being falsely penalized. This will serve as a starting point to incorporate a longstanding concern about a potential chilling effect into the system design of adjudication and cyber laws.
Our research findings can offer policymakers valuable insights on how to mitigate any unnecessary and undesirable uncertainty in CMA enforcement. First, policymakers should acknowledge the limitations of legal systems and initiate targeted deliberations within legal communities. This proactive approach will help develop additional legal cases to prevent false prosecutions in cybersecurity-related contexts. Second, our research demonstrates the significance of experience for decision makers grappling with unwanted uncertainty. In particular, policymakers may contemplate the implementation of tailored communication strategies aimed at less experienced professionals or students, which can alleviate uncertainty. By addressing the uncertainties surrounding enforcement and providing clear guidance on compliance, such targeted strategies can effectively reduce the chilling effect on legitimate knowledge-sharing activities. Furthermore, policymakers should consider market mechanisms and social norms alongside law enforcement. Our findings support the adoption of licensing, credibility tracking, and community recognition as supplementary measures for CMA enforcement. To directly address the chilling effect, policymakers should establish a neutral mechanism as a buffer between law enforcement and the user community. Such a mechanism could take the form of a panel comprising cybersecurity users, nongovernmental organizations, and other neutral parties who can evaluate if the tools were developed in good faith. This approach can provide a transparent and accountable process, ensuring that legal interpretations are consistent with the community's norms and values.
Our findings also offer guidance to forum administrators in addressing the chilling effect caused by CMA enforcement. Forum administrators can provide less experienced users with additional information and guidelines, helping them understand the enforcement process and avoid undue restraint. Because peers' feedback in cybersecurity-relevant discussions can reduce uncertainty and mitigate the chilling effect, it is advisable for forum administrators to foster a responsible and informative online environment. This approach will help mitigate any negative consequence of the chilling effect on knowledge-sharing activities. Because our study shows that CMA enforcement leads forum users to create content resembling that of cybersecurity professionals, forum administrators can provide resources and guidelines aligned with professional standards, which helps users more effectively navigate the uncertain legal landscape.
Our study is not without limitations. First, because estimation of a chilling effect is limited to the major publicly accessible hack forums, we were unable to observe whether legitimate cybersecurity-relevant posts possibly migrated to private underground channels. However, if they did, this still means they have been chilled from public forums and the cost of communicating cybersecurity techniques purposed for defense increases accordingly. Therefore, even when such migration to private channels occurs, we still consider it as a realization of a chilling effect. Second, we do not have the identities of the users on the forums we studied. Thus, we are unable to identify whether the same users use different user IDs in the two forums. However, because participants in publicly accessible hack forums have heightened dedication to meritocracy, most users, especially the more knowledgeable ones, are likely to maintain a single user ID. Furthermore, ID has been widely adopted to identify online users in the literature. Third, despite our robustness check, our proxy for removed leading posts may not capture all the moderations by users and forum administrators. Nevertheless, this feature of the data set, if it exists, actually helps us focus on the contributions that are not directly targeted by the law enforcement and measure the chilling effect. Fourth, the extent of the chilling effect may differ across the types of hacker communities. For example, a hack forum that does not strive for any form of legitimacy may not be chilled much by the CMA. Although the heterogeneity of hack forums is beyond the scope of this paper, it would be certainly interesting and important to examine such a differential impact in future research. Last, we were not able to find another hack forum with a closer location and the same language as our treated forums-but never subjected to CMA enforcement-to use as a control group. However, the results from our parallel trends analyses and PSM can alleviate concern about the control group and provide confidence on the causality. Further, it is unlikely that these two forums had the power to trigger CMA enforcement in China.
This study can be extended in two ways. First, the chilling effect of CMA enforcement can be examined in the context of a vulnerability investigation. Second, the effects of CMA enforcement can be studied in other countries and compared across different cultures and geographic locations. We believe the chilling effect deserves further investigation in the context of cybersecurity because a balance between deterrence and a chilling effect is crucial for cybersecurity. Cybersecurity professionals need to understand their adversaries' technology and mindsets to protect their systems and networks from ubiquitous attacks. When CMA enforcement blocks the communication of cybercriminals in publicly accessible online hack forums, it also blocks an easily accessible channel for cybersecurity professionals. Furthermore, enforcement may encourage individuals with malicious intent to take their communication into private channels or onto the darknet, increasing the information gap between perpetrators and defenders. An awareness of the risks in computer misuse should be protected and grow in an environment in which the uncertainty of false penalties can be minimized by leveraging the resources from legal agencies, communities, and public policies.

title: Excessive Dependence on Mobile Social Apps: A Rational Addiction Perspective
abstract: Drawing on the rational addiction framework, this study explores the digital vulnerabilities driven by depen dence on mobile social apps (e.g., social network sites and social games). Rational addicts anticipate the future consequences of their current behaviors and attempt to maximize utility from their intertemporal con sumption choices. Conversely, myopic addicts tend toward immediate gratification and fail to fully recognize the future consequences of their current consumption. In lieu of conducting self-report surveys or aggregate level demand estimation, this research examines addictive behaviors on the basis of consumption quantity at an individual level. To empirically validate rational addiction in the context of social app consumption, we collect and analyze 13-month, individual-level panel data on the weekly app usage of thousands of smartphone users. Results indicate that the average social app user conducts herself in a forward-looking manner and ratio nally adjusts consumption over time to derive optimal utility. The subgroup analysis, however, indicates that substantial variations in addictiveness and forward-looking propensities exist across demographically diverse groups. For example, addictive behaviors toward social network sites are more myopic in nature among older, less-educated, high-income groups. Additionally, the type of social app moderates the effects of demographic characteristics on the nature of addictive behaviors. We provide implications that policymakers can use to effec tively manage mobile addiction problems, with the recommendations focusing on asymmetric social policies (e.g., information-and capacity-enhancing measures).
