In all subsequent analyses, we used obtained factor scores as well as z-standardized scores.
Average Silhouette Values and Davies-Bouldin-Indices indicate a robust three cluster solution (see Supplemental Appendices E and F). Supplemental Appendix G exhibits that all clustering approaches produce similar results, that is, there is an average agreement of 92.3 percent between the different clusterings. This agreement is backed by a contingency analysis. All χ 2 tests are statistically significant (p < 0.01) and an average Cramer V of 0.87 indicates a very high correlation between the nominal clusterings. We report results for the Spherical K-Means clustering using Cosine distance only. Based on our theoretical considerations, the implementation of API design characteristics reflects a conscious design decision of an API provider. Following this line of reasoning, Cosine distance is an asymmetrical distance measure and, thus, takes into account such conscious design decisions only [31]. By contrast, other applicable distance measures also take into account non-implemented API design characteristics for which we cannot infer conscious design. After validating the cluster structure, we report frequency distributions to characterize the API clusters (see Table 4). We calculate Cramer Vs to test whether or not the API design characteristics significantly differ across the three clusters. We analyze global differences across all clusters and apply posthoc tests, comparing single clusters. In order to ensure that the analysis represents a realistic picture of API design characteristics, the assignment of APIs was manually verified for plausibility. We report cluster centroids (i.e., the API characteristics' values for the three archetypes) and archetypical examples in Table 5.
Professional Services. APIs in the professional services cluster are characterized by a high probability of offering sophisticated information processing functionalities that go beyond the simple provision of data and for which API providers request transaction-and subscription-based charges. User authorization and security measures are also quite strongly associated with this cluster. This cluster can be well matched to the group of professional services [7,61,106]. Choosing the professional service archetype, API providers create an API that enables their clients to integrate the functionality of the API provider's offerings directly into the client's existing information systems and the evolving business operations. These APIs are frequently built to leverage an already existing service or product of the API provider for which the API usually represents an alternative access channel. With a share of 67 percent, the professional service cluster is the biggest API cluster. As an archetypical example, Salesforce's Analytics API offers programmatic access to analytics features [2].   Mediation Services. APIs in the second cluster are characterized by providing developers access to end customers; the provider of a mediation service, however, entertains its own direct relationship with these end customers. APIs in this cluster most frequently engage in revenue sharing approaches and make strong use of user authorization. As for professional services, API providers offer a broad range of functionalities that go beyond infrastructure and data access. Given these characteristics, this cluster matches well with the mediation service [75,79,94]. Based on extant information processing functionalities that mediation services provide, API developers can develop new service offerings for the API providers' end customers. This API cluster accounts for 18 percent in our sample. The Dropbox API, as an archetypical mediation service, allows app developers programmatic access to file synchronization and storage functionalities [23]. Dropbox provides marketing for apps that integrate with the Dropbox API on its website and requires app customers to have their own Dropbox subscription.
Open Asset Services. APIs in the third cluster are characterized by providing multichannel access to IT infrastructure or data resources, that is, the API reflects an alternative access option. API providers apply neither transaction-, nor subscription-based charges. Also, they offer no revenue sharing options. Further, they show the lowest usage of user authorization and security options. Given these traits, APIs in this archetype match well open asset services [48,56,64,84]. With low access barriers and their high versatility, such APIs are intended to involve the general public in approaches to open innovation. This API cluster accounts for 15 percent of all surveyed API providers. The New York Times Article Search API is an archetypical open asset service that offers free access to article data and metadata that is also available via the New York Times website [98].
In order to test our hypothesis, we again present results that are based on the Spherical K-Means clustering only. However, results are very consistent between the different clustering approaches. API ROI reflects a single item that has been measured with a fivepoint Likert scale. Thus, API ROI can be best described as being of ordinal nature such that ordinal logistic regression is an appropriate modeling choice [13,43,45]. Similarly, we apply negative binomial regression in order to account for the fact that the API diffusion measure relies on count data. We first test our API ROI hypotheses (Hypothesis 1 and Hypothesis 2). Ordinal logistic regression is a generalization of binary logistic regression and can accommodate dependent variables that consist of more than two ordinal levels by applying a cumulative logit model. A central pre-requisite of ordinal logistic regression is the proportional odds (also known as parallel regression) assumption that claims that the relationship between each pair of outcome categories of the dependent variable is the same [43]. We applied Brant's [13] test in order to test this assumption. We yielded non-significant test statistics indicating that proportional odds can be assumed. We estimated the following regression:
API ROI reflects the level of financial goal attainment (1 = API ROI goals are not met at all; 5 = API ROI goals are completely met), X the vector of predictor variables, β the vector of estimated coefficients, α the intercepts, and j the number of ordinal response levels for API ROI. Consequently, Pr(API ROI ≥ j | X) is the probability that API ROI is higher or equal to the API ROI level j, conditional on the predictors X. We test model 1 in a stepwise fashion. We first test for direct main effects excluding the interaction terms (model 1a). Then, we included the moderation effects in order to test our hypotheses (model 1b). Table 6 shows the results of the ordinal logistic regressions. Model 1a indicates that we cannot detect any significant main effect of economies of scope in production and the variables measuring the similarity to the design archetypes of professional/mediation services. Model 1b reveals positive interaction effects for economies of scope production and similarity to the professional service archetype (β = 0.46, p ≤ 0.01) as well as to the mediation archetype (β = 0.39, p ≤ 0.05).
A likelihood ratio test reveals that R 2 increases significantly (p ≤ 0.01) from 0.25 to 0.30 when comparing the models with (model 1b) and without moderation effects (model 1a). The log odds (exponentiated beta coefficients) for both interaction effects are > 1, that is, indicating that API providers following a mediation or professional service design and targeting economies of scope in production have a higher API ROI than others. In order to better understand the results of these interaction effects, we evaluate how the predicted probabilities of the different levels of API ROI change with varying degrees of similarity to the API design archetypes and economies of scope in production. Table 7 shows that API providers that simultaneously target economies of scope in production and follow a professional service or a mediation service design have higher probabilities of reaching high to very high levels of attaining their API ROI goals. For instance, API providers that follow professional service design and have reported high levels of economies of scope in production have a 68 percent chance of reaching high to very high level of goal attainment. By contrast, API providers that follow a professional service design without explicitly targeting economies of scope in production or vice versa have lower probabilities of reaching the same levels of goal attainment (36 percent and 39 percent). Thus, we find support for our hypotheses 1 and 2. 2  Testing our API diffusion hypotheses, we first applied a chi-square test for dispersion and found our data to be overdispersed with p < 0.01 [45]. We believe that this overdispersion (conditional variance of API diffusion is greater than its conditional mean) is  caused by a distribution that is found in many online-contexts. Most APIs have a low to moderate diffusion and a handful of APIs show very high diffusion. In order to deal with this overdispersion, we tested a variety of alternatives including quasi-poisson, negative binomial, or zero-inflated regression models [45,106]. However, likelihood ratio and deviance tests revealed that negative binomial regression best represents our data such that we have chosen this approach. Thus, E(API diffusion | X) reflects the expected value of API diffusion given the predictor variables in the model [95]. Again, we test this equation in a stepwise fashion in order to disentangle main and interaction effects. Table 8 shows the negative binomial regression results. In model 2a, we find no main effects of our API design measures and the targeted level of economies of scope in innovation. Model 2b shows that the interaction between economies of scope in innovation and similarity to the open asset archetype is significant (β = 0.45, p < 0.05). This interaction effect significantly increases R 2 from 0.25 (model 2a) to 0.3 (model 2b) with p < 0.01. These results indicate that neither increasing the similarity to the open asset archetype nor following an economies of scope in innovation strategy is associated with a significant increase in API diffusion in isolation. The exponentiated beta coefficient for designing APIs according to the open asset archetype is 1, that is, striving towards open asset design alone has no positive or negative effect on API diffusion. By contrast, the exponentiated beta coefficient for the interaction term of similarity to the open asset design and economies of scope in innovation strategy is 1.57. This means that API providers that embark on economies of scope in innovation in conjecture with an open asset design increase the diffusion of their API by 57 percent when being compared to API providers that follow an open asset design only. We find no support for the interaction between economies of scope in innovation and the similarity to the mediation archetype. Thus, we can support Hypothesis 3, while we have to reject Hypothesis 4. 3  Finally, we probe our moderation analyses through visual representations (Figure 2, 3, and4). These plots support our fit as moderation perspective showing that an alignment between API design archetypes and targeted economies of scope leads to superior API ROI and diffusion.
Our analysis of how a provider's choice of API archetype interacts with its targeting of platform-based value creation mechanisms in influencing API ROI and diffusion provides support for the theoretically derived hypothesis that the interaction of targeting economies of scope in production and an API's similarity to the professional service archetype is positively related to API ROI (Hypothesis 1). Second, our results support our theoretical argumentation that the interaction of targeting economies of scope in production and an API's similarity to the mediation archetype is also positively related to API ROI   (Hypothesis 2). Third, our analysis shows that the interaction of targeting economies of scope in innovation and an API's similarity to the open asset service archetype is positively related to API diffusion (Hypothesis 3). Our results do not provide support for the fourth hypothesis that the interaction of targeting economies of scope in innovation and an API's similarity to the mediation service archetype is positively related to API diffusion (Hypothesis 4). A strategy that targets economies of innovation, thus, does not suffice for achieving high diffusion with APIs that are similar to the mediation service archetype.
This finding conforms with prior literature, which suggests that diffusion of mediation services requires careful coordination of cross-platform externalities and the execution of platform ignition strategies [28]. External developers will only become aware of and adopt a mediation service if it provides access to enough customers that external developers target [94], if there is complementarity between the API provider's and the developer's capabilities [52], and if there is an adequate level of platform governance [99].
We provide three contributions to the literature on digital platforms. First, we develop a unifying theory that consolidates different theoretical perspectives on API design and strategy. Prior literature on API design is scattered and discusses selective aspects of API design in disparate contexts. Some authors study APIs that provide marketing and distribution capabilities to third-party developers on two-sided platforms [e.g., 79]. This stream of literature focusses on an API's ability to provide end customer access and to spur novel end-customer-facing value propositions from third parties. It produces theories with limited transferability to APIs on one-sided platforms that primarily focus on value appropriation. A second group of authors studies APIs that provide open data services [e.g., 56]. It focusses on an API's ability to expose assets to external developers free of charge in order to achieve high API diffusion. The research results are not applicable to fee-based APIs that do not target API diffusion but API ROI. A third group of authors considers APIs as distribution channels for cloud-based professional services [e.g., 7]. This perspective focusses on fee-based offerings to API developers and excludes indirect value appropriation mechanisms on two-sided markets. Considering that APIs represent key strategic resources of platform providers that determine a platform's prosperity [9], a generalizable theory on API design is required [108] that integrates the disparate perspectives on API design and explains the strategic impact of design choices across these isolated contexts. Our unifying perspective on API design that is grounded in contemporary literature on platform architecture and governance [99,100] synthesizes prior API literature. We differentiate between three API archetypes with archetypal design -professional services, moderation services and open asset servicesand offer a fit-as-moderation perspective on the applicability of economies of scope in production and innovation to these API archetypes. In so doing, we respond to Yoo et al.'s [108] call for further research on the strategic role of design decisions regarding boundary resources for digital platforms.
As our second contribution, we choose the individual API as our focal unit of analysis and, thus, extend the knowledge on the performance effects of API design. Prior research studies the aggregate use of APIs and discovers positive performance effects of API adoption on the firm level [9] and on the platform level [8,93,101,107]. Thus, prior empirical research studies sets of APIs offered by a firm or by a platform and look at the collective role of APIs for firm and platform performance, respectively. Firm-level and platform-level analyses do not allow a direct linkage between individual APIs (particularly API design characteristics) and their performance impacts. At the firm level, Benzell et al. [9] compare firm performance (market value, R&D expenditure, data breaches) before and after the first introduction of APIs. They show that whether or not a firm adopts APIs predicts a substantial increase in a firm's market value. At the platform level, Xue et al. [107], for example, study how developer's adoption of APIs, which are offered by a platform, influences their likelihood to continue developing new applications for this platform. They examine how the adoption of APIs generally influences platform performance (in terms of the number of apps hosted by a platform). Benlian et al. [8], as a second example for a platform-level analysis, regard the scope of functionalities APIs collectively offer as part of their operationalization of platform openness, and show a positive relationship of platform openness with a platform's perceived usefulness and developer satisfaction. Because most platforms offer multiple APIs and alternative boundary resources such as software development kits, these studies only allow limited implications on the design and performance effects at the level of individual APIs. We take into account different architecture-related and governance-related design decisions that APIs incorporate and distinguish between three API archetypes of professional, mediation, and open asset services. We relate these API archetypes to API ROI and diffusion. Our results extend our knowledge regarding the distinct consequences of different API-level design choices. We, thus, respond to de Reuver et al.'s [24] call for further research on platform boundary resources that creates direct platform design knowledge.
As our third contribution, we respond to Gawer's [36] call for empirical efforts to validate her proposed organization-theoretic platform perspective. We adopt Gawer's [36] organization-theoretic conceptualization of platform-based ecosystems that allows us to empirically study two modes of ecosystem value creation simultaneously: economies of scope in production and innovation. With our moderation-as-fit-perspective, we establish that the provider's API design must match the targeted mechanism of interorganizational value creation and the business objective (ROI or API diffusion). Our results suggest that, depending on the design, APIs facilitate economies of scope in production or innovation. Moreover, the fit of API design with value creation strategies determines whether value exploration targets (via API diffusion) or value appropriation targets (via ROI) are achievable.
Our results generate two practical implications. First, API providers are challenged with overlooking an API's relevance for strategic competitiveness [51]. Our results show that API providers should carefully align API archetype choice with the value creation strategy and the superordinate business objective. Offering professional services may result in a positive ROI if they improve a software solution's integrability. Mediation services may increase direct or indirect revenues in case they facilitate the integration of platform resources, such as end customer marketing capabilities for third-party developers. Open asset services, in contrast to the other two API archetypes, do not focus on value appropriation but on value generation only. They may generate high levels of API diffusion if the API provider successfully involves third-party developers in joint innovation. Second, API providers have difficulties in attracting third-party developers and in defining appropriate approaches to value appropriation [3,12]. We suggest that API providers should align approaches towards value generation and appropriation with the value creation strategy. Leveraging economies of scope in production legitimates transaction-based or subscription-based API pricing. The realization of economies of scope in innovation, on the contrary, is not linked to value appropriation, but is an effective instrument for attracting third-party developers.
One should interpret the results cognizant of the following limitations that open up avenues for further research. First, owing to our focus on public Internet APIs, the results do not apply to private APIs or non-Internet APIs that local applications expose. Further research may apply our model to investigate non-Internet APIs in local applications. Second, our study is limited to APIs offered by for-profit providers. Further research may adapt our research model to study APIs that non-profit providers such as governmental institutions offer. Third, we do not study the effects of simultaneously offering more than one API. An avenue for further research is to build on our theory and explore the interaction effects that result from offering multiple APIs. Fourth, we limit our conceptualization of economies of scope in production to linkage effects resulting from facilitating the vertical integration of provider and customer systems. We do not study production economies relating to horizontal bundling and the use of shared inputs in digital platforms, to which future research may attend. Fifth, apart from economies of scope in production, this research only studies economies of scope in innovation. Another area for further research is a focal study of mediation services and how API design aligns with economies of scale in demand, which will require a detailed analysis of cross-platform externalities. Sixth, our measurement approach is limited in that, while the set of analyzed API design elements is theoretically motivated, backed by a thorough synopsis of the available literature, and empirically verified, we do not claim exhaustiveness of API archetypes. Also, API ROI is the product manager's perception rather than an objective measure. Moreover, we analyze the levels to which an API provider targets the value creation mechanisms and do not provide objective measures for economies of scope in production and in innovation. Further research may introduce other measurement approaches to extend our findings. Seventh, our cross-sectional analyses only ascertain association, but not the causal relationships inherent in our theoretical arguments. A fruitful area of further research that may expand on our results deals with investigating longitudinally how a time-varying API strategy impacts a provider's platform evolution.
In spite of the rich literature on digital platforms, there is sparse knowledge on the design of APIs and on how to successfully align API design with an API provider's contextual conditions. In this research, we developed and validated a theoretical model that explains how the choice of API design interacts with the levels to which an API provider targets different value creation mechanisms and how this interaction affects API ROI and diffusion. We contribute to the IS literate an overarching theory of API design that unifies prior theoretical perspectives and that extends current knowledge on the performance effects of API design.
1. The basic idea of Frigyesi and Höglund [33] is to investigate how well an extracted factor or a number of extracted factors can reproduce the initial items from which the factor(s) were formed. They suggest to calculate the residual errors for an increasing number of factors for a data set and a permuted version of that data set. If the residual errors calculated from the permuted data set have the same size as the residual errors from the original data set, nonnegative matrix factorization has captured all the "noise" within a data set such that the extracted factor(s) do not contain useful information. However, the factors in the original data set show considerably smaller residual errors than the factors extracted from the permuted data set. Differences are biggest for one single factor such that we conclude that this single factor captures the relevant information from the underlying items. 2. We also performed a robustness check in which we considered API ROI as interval-scaled data and applied ordinary least square regressions. Results are consistent and lead to identical implications. 3. We also performed a robustness test for verifying these results. In greater detail, we applied log transformation to the three items with an offset of 1 [44] as well as applied exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis. The psychometrical properties of this latent API diffusion factor were excellent. All three items loaded unambiguously and significantly with p < 0.01 on that factor. Chronbach α was 0.86, the Average Variance Explained was 0.68, and the Composite Reliability was 0.86. Using the Fornell-Larcker-Criterion the factor was clearly distinguishable from the other ones. Testing Model 2 by means of ordinary least square regression, we found very consistent results that lead to the identical implications.

title: Effects of Freemium Strategy in the Mobile App Market: An Empirical Study of Google Play
full_text:
HOON SEOK CHOI is a fourth-year Ph.D. student in the Department of Information Systems and Cyber Security at the University of Texas at San Antonio. He received a B.A. in journalism and advertising and a B.Sc. in chemical engineering from Dankook University, South Korea, and an M.A. in advertising and marketing from the University of Leeds, United Kingdom. His research interests include mobile applications, online gaming, social media, cybersecurity (software piracy, securityrelated user behavior), and human-computer interaction (usability testing on prototyped IS products).
ABSTRACT: This paper examines the effect of the freemium strategy on Google Play, an online marketplace for Android mobile applications. By analyzing a large panel data set consisting of 711 ranked mobile apps, we found that the freemium strategy is positively associated with increased sales of the paid mobile apps. Positive trial experience as represented by high review rating of the free version of a mobile app leads to higher sales of its paid version, whereas high visibility of the free version of a mobile app as represented by its product rank does not have a significant impact on the sales of its paid version. This finding suggests that although offering a free trial version is a viable way to improve the visibility of a mobile app, offering a quality free app is more important in boosting sales of the paid app. Moreover, we found that the impact of review rating is reduced when the free version is offered, or when the mobile app is a hedonic app, because consumers have the ability to experience the app themselves before purchase. These findings extend understanding of the freemium business model to include a market characterized by simultaneous intramarket competition for both the freemium and paid products and demonstrate how such dynamics may influence sales of the paid products. KEY WORDS AND PHRASES: Android, freemium, Google Play, mobile apps, online product rank, online reviews. MOBILE APP REFERS TO APPLICATION SOFTWARE-a type of software that allows the user to perform a specific task that can be installed and run on a range of portable digital devices such as smartphones and tablets. A mobile app can be distinguished from general software by the following characteristics: it is optimized for touch-screenbased mobile devices, it is designed mostly for personal use, it is offered free of charge (except for mobile data use costs) or for sale, and most important, it is made available for download to mobile devices directly through a centralized online marketplace where users can rate and review the app and access various app ranking lists.
Since Apple made a key turning point in the business by launching its App Store in 2008, there has been remarkable growth in the mobile app market. Digi-Capital, an investment bank for mobile apps and games, has forecast that by 2017 mobile apps could reach a revenue of more than $70 billion globally, with nongame apps set to double revenue share from 26 percent to 51 percent [15]. In the United States, as of November 2013, the Android mobile operating system (OS) currently leads the competition with 50.3 percent market share, beating Apple's iOS and Windows Phone, which have 43.1 percent and 4.7 percent of market share, respectively [52]. Furthermore, in terms of percentage of time spent, statistics have shown that mobile apps already have overtaken the mobile web 1 since 2011 [38].
For the Android consumers, Google Play (https://play.google.com) is such a onestop shop for thousands of Android apps. Initially launched as Google's Android Market (or "the Market"), the Android web portal was rebranded and integrated into one of the categories of Google Play in March 2012. 2 This online storefront has been growing at a rapid pace, surpassing the 500,000 available mobile apps milestone on May 2, 2012 [17], not too long after its record high 10 billion downloads in December 2011 [13] and the previous milestones of 200,000 and 300,000 available apps only a few months before, in April and August 2011, respectively. The Netherlands-based app analytics firm Distimo has attributed the surging numbers to the new "freemium" applications that keep flooding the Market. In fact, two-thirds of Android apps are freemium, establishing the Market as the largest free mobile app store in the world [16].
Freemium, a combination of the words "free" and "premium," is a business model by which a service or a product is offered free of charge, but a premium is charged for advanced features, functionality, or related products and services [30, p. 195]. This strategy is widely utilized in the offering of digital-based products or services, including software, games, and web services. In the mobile app market, freemium apps are free to download but typically include offers to upgrade to the paid version, which is ad free or has richer features, to buy additional content or services within the app (i.e., in-app purchase), or to unlock additional levels of game stages.
Today, the freemium strategy is observed in virtually all mobile app marketsincluding Apple App Store, BlackBerry App World, Google Play, and Windows Marketplace for Mobile. Free apps are often listed side by side with their paid counterparts to provide consumers the opportunity to test run a mobile app before purchase. The flowchart shown in Figure 1 illustrates how a typical consumer selects and purchases a mobile app in a mobile app store such as Google Play.
A consumer may, of course, purchase a paid app directly without trying out its free version. However, a 2013 study reveals that the majority of consumers take advantage of the free apps offering in online mobile app stores [27]. Hence, we believe that the process depicted in Figure 1 represents a typical scenario that can occur when a consumer searches for a mobile app on Google Play. As do other e-commerce sites, Google Play allows consumers to share their feedback on these apps through reviews and ratings. More interestingly, these mobile app stores also publish ranking lists of both free and paid apps based on various factors such as the number of downloads, average rating, and the number of reviews. The simultaneous presence of two competitive markets for both the free and the paid apps and the availability of ranking and rating information in both markets have generated interesting dynamics in the mobile app market. For example, there are contradictory viewpoints among mobile app vendors about the effect of free apps on their paid version. Some vendors believe that providing free apps decreases the total sales of the paid versions of the apps. Despite the potential revenue streams from free apps' in-app purchases, advertising, and subscriptions, these mobile app vendors still see the traditional pay per download as the most prolific revenue source to target. And to them, the effect of a free app on its paid version is potentially negative, as the free version may cannibalize the sales of the paid version, leading to lower overall revenue and profit.
Other mobile app vendors, however, believe that offering a free version of their app is an effective way to attract consumers, as some consumers who purchased their app would not have done so if they had not experienced the free version of the app. Moreover, a free app that makes it to or near the top of the ranking list can significantly increase the visibility of the app because it will be displayed on the main page of the website. This creates a vicious loop and will lead to more trials of the free app, which in turn can potentially boost sales of the paid version. Hence, these vendors explicitly encourage consumers to try the free version first before making a purchase.
These contradictory viewpoints leave us with several interesting questions: How does the free version of a mobile app affect the sales of its paid version? Do the results learned from use of the freemium strategy in other product markets still hold in the mobile app market? And last but not least, what is the role of the ranking systems for both free and paid apps in the Android mobile app market? To answer these questions, we developed a set of hypotheses and empirically tested them using a longitudinal data set collected from Google Play's website. From our findings, we attempt to offer insights to app developers and marketplace designers into how consumers make their purchase decisions in the presence of widely available free apps.
The effects of the freemium strategy in the software market have been studied extensively in the literature [10,22,28,41]. Bawa and Shoemaker [6] maintained that free samples can create three potential effects on sales: (1) an acceleration effect, whereby consumers decide to purchase a product earlier than they would have if the free sample had not been given; (2) a cannibalization effect, whereby the free sample reduces sales of the product; and (3) an expansion effect, which occurs when consumers would not otherwise purchase a product without the free sample. Because the outcome of the freemium strategy depends on the interplay of these three effects, which are in turn determined by various factors, the impact of free samples can differ significantly across different categories.
In the traditional software market, in addition to the widely established brand building [37,41] and learning effects [14], software vendors often exercise the freemium strategy to exploit economic rents ascribed to positive network effects [23], product complementarity [47], or an accelerated diffusion process [34]. However, unlike traditional software applications, which often exhibit demand side economy of scale, mobile apps are generally characterized by minimal learning and switching costs and a low degree of interdependence among apps from the same developer. Hence, the classic network effects or product complementarity theory cannot be used to account for the dynamics in the mobile app market. Rather, adoption of paid mobile apps depends critically on two important factors: product visibility and product quality.
The importance of product visibility and product quality in determining the success of mobile apps in the market can be explained in the context of a new product adoption process. In the process, consumers generally go through five steps: (1) awareness, (2) interest, (3) evaluation, (4) trial, and (5) adoption [51]. The first step, awareness, is when consumers are informed about the product attributes [36]. In a competitive market environment, as the number of products in a category increases, generating awareness of a new product becomes more difficult [35]. Android app market presents such a challenge not only because there are now close to 1.3 million apps [4] but also because every month some 15,000 new apps are introduced [50]. Product visibility, measured by the rank of the app, is therefore essential to generating a high level of awareness of an app. This is especially true if we consider that most consumers find the apps they are to download through the ranking list published by online marketplaces such as Google Play [1]. Highly ranked apps also generate more interest among potential users because they reflect the interest of other consumers, and such peer influence has been shown to be one of the primary drivers of purchase decisions in online shopping [7].
During a new product's evaluation and trial steps, product quality is critical in determining whether consumers will purchase it. In the software market, consumers are likely to judge the quality of software on the basis of the quality of the free trial version [10]. In the mobile app market, the quality of a free app plays a critical role in the purchase decision of its paid version. This is because many app developers provide free apps with similar quality to their paid version albeit containing ads or with reduced functionality. A study conducted by AdMob [1] revealed that the primary reason for purchasing paid apps was that consumers liked the free version and decided to upgrade to the paid version. Furthermore, other studies have shown that on Google Play and Apple's App Store, a large portion of paid app consumers had tried the free version first before purchasing [49].
In the online environment, product quality can also be inferred from online customer reviews, which are generally left by customers who have purchased and experienced the product, and so the reviews are very relevant and informative. The impact of online reviews, along with product ratings and number of reviews, on the purchase decision of customers has been studied extensively in a variety of markets, such as movies [34], online book stores [35], online shopping stores [36], and video games [37]. The results of these studies generally support the idea that online reviews have become a primary reference for consumers, and the consumer-generated information plays a significant role in the purchase decisions of buyers [44]. However, the extent to which online reviews affect consumers' purchase decisions differ due to a variety of factors, such as product type, product visibility, quality and quantity of the reviews, reputation of the reviewers, and freshness of the reviews.
Product characteristics are one of the most significant factors moderating the effect of online reviews. The impact of online reviews on sales of utilitarian products, compared with that on sales of hedonic products, is relatively high due to the focus on product functionality rather than on individual preferences in product evaluations [38]. Similarly, such an impact is more significant in the evaluation of search products [31,39], whose quality can be evaluated before consumption (e.g., a calculator), than in that of experience products (e.g., wine), whose quality can only be determined after consumption [36,40].
The popularity of a product may also moderate the impact of online reviews. With thousands of products competing for consumer attention and media coverage, less attractive products receive little attention and product coverage, resulting in a higher degree of product uncertainty. Online reviews thus become a primary source of information for consumers to reduce such uncertainty. Hence, it is not surprising to see that products less popular in the market are more significantly influenced by online reviews [37].
In terms of the direction of feedback, negative online reviews are found to be more critical in the decision-making process than positive online reviews due to the overall risk aversion among consumers [35]. This is consistent with the results of previous research demonstrating that in the traditional brick-and-mortar stores, negative word of mouth more strongly decreases the willingness to purchase than positive word of mouth increases the willingness to purchase [41].
The quality and quantity of reviews also play an important role in increasing sales volume. Prospective consumers tend to rely more on online reviews that are more thoroughly composed [36] and those with a higher number of reviews [34]. In addition, the impact of reviews is more substantial if the reviews are written by reputable users, although such an effect on sales performance decreases over time [42].
Although the foregoing results have been consistently demonstrated in the literature, almost all of the aforementioned studies examined the impact of product visibility and product quality on sales of the same product. Therefore, it will be interesting to see how the free version of a product affects the market performance of its paid version in a market where the freemium strategy is implemented. In particular, it is compelling to ask whether the findings in the extant literature still hold when both the free and the paid versions of the same product are ranked and rated in the same online marketplace.
Google Play is not the first website to publish product ranks and review ratings. With the rapid advance in data analytics technology, more and more electronic commerce sites (such as Amazon.com) have provided product rank and user reviews of the products listed on their websites to assist consumers in making their purchase decisions. In turn, researchers have keenly identified the rich research opportunity associated with the vast amount of data available on these websites and proposed innovative ways to take advantage of the data resources [24,26]. In the past decade, researchers have studied the relationship between product rank and actual sales and used the demand data recovered from product rank to estimate consumer surplus [7], analyze price elasticity [11], and study product cannibalization [25]. These studies offer a solid theoretical foundation for our research.
Although Google Play adopts a ranking system similar to the ones implemented by many e-commerce sites, one important distinction lies in the simultaneous publication of the ranking lists for both the free and the paid apps on Google Play, which is typically not present in other websites that sell regular commodities. This offers us a unique opportunity to examine the impact of the adoption of the free version of a mobile app on its paid version. On Google Play, the visibility and quality of a mobile app are largely manifested through two important indicators: the product rank and the review rating. In the next section, we develop several hypotheses to investigate how these two factors contribute to the adoption of the paid version of a mobile app.
In the traditional software market, due to the difficulty in obtaining sales data, studies involving the freemium strategy have largely adopted analytic tools, and the findings are highly contingent upon a variety of factors. For example, the performance of sampled software has been found to differ by software categories [22] and strategies for sampling (e.g., full functionality with limited time period or limited functionality without time limitation) [42]. The profitability of the freemium strategy often depends critically on the demand for product compatibility and the strength of network effects [9,10]. However, even without strong network effects, offering a fully functional software for free in the early stage may boost a software vendor's profit in the long run [34].
In the mobile app market, we expect the net impact of the freemium strategy on sales to be positive due to the unique characteristics of mobile apps. As a highly centralized marketplace, Google Play is an official portal for app developers to publish their apps and is therefore extremely competitive due to the large number of competing apps in each category, the very low search cost, and the ease of comparison across a variety of offerings. 3 This market structure leads to a fourth "competitive" effect beyond the acceleration, cannibalization, and expansion effects identified in Bawa and Shoemaker [6]. When a large number of substitutes in a product category are available for free, there is probably a higher degree of cannibalization of these free substitutes than of a paid app's own free version. Moreover, not offering a free version may significantly reduce the awareness of and interest in the product, which may hurt sales more than cannibalization does [3]. Given that cannibalization is more likely to emerge in markets with a high degree of product differentiation [25], and in the mobile app market there exists a relatively low degree of product heterogeneity, one would expect the competitive effect to dominate the cannibalization effect in this market.
In addition to economics reasons, the freemium strategy may also stimulate demand due to consumer psychology. Kim and Morris [40] showed that consumers experiencing a trial of low-involvement products tend to have better affective and cognitive responses to the products than to products requiring high involvement. Similarly, Kempf [39] argued that consumers with personal experience with a product tend to demonstrate stronger belief, confidence, attitudes, and purchase intentions than those with indirect experience with it, such as through advertising. Given the similarity between mobile apps and the product types examined in the foregoing studies, we expect that the freemium strategy would have a similar impact in the mobile app market. Therefore, we predict that offering the free version of a mobile app is more likely to improve the market performance of its paid version, as represented by the number of downloads of the paid app.
Hypothesis 1: Offering the free version of a mobile app is positively associated with a larger number of downloads of its paid version.
The existing literature has suggested that product rank and online reviews are good indicators of product visibility and product quality, and both have been shown to have a significant impact on consumer's online purchase decision [12,19,45,53]. In the case of mobile apps, an interesting difference arises from the fact that a lot of mobile apps offer a free trial version for consumers. As mentioned earlier, there is ample anecdotal evidence that shows that consumers interested in purchasing a mobile app always prefer to try the free version when one is available [29,32]. Consequently, the experience from the free version trial will be highly influential in the subsequent purchase intention. Because Google Play publishes information about the ranks and ratings of both the free and the paid apps, an interesting question arises: How do the visibility and user satisfaction of the free app, as represented by the rank and the rating of its free version, influence sales of its paid version? Drawing on the extant literature, among paid apps that offer a free version, we expect that a higher rank of the free version would increase the visibility of the app, which in turn would result in more trials of the free app. Because some consumers who try out the free version of the app will decide to buy the paid version, all else being equal (e.g., the quality of the app), the larger the user base of the free app, the more users will buy the paid version (note that the ratio of conversion might decrease, but the absolute number of users will always increase with more free trials). At the same time, sales of the paid apps also depend critically on the quality of the free app. For a given paid app, the impact of a high-quality free version may be ambiguous. On the one hand, a highly rated free app can effectively promote the sales of its paid version. On the other hand, some users who are very satisfied with the free version will end up not purchasing the paid version, leading to some cannibalization of the paid app. However, if we compare two paid apps that both offer a free version, given the highly competitive nature of the mobile app market and the abundance of substitute products, the app with a lower quality free version is even more likely to discourage potential buyers from purchasing its paid version. In other words, both apps may suffer from the cannibalization effect, but net sales will still favor the app with the better rating. Therefore, for paid apps that offer a higher quality free version (as reflected in the review rating of the free version), we expect the impact of the freemium strategy to be more significant than it is for apps that offer a lower quality free version.
Hypothesis 2a: Among paid mobile apps that offer a free version, the number of downloads of the paid version is positively associated with the rank of its free version.
Hypothesis 2b: Among paid mobile apps that offer a free version, the number of downloads of the paid version is positively associated with the rating of its free version.
When consumers search for products that they are not familiar with, they tend to rely on feedback provided by professionals or other consumers who have experienced the product to reduce uncertainty. This is especially true for experience goods such as PC software. However, in the mobile app market, for apps offering a free version, consumers can test the features and functionalities of the apps before purchase, technically turning them into search goods. Consequently, we expect the impact of review rating will be less significant for apps that offer a free version than for those that do not offer a free version. Among mobile apps that do not offer a free version, we expect the findings from the extant literature about experience goods will still hold here. In this case, less popular products typically present a higher risk due to limited professional review coverage and customer feedback. In the absence of this information, it has been shown that the influence of user reviews is more significant in the purchase of less attractive products [53] and increasingly insignificant in the adoption of more popular products [21]. In our context, these findings imply that the impact of rating will be more salient for paid apps with a lower rank than for those with a higher rank, which leads to the following hypotheses: Hypothesis 3a: The impact of the rating of a paid mobile app on the number of downloads is less significant for mobile apps that offer a free version than for those that do not offer a free version. Hypothesis 3b: Among paid mobile apps that do not offer a free version, the impact of rating on the number of downloads is more significant for paid mobile apps with a lower rank than for those with a higher rank.
As with traditional software, mobile apps may be categorized into two subgroups: hedonic and nonhedonic. Game and entertainment apps, which are mainly used for fun, can be classified as hedonic apps, and such apps as utility and business programs can be classified as nonhedonic apps. The evaluation of hedonic products is usually subjective and tends to vary from person to person, as it is largely based on individual preferences rather than commonly accepted standards, whereas the evaluation of nonhedonic products is usually objective and consistent across users. Researchers have found that the impact of online reviews on hedonic products is relatively smaller than the impact on nonhedonic products [8]. Such a finding is expected to be more apparent in the mobile app market because there is often a free version of the app. In the mobile app market, because the majority of the free apps offer features and functionalities similar to their paid versions, consumers have plenty of opportunity to thoroughly evaluate the apps before they make a purchase. When it comes to hedonic apps, due to their more engaging nature (e.g., games), consumers tend to spend more time when they get to try the apps, relative to nonhedonic apps. This in turn leads to more confidence in the consumers' own evaluations of the app and, therefore, greater likelihood of the consumers' relying on their personal experience rather than the review ratings of other people to determine whether they will purchase the paid version. Hence, it can be expected that the impact of the rating of the free version of a mobile app on its paid version will be less significant for hedonic apps than for nonhedonic apps.
When consumers rely primarily on their own experience in determining whether to purchase an app, their awareness of the app (and hence the chance the app will be picked for free trial) becomes a more salient factor in ultimately driving the sales of the app. Because there are more than a million apps in the Google Play store, one that makes it to the top-ranked list achieves much greater visibility and hence an increased chance of being purchased.Therefore, we argue that, relative to a nonhedonic app, the chance that a hedonic app will be adopted by a consumer depends more on its visibility to consumers (as represented by its rank 4 ) than on the opinion of other consumers (as represented by its rating). Therefore, we expect that the impact of the rank of the free version of a mobile app will be more significant for hedonic apps than for nonhedonic apps.
Hypothesis 4a: The impact of the rank of the free version of a mobile app on the number of downloads of its paid version is more significant for hedonic apps than for nonhedonic apps.
Hypothesis 4b: The impact of the rating of the free version of a mobile app on the number of downloads of its paid version is less significant for hedonic apps than for nonhedonic apps.
To better illustrate the relationships among the various hypotheses proposed in this section, we provide an integrated view of our research framework in Figure 2.
To test our hypotheses, we collected data from Google Play and focused on its Android apps store, an online marketplace dedicated to promoting the adoption of mobile apps compatible with the Android platform. In addition to providing links for downloading apps, Google Play's Android apps store also publishes various ranking lists. Among them, the Top Free, Top Paid, and Top Grossing lists are the most relevant for our research questions. The Top Free and Top Paid ranking lists include the top 504 applications in the free and paid categories based on the number of downloads, whereas the Top Grossing list includes the top 504 apps based on their revenue, which consists of both upfront app purchase revenue and in-app purchases (i.e., fees to obtain an advanced feature or to unlock a level in a game). Because these lists are updated daily, we created three software agents to automatically parse on a daily basis the three ranking lists and product web pages related to the ranked apps in each of the three lists. We ran the software agents for two months, 5 from November 2011 to January 2012, and collected daily data on the following variables: type of application (paid vs. free), rank of the app in each of the three aforementioned ranking lists, usage category (utility, financial, games, entertainment, etc.), price (for paid apps only), overall user review rating, rating count (number of reviews), developer, app version number, date a new version was released, file size, minimum version of Android OS required, and content rating (level of maturity). During our two-month sample period, 1,567 paid apps, 1,740 free apps, and 704 top-grossing apps appeared on the three ranking lists. 6  Because we are interested in how the free version of a mobile app affects adoption of the paid version, we used the Top Paid ranking list as the basis for constructing our data set. We created a dummy variable, FreeVersion, to indicate whether an application had a free version or not. Of the 1,567 ranked paid applications, 1,020 (65.1 percent) offered a free version on Google Play and were assigned a value of 1 to the dummy variable, FreeVersion. 7 Furthermore, among these 1,020 free apps, 379 (37.2 percent) made it to the Top Free ranking list. For these top free apps, we were able to include their Top Free ranks, ratings, and rating counts in our data set.
As the data are both cross-sectional and longitudinal, the initial data set is a large panel data set that consists of 60,142 observations from 1,567 product panels 8 across two months, covering thirty mobile app categories with prices ranging from $0.99 to $39.95. Each product panel represents an Android app i ranked during day t. The app-level panels allow us to control for variation due to the individual characteristics of the app, whereas the time series data allow us to control for variation due to potential "seasonal fluctuations" (e.g., new version being released) and time trends (e.g., declining consumer interest over time).
The data for the majority of the variables were readily available from the web pages we parsed on Google Play. However, a major data challenge in our study was the lack of actual sales data. Like many electronic commerce sites such as Amazon.com and other mobile app providers such as Apple, Nokia, and RIM, due to competitive reasons, Google does not reveal the actual number of downloads for the apps purchased through Google Play. Without these data, we could not test hypotheses related to the impact of the free version of an app on the sales of its paid version. This challenge is very similar to the one confronting many IS researchers who seek to understand the relationship between product rank and actual sales on various online marketplaces [7,11,25]. In most of these studies, product rank is publicly available, whereas actual sales data are not. However, it is generally assumed that product rank is largely determined by the actual sales on the majority of these e-commerce sites. Given this assumption, by analyzing the available historical sales and product rank data, researchers have found that there exists an inverse relationship between product rank and actual sales [7,11,24,25], which can often be represented by the power law, or Pareto Type I distribution (Pareto 1896), as shown in the following equation:
where β is a scale parameter and α is a shape parameter.
Given this relationship, if the scale and shape parameters are known, researchers can estimate actual sales based on the publicly available product rank. To estimate these two parameters, prior studies have adopted various approaches. Chevalier and Goolsbee [11] examined how the product rank changes in response to a change in demand by purchasing a large quantity of several low-ranked books on Amazon.com. More recently, Garg and Telang [24] developed a simple yet effective approach to estimate the demand parameters by jointly solving the foregoing Pareto equation for both the Top Paid and the Top Grossing ranking lists in Apple's App Store.
Although the foregoing methods have been widely adopted in studies that seek to recover the actual sales from publicly available product rank data, these methods are less applicable to our case. As revealed by several studies [46,48], unlike other e-retailers, Google Play does not rank its Android apps based solely on the number of downloads. Although the download number still plays an important role in the ranking algorithm adopted by Google Play to unknown degrees, other factors such as rating, freshness of the app, retention rate, and history of growth have all been found to influence the rank [18]. Given the unknowns involved in the ranking algorithm, the inverse function used by prior studies could no longer be applied to our data. In light of this new challenge, we had to resort to another, nontraditional approach to recover the sales data.
After careful investigation of all the information published on Google Play's website, we found that we were able to develop a computational method to recover the download numbers for many, if not all, of the apps in our data set through two pieces of information. The first piece of information was a graph posted on the individual app's web page that shows the fluctuation in the number of downloads for a given app in the previous thirty days. Using graph-to-data digitizing software (i.e., Engauge Digitizer), we were able to recover the relative number of downloads within a given period (i.e., thirty days) for a given app. Table 1 shows sample data resulting from the graph-to-data conversion process. However, because Google does not define the vertical axis of the graphs, the converted data from the graphs cannot be used to directly recover the absolute number of downloads. To obtain the actual download counts, we incorporated another piece of information presented on Google Play's app web page, that is, the range of download counts. As of the end of our data collection period (January 18, 2012), Google Play classified the number of downloads for its mobile apps into one of the following eleven categories:
1. 10-50 2. 50-100 3. 100-500 4. 500-1,000 5. 1,000-5,000 6. 5,000-10,000 7. 10,000-50,000 8. 50,000-100,000 9. 100,000-500,000 10. 500,000-1,000,000 11. 1,000,000-5,000,000
On day 5 of our data collection period, the range of download counts changed from the previous day's 500-1,000 to 1,000-5,000, and on day 15 the download range changed from 1,000-5,000 to 5,000-10,000. With this information, we can derive that the number of downloads reached the 1,000 milestone on day 5 and the 5,000 milestone on day 15. Accordingly, we can derive that there were a total of 4,000 downloads between day 5 and day 15. In this case, we can add the relative number of downloads from day 5 through day 15 (which equals 741 based on the data presented in Table 1). We can then divide the total number of downloads (4,000) by the relative number of downloads (741) to obtain the ratio of the actual number of downloads to the relative number of downloads in Table 1. Multiplying this ratio by each day's relative download counts yields the actual number of downloads for this mobile app for the past 30 days.
Following this approach, we were able to recover the actual number of downloads for mobile apps in our data set where there were changes of download ranges during our sample period. However, such changes of download range did not occur for all of the apps in our data set during our sample period. Some apps remained in the same download range, and some only had one change in download range during our sample period. Without the necessary download range change data, we could not recover the actual number of downloads for these apps.
To maximize the number of data points for the number of downloads variable, we checked several other websites to collect additional download range change data to compute the actual number of downloads. For example, we found a website named AppBrain (www.appbrain.com) that provides a comprehensive summary of the activity history of almost all Android mobile apps that have appeared on Google Play. Among the rich information presented on this website, of particular interest to us is the history of the download range change, such as the one shown in Figure 3.
The app highlighted in Figure 3, App Folder Pro, is one of the apps in our data set that had only one change in download range (i.e., on January 10, 2012) during our sample period (from November 18, 2011, to January 18, 2012). But with additional download range change data from the AppBrain website (the number of downloads passed the 1,000 milestone on November 14, 2011), we were able to derive that there were 4,000 downloads between November 14, 2011, and January 10, 2012. Therefore, using the computational method illustrated earlier, we were able to recover the actual number of downloads for this app during our sample period. Note that for the period between January 11, 2012, and January 18, 2012 (the end of our sample period), we can still recover the actual download data for the remainder of the sample period using the download trend graph on January 18, 2012, although the next change in the download range occurred after our sample period (on May 15, 2012), because the actual number of downloads on January 10, 2012, is known.
In addition to AppBrain.com, we also collected download range change data from other sources, such as the developers' websites and from a pilot data set we collected prior to our formal data collection. As a result, we were able to compute and verify the actual downloads for 711 apps out of the total 1,567 apps in our original data set. 9 This resulted in a final data set with 23,771 data points.

In all three models, the dependent variable Downloads i,t is the number of downloads of a paid app i on date t. Model 1 is estimated based on all of the apps in our data set and is used to test H1 and H3a, which examine the impact of the freemium strategy on sales and the moderating effect of free apps on the rating of their paid version. Model 2 is estimated against all paid apps that offer a free version and is used to test H2a, H2b, H4a, and H4b, which examine the impact of the rank and the rating of the free apps on their paid version and their differential impact on different app types. Finally, Model 3 is estimated against all paid apps that do not offer a free version and is used to test H3b, which examines the interaction between the rank and the rating of the paid apps.
Because our data set is a typical panel data set, we started the analyses with several specification tests to examine whether our models are subject to specification errors and violations of the ordinary least squares (OLS) estimation assumptions and to determine the appropriate econometric treatments. We started with the standard heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation checks. A Breusch-Pagan/Cook-Weisberg test for heteroskedasticity yields a high χ 2 for all three data sets, suggesting the presence of heteroskedasticity. This is consistent with a plot of the residuals versus fitted (predicted) values, which exhibits a wider scatter with greater x-axis values. The Wooldridge test for autocorrelation in the panel data also shows that first-order autocorrelation (AR1) cannot be ruled out for our data set. This is not surprising, given the longitudinal nature of our data. The presence of heteroskedasticity and AR1 autocorrelation suggests against the use of OLS. To address these issues, we applied the generalized least squares (GLS) estimation procedure 10 with corrections to adjust for both heteroskedasticity and panel-specific first-order autocorrelation. We also used the lagged independent variables to account for any potential time lag between the independent variables and the dependent variable. The results reported in Table 4 are coefficient estimates obtained from the GLS estimation.

More specifically, the main effect of FreeApp should be computed as the partial derivative of the dependent variable with respect to the variable of interest.
