title: Personalized Ranking at a Mobile App Distribution Platform
abstract: The ease of customer data collection has enabled the widespread personalization of content and services in digital platforms. We examine personalization in a hitherto unaddressed context: that of mobile app distribution. Specifically, we develop a comprehensive framework for the personalized ranking of app impressions, leveraging revealed preferences embedded in consumer clickstream data. To improve platform revenues, the framework jointly accounts for consumer utility and cost per action (CPA) margin, which is the revenue earned by the platform per app installation. To this end, we specify a structural model of click and installation choices, jointly estimated as a function of a comprehensive set of numerical (screen rank, quality, and popularity) and textual (titles, descriptions, and reviews) covariates. Our novel data set is at the granular user-impression level and uniquely includes app CPA margins paid to the platform. We conduct a series of policy experiments to quantify the value of personalization. Specifically, we show that a personalized hybrid margin and utility margin ranking scheme outperforms other personalized methods, including those based on utilities alone or a combination of utilities and margins. Overall, our analysis demonstrates how platforms can leverage routine consumer clickstream data to personalize the ranking of app impressions, thereby more effectively monetizing mobile app distribution.
full_text:
The market for mobile apps has seen exponential growth over the last two decades with 218 billion apps downloaded in 2020 contributing to sales of $143 billion (App Annie 2021). In addition to the handful of native app stores (most notably Google Play and Apple App Store), third-party app distribution platforms have emerged, including the one we study here. More than 100 billion app downloads are expected through such platforms, which will generate annual revenues of $36 billion by 2021, and both downloads and revenues are growing at an annual rate of 12% (App Annie 2017). 1 Third-party platforms typically run a cost-per-action (CPA) business model, whereby they are compensated by app developers at a precontracted rate for each app installed. The revenues collected by the platforms, as with product search engines in general, depend on what app impressions are shown to users and in what order (e.g., Ghose andYang 2009, Agarwal et al. 2011). Yet third-party app distribution platforms are generally naïve in terms of app ranking strategies (Dogtiev 2019), resorting to such simple metrics as click-through rates (CTR), conversion rates, and CPA margins and ignoring fundamental drivers of user valuation for the apps. Indeed, prior work (e.g., Ghose et al. 2014, De los Santos andKoulayev 2017) shows that accounting for average consumer utilities in the ranking of impressions can yield higher platform revenues. We build on this to show how personalized rankings-that is, rankings based on individual utilities rather than the average utility-can further increase both platform profits and consumer utilities.
Personalization is defined as the capability to match content, products, and services to individual users based on the knowledge of their past behaviors and revealed preferences (Hagen et al. 1999). It is studied in a variety of contexts, including search engines (Yao andMela 2011, Yoganarasimhan 2020), recommender systems (Ansari et al. 2000, Bodapati 2008), personalized pricing (Zhang and Wedel 2009), targeted marketing (Ansari and Mela 2003, Arora and Henderson 2007, Goldfarb and Tucker 2011), and more (see Adomavicius et al. 2008 for a survey). Users benefit from personalization because it reduces their search costs, helping them find more relevant offerings at the right place and time. Higher customer satisfaction translates into higher customer retention and conversion rates, greater willingness to pay, and generally higher average revenues per user per unit of time. In a sense, personalization is an effort to turn customer heterogeneity into incremental revenue opportunities through the appropriate matching of customer revealed preferences to suitably tailored content and offerings. It is helpful to distinguish between personalization and customization-terms that are often used synonymously but are subtly different (Davis 2018, Muhamad 2019). A succinct distinction between the two is discussed by Muhamad (2019): "While customization is initiated by the user, personalization is done for the user." In other words, when users proactively configure products to meet their preferences, that is customization; when the platform ranks the preferred products for individuals as studied in this research, that is in the realm of personalization.
We now place our instance of personalization within the framework of Adomavicius et al. (2008), which highlights four key dimensions of the type of personalization: offering (personalization of recommended products, content, or price), approach (provider-, consumer-, or market-centric), granularity (individual or segment-based), and intrusiveness (intrusive or nonintrusive). Within this framework, our offering is the personalization of recommended products (i.e., apps) using a consumercentric approach. In terms of granularity, our analysis is at the individual level (as in Balabanović and Shoham 1997) rather than the segment level as the analysis of sponsored search advertising by Yao and Mela (2011) in an anonymous search engine. 2 Finally, ours is a case of nonintrusive personalization, in the sense that the personalized app impressions are presented passively on the offer wall and do not interfere with the user's browsing process.
Indeed, the premise of our consumer-centric ranking scheme is that revealed preferences embedded in clickstream data can be analyzed to recover consumers' preferences and, in turn, used to personalize the ranking of app impressions. When clickstream data are collected by all manner of product search engines, the mobile app distribution context has relatively more frequent click and conversion interactions because of the numerous free apps available for download. 3 Over time, this translates into substantial volumes of click and install choices (i.e., revealed preferences) from heterogeneous users. This offers an actionable opportunity for the platform to learn about the nature of app demand and then leverage that knowledge for more effective ranking and monetization. When ranking design has drawn attention in prior research (see Table 1), we ask a set of hitherto unaddressed questions: (1) How are consumer utilities from app click and install influenced by app and impression characteristics? (2) How should the platform balance the drivers of these utilities with app revenue margins and design a personalized ranking of impressions? (3) How do alternative personalized ranking schemes compare in terms of contributions to platform revenues?
To address these questions, we obtain a unique data set of click and download data from a marketing agency that manages the home screen for one of the prominent mobile networks in the United States. The agency hosts an offer wall that serves as an app distribution platform. The user impression-level data contain app impressions along with the corresponding click and install responses. We estimate a structural model of click and download utilities as a function of a broad set of numerical and textual app characteristics using a two-stage bivariate probit model in a hierarchical Bayes framework. The numerical variables include screen ranks, star ratings, review volume, and the number of downloads; the textual features consist of informativeness, ambiguity, and sentiment extracted from titles, descriptions, and reviews, using suitable natural language processing methods.
The parameter estimates provide a number of insights. First, consistent with prior work (e.g., Ghose and Yang 2009), we confirm salient ranking and quality effects. Quantitatively, moving an app impression one slot upward in the screen is associated with a 4.26% higher click-through rate; having one additional star in rating boosts click and install performances by 2.91% and 1.37%, respectively. Second, consumers generally prefer more informative app titles so that a 1% increase in the length of app titles is associated with a 2.12% We leverage our structural parameter estimates to conduct a series of policy experiments to evaluate the incremental value of personalization. Specifically, we compare the mean utility based ranking (Ghose et al. 2014) with personalized ranking at the individual level. We show that personalization enhances the platform's expected revenues substantially. To further improve platform profitability, we propose a novel personalized ranking scheme, namely, the hybrid margin and utility margin (HMUM) ranking. The hybrid ranking approach alloys two ranking methods and exquisitely balances download performance with revenue margins. We demonstrate that this hybrid ranking outperforms alternative ranking strategies based on either utilities or a combination of utilities and margins, especially when personalization is incorporated. It is noteworthy that, whereas prior research tends to focus on picking "a" best algorithm from among alternatives, it tends to discard the potential of a hybrid approach that combines multiple schemes in an optimal ranking scenario. 4 The proposed ranking scheme presents a personalized list of app impressions to each user, which consists of two sections. The top few positions on the screen are populated with the user's most favorite apps sorted in decreasing order of CPA margins. The user is likely to click on these highutility impressions anyway, irrespective of precise screen ranking, making app CPA margins the most significant determinant of incremental revenues. The lower section consists of the remaining app impressions sorted in decreasing order of the product of utility and margin (i.e., utility × margin), again, on a personalized basis. The resulting hybrid ranking scheme is designed to balance the forces that drive individual user utility versus revenue margins in a manner that enhances platform revenues along with customer value. Further contributions of our work to the literature and practice are discussed in the concluding section.
The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews the related literature and describes the conceptual framework for our empirical analysis. We detail the research context and data in Section 3. Section 4 describes our empirical model and estimation strategy. In Section 5, we describe our results and robustness checks. A series of policy experiments are conducted to compare alternative ranking methods in Section 6. Section 7 concludes this research with our contributions and managerial implications. There is an online appendix that presents a simple analytical model and some additional results.
At a high level, this work contributes to the emerging literature on the mobile app economy. Although prior studies focus on how aggregate demands are affected by app and consumer characteristics (e.g., Ghose and Han 2014, Han et al. 2016, Li et al. 2020), our work takes a "micro" perspective on app consumption, focusing on personalized ranking designed for third-party app distribution platforms. In so doing, we contribute to two interrelated areas of prior work: (i) ranking of search impressions and consumer choice thereof and (ii) the personalization of online content and services. We discuss each in turn and conclude with our conceptual framework.
Our modeling of consumer click and conversion utilities builds on prior work that studies online consumer choice of search results as summarized in Table 1. What is common across these studies is that consumers choose from a ranked list of information, content, or product offerings. Further, the outcomes of interest are a combination of clicks and conversions. We highlight whether these studies explicitly consider ranking design, and if so, what is the basis for screen ranking? A consistent theme in the literature is that screen rank plays a significant role in consumer propensity to click. For example, in an online shopping context, Brynjolfsson et al. (2010) show that consumers tend to choose product offerings on the first page. In sponsored search, Ghose and Yang (2009) find that low-ranked sponsored listings attract more clicks and conversions using keyword campaign data from an advertiser. In a similar setting, Agarwal et al. (2011) notice that the click-through rate decreases with position, but the top positions are not necessarily the most profitable for an advertiser to bid because of higher placement costs.
These studies consider screen ranking as a covariate for explaining online click and conversion decisions. In contrast, other works focus on the design of ranking systems themselves (Ghose et al. 2012(Ghose et al. , 2014;;De los Santos and Koulayev 2017;Ursu 2018;Choi and Mela 2019). In a hotel search setting, Ghose et al. (2012) propose a ranking system that sorts products in decreasing order of the average utility for all users (i.e., their "best value" ranking). They find that consumers prefer such a ranking over price-or ratingbased rankings. Ghose et al. (2014) further show that such average utility-based ranking can increase platform expected revenues significantly. In this direction, the mean utility-based ranking is shown to benefit the platform by Ursu (2018) in her field experiments on Expedia. She further finds that ranking affects consumer clicks only and not purchase decisions. Finally, De los Santos and Koulayev (2017) extend the mean utility-based ranking by considering price sensitivity at the segment level. This scheme outperforms naïve ranking by price or popularity alone. We also leverage structural modeling (i.e., structural estimation followed by counterfactual analyses), but our study departs from prior work by examining incremental revenues from a personalized ranking of utilities at the individual level. Another point of departure is that prior studies are not privy to revenue-sharing details between the platform and advertisers. 5 By contrast, the actual CPA margins are observed in our context, enabling us to explicitly study the interplay between consumer utility drivers and platform revenues.
It is also worth noting that the existing literature tends to propose a single performance metric to rank all products. Such a one-size-fits-all approach may incur undesirable outcomes, especially when utilitybased methods maximize consumer utilities at the expense of a platform's revenues. A hybrid algorithm that blends rankings based on utilities and margins might help generate higher overall revenues. Choi and Mela (2019) showcase this approach in an online marketplace, which is monetized through sales commissions and advertising revenues. Their hybrid scheme optimizes overall platform revenues, wherein the top 5 slots are reserved for cost-per-click auctions to enhance advertising revenues with the lower positions sorted in terms of expected sales revenues. A similar logic is applicable in our analysis of a hybrid ranking method, but two key differences are worth noting. We balance the factors that affect consumer utilities and platform revenues, whereas Choi and Mela (2019) trade off advertising and sales revenues. In addition, our analysis quantifies the value of both hybridization and personalization, whereas the prior study proposes a nonpersonalized hybrid approach.
Personalization is the ability to provide tailored content and services to individuals based on their revealed preferences in past behaviors (Hagen et al. 1999). Personalization is studied in different contexts with attention paid to the impacts of personalization on consumer surplus on the one hand and seller profits on the other. As a representative example, Rossi et al. (1996) study target couponing by designing various coupon face values for heterogeneous consumers. The results show that target couponing generates revenues 2.5 times higher than blanket couponing. Ansari and Mela (2003) propose personalized marketing emails, finding that the contenttargeting approach improves click-through rates. Also, prior studies examine recommender systems, which are designed to predict users' preferences using their own past choices or similar users' (e.g., Ansari et al. 2000, Bodapati 2008). In a personalized search setting, Yoganarasimhan (2020) adopts a machine-learning approach to implement personalization that maximizes consumer utilities. 6  Personalized online engagements, however, may harm platform profits when increasing consumer surplus. Zhang and Wedel (2009) investigate the effects of personalized promotions at different levels of granularity. They find that individual-specific personalization does not always result in a higher payoff than segment-specific personalization or no personalization at all. Similarly, in the targeted advertising context, Goldfarb and Tucker (2011) show that obtrusive ads aggravate privacy concerns and thereby lead to lower purchase intent. Finally, Ghose et al. ( 2014) find a negative effect of "active personalization" on platform revenues in a randomized experiment on a mock hotel search engine. 7 These studies suggest the possibility that higher personalization may create benefits for consumers at the expense of a platform. An underlying reason might be that consumer preferences are not always aligned with revenue margins. Our goal, in part, is to craft exquisite personalization that creates incremental value for both consumers and the platform in the app distribution context.
We illustrate the conceptual framework for our empirical analysis in Figure 1. The ultimate goal is to study personalized ranking on platform revenues, jointly considering consumer utilities and CPA margins. Consumer latent utilities are structurally modeled in a two-stage decision-making process of click and conversion. Covariates used to estimate the latent utility functions include a variety of impression and app characteristics, including screen rank, quality, popularity, and other variables motivated by prior research. We recover the utility function at the individual level by specifying full user heterogeneity in a hierarchical Bayes framework. Finally, we leverage the structural parameter estimates, in conjunction with data on platform revenue margins, to conduct a series of counterfactual policy experiments to evaluate a set of nonpersonalized and personalized ranking schemes. These experiments demonstrate the incremental value of personalization and shed light on the nature of the most fruitful personalized ranking scheme, which aligns consumer preferences with enhanced platform revenues.
To characterize the nature of the optimal ranking scheme, we develop a simple analytical model (see the online appendix), which considers app consumption via an offer wall. The model incorporates search (or exploration) costs, different app qualities, and user heterogeneity in taste for quality. 8 We solve the model to compare platform revenues under the optimal personalized with nonpersonalized ranking schemes. One of the key results is that a hybrid ranking scheme could be most effective. Extrapolating from the analytical model, the logic for a hybrid personalized ranking scheme in a real-world platform is as follows. The top of the list should include the highest utility apps for a given user, sorted in decreasing order of revenue margins. Because the user is likely to click on all these high-utility impressions (i.e., the utility differences among them are negligible), ranking is the most significant determinant affecting click performance. As such, the platform maximizes revenues from these slots ranked by margins. The remaining spots are sorted in decreasing order of the product of utility and margin (utility × margin) to align consumer download utility with revenue margins. The resulting hybrid scheme demonstrates higher platform revenues relative to alternative rankings based on utilities or margins alone.
Though we gain useful guidance from the analytical model, the primary engine that drives our empirical analysis is a structural utility model that considers a two-stage choice process (i.e., click and install) at the individual level. Our high-resolution model grants two benefits with respect to ranking design. First, we are able to characterize each consumer's preference precisely, whereas prior literature (e.g., Ghose et al. 2012Ghose et al. , 2014;;De los Santos and Koulayev 2017) has to average out preference heterogeneity. It is also worth noting that our two-stage modeling better reflects users' decision making compared with simultaneous equations that ignore the conditional dependence of clicks and conversions. Second, we specify how to balance the recovered utility functions with CPA margins to yield more effective personalized ranking. Specifically, in order to maximize expected revenues at the individual level, we explicitly balance conversion performances with CPA margins by hybridizing ranking schemes. In this regard, the structural parameter estimates allow us to infer a consumer's favorite apps, which are ranked in terms of margins, yet the consumer is most likely to click on them. The remainder of the list is sorted on the basis of both utility and margin. Indeed, this is the logic behind our hybrid personalized ranking scheme based on the context and data described next.
We obtain a unique data set from a marketing agency that monetizes the home screen for one of the major mobile service operators in the United States. The home screen provides common features, including local and web search, content display (e.g., news, weather, and horoscope), and a mobile app offer wall. We focus on the role of this service provider as an app distribution platform. Note that third-party app distribution platforms, such as this one, account for some 32% of overall app installs (App Annie 2017).
We illustrate the business model of this app distribution platform in Figure 2. A user visits the offer wall and explores the app impressions. 9 If an app draws the user's interest, the user can click on the impression and get redirected to the corresponding app store (e.g., Apple App Store and Google Play). The landing page provides the user with more details about the app, including description, download volume, reviews, and other information. This information is pertinent to the user's decision whether to install (i.e., download) the app. The app distribution platform earns revenues on a CPA on a pay per download basis, whereby each app has a precontracted CPA margin. Figure 3 shows some representative screenshots of the app offer wall and landing pages. In summary, consumers are provided with app titles and average star ratings as part of the app impressions on the offer wall. After clicking on an impression, they observe the number of downloads, Information Systems Research, 2023, vol. 34, no. 3, pp. 811-827, © 2022 INFORMS detailed app descriptions, and full-text reviews on the landing page.
Our clickstream data are derived from server logs collected during the first three weeks of July 2015. The logs capture the impressions served to each user along with their clicks and installs. All impressions are organized in chronological order at the user-impression level, enabling us to recover the screen rank of each impression and the total body of impressions displayed during a given session. In addition to mobile clickstream data, we also consider app characteristics from both numerical (screen rank, review volume and valence, the number of downloads) and textual (app titles, descriptions, and reviews) data.
Recent research emphasizes the importance of supplementing quantitative data with textual variables, such as readability (e.g., Ghose and Ipeirotis 2011) and sentiment (e.g., Goh et al. 2013). To this end, we consider a pair of objective and subjective measures. Informativeness captures how much objective information a text contains, whereas sentiment measures consumers' subjective feelings expressed through the text. We follow prior literature to include three constructs for informativeness, including length (e.g., Ghose and Han 2014), word frequency (e.g., Yamamoto and Church 2001), and ambiguity (e.g., Klapdor et al. 2014). These are supplemented with the polarity of sentiment (e.g., Archak et al. 2011).
We apply multiple text-analytic tools to operationalize these two types of textual variables. Specifically, we construct informativeness and ambiguity measures for objective information and extract sentiments from the text for subjective opinions as described. 10 Informativeness is operationalized based on word frequency and the length of texts. Word frequency characterizes how specific a word is. The more frequently a word is used, the less specific information it conveys. The overall informativeness of a text is taken to be negatively related to the average word frequencies. 11 Thus, we follow Leech et al. (2001) to compute the frequency of each word in a text using the corpus-based word frequency and compute the average. Also, longer texts generally contain more information than shorter ones. We count words in the texts to approximate the richness of information; an  2014), we measure ambiguity at the word level by calculating the number of semantic interpretations that a word possesses. 12 We use the average of word ambiguities as a measure of the overall ambiguity of each text object. Finally, to capture the sentiments of text, we adopt a polarity classifier. We let the polarity range from zero to one, wherein the two extremes indicate completely negative and completely positive sentiments, respectively. We implement the classifier in a logistic regression model and estimate it using an L1-penalized maximum likelihood estimator. 13  App titles, descriptions, and reviews are run through the trained model to obtain the corresponding sentiments.

Following the preceding hierarchical model specifications, we develop a Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) procedure to make recursive parameter draws from the corresponding full conditional distributions as
We implement the random walk Metropolis-Hastings algorithm because the posterior distributions do not have closed-form specifications. Our adaptive estimation strategy consists of two steps to search the parameter spaces more efficiently. In the first step, we run a pilot MCMC for 50,000 iterations and discard the first 20,000 draws as the burn-in samples. We next utilize the remaining 30,000 draws to compute the empirical posterior means and covariance matrices. In the second step, we run a separate Metropolis-Hastings sampler using the posterior means and covariance matrices as the initial values and covariance parameters for the proposal distributions. We run the sampler for 50,000 iterations and keep every 20th draw to approximate the posteriors. To test the convergence of the MCMC procedure, we perform the Gelman-Rubin diagnostic that compares the estimated between-and within-chain variances for each parameter (Gelman and Rubin 1992). We ensure convergence by running three parallel chains with different initial values and random seeds. The diagnostic concludes that the chains converge. The resulting potential scale reduction factors (PSRF) are all below 1.08-well below the suggested threshold (i.e., PSRF 1.2) for the assessment of convergence (Brooks and Gelman 1998).

We summarize the effects of the covariates on click and install decisions in Table 4. 16 Starting with the click stage, Rank has a negative and significant coefficient, indicating that app impressions higher up on the screen are more likely to be clicked on. The positive and significant coefficient on Rating suggests that higher rated apps are associated with a higher click-through rate. Turning to the textual variables, ln(TitleLen) is positive and significant, and TitleFreq is negative and significant, jointly indicating that consumers prefer apps with more informative names.
The coefficient of TitleAmb is negative and significant, implying that a more ambiguous app title deters click performance. The sentiment of app title has a significant impact on clicks. TitleSent is negative and implies that app titles with more restricted words (e.g., kill, shot, and ruin) generally draw more attention from consumers. The insignificant coefficient of Game suggests that the click performance is similar across game and nongame apps. The negative impact of the number of competing apps on the click-through rate is illustrated by the significant coefficient of ln(Num-CompApp), indicating substantial substitution effects between competing apps in the same category.
In the install stage, DescLen and DescFreq are not significant, indicating that the informativeness of descriptions does not significantly affect the install decision. The insignificant coefficient of DescAmb shows no evident correlations between the ambiguity of description and the willingness to install. However, DescSent is significantly positive and shows that descriptions written in more positive tones are more favorable. These results together suggest that consumers do not pay much attention to the details (e.g., features and functions) in descriptions-at least not on their mobile devices-but they are swayed by emotional cues in the descriptions. Conditional on a click, Rating remains significantly positive and shows that consumers are more likely to install higher quality apps, consistent with the importance of quality to sales of experience goods in other online contexts (e.g., Chevalier and Mayzlin 2006). The insignificance of ln(NumRatings) means that the volume of ratings does not influence consumers' propensity to install. It is worth noting that Popularity is insignificant at this stage. In other words, popular apps do not recruit more installs than less popular apps. One possible explanation is that consumers generally have installed the majority of the most popular apps (e.g., Facebook and Twitter). This pattern is consistent with the finding that product popularity is not always directly correlated with the conversion rate (Yang and Ghose 2010).
Based on the coefficient estimates in Table 4, we can quantify the economic significance of the factors. To interpret the coefficients of a probit model, we calculate the marginal effects of each variable when fixing the others at their mean values. Quantitatively, a 1% increase in the app title length is associated with a 2.12% increase in CTR. One more synonym for a word in an app title decreases CTR by 3.15%. Changing the tone of an app title from positive to relatively negative boosts the click performance by 3.01%. However, the role of sentiment in descriptions gets flipped so that a positive sentiment of app descriptions brings a 1.22% increase in the propensity to install compared with a negative sentiment. For the significance of the numerical variables, moving an app one position up on the screen increases CTR by 4.26%. Having one more star in ratings increases the click-through and install rates by 2.91% and 1.37%, respectively. When the list of impressions includes one more competing app in the same browsing session, the click performance of the focal impression drops by 2.66%.
We also find some interesting differences when we investigate the impacts of textual versus numerical information on click and download behaviors, which we highlight throughout appropriate grouping of variables in Table 4. Textual covariates based on app titles and descriptions play a more significant role in the click stage than in the download stage. A likely explanation has to do with the relative salience of the two types of information in the two stages. At the click stage, textual information is brief and can be processed as efficiently as numerical data. On the landing pages, however, textual descriptions are substantially longer, whereas the numerical information can be processed more economically, especially on the cramped real estate of a mobile screen. Accordingly, in the install stage, users are influenced by the numerical covariates and by the overall sentiment of the textual descriptions rather than detailed textual features.

Starting with in-sample predictions, the main model (i.e., Model 1) with full heterogeneity outperforms the others in terms of root mean square error (RMSE), mean squared error (MSE), and mean absolute deviation (MAD), the performance measures suggested by Ghose et al. (2014). The comparisons between Models 1 and 2 indicate that incorporating textual information significantly improves the model fit by 13.33%, 12.50%, and 17.65% in RMSE, MSE, and MAD, respectively. The full-heterogeneity model (i.e., Model 4) consistently remains superior to the other two. Overall, both in-and out-of-sample validations confirm the importance of accounting for consumer heterogeneity and textual covariates.

In the main model, we operationalize the textual information of app titles and descriptions using word frequency, the length of texts, ambiguity, and sentiment measures. We consider a series of ranking approaches in our policy experiments to illustrate the impact of personalization on platform revenue improvements. Table 9 summarizes the results. Columns (a) and (b) list the performances of nonpersonalized and personalized rankings, respectively. Focusing on nonpersonalized methods in column (a), we first consider a mean utilitybased ranking (1a) in Table 9, corresponding to the mean-utility ranking of Ghose et al. (2014). Impressions are ranked in decreasing order of mean utility (CTR j × CR j ) to all users. The third nonpersonalized ranking (3a) is a hybrid one, which displays the highest utility apps in decreasing order of margins on the top section followed by the remaining apps in decreasing order of the utility-margin product (Utility × Margin). 18  This method results in a revenue improvement of 2.38% relative to (1a). Next, we discuss the personalized counterparts of (1a)-(3a), wherein app listings differ across users. Thus, the personalized utility-based ranking for user i displays apps in decreasing order of CTR ij × CR ij , resulting in an increase in revenues of 4.92% relative to (1a). The personalized counterpart of (2a), which accounts for both user utilities and app margins (CTR ij × CR ij × Margin j ), substantially increases revenues by 15.56%. The personalized hybrid method implemented at the individual level provides the highest expected revenue with an increase of 16.73% relative to (1a). The side-by-side comparisons between personalized and nonpersonalized methods jointly highlight the value of personalization on ranking design. In every case, the personalization of rankings increases revenues, ranging from 5% to 17% improvements relative to (1a). Finally, we note that the hybrid approach is more effective than the utility-margin approach only under personalization.
The policy experiments provide several insights with respect to how platform revenues can be increased via screen ranking methods. To begin with, we confirm that accounting for average consumer utilities in the ranking of impressions can yield higher platform revenues (e.g., Ghose et al. 2014, De los Santos andKoulayev 2017). Indeed, the average utility case serves as the benchmark in our comparative analysis of ranking methods. The first thing we learn from the policy experiments is that incorporating app margins into the average utility methods can further enhance platform revenues even in the absence of personalization. This echoes how Google's ranking of sponsored search results accounts for both landing page quality (analogous to average utility in our case) and bid amounts (analogous to margins in our case). However, true gains in platform revenues are only available through personalization, which leverages the heterogeneity of user preferences. When personalization lifts the revenues of the utility-based scheme (1b), it raises the revenues of the Utility × Margin scheme (2b) even more. The reason is that the platform implements (2b) by not only balancing the trade-off between consumer utilities (which drives click and conversion) and app margins (which drives marginal revenue contribution), but personalizing the trade-off across users. In a sense, personalized Utility × Margin more precisely characterizes the individual-specific trade-off regarding salient heterogenous user preferences, significantly raising platform revenues. The revenue improvement can be further enhanced in the personalized case of the HMUM ranking (3b). On top of the personalized tradeoff, (3c) cherry-picks each user's favorite apps that are most likely to be downloaded. Accordingly, in this scheme the platform benefits by placing a user's favorite apps (sorted by app margin) on the top and listing the remaining apps in decreasing order of Utility × Margin.
We develop a comprehensive framework to leverage clickstream data for more effective mobile app distribution monetization through a personalized ranking in the context of third-party app distribution platforms. Such platforms account for 32% of all app downloads, so this setting is of considerable interest in its own right. Besides, these platforms also serve as advertising and retail channels for app developers in partnership with telecom companies and online communities. In this regard, these platforms help developers to market apps and consumers to explore apps by maintaining a variety of app categories.
Our empirical analysis proceeds in two stages. First, we implement a two-stage click and conversion model in a hierarchical Bayesian framework that incorporates individual heterogeneity. Second, we recover individual utility parameter estimates and use them in a counterfactual analysis through suitable policy experiments to study several nonpersonalized and personalized ranking methods. To summarize the results of the click and conversion models, we find that our set of numerical and textual covariates are collectively highly significant in explaining consumer choice on the platform. We find that screen rank is a critical determinant of which app impressions consumers choose to click on; moving an impression up one slot on the screen is associated with a 4.26% increase in click-through rates.
The valence of reviews is also important, more so with respect to which apps are installed than which impressions are clicked on. Also, there exist significant substitution effects among the competing apps in the same browsing session. Interestingly, we find that the popularity of apps does not explain download behavior.
The reason, we suspect, could be that the most popular apps are downloaded already, nullifying the incremental impact of this factor on conversions. Moreover, we find that users pay attention to textual information. In the click stage, the informativeness of app titles has a significant and positive impact, whereas ambiguity and sentiment have a negative relationship with CTR. Consumers are persuaded to click on the titles consisting of less frequently used and less ambiguous words. App titles with more restricted words (e.g., kill, shot, and ruin) generally catch more eyeballs. In the conversion stage, only the sentiment of descriptions positively affects consumer decisions. We also notice that review text features are insignificant for explaining app installs. A likely explanation is that users tend not to read detailed review texts on their cramped mobile screens, relying on numerical summaries instead.
In the policy experiments, we manipulate the positions of app impressions using the recovered consumer utility parameters and calculate the expected platform revenues based on the actual CPA margins. The results indicate that a personalized ranking method accounting for utilities and margins outperforms all other ranking methods we consider. Remarkably, personalized rankings outperform nonpersonalized counterparts ranging from 4.92% to 16.73% in which the proposed hybrid approach is more effective than other personalized alternatives. In terms of implementation, personalized ranking could be deployed via a nightly batch process, wherein the utility functions are reestimated using all the available clickstream data in the archive. These updated utility function parameters are used to determine the personalized rankings in advance for each user such that the impressions are presented with a minimal real-time computational burden.
These results contribute to the literature in several ways. First, as Table 1 summarizes, this study is one of the first to examine app install monetization, adding to the range of contexts studied in prior work, including search engines and the downloads of music and movies. Further, we deploy a comprehensive set of both numerical and textual covariates. Second, we are able to implement a unique study of personalization in the app monetization context because of the fine granular clickstream data at the user-impression level. Thus, we model individual heterogeneity, which allows us to examine a personalized ranking through suitable policy experiments; in contrast, prior studies (Ghose et al. 2012(Ghose et al. , 2014;;Choi and Mela 2019) discuss earlier estimate drivers of weekly aggregate click and conversion rates. At the same time, we have access to each app's CPA margin-we have not seen this in any prior work-which enables us to analyze the precise revenue impact of alternate ranking strategies. The optimal hybrid scheme that we propose balances drivers of consumer utilities with revenue margins. Finally, with respect to understanding the consumer utility for mobile apps, we focus on the microeconomy of an app distribution platform, whereas prior work focuses on market-wide demand drivers (e.g., Ghose and Han 2014).
Our work also provides actionable managerial implications. The majority of content distribution platforms, such as the one we study, exercise simple monetization heuristics. Our empirical analysis provides executable guidance on how such platforms can better monetize app distribution using clickstream data. These data, combined with CPA margins, help deploy ranking schemes that are substantially more profitable than extant algorithms. Specifically, the platforms can personalize rankings to individual users in an optimal way, generating higher platform revenues along with higher consumer surplus at the same time. Such personalized rankings are increasingly feasible to implement in real time as more data processing and analytical capabilities are available to mobile service operators. We expect that our hybrid personalized ranking is also applicable in other contexts as long as consumer utility and revenue margins matter, such as movie or music distribution and product search engines. Indeed, our empirical framework provides step-by-step guidance on how to implement such a novel personalized ranking method.
Our analysis also points to the importance of considering textual content (i.e., titles and descriptions) for both platforms and developers, shaping titles, descriptions, and sentiments for more effective monetization. The significance of the textual variables suggests that platforms could use app titles and descriptions to promote new apps that do not yet have enough ratings and review data. Finally, marketers can learn to leverage the preference heterogeneity on textual information to perform targeting. For instance, the platform can engage users who are used to reading descriptions by providing additional product details in texts. Similarly, phrasing in various sentiments can be utilized to target specific consumers given the significant heterogeneous preference on sentiment.
Our study, as is other empirical work, is constrained by data limitations. First, we cannot collect consumer demographics because of privacy protections. In this regard, we manage to implement a hierarchical model to account for unobserved consumer heterogeneity. Platforms with access to such demographics can further sharpen personalized rankings given a lower bound on revenue improvements via the personalization we show. Second, we have not evaluated the proposed ranking strategy in a randomized field experiment; instead, we exploit the individual heterogeneity estimates through policy experiments. However, it would be a fruitful exercise for further research to conduct experiments to obtain more robust insights into the impact of personalization. Third, we do not estimate the temporal effects on users' click and install decisions from a dynamic perspective. We precisely model the stage-dependency between the click and install decisions with full heterogeneity at the individual level. This approach enables us to study consumer heterogeneity and personalization in the ranking design as the main focus of this paper. As expected, incorporating dynamic components into the model could incur substantial difficulties in empirical identification and computational burden given the existing estimation challenges. We, thus, leave this area for future research. Overall, our analysis provides a platform with executable actions to enhance app distribution monetization along with potential benefits to multiple stakeholders in a mobile ecosystem.

title: Network Interconnectivity and Entry into Platform Markets
abstract: Digital technologies have led to the emergence of many platforms in our economy today. In certain platform networks, buyers in one market purchase services from providers in many other markets, whereas in others, buyers primarily purchase services from providers within the same market. Accordingly, network interconnectivity-which measures the degree to which consumers in one market purchase services from service providers in a different market-varies across different industries. We examine how network interconnectivity affects interactions between an incumbent platform serving multiple markets and an entrant platform seeking to enter one of these markets. Our model yields several interesting results. First, even if the entrant can advertise at no cost, it still may not want to make every user in a local market aware of its service, as doing so may trigger a competitive response from the incumbent. Second, having more mobile buyers, which increases interconnectivity between markets, can reduce the incumbent's incentive to fight and, thus, increase the entrant's incentive to expand. Third, stronger interconnectivity between markets may or may not make the incumbent more defensible: when advertising is not costly and mobile buyers consume in both their local markets and the markets they visit, a large number of mobile buyers will increase the entrant's profitability, thereby making it difficult for the incumbent to deter entry. However, when advertising is costly or mobile buyers only consume in the markets they travel to, a large number of mobile buyers will help the incumbent deter entry. When advertising cost is at an intermediate level, the entrant prefers a market with moderate interconnectivity between markets. Fourth, we find that even if advanced targeting technologies can enable the entrant to also advertise to mobile buyers, the entrant may choose not to do so in order to avoid triggering the incumbent's competitive response. Finally, we find that the presence of network effects is likely to decrease the entrant's profit. Our results offer managerial implications for platform firms and help understand their performance heterogeneity.
full_text:
Digitalization has led to the emergence of numerous platforms in our economy today (Rochet and Tirole 2003, Iansiti and Levien 2004, Parker and Van Alstyne 2005). Examples of popular platforms include Uber in the transportation industry, Airbnb in the accommodation industry, Craigslist in the classifieds market, and Groupon in the local daily deals market. A growing body of literature on information systems attempts to understand the optimal strategies required for digital platforms to scale and compete. Scholars have examined a variety of issues, including optimal pricing (e.g., Parker and Van Alstyne 2005), interactions between competing platforms (e.g., Koh and Fichman 2014, Niculescu et al. 2018, Zhang et al. 2018), optimal business models (e.g., Chen et al. 2016, Parker et al. 2017, Tian et al. 2018), strategies to motivate third-party providers (e.g., Huang et al. 2019, Kuang et al. 2019), matching efficiency between buyers and sellers (e.g., Hong andPavlou 2017, Xu 2018), platforms' investment decisions (e.g., Anderson et al. 2014), managing multigenerational platforms (e.g., Hann et al. 2016), and contractual relationships or tensions between platform owners and third-party providers (e.g., Huang et al. 2013, Hao et al. 2017, Li and Agarwal 2017).
Our study adds to this literature by examining how network characteristics affect the strategies and performance of competing platforms. All platforms exhibit two-sidedness in that they facilitate matching and transactions between consumers and service providers in their markets, but the interconnectivity of their businesses-which measures the degree to which consumers in one market purchase services from service providers in a different market-varies considerably across industries. For example, the network structure of Upwork, an online marketplace that connects millions of businesses with freelancers around the globe, exhibits high interconnectivities among different markets. In contrast, Uber's network consists of local network clusters with some interconnectivity among them: riders transact with drivers in their own city and, except for frequent travelers, they care mostly about the local availability of Uber drivers. We observe similar local network clusters with some interconnectivity in group buying platforms such as Groupon, classifieds sites such as Craigslist, food delivery platforms such as Grubhub, restaurantreservation platforms such as OpenTable, and marketplaces that match freelance labor with local demand such as TaskRabbit, Instacart, and Rover.
The network interconnectivity of a platform market has important implications for the profitability and defensibility of incumbent platforms. When the network is strongly interconnected, it is difficult for a new entrant to compete, particularly when consumers in one local market mostly purchase services from other markets. A platform that enters one local market, for example, would waste a significant amount of marketing resources to build awareness among local consumers and service providers without generating a large number of transactions. Therefore, for a new platform, entry into highly interconnected markets is costly. In contrast, when consumers and service providers mostly transact within their local clusters, it is relatively easy for a new platform to enter, as it can specialize in one local cluster and build awareness from there. In the ride-sharing industry, many entrants have challenged market leaders in local markets. Fasten entered the Boston market in 2015 to compete with Uber and Lyft with a much smaller budget. In New York City, Juno and Via have been competing with Uber and Lyft for years, and Myle was launched recently. Uber also faced a wave of rivals in London, including Estonia's Bolt, France's Kapten, Israel's Gett, and India's Ola. Didi, the largest ridesharing company in China, constantly faced new entrants in multiple cities.
In this paper, we adopt a game-theoretical approach to examine how network interconnectivity affects competitive interactions between an incumbent platform and an entrant platform. The incumbent platform has an installed base of buyers and service providers in multiple local markets; the entrant is interested in entering one of these markets. To capture interconnectivity between local markets, we assume that some buyers are mobile: they travel between markets, purchasing services in each. In the first stage, the entrant invests money to build brand awareness in one of these markets. In the second stage, the incumbent and the entrant set prices for buyers and wages for service providers in that market. In the third stage, buyers and service providers in that market choose one platform on which to conduct transactions.
Our model yields several interesting results. First, even if the entrant can advertise at no cost, it still may not want to make every user in a local market aware of its service, as doing so may trigger a competitive response from the incumbent. Second, having more mobile buyers, which increases interconnectivity between markets, can reduce the incumbent's incentive to fight and, thus, increase the entrant's incentive to expand. Third, stronger interconnectivity across markets may or may not make the incumbent more defensible. When advertising is not costly and mobile buyers consume in both their local markets and the markets they visit, a large number of mobile buyers (i.e., great interconnectivity) will increase the entrant's profitability, thereby making it difficult for the incumbent to deter entry. This result is somewhat surprising: great interconnectivity is supposed to provide the entrant with disadvantage because it increases the size of the incumbent's potential market while retaining the size of the entrant's potential market. When advertising cost is at an intermediate level, the entrant prefers a market with moderate interconnectivity between markets. When advertising is costly or mobile buyers consume only in the markets they travel to, a large number of mobile buyers will help the incumbent deter entry. Fourth, we find that even if advanced targeting technologies can enable the entrant to also advertise to mobile buyers, the entrant may choose not to do so to avoid triggering the incumbent's competitive response. Finally, we find evidence that the presence of network effects is likely to decrease the entrant's profit.
In the literature on platform strategies, our paper is closely related to the literature examining entry into platform markets. Studies have identified a number of factors that influence the success or failure of entrants in platform markets, such as the strength of network effects (e.g., Zhu andIansiti 2012, Niculescu et al. 2018), platform quality (e.g., Liebowitz 2002, Tellis et al. 2009), multihoming (e.g., Cennamo and Santalo 2013, Koh and Fichman 2014, Anderson et al. 2019), and exclusivity (e.g., Corts and Lederman 2009). All these studies assume a strongly interconnected network. As indicated in Afuah (2013), this assumption does not reflect the actual networks in most industries. Our study extends this literature by examining how network interconnectivity affects the strategies and performance of incumbents and entrants.
Broadly, our paper is related to competitive interactions between incumbents and entrants. Theoretical models in the literature focus on incumbent strategies such as capacity investment to deter or accommodate entry (e.g., Fudenberg andTirole 1984, Tirole 1988). Empirical studies often find that incumbent reactions to entrants are selective (e.g., Geroski 1995): whereas some incumbents choose to react to entrants aggressively, others do not appear to respond to entry. Studies have also shown that this variation in responses often depends on entrant characteristics, such as scale (e.g., Debruyne et al. 2002, Karakaya andYannopoulos 2011). Our model finds support for these empirical results. Chen and Guo (2014) document a similar result regarding an entrant refraining from overadvertising to avoid competitive response from a competitor but in a very different setting. In their setting, a third-party seller sells the same product as a retail platform and the seller needs to decide how much to advertise through other channels, such as search engines and social media. Our paper differs from these studies by examining how network interconnectivity changes the incumbent's incentives to react, the entrant's incentives to advertise, and the entrant's profit. We show that buyers' consumption behavior matters: when mobile buyers consume in local markets, greater network interconnectivity sometimes increases entrant profits; however, when they do not, greater network interconnectivity reduces entrant profits.
Our paper is also related to studies that examine how network structures affect product diffusion (e.g., Abrahamson and Rosenkopf 1997, Suarez 2005, Lee et al. 2006, Sundararajan 2007, Tucker 2008). These studies typically focus on social networks, like instant messaging platforms, and examine questions related to issues such as seeding within these networks (e.g., Galeotti andGoyal 2009, Manshadi et al. 2020), pricing policies to facilitate product diffusion (e.g., Campbell 2013, Leduc et al. 2017), network formation processes and how local network clustering leads to local bias (e.g., Lee et al. 2016), prediction accuracy (e.g., Qiu et al. 2014), and market segmentation (e.g., Banerji and Dutta 2009). These networks have more complicated connections because they depend on individuals' own social networks and, consequently, these studies rely on simulations or descriptive results. We adopt a different perspective to focus on how interconnectivity between local markets affects market entry and derive closed-form solutions.
The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we introduce the model and analyze the competitive interactions between an incumbent and an entrant. In Section 3, we examine extensions to our main models. In Section 4, we conclude by discussing the implications of our results and potential future research.
Assume that there are multiple local markets each with N buyers who are currently using the incumbent's platform (denoted by I) for transactions. A fraction of buyers in each market are mobile-r percent of them travel between markets. Assume the movement is random, so that in equilibrium, in each market, rN buyers visit other markets and rN additional buyers come from other markets to make purchases. Hence, r measures the interconnectivity between these markets. Each mobile buyer places one order for the service in his local market and another order when he travels. For example, riders use ride-sharing services in their local markets; when they travel, they use ridesharing services in other markets. 1 Each service provider fulfills one order at most. To accommodate these mobile buyers, each market has (1 + r)N service providers. Table 1 provides a summary of the notation used in the main model.
Before an entrant (denoted by E) enters one of these markets, the incumbent serves the market as a monopoly and all the users (i.e., both service providers and buyers) are aware of the incumbent. 2 Neither the buyers nor the service providers are aware of the entrant, but the entrant can advertise to build awareness.
The game proceeds as follows, as depicted in Figure 1. In the first stage, the entrant invests to build brand awareness among users in the local market. Advertising is costly, and it costs the entrant L(n) to reach n potential users. The entrant decides on θ, a fraction of the potential users reached through advertising. 3 Because we have N buyers and (1 + r)N service providers, n θ(2N + rN). Following the literature (Thompson and Teng 1984, Tirole 1988, Esteves and Resende 2016, Jiang and Srinivasan 2016), we assume the advertising cost is a (weakly) increasing and convex function of n: L (n) ≥ 0 and L (n) ≥ 0. Note that even with digital technologies, it remains costly to build awareness. While certain platforms may be able to attract their first tranche of customers relatively inexpensively, through word-ofmouth or other low-cost strategies, the cost typically begins escalating when the platform begins to look for new and somewhat different customers through search advertising, referral fees, and other marketing strategies (see, e.g., Dennis 2017). Consequently, many platforms exit the market after burning too much money on customer acquisition. In our model, we allow advertising cost to vary and examine its implications on platform strategies and performance. In the main model, we also assume that the entrant is not able to advertise to mobile buyers. We relax this assumption in an extension.
In the second stage, the incumbent sets the price to each buyer, denoted by p I , and the wage to each service provider, denoted by w I , in the local market. The entrant also sets the price for the service buyers, denoted by p E , and the wage for the service providers, denoted by w E . Here, the subscript denotes the platform (I for incumbent and E for entrant). For example, Instacart, decides the prices for users and the wages for shoppers. Uber decides the rates for riders and the commissions it takes before passing on the revenue from riders to drivers, which effectively determines the wages for drivers. Consistent with the practice, we allow firms to set different prices and wages in different markets, but they do not price discriminate based on whether a buyer is local or mobile within a market. Hence, the entrant and the incumbent compete for buyers and service providers from the local market, but the mobile buyers will only use the incumbent platform.

Prior studies have often had to make simplifying assumptions, such as a fixed price (or royalty rate) on one-side of the market, symmetric pricing, or one platform being an open source platform and, thus, free (e.g., Rochet and Tirole 2003, Economides and Katsamakas 2006, Casadesus-Masanell and Halaburda 2014, Adner et al. 2020). In this study, we take advantage of a market clearing condition to derive the optimal prices and wages for the two competing platforms. It continues to charge the monopoly price, v, and offer the monopoly wage, zero, although its profit does decrease as θ increases because it loses market share to the entrant. The entrant platform incentivizes some buyers and service providers to switch by charging a lower price and offering a higher wage.
The threshold for θ (weakly) increases with r because mobile buyers are only aware of the incumbent platform (i.e., the incumbent platform has monopoly power over them) and their existence reduces the incumbent's incentive to respond to the entrant. It is thus not surprising that the entrant can take advantage of this lack of incentive and increase its advertising intensity. The number of transactions hosted on the incumbent platform increases with r because of mobile buyers from other markets, even though the incumbent loses more transactions from local buyers to the entrant when r increases. The incumbent platform's profit increases with r because of the increase in transactions at the same monopoly price it charges. The number of transactions the entrant serves also increases with r because it can advertise more aggressively without triggering a competitive response from the incumbent. The entrant's profit increases with r without taking the advertising cost into account. If advertising cost increases significantly with r, the entrant's profit may decrease with r, a scenario which will be examined later.
When θ is larger than the threshold, however, the entrant platform has the potential to steal a large market share from the incumbent. The incumbent platform chooses to respond by lowering its price to buyers. The entrant platform thus lowers its price to buyers as well. The results suggest that under certain circumstances (e.g., when advertising is cheap), network interconnectivity, which does not influence the size of the entrant's potential demand in a single market but is supposed to benefit the incumbent that operates in multiple interconnected markets, may, in fact, encourage the entrant to enter the market and increase entrant profit. In this case, a higher network interconnectivity will make it even more difficult for an incumbent to deter entry. These results have important managerial implications for platform owners to understand their competitiveness in markets with a given level of market interconnectivity for resource planning and marketing strategy design, and for policy makers to take into account the network interconnectivity when considering the anticompetitive issues in platform markets. These results also have important implications for the entrant regarding the choice of market to enter when the fraction of incoming mobile buyers varies across markets; we will examine this further in the next section.
In our main analysis, we assume that all markets are homogenous. Consequently, the entrant could begin by entering any one of these markets. If these markets have different fractions of mobile buyers visiting from other markets, assuming the entrant only has the budget to enter one market only, which market should the entrant choose to enter?
Suppose there are H markets. Let r h be the fraction of mobile buyers coming into market h (h 1, 2, … , H). Hence, market h has N local buyers, (1 + r h )N service providers, and r h N incoming mobile buyers. We obtain the following proposition. 9 Proposition 4. When k is small, the entrant should choose the market with the highest fraction of mobile buyers from other markets, r, to enter; when k is large, the entrant should choose the market with the lowest fraction of mobile buyers from other markets, r, to enter. For an intermediate value of k, the entrant may choose a market where r is also intermediate. 10   The result echoes Proposition 3, where we find that the entrant's profit increases with r when k is small, decreases with r when k is large, and has a nonmonotonic relationship with r for an intermediate value of k. Whereas Proposition 3 focuses on how the entrant's profit changes when r in a local market increases, this proposition extends our finding to how the entrant should choose a market among the markets that vary in the fraction of incoming mobile buyers. The proposition suggests that when the fraction of visitors is high, the incumbent is less likely to fight the entrant. At the same time, however, a high fraction of visitors means that a large fraction of the entrant's advertising expenditure will be wasted on unmatched service providers. Hence, the entrant will find such a market attractive when advertising is not costly. For example, if Google wants to offer ride-sharing services because it already has a larger number of users from its current services and can build awareness at a low cost (k is small), Google should start offering these services in large cities with a large fraction of visitors. However, a new startup, for which advertising is rather costly, should target small cities with a small fraction of visitors in order to improve advertising efficiency.
Entire Market In our main model, we also assume that the incumbent owns the entire market (i.e., all potential buyers and service providers are aware of the incumbent) before the entrant emerges. In reality, it is possible that not every user in the local market is aware of the incumbent. Thus, it is possible for the entrant to attract users who are not aware of the incumbent. We consider this possibility in this extension. Assume the incumbent's market share before the entrant arrives is s, where 0 < s < 1. We then have the following proposition. The results from the main model remain qualitatively the same as long as s is sufficiently large. But when s is below a certain threshold, the results differ from our main results. When the incumbent has a small share of the market, the entrant and the incumbent can effectively avoid direct competition by targeting different segments of that market. Hence, both will charge monopoly prices and offer monopoly wages, and no buyers and service providers will switch from the incumbent to the entrant.
They Travel In our main model, mobile buyers purchase services in both their local markets and the markets they visit. This assumption fits with markets such as those in the ride-sharing industry, where riders hail cars in their own markets and also in other markets when they travel, or daily local deal markets, where consumers buy deals in their own markets and also in other markets when they travel. In this case, interconnectivity affects the size of the potential market for the incumbent but does not affect the size of the potential market for the entrant. Our main model thus enables us to examine the impact of market interconnectivity on the entrant independent of the market size effect. Interestingly, although the size of the potential market for the entrant is unchanged, its profit may increase with the interconnectivity between markets. This possible profit enhancement for the entrant, independent of the market size effect, is the most interesting result of our model and provides novel insights regarding the role of market interconnectivity in influencing platform competition.
Although the assumption that mobile buyers purchase services in both their local markets and the markets they visit is consistent with the practice for many platforms, in this extension, we examine to what extent our results are affected by this assumption by looking at the scenario in which mobile buyers do not consume in their local markets. We obtain the following result under this assumption. Proposition 6. The results from the main model are qualitatively the same when mobile buyers do not consume in their local markets, except that the entrant's profit under the optimal θ always decreases with r.
Unlike in the main model, in this case, by assuming away local consumption, we keep the size of the potential market for the incumbent fixed. The size of the potential market for the entrant, however, changes with interconnectivity: a larger fraction of mobile buyers will have fewer potential buyers for the entrant. The results suggest that the incumbent's profit always increases with r, irrespective of whether local consumption occurs. However, although the entrant can continue to take advantage of the incumbent's disincentive to fight and advertise more aggressively, its demand decreases (i.e., the market size effect and interconnectivity effect take place jointly). Consequently, its profit decreases with r. In the case of Airbnb, for example, travelers typically do not care about the number of hosts in their home cities; they care more about the number of hosts in the cities they wish to visit. 11 This result explains why it is more difficult to challenge an incumbent platform like Airbnb for which local consumption occurs less frequently compared with one like Uber.

As we show in the main analysis, mobile buyers help deter the incumbent from fighting with the entrant. Hence, the entrant may not want to steal the mobile buyers from the incumbent even when it can target them and advertise to them at zero cost. The entrant is more likely to avoid advertising to the mobile segment when the value of these buyers to the incumbent is high (large v), the mobile segment is not large so the entrant does not lose a huge number of potential buyers (small r), and a small amount of advertising can steal a large number of mobile buyers away from the incumbent and thus trigger its response (small m). When the advertising cost for mobile buyers is higher than the cost for local users, the entrant will be even less likely to advertise to mobile buyers. The only situation in which the entrant will advertise to mobile buyers is when the entrant has advertised to all local buyers and has not triggered competitive responses from the incumbent, which is rarely observed in practice. Thus, Proposition 7 helps justify the assumption in our main model that mobile buyers are aware only of the incumbent.
In our main model, we focus on matching between the buyers and service providers. Similar to other matching models (e.g., Zhang et al. 2018), we do not model network effects. This approach enables us to separate the network-interconnectivity effect from the network effects, but network effects may have an impact on matching quality or speed. For example, in the case of ride-sharing services, a large number of drivers on a platform can reduce the wait time for riders. Similarly, a large number of riders reduces the idle time for drivers. In the accommodation market, a large number of hosts and travelers on a platform increase the likelihood that each traveler and each host is matched with a party close to his or her personal preference. Here, we use parameter e (e ≥ 0) to capture the strength of network effects. We first consider the case where e is small and both platform firms can coexist.
To avoid multiple equilibria due to network effects, we assume e to be much smaller than the value of the transaction itself. 12 This assumption is reasonable because in such markets most benefits to buyers or service providers come from the transaction itself. Proposition 8. The results from the main model are qualitatively the same in the presence of network effects when the strength of network effects is small.
We also examine how the strength of network effects affects the profits of both the entrant and incumbent. Given the computational complexity, we explore this effect as the strength of network effects, e, approaches zero. We find that as long as m is sufficiently large (e.g., m > v), because the incumbent has a larger market share, network effects make the incumbent more attractive to users, thereby reducing users' tendencies to switch to the entrant. Hence, as the network effects become stronger, the entrant's profit decreases and the incumbent's profit increases.
When e is sufficiently large, we find that the equilibrium in which the entrant has positive demand cannot be sustained and the incumbent becomes the monopoly. This result is expected because when network effects dominate pricing effects, if an entrant enters the market, the incumbent always has the incentive and is able to take advantage of its installed base advantage to drive the entrant out of the market.
Proposition 9. When network effects become sufficiently large, the incumbent can deter the entrant from entering the market and thereby monopolize the market.
