Extant studies in the platform strategy literature typically assume that each participant on one side of a market is (potentially) connected to every participant on the other side of the market. Our paper departs from this assumption to explore the impact of network interconnectivity on the defensibility of an incumbent with presence in multiple markets against an entrant that seeks to enter one of these markets.
As depicted in Figure 4, our model captures heterogeneous network interconnectivity across different industries, ranging from isolated network clusters (r 0) to a fully connected network (r 1). Examples of isolated local clusters (i.e., no mobile buyers) include Handy, a marketplace for handyman services, and Instacart, a platform that matches consumers with grocery shoppers. In such markets, consumers only buy services in their local markets and do not typically use such services when they travel. Toward the other end of the spectrum, we have strongly connected networks. This is the case for Airbnb, a platform on which travelers transact mostly with hosts outside their local clusters, and Upwork, an online outsourcing marketplace, where any clients and freelancers can initiate projects. Between the two extreme scenarios, we have networks that consist of local clusters with moderate interconnectivity. In the case of Uber, Grubhub, and Groupon, consumers primarily use their services in their local clusters but also use such services when they travel.
We find that the greater the interconnectivity, the lower the incumbent's incentive to respond and, hence, the stronger the entrant's incentive to reach more users in a local market. Whereas we find that the incumbent's profit always increases with interconnectivity, the entrant's profit does not always decrease with interconnectivity. When advertising is inexpensive and mobile buyers consume in both their local markets and the markets they travel to, the high interconnectivity between markets also increases the entrant's profit, thereby making it difficult for the incumbent to deter entry; on the other hand, when advertising is costly and/or mobile buyers consume only in the markets they travel to, high interconnectivity reduces the entrant's profit, thereby helping the incumbent deter entry. When the advertising cost is at an intermediate level, the entrant is more likely to survive under moderate interconnectivity between markets. We also extend our model to examine situations where markets are heterogeneous, the entrant is able to target mobile buyers, buyers and service providers have different switching costs, and network effects are present. Overall, these results help explain barriers to entry in platform markets and the resulting performance heterogeneity among platform firms in different markets.
These results corroborate empirical observations of many platform markets. For example, we show that it is optimal for an entrant not to trigger incumbent responses. The founders of Fasten, an entrant into the ridesharing market in Boston, were very clear from the beginning that they did not want to trigger Uber's response by strategically minimizing their advertising activities. 13  Fasten also chose not to target visitors in Boston: it did not advertise in Boston's Logan Airport or in its South Station Bus Terminals. Indeed, although Fasten grew rapidly in Boston during the period 2015-2017, Uber and Lyft did not change their prices or wages to compete. As a counterexample, when Meituan-a major player in China's online-to-offline services such as food delivery, movie ticketing, and travel bookings-entered the ridesharing business, it was able to build awareness of its service at almost no cost through its existing app, which had an extensive user base. Meituan's entry into the Shanghai ride-sharing market triggered strong responses from the incumbent, Didi, thereby leading to a subsidy war between the two companies. Meituan subsequently decided to halt ride-sharing expansion in China.
Our results also suggest that Airbnb's and Booking.com's business models are more defensible than Uber's because most of their customers are travelers and do not use the services in their local markets as often, whereas Uber's consumers primarily use its services in their local markets. The difference in defensibility is a key aspect for why Airbnb and Booking.com were able to achieve profitability, whereas Uber has been hemorrhaging money. 14  Our study offers important managerial implications for platform owners. We find that an incumbent's profit increases with interconnectivity regardless of whether mobile buyers consume in local markets; thus, incumbent platforms should seek to build strong interconnectivity in their networks. In our model, the level of interconnectivity is given exogenously; however, in practice, how firms design their platforms can influence interconnectivity. For example, although Craigslist is a local classifieds service, its housing and job services attract users from other markets. Our research suggests that such services are important sources of Craigslist's sustainability, and, thus, Craigslist should strategically devote more resources to grow these services. As another example, many social networking platforms such as Facebook and WeChat allow companies or influencers to create public accounts that any user can connect with. Such moves increase interconnectivity among their local network clusters.
Our research suggests that an entrant needs to conduct a thorough network analysis to understand the interconnectivity among different markets, the strength of network effects, the capability of its targeting technologies, and whether mobile users consume in their local markets. These factors, together with the cost of reaching users, can help inform the entrant's location choice and how aggressively it should build awareness in a new market. The entrant needs to realize that even if advertising incurs little cost, it is not always optimal for it to advertise to every user. The entrant should advertise to the extent that it does not trigger competitive responses from the incumbent. Equally important, it is not always the case that an entrant should choose a market with low interconnectivity. When advertising is inexpensive and mobile buyers consume in local markets, it could be more profitable to enter a market with high interconnectivity.
Our research also offers important implications for policy makers. With the growing popularity of digital platforms, policy makers around the world are increasingly concerned about the market power of these platforms. Our research suggests that regulators should pay close attention to the network structures of these platform markets to improve their understanding of market competitiveness and entry barriers.
As one of the first papers that explicitly models network interconnectivity of platform markets, our paper opens a new direction for future research on platform strategies. For example, our model focuses on an entrant's entry strategy and only allows the incumbent to react through pricing. Future research could consider the incumbent's perspective and examine other strategies for entry deterrence.
Our paper focuses on examining an entrant with limited resources (to overcome entry cost in each market) and an incumbent that already exists in many markets. Even if we allow the entrant to enter more than one market, as long as the number of markets the entrant can realistically enter is small compared with the total number of available markets available (which is true in most cases), our results would not change qualitatively because network interconnectivity (or awareness spillover) plays a rather minor role for the entrant relative to the incumbent. Take the Uber and Fasten cases as examples. Even if Fasten enters a second market, the number of Fasten users from that market to Boston is rather small compared with the number of Uber users from the hundreds of cities outside Boston to Boston. This also implies that Fasten's advertising in the second market has little impact, relative to Uber, on the first market that Fasten entered. Future research can extend our analysis to examine cases involving a resourceful entrant that can enter many markets at once, such as in the case of Uber versus Grab in Southeast Asia.
In our model, one buyer and one service provider are matched during each transaction. In other words, at a given time, a buyer cannot buy from multiple service providers (regardless of whether they are on the same platform or different ones), and a service provider cannot serve multiple buyers (regardless of whether these buyers are on the same or different platforms). This assumption matches with the ridessharing industry in that the same rider or the same driver does not show up in multiple cars at a time. 15 If we allow multiple transactions for each user, we may observe multihoming in that a rider may be matched to Uber drivers for certain transactions and Lyft drivers for other transactions. Future research can extend our model to incorporate multiple transactions for each user and allow buyers and service providers to multihome. In this case, the entrant needs to decide on the entry and advertising strategy based on how many transactions it expects to serve. Buyers and service providers will decide whether to adopt the entrant platform based on their switching costs and expected benefits from future transactions. Although the game will be more complicated, we believe that our key insights would continue to hold. For example, in equilibrium, only the buyers and service providers with low switching cost will adopt the entrant platform to multihome. Incoming mobile buyers will continue to disincentivize the incumbent to respond in each period, which ultimately drives the impact of network interconnectivity on the entrant's advertising strategy and profitability, as illustrated in our model.
Furthermore, to focus on the impact of network interconnectivity, we abstract away many factors that could influence competitive interactions between incumbents and entrants. For example, in the ride-sharing industry, riders may not care much about vehicle features. However, in the accommodation industry, travelers are likely to care about the features of properties, thereby making it easier for an entrant into the accommodation industry to differentiate itself from an incumbent and reducing the competitive intensity. In addition, because of tractability, we could not examine all possible parameter values after incorporating network effects into our main model. Future research could further explore how these factors affect competitive interactions.

title: The Role of Dynamic Capabilities in Responding to Digital Disruption: A Factor-Based Study of the Newspaper Industry
abstract: Internet and digitization are fundamentally changing and disrupting newspaper companies' traditional operating models. Disruptive innovation theory offers explanations for why companies succeed or fail to respond to disruptive innovations. This study builds on disruptive innovation theory by ascertaining the role of dynamic capabilities in the performance of response to digital disruption. Empirical results suggest that first-order dynamic capabilities that are created by changing, extending, or adapting a firm's existing resources, processes, and values are positively associated with building digital platform capabilities, and that these capabilities impact the performance of response to digital disruption. For information The authors acknowledge the valuable contributions by the JMIS
full_text:
systems (IS) researchers, this study clarifies the role of first-order dynamic capabilities in responding to digital disruption. For IS practice, it helps managers to focus on the most promising factors for creating first-order dynamic capabilities, for building digital platform capabilities, and for reinventing their core functions to accelerate digitization. KEY WORDS AND PHRASES: autonomous growth group, common language, digital disruption, digital platforms, digital transformation, digitization, disruptive innovation, innovative culture, multimedia mindset, organizational capabilities, resources-processes-values (RPV) framework, response performance, staged resource allocation.
Internet and digitization are changing the newspaper industry at an extraordinary pace. They have made technologies for e-commerce, social networking, finding and comparing choices, and entertainment easy and powerful. Internet information is now cheap and abundant; as information grows people become more comfortable and willing to spend more time using the technologies. The Internet's open standards have also facilitated open distribution platforms, which have further resulted in more flexibility for consumers to access digital content from any provider. As more content distribution moves to the web, readers are moving online to read news and share articles. At the same time, aggregative news services are becoming more important intermediaries in the dynamics of newspaper circulation [98]. Furthermore, the convergence of inexpensive digital information goods and computing and communication devices are changing not only the newspaper industry but also business and society as a whole through five digital forces: globalization, millenialization, prosumerization, business virtualization, and platformization [53]. 1 Nowhere are the effects of these digital forces more disruptive than in the communications, information, media, and entertainment (CIME) industries. In response to Internet and those digital forces, major CIME companies in both print and broadcasting have established significant online news services and are moving fast in (1) deploying digital platforms to create new ways of attracting and engaging audiences, (2) offering digital solutions and very different approaches to news, information, social networking, and entertainment, and (3) implementing a wide variety of online revenue models that draw away more and more newspapers' advertising dollars [5]. At the same time, those same digital forces that are changing CIME companies in general are radically changing newspaper companies in particular by changing their value chain [53,98]. By enabling community collaboration and citizen journalism, Web 2.0 platforms and digitization have facilitated the production of user-or community-generated digital content by nonjournalist readers, resulting in virtualizing news-gathering processes. Readers now have access to journalists' blogs and tweets about the news as it happens and can comment on articles and make suggestions on both online and print versions. Since digital news and information content can now be produced by amateurs in addition to professionals, Internet and digitization are competence-destroying and disruptive for the newspaper industry. Consequently, newspaper companies are seeing their dominance erode and Internet and digitization are fundamentally changing and disrupting their traditional business models. Readers' new online behavior has pushed newspaper companies to focus on digitization, digital platforms, digital transformation, and digital innovations [52]. Even so, some have raised serious concerns about the future viability of the print newspaper industry [30]. Many industry analysts believe that disruption to the newspaper industry is likely to follow the same pattern seen by disruptive innovations in other industries [6], and are predicting a complete eventual collapse of the century-old newspaper industry because the newspaper industry as a whole has lost tens of thousands of jobs since the digital disruption and its revenue level has returned to that of the 1950s [42,69,77].
According to disruptive innovation theory [28], the resources-processes-values (RPV) framework offers explanations for why big companies succeed or fail to respond to disruptive innovations, 2 and helps managers in assessing an incumbent's organizational strengths (capabilities) as well as its weaknesses (disabilities) in responding to disruptive innovations. Despite drawbacks brought about by a lack of clarity in the terminology used, Christensen's work on disruptive innovations has received extensive coverage not only in innovation literature [e.g., 10,32,35,39,54,116] but also in information systems (IS) literature [e.g., 81,87,88,101]. Through categorization and application of disruptive innovation theory to diverse disciplines, industries, and topic areas (such as new product development, marketing, strategy, health care, education, orthopedics, psychotherapy, political science, technology, and innovation management) (e.g., [27,36,86,119,126,129]), it has made a transition from a descriptive to a normative theory [24]. Despite the ongoing process of theory building [24,36,90], disruptive innovation theory is not mentioned as one of the widely used theories in IS research [83]. Not surprisingly, the emphasis in the theory has always been on nontechnology factors that are embedded in the RPV framework, and little attention has been paid to the enabling role of technology in responding to disruptive innovations [134]. Digital technologies, innovations [70,133], and transformation [15], however, are fundamentally transforming business processes, products, services, and relationships [16]. The complex patterns of dynamic interdependencies among environmental turbulence, dynamic capabilities, and IT systems have resulted in the phenomenon called "digital ecodynamics" [45]. However, most prior IS studies have not focused on the role of dynamic capabilities in responding to digital disruption. The identification of factors that create dynamic capabilities also aids IS researchers in identifying digital transformation drivers that are necessary for building digital platform capabilities in responding to digital disruption. Consequently, we integrate the literatures on dynamic capabilities, digitization, and digital transformation into the literature on disruptive innovations in order to build on disruptive innovation theory and gain new insights. In other words, we account for the interdependence among RPV factors as clusters of interconnected elements that create first-order dynamic capabilities and that lead to building digital platform capabilities. This will allow us to improve RPV categorization and trigger the cycle of improvement in disruptive innovation theory by identifying anomalies in the theory [24,36,134]. 3  In this study, we focus on the newspaper industry as an information-intensive industry to provide an empirical context to describe and measure RPV factors that create first-order dynamic capabilities for responding to digital disruption. Three research questions are addressed: (1) what are newspaper companies' key RPV factors that create first-order dynamic capabilities for responding to digital disruption? (2) what is the role of such capabilities in building digital platform capabilities? and (3) do digital platform capabilities mediate the impact of first-order dynamic capabilities on the performance of newspaper companies' response to digital disruption? This study, therefore, makes three main contributions. First, it provides definitions, measurements, and data for a firm's RPV factors that create first-order dynamic capabilities for responding to disruptive innovations. Second, it examines the role of these RPV factors as clusters of interconnected elements in building digital platform capabilities. This is especially important for shaping future research in digital innovations, digital infrastructures, and digital business strategy [15,16,120,133]. Third, it examines how building digital platform capabilities mediates the impact of first-order dynamic capabilities on response performance. By empirically examining the microfoundations of digital platform capabilities, this work also contributes to the extant literature in revealing how first-order dynamic capabilities help in reconfiguring a firm's resource base for responding to digital disruption [125].
A technology is considered disruptive when its use generates services or physical products with different performance attributes that may not be valued by a company's current customer base [40,47]. Disruption, however, is not an event or immediate phenomenon but a process that may take several years or even decades [28], "sometimes quickly and completely, but other times slowly and incompletely" [129, p. 58]. The literature on discontinuous innovations has often examined incumbents' resources and capabilities when trying to explain their difficulties in responding to these innovations. Christensen [25] proposed an alternative explanation for the recurrent pattern of incumbent's failure to respond to disruptive innovations and framed disruption as a theory (see Supplement A for an overview of disruptive innovation theory). Although prior case studies provide rich context for theory-building purposes, "the most promising area for research would be to provide data specifying resources, processes, and values" [36, p. 252]. As a normative (or a formal) theory, disruptive innovation theory can be further improved by "making definitions and measurements more precise, by refining the categories, and by clarifying the mechanism of causality" [25, p. 48], and by an "empirical study which tries to compare precisely which combinations of the enablers are most important" [134, p. 445]. Given that there are no studies on the role of technology in enabling response to disruptive innovations [134], it is clear that the extant literature on disruptive innovations has also largely ignored technology managers, and thus ill serves them with respect to providing insights into key RPV factors that create dynamic capabilities for responding to digital disruption.
To begin to address this knowledge gap, we build on disruptive innovation theory by drawing on strategic management literature on organizational ordinary and dynamic capabilities [41,125] and on the recent IS literature on digitization, digital transformation, and dynamics of digital ecosystems [15,45,121,133]. Organizational ordinary capabilities are defined as "high-level routine (or collection of routines) that, together with its implementing input flows, confers upon an organization's management a set of decision options for producing significant outputs of a particular type" [131, p. 991]. They are the zero-level and "how we earn a living now" capabilities [131]. A radical technological change, however, often creates capability gaps for incumbent firms in the industry because it introduces new technological knowledge and alternatives, new ways of performing organizational activities, and new ways of creating value. A capability gap is the distance between a firm's existing configuration of capabilities and the most valuable configuration potentially available post the technological change [84]. Such gaps require firms to develop or acquire new sets of capabilities to enter into a new technological subfield, commercialize new products, and incorporate the new technology to create value [84]. The literature has also explored the reasons for incumbents' reluctant or ineffective responses to such radical technological innovations [13,14,61]. Although the choice of a capability reconfiguration mechanism to narrow capability gaps depends on the pace and uncertainties of the technological change [84], the incumbents' responses are guided by their intrinsic resources, processes, and cultural influences [85,122].
In contrast to organizational ordinary (operational) capabilities, dynamic capabilities govern the rate of change in organizational ordinary capabilities and involve long-term commitment to specialized resources [41]. They are essential in (1) responding to disruptive technological shifts [114], (2) integrating e-business transformation with the existing operation of the business [15,34], and (3) connecting with customers and suppliers in response to disruptive innovations [86]. Dynamic capabilities theory is an extension of the resource-based view of the firm [11,46]. Research on dynamic capabilities has focused on technological innovation, adaptation, and strategic responses as streams of research to differentiate from the organizational (operational innovation) capabilities theory of a firm [125]. It has suggested that managers need to be able to integrate, build, and reconfigure internal and external competencies to address changing environments [125], or "to use resources . . . to match or even to create market change" [46, p. 1107]. Dynamic capabilities are theorized as existing at different levels. The first-order dynamic capabilities "extend, modify, change and/or create ordinary capabilities" [41, p. 255]. In the absence of the firm's ability to create the first-order dynamic capabilities, ordinary capabilities may well become core rigidities [85]. When deploying first-order dynamic capabilities may not be sufficient, a firm may need to adapt its current approach or adopt a completely new approach to develop second-order dynamic capabilities [33]. 4 The second-order (or higher-order) dynamic capabilities enable spontaneous responsiveness in novel situations and in recessionary conditions [33,131]. In theory, an infinite progression of orders of dynamic capabilities may exist; in practice, dynamic capabilities are unlikely to be sustained much beyond second-order [33,131].
Organizational ordinary and dynamic capabilities have been shown to influence performance at firm and process levels through various mechanisms [18,41,128]. As a matter of normal business practice, firms actively manage their capabilities and, therefore, attempt to limit their downside risks and are likely to abandon or replace capabilities if performance falls below a certain threshold [41]. However, an exogenous change (such as a radical technological change) could at any time tip an existing cost-benefit balance of capability investment in favor of lower-order capabilities. Therefore, a firm (1) may employ a capability that is disconnected entirely from its profit mechanism(s), (2) may not achieve any return from the higher-level capability to cover its costs of usage, or (3) may use a capability that has a negative effect on performance [41,131]. Our theoretical model investigates the effects of the first-order dynamic capabilities on response performance to digital disruption.
Recent research on how companies can transform themselves in response to disruptive innovations suggests that such transformation needs to happen as a result of two separate and simultaneous transformation efforts: (1) adapting the core business to the realities of the disrupted marketplace, and (2) establishing a "capabilities exchange" that allows for a new disruptive business to create the next source of growth by sharing resources with the core business without interfering with it [52]. The path forward for the incumbent companies will involve repositioning their core businesses by identifying the JOBS that their customers want them to perform more easily, conveniently, or affordably [129]. 5 The above two transformation strategies have been adopted by many newspaper companies as their responses to disruption [5], and some have seen great success in generating new revenue streams [52,69].
Accordingly, to respond to digital disruption, newspaper industry analysts and task forces have called for newspaper companies (1) to undertake digital transformation and act in a more complex value network (or "value web") of business-to-consumer and business-to-business so as to better address the needs of the actors in their value network [15]; (2) to collaborate with other content providers, independent Internet companies, and value web partners to offer a variety of digital products, and to organize them into electronic databases and back office content management systems [52]. These will increase the quality and quantity of original digital content on platforms of consumers' choice, and will go beyond the core products and core functions of reporting news and create a wide range of digital noncore products fulfilling JOBS [6]. The American Press Institute (API) views the newspaper industry's core products as traditional print products that rely primarily on display, classified, or insert advertising sold by sales representatives to traditional advertisers, and that use traditional production and distribution methods (e.g., paid daily or weekly newspapers, and all other products based on a similar business model) [6]. Specifically, these include (1) print dailies and weeklies, (2) niche publications, either content-focused or advertising-focused, (3) news websites relying mainly on cost per thousand (CPM) (display) advertising and classified [6]. The digital noncore products, however, include (1) niche websites targeting users' JOBS (such as community bulletin boards like craigslist, social networking portals, and user-ratings engines), (2) digital products that rely on new revenue streams (such as paid search, lead generation, and consumer direct marketing), and (3) digital products sold through nontraditional sales channels (such as self-serve advertising via Google AdWords) [6].
First-Order Dynamic Capabilities and RPV Framework Dynamic capabilities are shown to be the source of "variation" for technological innovation and adaptation among firms [32,125]. Recent research on dynamic capabilities has suggested that first-order dynamic capabilities for new product development [57,68,100] or for IS project portfolio management [33] are created by changing, adapting, or extending a firm's existing RPV. For example, recent research in product innovation capability has suggested that a firm's organizational culture, structure, innovation process, and senior leadership lead to dynamic capabilities in terms of radical product innovation capability [115]. Disruptive innovation theory also suggests that an incumbent is able to develop new innovative products in responding to disruptive innovations if the development of these new innovative products can be accommodated by the incumbent's resources (what it has), processes (how it works), and values (what it wants to do) [24]. Understanding how the first-order dynamic capabilities create innovation project management capabilities for building digital platform capabilities requires a process-or a project-level analysis rather than a firm-level analysis [33,41], since processes are where the resources are deployed and where their first-order effects are expected to be realized [111]. The firm-level analysis, however, fails to provide information regarding how changing, adapting, or extending existing RPV can directly lead to innovation project management capabilities in terms of effective decision-making processes for managing innovation projects [33]. Therefore, we take a process-and project-level perspective and draw on disruptive innovations research and factorbased information technology (IT) innovation research to identify the key constituents of RPV that need to be changed, adapted, or extended to create first-order dynamic capabilities for managing innovation projects. Table 1 summarizes prior literature on RPV constituents for responding to digital disruption.
In the RPV framework, resources are different from IT assets, which can be directly purchased from a vendor [97]. As summarized in Table 1, three classes of resources are critical for enabling responses to digital disruption in the context of the newspaper industry. Dedicated financial resources to fund innovation projects for enabling response to digital disruption are especially important because those projects are often seen as unlikely to generate sizable profits. As such, newspaper companies may find it difficult to assign high priorities for those projects, which would result in a lack of funding for them [9]. Similarly, without dedicating -It needs to permeate all aspects of a newspaper company and its overall mission.
-It must take hold institutionally, across the entire organization, and personally, in those leading the transformation [5,64,82,121].
sufficient human resources to responding to digital disruption, the digital transformation efforts are unlikely to succeed [63]. Furthermore, disruptive innovation literature points to the importance of senior management support for innovation projects that are designed to enable response to disruption through not only stressing their strategic importance but also actively participating in those projects. For newspaper companies, this implies that senior management needs to go beyond words, and in addition to leaning back and reviewing improvements in the core products, senior management needs to lean forward and work on growth initiatives for noncore products [8,63].
According to the RPV framework, processes that govern investment decisions are the most crucial processes in which many organizations' most serious disabilities reside when attempting to respond to disruptive innovations [28]. Companies that made above-average progress on responding to disruptive innovations had allocated a greater extent of their resources toward business processes for digital transformation efforts than those who made below-average progress [7]. As shown in Table 1, there are two critical processes for enabling response to digital disruption in the context of the newspaper industry. The staged allocation of funding resources allows for committing small amounts of resources to multiple innovation projects, filtering out unpromising innovative ideas, and refining promising ones. In addition, establishing an autonomous growth group, business unit, or "heavyweight" development team is essential for creating new processes or ways of working together because individuals of those groups or teams often do not represent their functional group interests [75].
In the RPV framework, values are defined as standards by which employees make prioritization decisions for judging whether "a particular customer is more important or less important than another, whether an idea for a new product is attractive or marginal" [28, p. 185]. To successfully manage innovation projects, then, requires firms to build and sustain an innovation-supportive culture, which can be nurtured through introducing advantageous culture artifacts [61,73]. As shown in Table 1, there are three critical cultural artifacts for developing an innovation-supportive culture in the context of the newspaper industry [5,6,7,63]. Innovative culture derives from values and informs an underlying belief structure that reinforces the daily practices [73]. Since enabling response to digital disruption is risky and unpredictable, newspaper companies need to establish or reinforce values for identifying high-growth opportunities [6]. Companies with a common language for disruptive innovations are able to avoid some of the mental traps that make enabling response to digital disruption difficult. These traps include pursuing perfection when "good enough" is often sufficient, overestimating knowledge of new markets, and making big bets when it is better to begin with small ones [7]. For executives and top management teams, however, their mindsets guide their strategic decisions and actions. Newspaper companies, therefore, are increasingly challenged to adopt a multimedia mindset and view their business as a portfolio of products and services with different business models, pricing, and distribution strategies. This will allow them to develop a new mindset that does not favor the status quo and further develops the innovation competence needed to successfully develop and execute strategies to respond [62,86].
As detailed in the next section, developing digital platform capabilities is a complex process encompassing various components of RPV that need to work in concert. Therefore, a more realistic representation of system development process requires that we consider how project-level RPV factors lead to building digital platform capabilities jointly rather than in isolation. This is consistent with the resource complementarity argument in the strategic management literature, which suggests that the presence of one resource enhances the value of another resource, and one may have little or no value without the other [11]. As such, we posit that first-order dynamic capabilities should be conceptualized holistically in order to account for the complementary combinations of project-level RPV factors for building digital platform capabilities. Our approach benefits from recent research on the dynamics of digital ecosystems in a turbulent environment, which suggests that digital ecodynamics requires a holistic convergence among dynamic capabilities, IT systems, and environmental turbulence [45].
Developing digital noncore products requires new digital platform capabilities that many newspaper companies do not necessarily possess. Gawer [48] defines platform as the building blocks that act as a foundation for developing complementary products, technologies, or services by an array of firms. Digital platforms organize IT capabilities into software frameworks for integration of transactions across diverse consumers and businesses [16,59,92,120]. Digital platform capabilities provide standards, connectivity, rules, and IT capabilities for mediating the production, search, and delivery of digital content and information goods among users of digital platform ecosystems. Although digital (product) platforms extend the functionality of products, there are a limited set of complementary products that could be developed using the basic features of the platforms, and such extensions are typically regulated by firms owning the platforms [95]. 6 Since digital platform users transact with each other at the same time they transact across digital platforms, the focus of value creation shifts from value chain to value networks [94]. This in turn has induced new forms of business and digital strategies [16,53,100]. To pursue a digital strategy, newspaper companies need to be "digital first and print last" by building compelling digital noncore products with original content on platforms of their customers' choice [76]. Digital strategy, however, does not mean web only or discontinuation of print. It means continuous development, and not just development around the schedule of print products, to ensure timeliness of content on websites or mobile platforms throughout the day. Some industry observers now believe that pursuing a digital strategy will result in (1) more audience (crowd) engagement by increasing the quality of shared content, (2) more robust growth of digital platforms and audiences, (3) more efficient cost structure by harnessing "both the cloud and the crowd," (4) more revenue opportunities, and (5) more profits by allocating resources to cost-effective creation of content and sales and not just to the legacy mode of production [76]. Pursuing such a strategy, however, demands development of a multiplatform or platform-free mindset by considering all forms of content (e.g., video, audio, article, photo, interactive features) when planning a reporting project. It will require developing a digital-first mindset, making digital strategy everyone's job, cultivating an open culture that embraces digital innovations [1], and ultimately building digital platform capabilities.
To respond to emerging threats and opportunities associated with digital disruption, API's Newspaper Next (N2) project has recommended that newspaper companies create two new digital platform capabilities. These are platforms to connect to consumers and platforms to connect to businesses. Building these digital platform capabilities is similar to digital transformations that are taking place in many industries [15,80]. This will allow newspaper companies to create new disruptive businesses and new sources for growth by concentrating on digital value creation and by restructuring them around their core functions when developing digital noncore products [5,6,53].
Platforms to connect to consumers: Building digital platform capabilities to unlock the community's collective wisdom supports those information needs of the local community that require tapping into prior experiences, opinions, and knowledge of people in the community (e.g., finding good home contractors or restaurants) [5,6]. Besides incorporating user-generated content and citizen journalism on their existing websites, newspaper companies are increasingly challenged to reach new audiences through building digital community platforms (e.g., photo-and video-sharing tools, bulletin boards, wikis, etc.) that allow virtual communities to self-form [5,12,52]. 7  Platforms to connect to businesses: Newspaper companies often have extensive local data about institutions, businesses, and local residents (e.g., databases for parks, medical facilities, and restaurant menus). However, most of this information is not organized for easy public access or search. Over time, newspaper companies could develop a range of digital noncore products such as numerous print and Internet business solutions to reach general and niche audiences; a broad and growing assortment of digital and online marketing solutions including but not limited to targeting, lead generation, promotions, email, paid search, self-serve ad creation, web site optimization, video, audio, mobile and other emerging technologies and media; a range of other services, including customer loyalty programs, back-office tools and platforms, transactional services, product delivery services, public events and other businesssupport services, and whatever else will meet important unsatisfied businesses "JOBS-to-be-done." [5, p. 9]. These will help them implement new revenue and service models that could have the broadest appeal to businesses in multiple sectors or verticals and could reach large numbers of nonconsumers [12,52].
Creating growth businesses can happen only if companies allocate necessary resources toward innovation projects [8]. A greater synergy among financial and human resources, and senior management support is necessary for setting up the staged allocation of resources and for giving the right autonomy to innovation projects [8,63,64]. Having a shared perspective or values on key innovation principles can dramatically change the way organizations think as well as strengthen their ability to identify and develop new ideas [6,99]. Most innovative organizations have effectively infused a pro-innovation value system throughout their companies' processes, and their employees behave according to it [99]. 8 Resource complementarity implies that project-level RPV should be conceptualized holistically to create first-order dynamic capabilities for managing innovation projects. In the dynamic capability literature, resource-picking mechanism refers to a firm's capability to create rent by effective selection of resources from the firm's own pool especially in the right combinations with other resources and to guide decision making. Disruptive innovation theory also suggests that RPV factors collectively determine organizational capabilities or disabilities in responding to disruptive innovations. Dynamic capabilities contribute to performance by reducing costs associated with providing products and services, improving their quality, and increasing their revenue [41]. Therefore, one would expect that the higher a firm's ability to collectively change, adapt, or extend its existing RPV to create first-order dynamic capabilities for managing innovation projects, the higher its response performance will be in terms of digital revenue generated from all online sources. Therefore, we propose the following:
Hypothesis 1: The greater the extent of the first-order dynamic capabilities, the higher a newspaper company's response performance will be in terms of digital revenue generated from all online sources. Dynamic capabilities also contribute to performance by allowing the firm to identify and respond to opportunities through developing new processes, products, and services [41]. By changing a firm's processes, products and services, and customer relations, these capabilities can have positive contributions to firm performance at both the process and firm levels [41]. First-order dynamic capabilities are created by changing core innovation processes and exploiting resources to search for new opportunities and by cultivating values to promote innovative risk-taking and creative actions. A firm is able to create first-order dynamic capabilities in terms of innovation project management capability by changing, adapting, or extending its existing RPV [33]. Innovation project management capability is necessary for building digital platform capabilities because without developing such capabilities a firm may not be able to improve the speed, effectiveness, and efficiency with which to respond to digital disruption. 9 Therefore, one would expect that the higher a firm's ability to create first-order dynamic capabilities for managing innovation projects, the higher its ability will be to build digital platform capabilities for responding to digital disruption. Hence, the following hypothesis is proposed:
The greater the extent of first-order dynamic capabilities, the higher a newspaper company's ability will be to build digital platform capabilities in response to digital disruption.
Newspaper companies can build audience by building digital platform capabilities for fulfilling JOBS beyond news [6,52]. Building relevant databases and platforms for collective conversation and wisdom can open excellent opportunities to help nonconsumers and small and medium-sized businesses get their information JOBS done better than any existing solutions [5,52]. The nonconsumers and "low end" of the business market represent the largest growth opportunities for newspaper companies in local markets [6]. Digital platform capabilities enable newspaper companies to progress faster toward digital transformations by offering digital products on platforms of a consumers' choice, by engaging them in new ways, and by better connecting to communities and communicating digitally, which is the way that most conversations are conducted in today's digital age. It will also enable them to add new services to the core physical products for businesses by offering new digital products and opportunities, and by creating new digital insights, experiences, and revenue streams. 10 Without developing digital platform capabilities, it will not be possible for newspaper companies to lead digital transformation efforts. Thus, we hypothesize that the higher a newspaper company's ability to build digital platform capabilities, the higher its response performance will be in terms of number of digital noncore products. Therefore, we propose: Hypothesis 3: The greater the extent of digital platform capabilities, the higher a newspaper company's response performance will be in terms of number of digital noncore products.
The literature on IT capabilities has emphasized the impact of IT capabilities on new product development for integration with suppliers and customers [102, 110] and on innovation creation process and performance [18,68,74,78,128]. However, such impacts depend on a firm's ability to change, adapt, or extend its existing RPV to effectively manage innovation projects. Without this ability, the existing RPV factors may well become core rigidities [85]. For example, financial and human resources affect the number of digital noncore products only to the extent that these resources are used effectively in managing innovation projects for building appropriate digital platform capabilities. Similarly, staged allocation of resources and autonomous growth groups have effects on the number of digital noncore products only to the extent that these processes are adapted effectively to improve decision making for the deployment of digital platform capabilities. 11 First-order dynamic capabilities are created by changing, adapting, or extending existing RPV to create innovation project management capabilities for effectively managing innovation projects. However, to build digital platform capabilities, firms must first develop such capabilities. Therefore, one would expect that the existing RPV may not necessarily be directly related to the number of digital noncore products because developing digital noncore products ultimately depends on a firm's ability to change, adapt, or extend its existing RPV to create innovation project management capability. This capability is needed for the effective management of innovation projects for building digital platform capabilities. Therefore, one would expect that building digital platform capabilities should mediate the impact of first-order dynamic capabilities on a newspaper company's response performance in terms of number of digital noncore products. Hence, we propose the following: Hypothesis 4: The impact of first-order dynamic capabilities on response performance in terms of number of digital noncore products is mediated by a newspaper company's ability to build digital platform capabilities.
Guided by the literature, we developed our research model as depicted in Figure 1. This model was tested through a web survey. The theoretical model in Figure 1 includes patterns of interaction between dynamic capabilities and the performance of newspaper companies' response to digital disruption.
First-order dynamic capabilities (FODCAP) are measured by assessing the strengths and weaknesses of a newspaper company's RPV for effectively managing innovation projects for responding to digital disruption. FODCAP is created (formed) by changing, extending, or adapting a firm's existing RPV. Each of the three Resources (RESOURCES) assess the extent to which a newspaper company has dedicated financial resources (DFR), dedicated human resources (DHR), and senior management support (SMS) for developing noncore products. RESOURCES is measured as a second-order reflective construct with three reflective factors: DFR, DHR, and SMS.
Processes (PROCESSES) assess the extent to which a newspaper company has established processes for staged allocation of resources (SAR) for developing noncore products and has autonomous growth group (AGG). It is measured as a second-order reflective construct with two first-order reflective factors: SAR and AGG. SAR assesses the extent to which a newspaper company takes a trial-and-error approach to innovation projects. AGG measures the extent of the growth group's ability to be self-directed and the extent of its authority to make decisions in developing noncore products.
Values (VALUES) assess the extent to which a newspaper company has established innovative culture (IC), a common language (CL), and a multimedia mindset (MM) necessary for establishing an innovation-supportive culture. It is measured as a second order reflective construct with three first order factors: IC, CL, and MM. IC measures the extent to which a newspaper company encourages experimentation and rewards innovative behavior. CL assesses whether (1) various stakeholders in a newspaper company understand and have a shared perspective on the key innovation principles, (2) they see their roles in it, and (3) the core concepts reflecting the key innovation principles are built into company documents and stakeholders share the same principles. MM evaluates the extent to which a newspaper company has defined its role and its business as delivering a portfolio of products and services to satisfy consumers' needs for news, information, entertainment, and communication.
Digital platform capabilities (DPCAP) assess the degree to which a newspaper company has built digital platforms to connect to consumers (PCC) and to connect to businesses (PCB). DPCAP is measured as a second-order reflective construct with two first-order reflective factors: PCC and PCB.
Response performance (RSPRF) is measured by assessing a newspaper company's performance in producing and selling digital noncore products as a response to digital disruption. By introducing a different set of features, performance attributes, and prices, the digital noncore products will allow newspaper companies to serve the needs of a new value network of customers and businesses via digital platform capabilities [4]. Developing digital noncore products to support digital strategy depends on having the freedom to create a unique cost structure and value network to be profitable in selling its earliest products. The response performance, therefore, needs to measure the quantity of digital noncore products and the revenue generated from such products. Therefore, the number of digital noncore products and the digital revenue generated from all online sources are considered to be important indicators of newspaper companies' response performance to digital disruption. 12  Therefore, we measure the number of digital noncore products on a monthly basis (RSPRF 1 ) and the percentage of revenue from all online sources (RSPRF 2 ). Because the two indicators of RSPRF are hypothesized to have different antecedents, RSPRF cannot be measured as a reflective construct; it can only be measured as a formative construct [65,103]. The complete final list of items for the ten constructs and for the dependent variable is listed in Supplement B. As discussed in Supplement C, a rigorous construct development and validation process, which included a pilot study, was followed to ensure construct validity and to ward off common method bias [31].
For control variables, firm size (SIZE) and first year of online publishing (YEAR) are used. YEAR values range from 1 (before 1990) to 4 (after 2000). Consequently, the smaller the response, the earlier the newspaper firm started online publishing. YEAR is a control variable for DPCAP. SIZE is measured with five variables that all reflect a firm's size: weekday circulation, weekend circulation, number of employees exclusively for web operations, total number of employees, and annual revenue. SIZE is a control variable for DPCAP, RSPRF 1 , and RSPRF 2 .
We determined that self-reported data from senior executives of newspaper companies would be reliable and free from common method bias. This is because: (1) the questionnaire items address the RPV of newspaper companies; such data can be obtained only from self-report; (2) the dependent variables measure revenue breakdown and number of noncore products; such information can be obtained only from executives of newspaper companies; and (3) both the independent and dependent variables tend to be objective in nature. Respondents were contacted through e-mails and data were collected through a web survey. To collect e-mail addresses, we used a website that had a comprehensive listing of all local newspapers in the United States by state, from very small local newspapers with under 25,000 in circulation to very large local newspapers with over 1,000,000 in circulation. We visited websites of all local newspapers listed and manually collected names, e-mail addresses, and job titles of senior executives of each newspaper, if its website listed such information. The e-mail addresses were divided into four groups according to time zones. Each solicitation was e-mailed according to the receiver's local time between 8:30 a.m. and 9:30 a.m. on weekdays. To improve response rate, the solicitation e-mail addressed each recipient individually. On the survey, respondents were instructed to answer each question as a representative of the newspaper as opposed to basing replies on purely personal views. The instructions stated that respondents could leave the survey at any time and that their responses would be completely anonymous and confidential. Similar to the pilot study for the measurement validation process (see Supplement C), for control purposes, the web survey recorded IP addresses, date/time survey started, date/time survey submitted, and a session ID for each survey. Respondent job titles and newspapers-working-for information were collected for further data control. A total of 158 responses were collected after three rounds of e-mail solicitations. However, due to a server problem, 10 data points were lost, resulting in a total of 148 responses. No submitted survey took less than five minutes. Using the IP addresses and newspaper names of respondents, we eliminated 10 data points where a respondent had a lower job title than an existing respondent from the same newspaper and 2 data points with no job title or newspaper-workingfor information but the IP address matched an existing respondent's. This resulted in 136 usable responses, all from different newspapers. This represented approximately 8-9 percent of all U.S. daily newspapers, which numbered 1,500-1,700 [67,96]. Table 2 lists job titles of respondents for both the pilot study (see Supplement C) and the main study, which shows that respondent job titles are similar between the two data sets. For the main study, 117 out of 136 respondents have titles of publisher, president, chief executive officer (CEO), chief financial officer (CFO), senior vice president of marketing or related functions, or director of marketing or related functions. Comparing combined data of job titles and newspapers-worked-for between the pilot data and the main data showed no overlapping respondents between the two data collections.
Descriptive statistics are listed in Table 3. Over half of the respondents represented newspapers that are the smallest, below 25,000 in circulation. This is, in fact, representative of newspaper size distribution and is typical of survey participants in any large-scale newspaper survey. For example, as shown in comprehensive audience survey conducted by the Newspaper Association of America (NAA) with over 33 percent of all U.S. newspapers participating has descriptive statistics on circulation size very similar to that of our study. To test for potential nonresponse bias, following the technique used in prior research (e.g., [93]), we divided the sample into two halves according to response date/time and compared the demographics of the two. We found that the subsamples have circulation size distributions that are similar to each other's. This gives reasonable assurance that nonresponse bias is not a major concern. The circulation size distributions of the subsamples are also similar to those of large-scale newspaper surveys conducted by the NAA, as shown in Table 4. To further evaluate nonresponse bias, we compared the demographics of our sample as seen in Table 3 with demographics of the large-scale NAA survey shown in Table 4. We found that they are similar. The similarity between our data (Table 3) and NAA survey data (Table 4) signals that nonresponse bias is not a concern. This is because the NAA newspaper survey is large in scale and over 33 percent of all U.S. newspapers participated. Furthermore, those demographic distributions are consistent across multiple NAA newspaper surveys that we have examined and consistent with other published figures that give a complete breakdown of all U.S. newspapers by circulation size (e.g., [108]), supporting the conclusion that demographic distributions in NAA surveys are representative of all U.S. newspapers and therefore so are those of our sample.
The measurement and path models were tested using partial least squares (PLS) structural equation modeling software, SmartPLS 2.0 Beta [113]. Psychometric properties of reflective constructs (all first-and second-order constructs) were assessed by examining internal consistency, convergent validity, and discriminant validity. SmartPLS calculates all factor loadings and t-statistics, cross-loadings, average variance extracted (AVE), Cronbach's alphas, and composite reliability scores. Item means and standard deviations for measurement items were obtained using SPSS. Internal consistency was evaluated by examining Cronbach's alpha and composite reliability score. Values higher than 0.70 for both Cronbach's alphas and composite reliability scores indicate that internal consistency is strong. As seen in Tables 5 and6 for those constructs, Cronbach's alpha values range from 0.75 to 0.94 for first-order reflective constructs and from 0.84 to 0.89 for second-order reflective constructs, showing strong internal consistencies. Composite reliability scores range from 0.85 to 0.96 for first-order constructs and from 0.88 to 0.91 for second-order constructs, also indicating high internal consistencies. Convergent and discriminant validities were verified through confirmatory factor analysis by examining factor structure, AVE, and interconstruct correlations. For convergent validity, in a confirmatory factor analysis of reflective constructs, loadings need to be 0.70 or higher and AVE needs to be 0.50 or higher for every construct. For discriminant validity, in a confirmatory factor analysis, an item needs to load more highly on its own construct than on a different construct, and the square root of AVE for a construct needs to be higher than its correlations with other constructs. As seen in Tables 5 and6, item loadings range from 0.72 to 0.95 for firstorder constructs and from 0.70 to 0.92 for second-order constructs. All loadings are highly significant (p < 0.001); AVE values range from 0.6 to 0.89 for first-order constructs and from 0.50 to 0.60 for second-order constructs. As shown in Table 7, all loadings for the first-order constructs are greater than all cross-loadings. Some of those cross-loadings are relatively high (the highest being 0.66). This is quite common in published research when the indicators reflect correlated constructs (e.g., [3]). Since the accepted criterion is that loadings are greater than crossloadings, these relatively high cross-loadings do not invalidate construct validity. Table 8 for first-order constructs and Table 9 for second-order constructs show that the square root of AVE of a construct is greater than its correlations with other constructs. Therefore, convergent and discriminant validities are established for firstand second-order constructs.
Construct reliabilities of the formative first-order construct, RSPRF, and of the formative third-order construct, FODCAP, were assessed by examining all path coefficients from subconstructs to the aggregate construct, all weights, and indicator multicollinearity. For RSPRF, path coefficients are 0.78 (RSPRF 1 → RSPRF, p < 0.001) and 0.58 (RSPRF 2 → RSPRF, p < 0.001). For FODCAP, path coefficients are 0.39 (RESOURCES → FODCAP, p < 0.001), 0.27 (PROCESSES → FODCAP, p < 0.001), and 0.45 (VALUES → FODCAP, p < 0.001). This shows that all path coefficients from subconstructs to the aggregate construct are sizable, significant, and with the right sign for both formative constructs. We also note that VALUES contributes most to FODCAP, followed by RESOURCES, and then by PROCESSES.
To investigate multicollinearity, we calculated the variance inflation factor (VIF) for both formative constructs. A lack of multicollinearity is needed to establish construct reliability [38]. The VIF was calculated to be 1.04 for RSPRF and 2.42 for FODCAP, both well below the cutoff value of 3.33 [38], indicating lack of multicollinearity for both formative constructs. Construct validity of formative constructs was assessed by examining Edwards's adequacy coefficient, which is calculated as the sum of squared correlations between each subdimension and the construct measured divided by number of subdimensions [44]. A value greater than 0.5 is required to establish construct validity. Edwards's adequacy coefficient was calculated to be 0.58 for RSPRF and 0.80 for FODCAP, satisfying construct validity. Discriminant validity of the formative constructs was assessed by  examining intercorrelations between its subdimensions. Intercorrelation between RSPRF 1 and RSPRF 2 was calculated to be 0.16. As shown in Table 9, subconstruct correlations for the third-order formative construct are 0.67 between PROCESSES and VALUES, 0.70 between PROCESSES and RESOURCES, and 0.70 between  VALUES and RESOURCES. These correlation values satisfy the discriminant validity criterion of not exceeding 0.70 for both formative constructs. Concerning common method bias, statistical remedies have been proposed in the literature and have been used by researchers to rule out common method bias. These remedies include Harman's single-factor test, partialling out a "marker" variable, and partialling out a common method factor [e.g., 89,105,132]. All three remedies were performed and the results passed suggested thresholds for all three. However, recent studies have questioned or discredited the validity of statistical remedies [22,31,112,130]. They have generally proposed or favored the control of common method biases through the design of the study's procedures, which includes a careful consideration of data or rating source, rigorous construct development process, demonstrated construct validity, and best practice in survey administration such as psychological separation of measurements, anonymity and confidentiality guarantees, and reduction of apprehension [31,104]. Since, as discussed in the measurement development and data collection sections and as demonstrated by the construct validity and reliability testing results, our research design followed those rigorous processes, we conclude that common method bias is not a concern to the validity of our empirical findings.
Table 10 lists descriptive statistics of both indicators of the dependent variable, which shows that the majority of newspaper firms reported one to ten noncore products on a monthly basis and 1-10 percent of revenue coming from all online sources.
RSPRF measures a newspaper company's overall performance in responding to digital disruption in terms of number of digital noncore products (RSPRF 1 ) and percentage revenue from all online sources (RSPRF 2 ). As mentioned earlier, RSPRF 1 and RSPRF 2 are formative indicators of RSPRF. FODCAP affects RSPRF 2 directly (H 1 ). FODCAP affects DPCAP positively (H 2 ) and DPCAP in turn impacts RSPRF 1 positively (H 3 ). Furthermore, FODCAP does not impact RSPRF 1 directly; its impact on RSPRF 1 is achieved through DPCAP (H 4 ). This means that impacts of FODCAP and DPCAP on RSPRF 1 are different from those on RSPRF 2 . Those hypotheses were tested by using two separate dependent variables: RSPRF 1 and RSPRF 2 . Significance tests were done using a bootstrap procedure with 1,000 subsamples for 136 cases. Figure 2 shows the testing results. All path coefficients are positive, indicating positive relationships between the predictor and the dependent variable, as hypothesized. FODCAP has a significant direct impact on RSPRF 2 (β = 0.19, one-tailed p < 0.01), therefore H 1 is supported. There is a strong and significant effect of FODCAP on DPCAP (β = 0.52, onetailed p < 0.001), therefore H 2 is supported. The direct effect of DPCAP on RSPRF 1 (H 3 ) is medium in size (β = 0.19) and statistically significant (one-tailed p < 0.01), therefore H 3 is supported. Our model explains 17.8 percent variance in RSPRF 1 and 15.1 percent variance in RSPRF 2 . To see the effect on aggregated response performance, we also ran the model by directly modeling RSPRF with two formative indicators. All paths to either RSPRF 1 or RSPRF 2 were modeled as paths to RSPRF. This model explains 21.7 percent variance in RSPRF. (Path coefficients of RSPRF 1 → RSPRF and of RSPRF 2 → RSPRF examined for formative construct validity in the Measurement Model section were obtained using this model.) The relatively low variance explained is not surprising given that the newspaper industry is still in the early stages of implementing its response strategies.
To test the mediation effect of DPCAP on RSPRF 1 (H 4 ), we used Shrout and Bolger's [118] tests. As recommended by Shrout and Bolger [118], we used a bootstrap procedure with 1,000 samples for 136 cases and obtained the standard error of the mediation path (a × b in Table 11) across the bootstrap samples to compute the confidence interval and significance level of the mediation effect. The mediation testing results are presented in Table 11. As discussed in Shrout and Bolger [118], the confidence interval was calculated using normal distribution and was also obtained empirically using bootstrapping samples. The two confidence intervals are very similar in our data, indicating minimum skewing. The p-values are calculated using right-tailed t-distribution.
Table 11 shows that H 4 is supported, that is, the impact of FODCAP on RSPRF 1 is achieved through DPCAP and there is no direct impact of FODCAP on RSPRF 1 . This conclusion is drawn because (1) FODCAP is positively associated with RSPRF 1 since the total effect (C in Table 11) is significant (β = 0.13, t-value = 1.86, 0 not within the confidence interval); (2) the coefficient for the mediation path (a × b in Table 11) is 0.10 and is significant at one-tailed α = 0.05 level; and (3) when the mediation path is controlled for, the direct effect of FODCAP on RSPRF 1 (c′ in Table 11) is small and not significant (β = 0.03, tvalue = 0.33, 0 within the confidence interval). The mediation effect ratio is 76 percent. These results indicate that the effect of FODCAP on RSPRF 1 is mediated through DPCAP, which supports H 4 . For comparison purposes, we also tested the mediation effect of DPCAP on RSPRF 2 . Table 11 also shows that FODCAP impacts RSPRF 2 directly and not through DPCAP. This conclusion is drawn because FODCAP has a significant total effect (C in Table 11) on RSPRF 2 (β = 0.19, t-value = 2.89, 0 not within the confidence interval); the coefficient for the mediation path (a × b in Table 11) is 0.01 and is not significant at one-tailed α = 0.05 level (t-value = 0.243). Regarding the control variables, the coefficient for the path from YEAR to DPCAP is small and not significant (β = -0.06, t-value = 0.815), indicating that newspaper firms that started publishing online at an earlier time are not more likely to have a higher extent of DPCAP.
